title: Multiscale evolution of the 3D genome: ( Trends Genet. 42 , 912–921; 2026)
abstract: Publication date: Available online 25 November 2026   Source:  Trends in Genetics  Author(s): Yizhuo Che, Stephen J. Bush, Kai Ye

title: GASTON-VI efficiently quantifies spatial axes and molecular gradients from multi-sample, multi-modal spatial-omics data
abstract: Many tissues exhibit an underlying spatial axis along which fundamental biological processes occur due to continuous spatial gradients of cell type and molecular state. Modern spatial-omics technologies measure molecular features (e.g. gene/protein expression) at 100,000s-1,000,000s of locations within a two-dimensional (2-D) tissue slice, with large-scale atlases profiling multiple tissue slices of the same organ type across different individuals and biological conditions (e.g. healthy versus diseased). However, existing computational methods for identifying spatial molecular gradients are limited to small spatial transcriptomics datasets (1000s of cells) of a single tissue slice, while methods for integrating multiple samples do not explicitly model spatial axes nor spatial molecular gradients along such axes. Here, we present GASTON-VI, a variational inference (VI)-based deep learning model which efficiently learns an underlying spatial axis and spatial molecular gradients along this axis from multi-sample, multi-condition spatial-omics data of any molecular modality (e.g. transcriptomics, proteomics). GASTON-VI jointly learns (1) a spatial coordinate (the "isodepth") for each individual tissue slice and (2) 1-D spatial modality functions that describe molecular gradients along the isodepth for tissues of the same biological condition, while utilizing a latent variable model to account for batch effects. Further, GASTON-VI implements a statistical test for identifying molecules with differential spatial gradients across biological conditions (e.g. healthy versus diseased). On spatial transcriptomics and proteomics data from the intestine, tonsil, and liver, we show that GASTON-VI recovers spatial axes and molecular gradients along these axes more accurately and efficiently than existing methods. In particular, applied to large-scale spatial transcriptomics and proteomics atlases, GASTON-VI reveals differential spatial gradients of gene expression along the portal vein-central vein axis in fibrotic livers, and differential spatial gradients of protein abundance along the muscularis-lumen axis across different regions of the intestine. Software availability: GASTON-VI is available at https://github.com/chitra-lab/GASTON-VI.

title: scOnion: Cross-Modal Concordance-Aware Joint Analysis of Cells and Features in Single-Cell Multiomic Data
abstract: Single-cell multiomic assays jointly profile gene expression and chromatin accessibility in the same cells, enabling direct analysis of cross-layer coordination. However, agreement between modalities varies across cells, and existing integration methods often emphasize shared structure, potentially averaging away cell-specific cross-modal discordance that carries biological signal. Here we present scOnion, a concordance-aware computational framework that quantifies cross-modality agreement and propagates this information into downstream analyses. Starting from paired low-rank representations obtained by spectral integration, scOnion computes per-cell concordance scores, a concordance-aware joint cell embedding, and an induced cross-modal feature embedding. The cell embedding preserves structure strongly represented in either modality, improving cell-type and state resolution, while the feature embedding scores candidate regulatory element(rE)-to-gene (rE2G) pairs. Across immune, neural, and developmental functional genomic datasets, scOnion's concordance patterns are reproducible and cell-resolved, with low-concordance cells enriched for modality-specific structure. scOnion also prioritizes candidate rE2G pairs, including distal links, with stronger support from external Hi-C contacts and fine-mapped eQTL data than the baseline linkage methods. In a B-cell fate bifurcation study, scOnion reveals remodeling of concordance and rE2G coupling during lineage commitment. scOnion embeds ~70,000 cells and computes rE2G links on CPU in 30 minutes, extends naturally to other multiomic assays such as CITE-seq, and is available as open-source software.

title: Evaluating the Generalizability of Machine-Learning-Guided Directed Evolution Across Protein Fitness Landscapes
abstract: Machine-learning-guided directed evolution (MLDE) prioritizes promising protein variants for experimental testing, but performance depends on campaign design. We present MLDEx, a systematic benchmark of 557,143 simulated campaigns across 16 protein fitness landscapes, covering 28 representations, eight regressors, three acquisition rules, four initial training-set sizes, and four batch sizes. Going beyond previous benchmarks, MLDEx jointly evaluates these design choices and tests whether recommended configurations generalize to unseen protein landscapes. With small initial sets, ML guidance required 2.2-2.8 times fewer assays than random screening for comparable success, but this advantage diminished with larger sets. At 200 total assays, zero-shot screening achieved 56.2% success versus 44.6% for MLDE, with similar performance at larger budgets. Representation-regressor rankings varied substantially between landscapes: configurations selected on 15 landscapes performed 13.3 percentage points worse on the held-out landscape. MLDEx identifies broadly applicable campaign-design principles but cautions against transferring model rankings to new proteins.

title: BRIDGE: inter-tissue imputation with contrastive learning improves recovery of donor-specific gene expression
abstract: Multi-tissue transcriptome resources are central to understanding tissue-specific regulation and inter-individual variation. Realistically, most tissues are measured in only a subset of donors, especially for less accessible tissues such as brain and heart. Accurately imputing gene expression values for such tissues, while accounting for individual heterogeneity, remains a daunting challenge. Here, we present BRIDGE (Body-wide Representation via Inter-tissue Decoding of Gene Expression), a lightweight framework that imputes donor-specific and tissue-specific expression measures using contrastive learning. When tested on real-world expression data from the Genotype-Tissue Expression (GTEx) consortium, BRIDGE recovered donor-specific variation more accurately than existing state-of-the-art methods while improving overall accuracy, with the largest advantage found in the most inaccessible tissues. We provide the BRIDGE-imputed completed GTEx v11 donor x tissue xgene expression tensor as a resource to the broader research community.

title: XenoType: Decoding cellular identity in breast cancer histology through molecular supervision
abstract: Characterizing the cellular composition of the tumor microenvironment from histological images is fundamental to understanding cancer biology and informing treatment decisions. Deep learning has enabled automated nuclear detection and classification from hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) images, yet cell classifiers remain largely confined to broad morphological categories owing to a reliance on manual annotations. Recent efforts have used spatial molecular measurements to supervise histological classification, but these approaches often require separate tissue sections or produce altered H&E staining, and the resulting cell-type annotations depend on subjective choices such as marker selection and clustering parameters. Here we develop XenoType, a framework that classifies cells into seven molecularly informed categories directly from routine histology, trained using paired same-section Xenium spatial transcriptomics. Cell-type annotations are reconciled from four single-cell RNA-sequencing references, reducing dependence on marker choices. Across eight held-out breast tissue sections, XenoType outperformed commonly used CellViT++ retrained on the same molecular annotations under both four-class (macro-F1: 0.703 vs. 0.569) and seven-class (macro-F1: 0.571 vs. 0.403) taxonomies, with the largest gains for myoepithelial (F1: 0.175 to 0.572) and endothelial cells (F1: 0.395 to 0.682). Molecular measurements are required only during training; at inference, XenoType uses the H&E image alone. Model-reference agreement increased consistently with annotation confidence, and XenoType generalized to an independently profiled breast tissue section from a different spatial transcriptomics platform, supporting scalable cell-type mapping from routine histology without per-specimen molecular profiling.

title: A pangenomic approach identifies new structural variants associated with gene expression in the CARTaGENE cohort
abstract: Structural variants (SVs) are major contributors to the genetic diversity of human populations. While many small variants have been associated with human traits and diseases, the challenge to genotype SVs using short-read DNA sequencing and a linear reference genome has made association testing with SVs more difficult. To address these limitations and investigate the associations of SVs with complex human traits, we used PanGenie, a pangenome-based short-read genotyper, together with the second release of the Human Pangenome Reference Consortium (HPRC) pangenome to genotype 645,680 SVs in 2,173 participants from the CARTaGENE cohort. Through conditional eQTL analyses that account for associations attributable to known variation identified using a standard approach based on the GRCh38 reference genome, we identified 103 independent SV-eGene associations involving 99 unique SVs (SV-eQTLs). Of these associations, 41 replicated in the 1000 Genomes Project cohort (same direction of effect, nominal P-value  0.8) with small genetic variants (SNPs and indels) that belong to Open Targets fine-mapping credible sets, suggesting that these SVs are candidate causal variants for associations identified by genome-wide association studies. Our results highlight new opportunities offered by pangenome methods to more comprehensively integrate SVs into the study of human phenotypic variation.

title: ChronoClone links temporal clonal behavior to lineage output and mutation responses
abstract: Distinct stem cell clones can yield similar lineage outputs via different developmental trajectories or dynamics and respond differently to perturbation. Here, we introduce ChronoClone, an unsupervised method that groups single-cell clones by time-resolved cell-state composition into metaclones. Benchmarked against simulated ground-truth scenarios, ChronoClone demonstrates high noise tolerance compared to existing methods. Applied to an adult mouse hematopoietic lineage-tracing dataset, ChronoClone showed that clones producing the same lineage mature at different speeds, a difference the original study did not examine. Furthermore, using WT metaclones as a baseline reference for Dnmt3a- and Npm1c-mutant sister-clones, ChronoClone uncovered hidden, clone-specific mutation responses including slowed maturation and lineage composition shifts. By connecting temporal dynamics, perturbation responses, and ancestral molecular states, ChronoClone adds temporal cell-state dynamics into clonal analysis.

title: Phirefly: hierarchical quantum haplotype phasing at the chromosome scale
abstract: Motivation: Read-based phasing links alleles on the same homologous haplotype. It plays a critical role in long-read variant calling and variant analysis. Many phasing algorithms have been developed. This includes QHap, the only quantum-inspired algorithm for read-based phasing. QHap does not run on quantum hardware due to the scale of the practical problems. Results: We developed Phirefly, the first practical quantum algorithm for read-based phasing with the key phasing step executed on quantum hardware. Phirefly uses a CPU-based algorithm to identify small disjoint groups of SNPs linked by strong, consistent read support. These groups are called phaselets and are easy to phase. To phase across phaselets, which is harder due to weak or conflicting read support, Phirefly locks the relative SNP phases within each phaselet and applies a quantum algorithm, effectively treating each phaselet as one heterozygous variant. Phirefly runs on physical quantum computers from D-Wave and IBM, as well as with a quantum-inspired classical solver using CPU or GPU. It achieves broadly comparable accuracy to QHap and mainstream phasing algorithms on HG002 datasets. Availability and implementation: https://github.com/wangyf1125/Phirefly

title: A method to disentangle enhancer-gene interactions from latent factors in single-cell multi-omics data
abstract: Mapping regulatory elements to their target genes in the cell types relevant to disease is essential for interpreting non-coding variants identified by genome-wide association studies. Single-cell multiome data, which simultaneously measure accessible chromatin and gene expression per cell, allow such peak-gene links to be inferred within individual cell types. However, shared technical and biological variation across genes and peaks, such as cell cycle, cell quality, and inter-sample differences, creates spurious links, while including sample covariates to control for this variation inadvertently removes true genotype-driven links. To address this trade-off, we developed CREMAP (Covariance-of-Residuals-based Enhancer-gene Mapping), a statistical method that estimates shared variation as latent factors from the data and adjusts for them before testing each peak-gene pair. Using CRISPRi perturbation experiments and fine-mapped eQTLs as validation benchmarks, we demonstrate that CREMAP improves the accuracy of inferred peak-gene links compared with existing methods across two cell lines and 13 cell types from human bone marrow, brain, and kidney. In kidney proximal tubule cells, CREMAP retains eQTL-supported and allele-specific links that standard approaches miss when samples are included as covariates. Furthermore, its latent factors capture previously unrecognized global signatures, including a tubular injury program. CREMAP thus enables accurate cell-type-specific peak-gene mapping from single-cell multiome data while preserving genuine genetic regulatory effects.

title: Structural and functional reference maps of transcriptional enhancers in the developing human cortex
abstract: Non-coding regulatory variation is the major driver of human phenotypic diversity, yet maps of cis-regulatory elements (CREs) and their variability across developmental cell types remain limited. Here, we integrated single-nucleus chromatin accessibility data from 54 mid-gestation human prenatal cortical donors to generate a CRE atlas comprising 1,165,697 candidate CREs across 104,266 cortical nuclei. Chromatin-state annotation classified 1.5% of CREs as bivalent promoters, 0.3% as active promoters, 39.8% as active distal enhancers, 1.3% as CTCF-associated insulators but 57.1% remain unresolved. Overlap with an external enhancer assay dataset showed that many unresolved CREs, nevertheless, exhibit regulatory activity; thus, current chromatin signatures underestimate the functional regulatory landscape. Pseudo-bulk analysis across major cortical lineages revealed that the prenatal cortical regulome is dominated by lineage-restricted CREs, with only a small core shared across all lineages. Restricted CREs were enriched for unresolved elements, intermediate-sharing classes were enhancer-dominant, and broadly shared CREs showed the strongest promoter-proximal and bivalent contribution. Lineage-selective transcription factor (TF) sequence grammar analyses identified progenitor-associated homeodomain programs and neuronal basic helix-loop-helix signatures, together with representative candidate regulators such as SOX10, NFIA, EMX2, DLX1, ARX, and RFX3. Across donors, developmental time, and sex, prenatal cortical CREs segregated into a stable versus variable regulatory compartments. Broadly, recurrent and developmentally persistent CREs had greater activity, on average, and greater enrichment for promoter-associated states, whereas donor-restricted and temporally restricted CREs had lower activity and were enriched for unresolved and enhancer-like elements. Sex-biased CREs were rare but highly specific: female-biased CREs were predominantly X-linked, broadly shared, and developmentally persistent, whereas male-biased CREs were more numerous, less resolved, and more restricted across lineage and developmental contexts. Together, these results define the prenatal cortical regulatory landscape at single-cell resolution, revealing a small, stable, promoter-rich core and a larger variable, enhancer- and unresolved-rich compartment in which lineage diversification is driven primarily by selective deployment of distal regulatory elements.

title: CyteArc: in-place analysis and reuse of remote atlases at 100-million-cell scale
abstract: Public repositories hold hundreds of millions of single-cell profiles, yet analyzing them still requires downloading full files. We present CyteArc, a framework that analyzes remote atlases in place, scaling to nearly 100 million cells on standard CPUs faster than benchmarked workflows, with the lowest memory from 10 million cells upward. Without copying counts, CyteArc integrates millions of cells across studies using 1% to 4% of the disk space of other tools. CyteArc saves every step with full provenance, keeping analyses reproducible and letting researchers branch without rerunning upstream stages. Because those saved steps stay linked, completed cloud atlases act as live references, annotating new datasets without exporting reference files. Using CyteBase, an open cloud repository of over 160 million single-cell and spatial profiles in CyteArc format, we screen over 30 million blood cells across cohorts in minutes and identify rare circulating progenitors whose expansion tracks COVID-19 severity.

title: Functional cooperation, adaptation and synchronization of subcellular processes in cellular neighborhoods as inferred from spatial transcriptomics
abstract: Tissue-level functions emerge from pathway activities distributed across neighboring cells. Yet analyses of spatial transcriptomics mostly focus on cell type composition or signaling through ligand-receptor pairs, leaving spatial relationships between effector processes undescribed. We inferred networks of functionally interacting subcellular processes (SCPs) that are independent of shared gene products and lie beyond sibling relationships defined in parent-child hierarchies. Using those networks for the analysis of published spatial transcriptomics datasets from human kidney biopsies, we identified functionally related SCP activities between a tissue spot and its neighbors. Identified pairs of adjacent SCPs indicate functional cooperation, e.g. basement membrane assembly and cell-matrix adhesion, functional adaption, e.g. complement synthesis and inhibition, and functional synchronization, e.g. folate cycle and cobalamin metabolism or pre-mRNA splicing and nuclear mRNA export. Two independent null models, shuffling of SCP labels within the network and shuffling of spots on the tissue slice, distinguish pairs that are functionally non-random and pairs that are additionally enriched within the immediate neighborhood, separating local from tissue-wide coordination. Our results suggest that tissue physiology reflects not only cell type composition but also functional coordination between neighboring regions.

title: BRISANCE: A GPU-Accelerated Pipeline for Somatic Short-Variant Detection in Whole-Genome Sequencing Data
abstract: Post-sequencing computational processing of tumor-normal whole-genome sequencing (WGS) remains computationally intensive and can delay somatic variant detection in clinical and translational workflows. We developed and evaluated BRISANCE, a graphics processing unit (GPU)-accelerated pipeline based on NVIDIA Parabricks for detecting somatic single-nucleotide variants and short insertions/deletions, using matched tumor-normal WGS data from the Cancer Genome in a Bottle HG008 pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma model. Concordance with the DRAGEN-derived comparator call set was assessed using allele-level variant-set comparison, RTG Tools haplotype-aware benchmarking, and IGV manual review of four literature-reported HG008-T sample loci. Runtime was measured in two analyses: a fixed CPU-GPU comparison and GPU-scaling experiments. At the analyzed whole-genome call-set level, the PASS-filtered, positive-TLOD Parabricks set and the PASS-filtered DRAGEN set contained 17,134 and 16,885 variants, respectively, sharing 14,430 variants and yielding an intersection-over-union overlap of 73.66%. Shared fractions were 76.09% for single-nucleotide variants and 69.06% for insertions/deletions. Using the DRAGEN-derived call set as a comparator rather than a validated truth set, RTG score-based filtering increased comparator-based precision from 0.8375 to 0.9110 and F-measure from 0.8569 to 0.8821. Qualitative IGV review showed consistent read-level support at the four selected HG008-T loci. In the fixed CPU-GPU comparison using the HG008 tumor-normal dataset, the summed runtime of the evaluated preprocessing and somatic variant-calling components was 10.6 hours for the GPU-accelerated workflow versus 219.4 hours for the CPU-based workflow, corresponding to a 95.1% reduction and a 20.6-fold speedup under the evaluated conditions. In GPU-scaling experiments, alignment/preprocessing reached its shortest runtimes with 6-8 GPUs, whereas MutectCaller reached its shortest runtime with 2-3 GPUs, depending on CPU-thread configuration. Full-input Nextflow execution reproduced the historical CHROM/POS/REF/ALT record set, and a configuration-based interface was developed for user-defined analyses.

title: Niche-FATE: niche-aware inference of cell-state transitions from spatiotemporal data
abstract: Cell-state transitions depend on intrinsic transcriptional programmes and local signals. Existing spatiotemporal mapping methods largely match cells by expression or position, not by received signals. Here we introduce Niche-FATE, an optimal transport framework integrating gene expression, spatial neighbourhoods and inferred ligand-receptor signalling to estimate transition probabilities and prioritise fate-associated signals. In simulations with changing tissue organisation, Niche-FATE improved fate inference and recovery of known fate-determining signals (mean AUPRC of 0.46 versus 0.29 for the best-performing alternative). In digit tip regeneration, Niche-FATE reduced inconsistent regenerative-to-scar transition assignments from 28% without niche information to 7%. Niche-FATE also improved developmental transition inference in mouse organogenesis. In two mouse models of Alzheimer's disease, Niche-FATE linked predicted microglial transitions to local signalling, recovered amyloid plaque associations without plaque-location input and predicted transitions from disease-associated towards homeostatic-like states. Niche-FATE enables researchers to resolve divergent cellular outcomes and investigate their associated signalling environments.

title: RNAhub2: prefiltering and compression enable scalable structure-based RNA discovery
abstract: RNAhub is an established web server for structure-agnostic RNA homology search that builds multiple sequence alignments with nhmmer and performs downstream structural covariation analysis with R-scape and CaCoFold. RNAhub is efficiently applied to smaller genomes, including viruses, bacteria, and fungi. However, searches against large eukaryotic genomes remain computationally expensive, and genome storage requirements currently limit its taxonomic coverage, thereby reducing the opportunities to identify novel structural RNAs. Here, we present RNAhub2 which introduces three key advances to address those limitations: (i) query-adapted pre-filtering that creates a reduced query specific search database prior to iterative alignment construction; (ii) parallelized genome-level searches with job resumption; (iii) Nucleotide Archival Format (NAF) compression of genomes, reducing storage by approximately 4.2 fold and enabling the addition of nearly 5,000 species across major eukaryotic kingdoms within the original storage quota without increasing computation time. These combined updates yield significantly improved runtimes and comparable or stronger covariation signal. RNAhub2 is now scalable for eukaryotic comparative RNA searches without sacrificing sensitivity. The web server is freely available at https://rnahub.org.

title: mRNAspect: Real-Time Quality Control of Therapeutic mRNA with N1-Methylpseudouridine Bias Correction Using Nanopore Direct RNA Sequencing
abstract: Quality attributes of therapeutic mRNA include sequence identity, transcript completeness, and poly(A) tail length. While these attributes require monitoring from development through manufacturing, each needs a separate assay. Nanopore direct RNA sequencing enables rapid quality control because it measures all three on the same molecules within a single run, and the resulting data are available during sequencing. However, N1-methylpseudouridine (m1{Psi}), which often replaces uridine in therapeutic mRNAs, alters the nanopore signal, biasing basecalling and poly(A) estimation. We present mRNAspect, a pipeline combining real-time analysis and m1{Psi} bias correction. mRNAspect includes a fine-tuned basecaller and a poly(A) correction based on the reference sequence. mRNAspect is a packaged macOS app that ingests POD5 or BAM files by watching the MinKNOW output directory as sequencing proceeds. Its graphical user interface shows the latest snapshot of the results, and it writes HTML reports as each input file is processed and a PDF report when the run is finished. When measured on Linux with a single NVIDIA RTX 2080 Ti, each 3-min batch of sequencing (about 5,700 reads) was processed in 38 s. The basecaller was fine-tuned on in vitro transcribed (IVT) constructs and cDNA-IVT libraries. Across 10 m1{Psi} constructs held out from training, the fine-tuned basecaller reduced the error rate from 20.1% to 7.2%, compared with 3.0% for unmodified RNA. A poly(A) correction was fitted to constructs with both modified and unmodified pairs. The correction accounts for the fraction of uridine in the reference sequence and the number of uridines within the 12-nt sequence adjacent to the tail. Across eight constructs, the correction reduced the poly(A) tail length difference between modified and unmodified pairs from up to 9.0 nt to within 1.8 nt.

title: Heterogeneous Effects Across Clonal Hematopoiesis of Indeterminate Potential (CHIP) Driver Mutations Challenges a Unified Model of CHIP
abstract: Clonal Hematopoiesis of Indeterminate Potential (CHIP) is an age-associated expansion of hematopoietic stem cells harboring somatic mutations in the absence of overt malignancy. CHIP driver genes impart divergent effects on many biological processes, yet the mechanisms underlying these gene-specific effects, particularly in non-hematologic disease contexts, remain poorly understood. We analyzed 466 samples from the Multi-Ancestry Genomics, Epigenomics, and Transcriptomics of Alzheimer's Disease dataset, and identified function-specific differences between CHIP categorizations. Uniquely, DNMT3A CHIP was associated with global hypomethylation, STAG2 CHIP increased mutation burden, HSC differentiation CHIP strongly triggered adaptive immune response, and proliferative signaling CHIP induced coagulation and cell adhesion. These divergent functions differentially modulate inflammatory pathways and suggest investigating CHIP's downstream effects through a driver gene function-based approach rather than treating CHIP as a single entity. Our multi-omics analyses provide such a framework to improve mechanistic interpretation of conflicting relationships between CHIP and diseases such as Alzheimer's disease, cardiovascular disease, and cancer.

title: Random-walk-based Probabilistic Microglia Morphology Reconstruction in 2D and 3D from Confocal Microscopy Images
abstract: Reconstructing individual microglia from confocal images is challenging when fine processes have weak fluorescence or neighboring cells form connected structures. Inspired by Grady's random-walker framework, we propose a soma-guided probabilistic method for three-dimensional microglial reconstruction and cell-of-origin assignment. Signal-weighted random walks quantify voxel connectivity to each soma by the probability of reaching that soma before background or another soma. A path-length adjustment reduces the penalty on distal processes. Adjusted scores are compared across somata to assign voxels, subject to score and image-intensity thresholds. We assess process recovery and cell assignment separately using exact three-dimensional matching to manual tracings. In a P28 single-cell example, the reconstruction covered 83.98% of traced voxels within the analyzed region. For a connected cell pair in sample 12hrMD82, coverage was 71.86% and 82.31%, with a pooled incorrect-assignment rate of 4.61% among detected traced voxels. Local analyses were also combined to produce an overview of 13 cell reconstructions in the same sample. We additionally provide a two-dimensional version that tolerates short signal gaps in maximum-intensity projections. These initial examples demonstrate the potential of soma-specific connectivity for microglial reconstruction.

title: Does embedding impact classification performance ? A small sample perspective
abstract: Deep learning (DL) methods can address many challenges posed by high-dimensional and sparse microbiome data. In this study we applied and compared deep (DNN) and shallow (SNN) feedforward neural networks combined with five dimensionality-reduction techniques: Principal Component Analysis (PCA), Singular Value Decomposition (SVD), Non-negative Matrix Factorization (NMF), Autoencoder based Embeddings (AE), and convolutional layers (Conv). To establish baseline classification performance, the XGBoost was used, as it represents a robust machine learning based classifier with a relatively low number of hyperparameters. The task was to classify effective microorganism (EM) treatments based on intestine bacterial family abundance in common carp. In particular, the experiment involved 25 ponds that were divided into experimental groups. In each pond, the intestinal microbiome of five individuals was determined by sequencing two hypervariable regions of the gene encoding the 16s rRNA gene sequencing. The sequence reads were processed by QIIME2 and taxonomically annotated to the SILVA database, what resulted in 126 annotated families that were used as features in all downstream analyses. Abundance tables from 125 samples, transformed using the Centered Log-Ratio (CLR) method, were used to evaluate ten dimensionality-reduction and Deep learning configurations considering five-, three-, and two-classification scenarios. The DL models were optimized using cross-validation. To combat the overfitting that was present due to sparsity and small sample size, dropout and kernel regularization were implemented. During testing autoencoder embeddings achieved the highest classification accuracy (0.84), exceeding the XGBoost baseline (0.64), while embedding based on convolutional layers significantly reduced performance (0.44). PCA and SVD transformations showed comparable results (0.65), whereas NMF often failed to converge, likely due to incompatibility with CLR-transformed data. Best classification results were obtained for models that implemented AE embedding, it is most likely caused by their ability to capture non-linear patterns in the data. All models showed stable training behavior, with loss functions consistently decreasing across epochs. The SNN models were markedly less computationally intensive, than DNN. AE and NMF based embeddings were the most resource hungry (Wall Clock Time and RAM). Our results show (1): SNN architectures performed slightly worse than DNN, due to the fact of lesser informative capacity of the models. (2): Dimensionality reduction impacts model performance, though not always positively. (3) EM supplementation causes significant changes in microbiome that can be captured by DL architectures. Future work will include feature-importance analysis, integration of environmental and host metadata, exploration of larger datasets and more advanced architectures. As well as validation of model quality on simulated datasets. Overall, these results indicate that DNN architectures combined with AE embeddings have potential to be used as high accuracy classification tools. Those tools when combined with feature importance can help researchers to understand changes made by EM supplementation in a microbial community.

title: SYNDRI: Context-aware removal of transcript spillover in imaging-based spatial transcriptomics
abstract: Imaging-based spatial transcriptomics (ST) measures gene expression at single-cell resolution, but imperfect segmentation often misassigns transcripts between neighboring cells, a problem known as transcript spillover. This spillover is niche-dependent and can therefore confound downstream analyses that rely on niche-specific differential expression. True spillover cannot be directly quantified in experimental ST data, so existing correction methods infer contamination indirectly from transcript positions or expression structure. Here we introduce SYNDRI, a post-segmentation correction method that frames spillover detection as a supervised, gene-level classification task. We develop SYNDRI-SIM to generate labeled training data by simulating spillover between spatially mapped scRNA-seq profiles. SYNDRI uses a transformer to predict gene-level spillover probabilities conditioned on each cell's expression, identity, and local neighborhood, without requiring transcript-level coordinates or deconvolution. On held-out simulated data, SYNDRI achieves an AUPRC of 0.86, compared with 0.64 for the next-best method. Across MERFISH, CosMx, and Xenium datasets, SYNDRI achieves the highest aggregate performance across metrics of cell-type separation, reference similarity, and preservation of within-cell-type heterogeneity. In a CosMx lung cancer dataset, SYNDRI removes nearly all potentially contaminating tumor and macrophage markers from differential expression between tumor-associated and stromal fibroblasts while retaining native fibroblast markers. These results demonstrate the utility of learning from simulated spillover to improve the interpretation of spatial gene expression.

title: Genomic variation of Dutch traditional cattle breeds captured in a Dutch cattle pangenome
abstract: Traditional livestock breeds are reservoirs of genetic variation lost elsewhere by selection for productivity, yet are rarely represented in reference genome resources. Traditional cattle (Bos taurus) in the Netherlands are severely endangered, with some populations having declined by up to 95 % between 2020 and 2026. We generated 12 assemblies from seven traditional Dutch breeds and combined them with a Holstein Friesian assembly and the Hereford cattle reference to build the first Dutch cattle pangenome (2 881 293 997 bp), a graph containing 193.4 Mb of sequence absent from the international reference. More than 80 % of this sequence was breed private, and this fraction rose with variant size to 99 % for segments of at least one kilobase. Genotyping 54 short-read sequenced animals of these Dutch breeds against the graph recovered 55 865 structural variants and resolved four genetic clusters. The Groningen White Headed was the most differentiated breed while carrying the lowest nucleotide diversity, whereas the recently derived Improved Red and Deep Red remained close to their Meuse-Rhine-Yssel progenitor. Holstein Friesian formed no cluster of its own and contributed the least amount of novel sequence, a reflection of its historical use in upgrading traditional breeds. Ten structural variants located within genes were fixed within a single breed and ranked among the most breed-differentiated of all 55 865 SVs by VST , including a 174 bp deletion in KIT in the Dutch Belted. Pangenomes recover breed-defining variation that linear references cannot represent, supporting conservation and selection in traditional cattle.

title: SPECTRE: A versatile data framework for integrating spectral, environmental, and ecophysiological trait data
abstract: With the increasing availability of large datasets and the growing importance of artificial intelligence (AI), robust and sustainable data management systems have become essential for plant and ecosystem research. In particular, the integration of heterogeneous spectral data with plant functional traits and environmental measurements from multiple sensors poses a major challenge, requiring significant time investment and long-term planning. Here, we present SPECTRE (Spectral, Trait, and Remote-sensing Ecophysiology data framework), a versatile data framework based on simple, open data formats that addresses the need of many research groups for a standardized organization of heterogeneous datasets, facilitating their integration and joint analysis without relying on proprietary software or external service providers. SPECTRE integrates a wide range of datasets linking spectral measurements to plant traits, including LiDAR, hyperspectral imagery, chlorophyll fluorescence, geospatial data, soil moisture, climate variables, and ecophysiological traits, organized into three main categories: (i) unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV)-acquired data, (ii) ground-based trait measurements, and (iii) environmental data. All datasets are stored using a standardized folder structure and converted to comma-separated values (CSV) format. A unified primary key enables consistent linking of spectral signatures to functional traits across datasets by species and site, facilitating trait-based analyses, data framework extension, and long-term usability. The widespread use of lookup tables reduces data redundancy and facilitates the integration of data with different naming conventions, while the use of Markdown for metadata and documentation ensures easy access to information without relying on complex or proprietary formats, simplifying documentation creation and maintenance. Overall, SPECTRE offers a simple, transparent, and scalable solution that can be readily adopted by plant ecophysiological laboratories, facilitating future AI-driven trait prediction analyses.

title: Archetypal analysis provides interpretable mixture representations of microbiome community structure
abstract: Microbiome studies routinely reduce high-dimensional community profiles to a small number of coordinates for visualization and comparison. Ordination methods are powerful for detecting compositional differences, but their axes are often difficult to translate into explicit microbial community configurations; conversely, hard clustering can impose discrete states on variation that is frequently continuous. Here we evaluate Archetypal Analysis (AA) as an intermediate representation in which each microbiome is expressed as a convex combination of a small number of data-supported extreme community profiles. Across three applications, AA recovered biologically recognizable structure while preserving graded variation among samples. In a multi-biospecimen human microbiome dataset, different sample-source categories occupied characteristic regions of archetype space, while stool samples were represented by heterogeneous mixtures of archetypal profiles. In an early-life gut microbiome dataset, archetype usage changed systematically with age, describing microbial succession as changing contributions from community endpoints. In domestic dogs spanning forager, agrarian, pastoralist, urban, and industrialized lifestyles, groups showed characteristic but non-discrete combinations of archetypes, supporting generality across host species and ecological contexts. Across the displayed K-sensitivity analyses, the principal sample-source and early-life organization remained recognizable as model resolution changed, while repeated initialization and resampling analyses recovered similar archetypal structure. Held-out samples projected onto fixed training-derived archetypes retained metadata-associated organization within each dataset. Bray-Curtis principal coordinates analysis recovered the same broad biological structure, indicating that the value of AA is interpretive rather than simply greater separation, while taxa prioritized by AA retained substantial predictive information relative to equally sized random taxon sets. Together, these results support AA as a complementary microbiome representation that connects low-dimensional sample coordinates directly to interpretable taxonomic profiles and provides a natural framework for describing ecological states, gradients, and transitions without hard cluster assignments.

title: MEAM-OWL for browser-based analysis of motif enrichment and associations with gene expression
abstract: Motivation: Identifying functional regulatory motifs (such as cis-regulatory elements) remains challenging because conventional motif enrichment relies on binary comparisons between target and background sequences, overlooking quantitative relationships between motif copy number and gene expression or other quantitative traits. Existing tools for such analysis require specific and inconsistent input formats, incompatible with a streamlined workflow. Results: We present MEAM-OWL (Motif Enrichment Analysis Modules on the Web, Lite) to overcome those issues. As well as standard target-versus-background enrichment, MEAM-OWL can evaluate motif enrichment on the basis of either expression-ranked lists or Pearson correlation tests between motif counts and expression levels. These analyses can be preceded by sequence extraction and ingestion from genome and genome annotation files, and can be followed by annotation of detected motifs with known cis-elements from public databases. In pearl millet under dehydration, consistent with previous findings, MEAM-OWL detected the positive correlation between gene induction levels and the copy numbers of the drought-responsive ABRE (abscisic acid response element)-related motifs in their promoters. Furthermore, MEAM-OWL uncovered the correlations between the copy numbers of the VIP1-binding element in the promoters of Arabidopsis thaliana and the expression changes of mechanical stress-responsive genes across lines with perturbed expression of the transcription factor VIP1 and its homologs, as well as its enrichment that could be detected by a conventional tool. These results demonstrate that integrating quantitative expression-motif correlations can promote discoveries of biologically meaningful regulatory relationships and seamlessly connect them to hypothesis building and wet-lab validation. Availability and implementation: Source code and documentation are available at https://github.com/tsugama-eng/meam-owl. The archived v1.0.1 release is available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24264754.

title: An interpretable framework for decoding transcriptomic foundation models
abstract: Transcriptomic foundation models are pretrained on millions of single-cell profiles, but what their hidden states encode, and whether it holds on targeted spatial panels, is uncertain. We present interpreTFM, a layer-resolved framework that extracts frozen activations from scGPT, Geneformer, and C2S-scale, decomposes each evaluated layer with a sparse autoencoder (SAE), and evaluates the resulting features against raw hidden dimensions, an untrained SAE of the same width, and single genes, holding out either gene-token rows or whole genes. Concept-associated features are then projected to cells for spatial niche discovery and interface analysis. We applied the framework to a CosMx lung-cancer section (81,236 cells, 960 genes) and a Xenium renal-cell-carcinoma section (465,220 cells, 399 model-compatible genes), screening 29 model-layer combinations per dataset. On held-out observations of known genes, sparse features marked 262--593 biological concepts per analysis layer, against 0--70 for raw hidden dimensions and 0--249 for the untrained SAE; on genes held out during feature selection, concept F1 was 0.01--0.12 for every representation and lowest for sparse features, so a feature's concept label reflects the genes it detects, and randomly re-initialized models scored the same. A linear readout of the hidden states recovered the concept membership of unseen genes (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve 0.66--0.75, versus 0.59--0.61 for co-expression and cell-type profiles, and chance level for randomly re-initialized scGPT and Geneformer), so this information is learned and distributed across dimensions. At the cell level, sparse features were about twice as population-specific as raw hidden dimensions and approached single marker genes, and this held in four further CosMx donors. In the analyzed CosMx section, niches built from sparse features agreed with author cell types more closely than label-composition and expression-only niches and converged across models; in the further donors their concept-level definition recurred, whereas their composition did not. In the single Xenium section, three of five niches per model (lymphoid, tumor/myeloid, tumor/vascular) were shared across models and also emerged from measured expression alone. A macrophage's sparse profile predicted the myeloid composition of its neighborhood about as well as the full gene panel, also in three further donors. Within model niches, ligand--receptor co-localization recurred directionally across CosMx donors and placed CCL19--CCR7 in the Xenium lymphoid niche, whereas the models' own interface calls, under a local, stratified null with a threshold calibrated on contact-free fields, were at chance level in CosMx and tracked transcript spillover in Xenium. interpreTFM thus provides held-out tests that separate gene detection from concept generalization, and features that make cells and niches comparable across models and patients while carrying the information of the measured panel. Source code is available at href{https://github.com/OliiverHu/interpreTFM}{github.com/OliiverHu/interpreTFM}.

title: A discovery of emergent drivers pipeline uncovers parameter hierarchies in spatiotemporal agent-based tumor models
abstract:
by Po-Hao Chiu, Jacob I. Evarts, Jason Y. Cain, Neda Bagheri 

Tumor heterogeneity is a confounding factor that stems from individual cell decisions, regulation among diverse cells, and regulation between these cells and the tumor microenvironment. Identifying cellular and microenvironmental factors that drive tumor heterogeneity is critical to effective therapeutic targeting. However, current experimental methods to uncover the drivers of such heterogeneity can obscure the relative contributions of the microenvironment and cell-intrinsic properties. Similarly, standard parameter estimation methods for spatiotemporal models do not rank parameter importance or resolve equifinality, the property by which different parameter combinations yield equivalent emergent behaviors. Here, we introduce a likelihood-free discovery of emergent drivers pipeline to uncover combinations of parameter distributions that lead to observed emergent tissue dynamics and compare parameter–output dependence among equifinal fitted regions. This pipeline couples approximate Bayesian computation with sequential Monte Carlo and distributed random forests to fit target metrics and characterize these associations within spatiotemporal agent-based models. Mutual information analysis compares these dependence profiles among regions. We leverage correlations among the gen-4 particles to reduce the parameter search space via pairwise linear regression substitution and hierarchical clustering-based grouping without degrading fit to emergent target metrics. When applied to breast cancer data, the pipeline identifies separated fitted parameter regions that reproduce similar target metrics and exhibit different parameter–output dependence profiles. These findings identify candidate parameter relationships for direct tests of mechanistic redundancy.

title: Generating scRNA-seq data from bulk RNA-seq using a Gaussian mixture variational autoencoder
abstract:
by Myles Kim, Corey M. Williams, Guangzhi Xiong, Hyun Jae Cho, Steven Siadaty, Eric Xie, Aidong Zhang, Stefan Bekiranov 

Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) provides detailed, genome-wide gene expression profiles at single-cell resolution, enabling the identification of disease-driving cell types and genes. However, scRNA-seq remains costly, and there are extremely limited samples generated in even the most extensive human disease studies. In contrast, bulk RNA-seq data is abundant but averages gene expression across all cell types, losing cell-specific detail. To further leverage this abundance of RNA-seq data, methods have been developed to infer cell type proportions and average expression from bulk data using scRNA-seq as a reference. Additionally, generative AI models have been developed to generate more of an existing scRNA-seq dataset, spatial transcriptome data from bulk, and a complete single-cell dataset from bulk, with an incomplete set of single-cell data, for large cohort studies. However, there is a lack of tools specifically dedicated to generating representative single-cell RNA-seq from bulk RNA-seq data. To address this, we develop an innovative, modular framework, termed Bulk2SC, that takes full advantage of powerful generative AI approaches and existing scRNA-seq data to generate representative scRNA-seq data from bulk RNA-seq. Bulk2SC uses a Gaussian mixture variational autoencoder for data generation together with any tool that predicts cell type proportions from bulk RNA-seq data. We demonstrate the superior performance of Bulk2SC relative to tools that generate scRNA-seq from bulk RNA-seq as part of broader computational frameworks on published datasets from multiple tissue types. We also apply and assess Bulk2SC on a benchmark deconvolution dataset that contains paired bulk and single nucleus RNA-seq data. The modular design of Bulk2SC allows for deconvolution of single datasets as well as straightforward implementation within larger computational frameworks.

title: Protein sequence domain annotation using a language model
abstract:
by Arpan Sarkar, Kumaresh Krishnan, Sean R. Eddy 

Protein domain annotation underlies large-scale functional inference and is commonly performed by scanning sequences against libraries of profile hidden Markov models (profile HMMs). We describe PSALM, a protein domain annotation method that combines (i) a pretrained protein language model (ESM-2) with (ii) a per-residue domain-state classifier and (iii) a structured probabilistic decoder that produces a single, non-overlapping set of domain calls with explicit boundaries and scores. On a benchmark of 76.9M protein sequences with 107M annotated domains, PSALM attains a domain-detection sensitivity-specificity tradeoff comparable to HMMER. We characterize sequence and residue-level coverage on UniProtKB, observing higher coverage for HMMER at stringent expected false positive counts (E-values) and higher coverage for PSALM at relaxed E-values. We release code for data processing, training, and inference, along with the model weights and datasets used for training, validation, and benchmarking.

title: Biophysically grounded deep learning improves protein–protein ΔΔ G  prediction
abstract:
by Jonathan Feldman, Dianzhuo Wang, Antoine Maechler, Eugene I. Shakhnovich 

Accurate prediction of mutation-induced changes in protein–protein binding free energy (ΔΔG) remains limited by small, redundant datasets and train–test homology leakage. We show that commonly used SKEMPI2 splits inflate model performance, with every tested AI predictor declining under a stringent split that controls homology at the level of individual chains (60% sequence identity). We introduce ProtBFF, a modular framework that integrates five residue-level biophysical descriptors into pretrained protein representations through cross-embedding attention. Under leakage-controlled evaluation, ProtBFF improves performance across five sequence- and structure-based encoders. ESM-C achieves the highest Pearson correlation (0.469), while SaProt achieves the highest Spearman correlation (0.437), surpassing specialized ΔΔG predictors. Ablations identify interface features as the dominant contribution and show that pretrained embeddings and biophysical features provide complementary information. ProtBFF also improves low-data transfer to SARS-CoV-2 binding datasets, demonstrating the value of explicit biophysical priors for robust ΔΔG prediction.

title: Systematic clustering alignment and feature characterization for single-cell omics using ACE-OF-Clust
abstract:
by Xiran Liu, Ritambhara Singh, Sohini Ramachandran 

Clustering is widely used to identify cell types in cellular-resolution transcriptomic data, including single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) and spatial transcriptomics (ST). Mixed-membership clustering assigns fractional memberships across clusters and captures continuous variation beyond hard clustering, but integrating and interpreting results from either approach is complicated by the “clustering alignment problem,” which arises from label switching, multi-modality, and differences in model settings (including differing numbers of clusters). We introduce ACE-OF-Clust, enabling a four-step workflow for single-cell clustering: multiple clustering, clustering alignment, model comparison, and identification of informative features. ACE-OF-Clust introduces direct comparison of clustering solutions, assesses consistency against annotations, and leverages feature-level clustering profiles to prioritize genes discriminating among cell types, as well as to evaluate how gene sets contribute to clustering patterns. We demonstrate its utility using PBMC scRNA-seq data, breast cancer and mouse embryo ST data, and single-cell multi-omic data. ACE-OF-Clust quantifies cross-omic clustering variability and suggests putative cross-omic regulatory links. Overall, ACE-OF-Clust increases the interpretability, flexibility, and robustness of single-cell clustering, providing a scalable tool for studying cellular heterogeneity and gene expression dynamics.

title: mirCCC: Repression-aware graph learning for miRNA-mediated cell-cell communication inference
abstract:
by Yifan Chen, Jiaming Cui, Shilong Zhang, Enyan Liu, Luyao Xie, Cong Feng, Ming Chen 

Cell-cell communication analyses usually focus on protein ligands and receptors and therefore miss extracellular vesicle transfer of microRNAs, an important route of signalling in cancer. Here we show that microRNA-mediated communication can be inferred from standard single-cell RNA sequencing by detecting coordinated decreases in the expression of validated miRNA target genes. We developed mirCCC, a computational framework that estimates cell-specific microRNA activity, models cellular sending and receiving capacity for extracellular vesicle transfer, and learns microRNA-resolved communication graphs from transcriptomic data. In synthetic benchmarks with strong confounding signals, mirCCC improved whereas all comparison methods declined. Applied to a human colorectal cancer atlas, mirCCC recovered known colorectal cancer-associated microRNAs and identified stromal- and myeloid-to-epithelial communication converging on a plasticity program linked to TGF-β and Wnt/β-catenin signalling. These results provide a practical route for studying extracellular vesicle-mediated communication in existing single-cell atlases.

title: A structure-derived contact-network responsiveness atlas of human proteins
abstract:
by Ran Huang, Xin Ma, Dean Ta 

Protein structures encode non-local contact organization, but static coordinates do not directly quantify how a contact network responds when effective stabilizing interactions are strengthened or weakened. Here we introduce Contact-Network Responsiveness (CNR), a structure-derived framework that converts residue-level protein coordinates into density-controlled and topology-corrected response descriptors. The method is structure-source agnostic and can be applied to experimentally determined PDB structures, AlphaFold models, or other predicted structures; here, human AlphaFold models serve as the high-coverage structural substrate. Across 22,167 valid human protein models, hydrophobic non-local contact density defined a nearly exact Bethe mean-field baseline for the conformational susceptibility threshold. A graph-aware residue-level extension then revealed systematic graph-dependent deviations from this density-only prediction. We define a topology correction ratio, Rtopo=λfGraph/λfBethe, which provides an operational comparison of the two response models; empirical atlas tails define topology-facilitated, density-dominated and topology-suppressed regimes. CNR descriptors were associated with curated DisProt disorder annotations and broad-coverage UniProt/MobiDB-lite disorder fractions, supporting the interpretation that CNR captures a structural organization axis related to non-local contact availability and responsiveness.

title: A long-read metagenomic catalog of near-finished bacterial genomes from Shanghai pet dogs captures gut microbial diversity across geographically distinct cohorts
abstract:
Background
                      Pet dogs are considered part of the family, and understanding their gut microbiomes can provide insights into both animal and household health. Most comprehensive studies, however, relied on short-read sequencing, resulting in fragmented metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) that miss mobile genetic elements, antimicrobial resistance genes, and ribosomal genes. 
                  
                     Results
                      We apply deep long-read metagenomics, polished with short reads, to fecal samples from 51 urban pet dogs in Shanghai, generating 2,676 MAGs representing 320 bacterial species. Approximately 72% of these MAGs achieve near-finished quality and often improve on the corresponding publicly available reference genomes. Comparisons with external datasets show that our Shanghai-based MAG catalog is representative of urban pet dogs worldwide, with a median read-mapping rate above 90%. Moreover, we retrieve 185 nonredundant clusters of circular extrachromosomal elements, including elements linked to antimicrobial resistance, which are also detected in external dog gut datasets. Finally, long-read metagenomics reveals a dynamic genome architecture, including a putative secondary chromosome in a  Fusobacterium  species. 
                  
                     Conclusions
                      We provide a high-quality reference resource and demonstrate the power of deep long-read metagenomics to resolve microbial diversity and genome architecture in complex host-associated microbiomes.

title: Long-range genomic loci stochastically assemble into hierarchical chromosome structures
abstract:
Background
                      One fundamental yet open question is how eukaryotic chromosomes fold into segregated territories, a process essential for gene transcription and cell fate. Although several models describe how chromosomal loops form at shorter scales, the mechanisms governing large-scale chromosome organization across distances greater than 100 Mb remain poorly understood. 
                  
                     Results
                      Through analyses of multiple sequencing- and imaging-based datasets, we identify long-range chromosomal backbone loop structures that span more than 100 Mb, extending beyond the scale explained by several existing DNA loop models. Live-cell imaging using sequence-specific CRISPR-dCas9 fluorescent labeling shows that some long-range loops remain stable for at least 10 min. Biophysical modeling further demonstrates that their formation is driven by a multivalent binding mechanism. Epigenetic profiling and spatial density analyses indicate that many of these structures form independently of known large-scale nuclear structures. 
                  
                     Conclusions
                      Our findings suggest a redundant, distributed clustering mechanism that ensures the robustness of chromosome organization across cell types and against mutations. This mechanism coordinates large-scale chromosome compaction while simultaneously guiding the formation of smaller-scale chromosomal structures, offering a new framework for understanding genome folding and its role in cell identity.

title: Unsupervised multi-omics analysis reveals potential interactions and candidate features for phenotype classification in equine pituitary pars intermedia dysfunction
abstract:
Background
                      Pituitary pars intermedia dysfunction (PPID) is a progressive neuroendocrine disorder that primarily affects aged horses, caused by the degeneration of hypothalamic dopaminergic neurons, leading to abnormal pituitary function. Diagnosing PPID is currently hampered by assay variability and the complexity of early-stage presentations. 
                  
                     Results
                      This study presents an unsupervised method of integrating proteomics, lipidomics, and metabolomics to reveal cross-omic trends in PPID, overlooked by traditional analysis methods. Using multi-omics factor analysis, we find trends not seen in the conventional approach, such as divergence of C4BPA with triglycerides in the factor explaining the most lipidomic variance between the control and PPID-diagnosed horses, contradictory to current literary knowledge. Using a random forest classifier, we highlight potential biomarkers for PPID, which can be further explored as potential diagnostic and therapeutic targets. 
                  
                     Conclusions
                      This study demonstrates an integrated and unsupervised multi-omics data analysis of equine PPID, highlighting the importance of complementary sample preparation procedures and statistical analysis methodologies to capture a broader image of the underlying biology. More extensive studies are required to verify these methods as diagnostic tools and validate potential biomarkers observed in the proteomic and lipidomic alterations.

title: Evaluating metagenomic analyses for undercharacterized environments
abstract:
Background
                      Non-human-associated microbial communities play important biological roles, but they remain less understood than human-associated communities. Environmental samples from soil, ocean, and other ecosystems often contain 70% to 90% uncharacterized species, representing considerable uncharacterized microbial diversity. Here, we assess the impact of key environmental sample properties, including sequencing depth, species diversity, and the proportion of uncharacterized taxa, on a variety of state-of-the-art metagenomic analysis methods. 
                  
                     Results
                      We evaluate reference-based methods, including Centrifuge, Kraken 2/Bracken 2, MetaPhlAn 2/3/4, mOTUs3, and Metaxa2, and assembly-based methods, including MEGAHIT and metaSPAdes with MetaBAT binning, on 300 simulated taxonomic profiles and 348 real environmental samples from diverse ecosystems. In simulated datasets, all methods perform similarly at high taxonomic ranks, but newer marker-based methods incorporating metagenome-assembled genomes outperform others at lower taxonomic levels. Assembly-based methods require sequencing depth of at least 7.5 gigabase pairs and struggle with high-diversity communities. In real environmental data, taxonomic profiles assigned to the same sample by different methods show little agreement at lower taxonomic levels, but the methods agree better on community beta diversity estimates and on estimates of the relationships between environmental parameters and individual microbial features. 
                  
                     Conclusions
                      We conclude that the choice of taxonomic profiler depends on several factors, including the diversity and characterization of the underlying metagenomes, sequencing depth, and the biological question of interest. We recommend using multiple complementary approaches for comprehensive environmental microbiome analysis.

title: Leaf hydraulic conductance and stomatal dynamics are associated with cell wall properties in rice
abstract:
SUMMARY 
 Stomata play a pivotal role in leaf photosynthesis and global carbon-water cycling. Cell wall (CW) properties and leaf hydraulic conductance ( K 
 leaf ) are critical determinants of stomatal function. However, how CW properties and stomatal function are regulated through manipulation of CW biosynthesis and modification remains unclear, and the impacts of CW properties on  K 
 leaf  are largely unknown. In the present study, we systematically characterized the mechanical properties, structure, and chemical composition of CWs in rice  Xylosyl arabinosyl substitution of xylan 1 (Osxax1)  mutants, and further investigated the impacts of CW properties on  K 
 leaf , stomatal dynamics and photosynthesis. Our results showed that  Osxax1  mutants exhibited significantly reduced contents of hemicellulose, lignin, ferulic acid and  p -coumaric acid in CWs at the whole-leaf level. In guard cell CWs of the mutants, we observed more loosely packed cellulose microfibrils, reduced polyphenolic lignin, and the significantly lower Young's modulus. Additionally, stomatal conductance and photosynthetic rate were significantly decreased in the  Osxax1  mutants, accompanied by impaired stomatal dynamics and significantly decreased  K 
 leaf  and leaf water potential. The two  Osxax1  mutants also displayed smaller and collapsed leaf venation, which may be associated with reduced CW thickness and lignin content in xylem vessel walls. The potential mechanisms underlying these alterations in CW properties were discussed. Overall, this study suggests that  K 
 leaf , stomatal dynamics, and leaf photosynthetic performance are closely associated with CW properties in rice.

title: The kinase regulator KR1 modulates cotton fiber length through the brassinosteroid signaling pathway
abstract:
The cotton ( Gossypium hirsutum ) kinase regulator GhKR1 regulates the GhBIN2 kinase in brassinosteroid signaling. By promoting GhBIN2-mediated phosphorylation and inactivation of BES/BZR transcription factors, GhKR1 forms a GhLBD42–GhKR1–GhBIN2 regulatory module that negatively controls cotton fiber elongation.

  
 ABSTRACT 
 In cotton ( Gossypium hirsutum ), the brassinosteroid (BR) signaling pathway regulates fiber elongation. Although this pathway has been extensively studied, some of its components remain unidentified, and the mechanisms regulating fiber elongation have not been fully elucidated. Here, we identified GhKR1 as a kinase regulator that restricts cell elongation in plants. Although GhKR1 was originally annotated as a Membrane Associated Kinase Regulator (MAKR) family member, GhKR1 lacks the canonical MAKR domain and localizes to both the plasma membrane and nucleus. Overexpressing  GhKR1  in cotton resulted in shorter fibers and dwarfism, phenocopying BR-deficient mutants, whereas RNAi knockdown resulted in opposite phenotypes. Ectopic expression of  GhKR1  in  Arabidopsis thaliana  supported its conserved role in suppressing cell elongation.  GhKR1  is transcriptionally activated by LBD42, and both are suppressed by BR. GhKR1 specifically interacts with GhBIN2 and enhances its kinase activity, promoting the phosphorylation of GhBZR3 and GhBES1.4. This phosphorylation facilitates their nuclear translocation and transcriptional inactivation, thereby downregulating genes involved in BR biosynthesis, lipid metabolism, and cell wall remodeling. These results uncover a LBD42–KR1–BIN2–BES/BZR signaling cascade. In addition, using a single-nucleotide polymorphism associated with  GhKR1 , we developed a KASP marker linked to fiber length that can be used for breeding selection. Together, this work refines our knowledge of the BR signaling framework in cotton fibers and provides valuable genetic resources and one molecular marker for improving cotton fiber quality.

title: Metal-meets-acid: catalysis for lignin depolymerization
abstract: Abstract Lignin, the most abundant renewable aromatic biopolymer on Earth, represents a highly promising feedstock for sustainable chemicals and biofuels. However, the efficient catalytic depolymerization of lignin remains challenging due to its robust interunit linkages and the tendency of reactive intermediates to form irreversible condensates. Acid-metal bifunctional catalysis has emerged as an effective strategy to address these challenges, as the acid sites and metal sites promote bond cleavage while stabilizing intermediates to suppress recondensation. This review focuses on the cooperative mechanisms between acidic sites and metal catalysts during lignin valorization. We examine the specific catalytic functions of these dual active sites, discuss how their bifunctional catalysis enables efficient depolymerization, and summarize recent advances in catalyst design. In the end, we provide perspectives on tuning the spatial distribution and matching degree of dual active sites, offering potential directions for the future development of effective lignin conversion catalysts.

title: Climate warming amplifies metabolic imbalance across global lakes
abstract: Abstract Lake metabolism remains a critical yet poorly constrained component of the global carbon cycle. Here we integrate satellite observations, climate reanalysis data, free-water measurements derived metabolic estimates and machine-learning approaches to quantify lake metabolism across more than 4000 lakes from 2003 to 2024. We show that global lakes are overwhelmingly net heterotrophic, with ecosystem respiration (ER) exceeding gross primary production (GPP) in approximately 95% of lakes, generating a global metabolic imbalance equivalent to ∼2 Pg C yr −1 . Temperature is the dominant control on metabolic variability, and warming stimulates ER more strongly than GPP across most climatic regions. Consequently, climate warming is projected to intensify both the annual mean and intra-annual variability of GPP and ER, leading to an 11% more negative annual net ecosystem production by the end of this century (−2.03 to − 2.26 Pg C yr −1 ). These findings highlight lake metabolism as an important component of carbon-climate feedbacks.

title: A Photoelectrically Activated Neural Stem Cell Matrix for Nerve Repair
abstract:
An injectable neural matrix integrates silicon PN‐junction microfragments and neural stem cells within a thermoresponsive hydrogel. Photoactivation at 635 nm enhances cellular excitation and neurotrophic factor secretion. The composite supports tissue preservation and functional recovery in rat optic and sciatic nerve injury models, combining local cell delivery with optical regulation of trophic activity.








ABSTRACT
Stem cell therapy for nerve injury requires a local environment that supports cell delivery and regulates neurotrophic output. An injectable PN‐junction‐based biomimetic neural matrix (PNBM) integrates silicon PN‐junction microfragments and neural stem cells within a thermoresponsive hyaluronic acid–methylcellulose‐laminin hydrogel. Under 635 nm illumination, the microfragments generate reproducible photovoltages and amplify intracellular calcium responses. Compared with light alone, PN‐junction photoactivation reduces first‐spike latency by 91% and increases firing frequency 3.45‐fold. Transcriptomic analysis identifies  phosphoinositide 3‐kinase/protein kinase B (PI3K–AKT) pathway enrichment, while protein assays demonstrate increased secretion of nerve growth factor, brain‐derived neurotrophic factor, and glial cell line‐derived neurotrophic factor. In noncontact cocultures, photoactivated PNBM increases process extension and burst frequency in HT22 hippocampal cells and promotes Schwann cell alignment and myelin basic protein expression. In rats with optic nerve crush, treatment preserves retinal structure, reduces the astroglial lesion response, and improves visual evoked potentials. In sciatic nerve crush, it improves locomotor performance, motor electrophysiology, axon–myelin organization, and gastrocnemius preservation. PNBM couples semiconductor photoactivation to enhanced stem cell trophic output and provides a locally delivered bioelectronic matrix for central and peripheral nerve repair.

title: Chemically Differentiated PdCuLn Surfaces Reconfigure Adsorption for Selective C–C Cleavage in Glycerol Electrooxidation
abstract:
Lanthanide-modified PdCu nanorings (PdCuLn NRs) construct complementary soft- and hard-acid sites that reconfigure glycerol adsorption from C1–C3 dual-carbon binding on PdCu nanosheets (PdCu NSs) to cooperative Pd(Cu)–C/Ln–O binding. The resulting charge redistribution strengthens C1–C2 polarization, facilitates C–C cleavage, and promotes selective formate production.

 
 
 ABSTRACT 
 Selective C–C cleavage while retaining formate remains challenging in glycerol electrooxidation on Pd-based catalysts. Here, trivalent lanthanides are introduced as hard-acid sites onto PdCu, creating chemically differentiated hard/soft-acid interfaces. This interfacial differentiation reconfigures glycerol adsorption from symmetric carbon-dominated binding to asymmetric Pd/Cu–C and Ln–O coordination, thereby polarizing C–C bonds and promoting selective cleavage. In situ Raman and FTIR spectroscopy directly resolve the adsorption reconfiguration, while operando X-ray absorption spectroscopy reveals reversible recovery of the Pd working state that suppresses C1 overoxidation and favors formate retention. PdCuDy achieves ∼94% formate Faradaic efficiency and reduces electricity consumption by 63.5% in a GOR||CO 2 RR electrolyzer. Moreover, the PdCuDy||Pt/C membrane electrode assembly (MEA) further delivers 0.5 A cm −2  at only 1.07 V at room temperature while maintaining ∼90% formate efficiency over 50 h. These results establish hard/soft-acid interfacial differentiation as an effective strategy for coupling adsorption geometry with selective bond cleavage in electrocatalysis.

title: A Solution‐Processable Microporous Polybenzoxazole Platform for Gas Separation Membranes via Pd‐Catalyzed Direct Arylation Polycondensation
abstract:
A Pd-catalyzed direct arylation polycondensation enables the synthesis of solution-processable polybenzoxazoles with rigid backbones and intrinsic microporosity. Precise control over linkage geometry and copolymer composition enables systematic modulation of microporous architecture and gas transport behavior. The resulting membranes surpass the Robeson upper bounds and enable high-performance thin-film composite gas separation.

 
 
 ABSTRACT 
 Polybenzoxazole (PBO) backbones are attractive for molecular-sieving gas-separation membranes, yet their development as processable microporous polymer platforms has been limited by conventional high-temperature conversion routes. In these systems, benzoxazole formation, chain packing, and micropore evolution are coupled during thermal treatment, making it difficult to define backbone-level structure–transport relationships or to translate the resulting materials into solution-processed membrane architectures. Here, we report a solution-processable microporous PBO platform prepared by Pd-catalyzed direct arylation polycondensation (DArP). This catalytic C–H activation polycondensation directly constructs benzoxazole-containing backbones while preserving polymer solubility, allowing linkage geometry and comonomer structure to be varied without thermal post-conversion. The resulting polymers reveal how backbone connectivity modulates segmental dynamics, interchain packing, fractional free volume, and ultramicropore distributions. Gas-transport analysis further shows that ultramicropore refinement mainly controls diffusion selectivity, whereas fractional free volume defines the accessible permeability range. Several PBOs approach or surpass the 2008 Robeson upper bound, and representative thin-film composite membranes demonstrate that the intrinsic molecular-sieving behavior can be translated into a polymer-supported configuration with high gas permeance and competitive He/CH 4  mixed-gas selectivity. By connecting catalytic backbone construction, solution processability, and transport-relevant microporosity control, this work establishes a synthetic platform for designing high-performance PBO membrane materials.

title: Phase Separation of the UAP56‐U2AF65 Module Promotes Intergenic circRNA Biogenesis to Confer Salt Tolerance in Grapevine
abstract:
Salt‑triggered liquid‑liquid phase separation of the VvUAP56a‑VvU2AF65b splicing module drives biogenesis of the intergenic circRNA  Vvcirc2656 . Acting as a ceRNA,  Vvcirc2656  sequesters VvmiRN3361 to de‑repress  VvPERK1 , activating salt tolerance in grapevine.

 
 
 ABSTRACT 
 Soil salinization threatens global agricultural sustainability and severely constrains grapevine ( Vitis vinifera  L.) production. Although splicing factors play crucial roles in plant stress responses, whether and how the conserved UAP56-U2AF65 module coordinately regulates downstream circular RNA (circRNA) biogenesis remains unclear. Here, we report that the grapevine DEAD-box helicase VvUAP56a and the splicing factor VvU2AF65b form a functional module. These two proteins interact directly, and VvU2AF65b acts genetically downstream of VvUAP56a to positively regulate salt tolerance. Importantly, salt stress induces their liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) in the nucleus, forming dynamic condensates that contribute to the biogenesis of an intergenic circRNA,  Vvcirc2656 . VvU2AF65b directly binds sequences flanking the back-splice junction of  Vvcirc2656 , and VvUAP56a enhances this binding.  Vvcirc2656  localizes to the cytoplasm and functions as an endogenous competing RNA (ceRNA) that directly binds VvmiRN3361, thereby antagonizing its repression of the target gene  VvPERK1 , which encodes a proline-rich extensin-like receptor kinase.  VvPERK1  subsequently enhances salt tolerance via an abscisic acid (ABA)-dependent signaling pathway. This study uncovers a stress-triggered phase separation mechanism that links splicing factors to circRNA-mediated ceRNA cascades, providing a new framework for improving crop salt tolerance.

title: Hsp20‐Promoted Protective Protein Aggregation Drives Stress Tolerance Heterogeneity in Bacteria
abstract:
The mechanisms regulating heterogeneity in stress tolerance among isogenic bacterial cells remain unclear. The small heat shock protein Hsp20 promotes the formation of protein aggregates that sequester functional proteins and drive cells into different depths of dormancy, thereby regulating the trade-off between stress tolerance and recovery. This mechanism translates fluctuations in  hsp20  transcription into phenotypic heterogeneity at the single-cell level.

 
 
 ABSTRACT
