We show that the outcome of the comparison rests on two matters: how abundant the k-mers are, and whether the hash tables fit in cache. Sorting is faster only when data is mostly unique and the hash tables do not fit in cache. We then design a k-mer counting algorithm in the light of this analysis. We adopt the consolidated paradigm based on first partitioning the k-mers by their minimizer, thus obtaining partitions of super-k-mers, and then counting each partition independently in parallel. In particular, super-k-mers are deduplicated before counting, and the number of partitions is chosen so that the hash tables fit in cache whenever possible. The algorithm avoids writing temporary data to disk if enough internal memory is available. Results: We implemented this strategy in a tool named Tuna and show that it is faster than KMC3 on all but one of our inputs, spanning bacterial and human assemblies, metagenomes and read sets, by up to 4.3x. The advantage of Tuna compared to KMC3 in the counting step alone widens to 6.8x as k-mer abundance grows, as the analysis predicts. On the largest input tested, 614 GB of human sequencing reads, Tuna counts within 4 GB of memory and 0.7 TB of temporary disk. On that input the two tools finish within 1.1x of each other under the full 256 GB budget, and restricting every tool to the same 8 GB budget widens the advantage of Tuna over KMC3 to 1.8x. Software: The software is freely available at github.com/vicLeva/tuna under the MIT license.

title: Biomedical Text Embeddings Weakly Capture Chromatin Accessibility Similarity: A Large-Scale Measurement Study
abstract: Text metadata provides the most readily available description of public chromatin accessibility data, but it remains unclear how well it reflects similarity between the underlying chromatin profiles. We systematically compared pairwise cosine similarity matrices derived from 12 embedding types across 32,245 human assay for transposase-accessible chromatin with sequencing (ATAC-seq) experiments obtained from ChIP-Atlas. The embeddings were two chromatin representations (Atacformer and regulatory potential, RP), three biomedical language models and one general-domain model applied to full metadata and to cell-type names alone, term frequency-inverse document frequency (TF-IDF), and a random baseline. We measured agreement using Spearman rank correlation, Mantel permutation tests, and top-k neighborhood overlap in the similarity matrices. Across the full dataset, text-derived similarities correlated with Atacformer similarities at {rho}=0.20 to 0.30. This text-Atacformer agreement was largely driven by experiments with relatively few called peaks, which were enriched for promoter regions (median 69 to 75% within 1 kb of a transcription start site for experiments with 100 to 10,000 peaks), resulting in similar chromatin representations regardless of cell type. Among the 17,232 experiments with at least 5,000 peaks, the text-Atacformer correlations dropped substantially ({rho}=0.011 to 0.016), with less than 0.1% of top-5 neighbors shared. Atacformer itself barely tracked cell type in this subset, with only 1.3% of an experiment's top-5 neighbors sharing its cell-type label (0.8% expected by chance). In contrast, text-RP agreement was weak but persisted ({rho}=0.06 to 0.10; 28 to 35% of top-5 neighbors shared), suggesting that both capture coarse cell-type identity. Most of the text-derived similarity signal in the full dataset came from sample titles, which mainly identify the submission and sequencing platform. Notably, TF-IDF matched or exceeded the language models in every correlation comparison. These findings indicate that text metadata is at best a coarse proxy for chromatin accessibility similarity, and highlight the importance of controlling for peak count when comparing chromatin representations across public repositories.

title: ModFormer: A unified structure-aware model of transcriptome-wide A-to-I RNA editing
abstract: Adenosine-to-inosine (A-to-I) RNA editing can recode transcripts without permanently altering the genome. ADAR-catalyzed editing depends on both local sequence and RNA secondary structure, making it difficult to anticipate which sites will be edited or how mutations will change their activity. Moving from observing endogenous A-to-I editing to using it as a programmable molecular tool requires predicting how editing responds to sequence changes. Here, we present ModFormer, a model that integrates RNA sequence representations with predicted secondary structure to predict ADAR-mediated editing. Trained on human data, ModFormer predicts editing sites and rates across substrates and species unseen during training, recovers established sequence and pairing preferences, and anticipates experimentally measured responses to RNA mutations. These predictions prioritize responsive sites in mutational screens and guide an autonomous AI agent toward candidate RNA designs. ModFormer provides a framework for predicting how sequence changes reshape RNA editing and can be adapted to new substrates with limited experimental data.

title: APEs: Agentic Prediction of Epitopes to Guide Antibody-Antigen Structure Prediction
abstract: Antibody-antigen complex prediction remains difficult because the surface recognized by a specific antibody is often uncertain, and model confidence may not distinguish alternative poses. We developed APEs (Agentic Prediction of Epitopes for Structure Prediction), an agentic system that retrieves public evidence, interprets predicted antibody and antigen structures, and produces ranked residue-level epitope hypotheses. For retrospective evaluation, web retrieval was restricted to sources released before each CASP target entry date. Across eight CASP16 and six released CASP17 targets, the top-ranked patch reached residue precision of at least 0.5 for nine of 14 targets. We then used the predicted epitopes to steer additional Protenix-v1 sampling and to compare steered finalists with the highest ipSAE unsteered model. The retrospective best selection across three independent router calls increased mean DockQ from 0.306 to 0.375; DockQ increased from 0.089 to 0.679 for H2321 and from 0.005 to 0.379 for H2346. These results show that publicly available evidence specific to the target antibody-antigen complex can serve as an inference-time signal for epitope localization, guided complex sampling, and model selection. We also release predictions for CASP17 targets whose experimental structures had not been released when the predictions were finalized, providing a prospective test of APEs (https://github.com/CSSB-SNU/ape).

title: A refined InDel taxonomy broadens the repertoire of mutational processes shaping multiple myeloma
abstract: Somatic aberrations have been extensively characterized in multiple myeloma (MM). However, the mutational processes underlying small insertions and deletions (InDels) remain poorly understood. Here, we used a recently developed 89-channel InDel classification schema which allows differentiating mutational processes. We analyzed whole-genome sequencing data from 887 MM samples, spanning both newly diagnosed (NDMM) and relapsed/refractory disease (RRMM). We identified InDel signatures associated with replication slippage, APOBEC mutagenesis, topoisomerase 1 (TOP1)-mediated mutagenesis, non-homologous end joining (NHEJ), and two rare DNA damage repair-deficiency signatures. In two randomized clinical trials, incorporation of the APOBEC InDel signature InD9a improved treatment outcome prediction as pertaining to progression-free survival (PFS) and achievement of minimal residual disease (MRD) negativity. InD29, a signature linked to NHEJ-mediated errors, was detected in both NDMM and RRMM, and was enriched in samples exhibiting melphalan-associated mutagenesis and high SV burden. Genome-wide analysis identified a recurrent InDel hotspot at TXNDC5, a highly expressed gene in MM located within a region implicated in complex genomic rearrangements, with predominantly noncoding alterations suggesting potential regulatory consequences. Finally, InDel signatures revealed the presence of mismatch-repair deficiency (MMRd) and homologous recombination deficiency (HRD) phenotypes, even in cases without germline predisposition. Together, these findings provide a comprehensive characterization of InDel mutagenesis in MM, revealing previously underexplored relationships and demonstrating potential to refine comprehensive genomic classifications of MM.

title: Unscored variants leave many comparisons of variant effect predictors undecided: evidence from ClinVar, published benchmarks and genomic language models
abstract: Background. Variant effect predictors leave different variants unscored, so reported accuracies often rest on different variants, and which predictor is better can depend on variants never scored. Results. Manski's sharp bounds contain each predictor's accuracy and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) whatever its unscored variants would score. A comparison is decided when the two bounds are disjoint, which cannot happen when the two shares scored (of variants or, for AUROC, pathogenic-benign pairs) sum to one or less. For 49 dbNSFP predictors on 328,328 ClinVar substitutions, 745 of 1,176 comparisons are undecided inside declared scopes and 1,093 on the whole panel. In ten benchmarks from one PubMed query, 1,045 of 2,842 stated orderings (36.8%) are undecided. Yet most orderings between well-known predictors are decided (177 of 287), among them AlphaMissense above REVEL in the sixth Critical Assessment of Genome Interpretation. AlphaMissense's canonical-transcript release scores no missense substitution in secondary-findings genes CALM1, CALM2 or WT1, and missense variants that REVEL's and AlphaMissense's releases leave unscored are pathogenic less often than the panel's (likelihood ratios 0.18 and 0.25, describing each release). Across nine species, the genomic language model Evo 2 does not outperform gene annotation (species-mean AUROC 0.943 against 0.958); its 8,192-bp margin is resolved over Ensembl's conservation track (+0.108) but not over the 241-mammal phyloP (+0.055). Conclusions. Benchmarks should report each predictor's reach (share of variants scored) per label class and which orderings the bounds decide; the deposited reach matrices and glmtrust package allow these checks without rescoring.

title: Confidence-guided spatial gene expression inference for reliability-aware prognostic analysis from histology
abstract: Inferring spatial gene expression from histology images offers a promising strategy for extending spatial molecular profiling to large-scale clinical tissue archives. However, existing approaches face two major challenges: limited generalizability of single-cell expression inference across datasets and platforms, and the lack of reliable estimates of prediction uncertainty, which compromise downstream biological and clinical analyses. Here, we present REGAIN, a framework for spatial gene expression inference at both single-cell and spot resolutions with prediction confidence. Across tissue sections, independent datasets and platforms, REGAIN improved spatial gene expression prediction and downstream analysis. Confidence-guided selection further enriched for cells with more accurately recovered expression profiles and improved cell-type annotation, while confidence-weighted clustering enhanced spatial-domain identification. Beyond assessing prediction quality, confidence mapping reveals greater heterogeneity in gene expression predictability across spatial domains than across broad cell types, with differences persisting within the same cell type and associated with tumor progression-related cell states and local microenvironmental context. Importantly, in 766 patients from the TCGA-BRCA cohort, confidence weighting enhanced the prognostic value of histology-inferred spatial molecular features, yielding stronger prognostic associations and identifying additional prognostic information beyond age and PAM50 molecular subtype. These confidence-weighted features also showed improved prognostic discrimination compared with clinical variables alone or combined with unweighted spatial molecular features. Together, REGAIN marks a shift in histology-based spatial gene expression inference from a focus on predictive accuracy toward a reliability-aware paradigm, demonstrating that prediction confidence provides biological insights into morphology-expression coupling and enhances the clinical informativeness of inferred spatial molecular features.

title: An AI agent guides a pipeline for selective protein interaction inhibitors from discovery across targets to preclinical evaluation
abstract: A protein can engage multiple partners, making it challenging to disrupt disease-associated interactions while preserving others. We developed Bivexia, an AI agent that guides a multistage pipeline from discovery and de novo design through preclinical evaluation. Its decision rules are fixed in advance, and each prospective selection by the agent is cryptographically committed before testing. The objective is to discover small molecules that disrupt specified interactions of a target protein while preserving others. A compound advanced by Bivexia bound LAG-3 with nanomolar affinity and disrupted its interactions with tau and amyloid-{beta} while preserving binding to MHC class II and FGL1. It reduced tau and amyloid-{beta} burden in independent cohorts across two mouse models. The same rules gave three of nine hits on PrP and two of nine on LRP1, none in random controls. Our findings establish a framework for AI agents to pursue defined interaction selectivity across targets.

title: Unipept in 2026: A Unified Web Platform for Comparative Metaproteomics Analysis
abstract: Metaproteomics studies the collective proteome of microbial communities to characterize their taxonomic composition and functional activity. Unipept has long supported such analyses, but organizing samples into projects, building targeted reference databases, and comparing samples across a study were only possible in a standalone desktop application. Here we present a major update that moves these workflows into the web application, so a complete multi-sample study can be assembled, analyzed, and shared without local installation. Samples can be compared both taxonomically and functionally, the latter by mapping enzymes onto metabolic pathways with the integrated PathwayPilot. The analyses also became more informative. The Peptonizer2000, now accelerated by the new NORI inference engine, adds confidence scores to taxonomic and functional results, and an optional filter removes common contaminants before analysis. The Unipept API itself was also reworked, with an optimized index and flexible memory loading that roughly doubled query throughput and lowered the memory needed for deployment. We demonstrate these capabilities on six datasets of a defined microbial community.

title: Local wavefront alignment with corrected free-end penalty
abstract: Background: Pairwise alignment of nucleotide and protein sequences is a fundamental problem in bioinformatics. Wavefront alignment (WFA) is a groundbreaking algorithmic advance that reduces the time complexity of exact (semi-)global pairwise alignment with affine gap penalties from O(N2) to O(sN). Despite its success, WFA has yet to be extended to the local sequence alignment scope. Results: In this work, we propose a local wavefront alignment (lWFA) which generalizes WFA to the local alignment scope and preserves both the O(sN) time and the O(sN) to O(s2) space complexity. We also propose the bidirectional lWFA (lBiWFA), which reduces the space complexity of lWFA from O(s2) to O(s) while maintaining the time complexity as O(sN). Benchmarks show that lWFA and lBiWFA outperform current exact local alignment libraries like SeqAn and Parasail in aligning long sequences with error rate less than 5%. Conclusions: We suggest to use lBiWFA over lWFA because it has negligible memory footprint for aligning reads up to 20kbp, and is faster than lWFA except for short reads with very low error rates. According to the real-data benchmarks, lBiWFA are faster than SeqAn and Parasail for aligning NGS short reads with 0.1%[~]1% error rate and ONT long reads with 3%[~]5% error rate. However, for reads sequenced by legacy long-read platforms with 10%[~]15% error rate, SeqAn and Parasail are faster. Nevertheless, lBiWFA has a competitive speed for reads with error rate up to 10%. One may choose lBiWFA over SeqAn and Parasail if the memory usage is the major concern.

title: A Two-Stage YOLO-Swin Transformer Pipeline for Cross-Dataset White Blood Cell Classification
abstract: Background: White blood cell (WBC) classification across datasets is challenged by differences in staining, image context, and class distributions. Methods: We developed a two-stage YOLO11-Swin Transformer pipeline. In the first stage, WBC detection and context-preserving cropping, a YOLO11 detector finds the leukocyte in each uncropped image and produces a cell-focused crop that retains the surrounding background. In the second stage, WBC classification, a Swin Transformer (Swin-B) assigns the crop to one of nine cell types. The classifier was trained on detector-cropped cells from five public datasets, so the first stage supplies the same kind of input at test time; morphology-preserving color augmentation addressed staining variation, and class-weighted cross-entropy addressed class imbalance. WBCBench2026, a public benchmark not used for training, served for external evaluation in seven harmonized classes, scored by macro-F1 (the mean of per-class F1). Further analyses removed the first stage or masked the background, compared classifier backbones, held out each training dataset (leave-one-dataset-out, LODO), and tested a second split (Phase-2) with about 60% synthetically degraded images. Results: The full pipeline reached an external macro-F1 of 0.879{+/-}0.006 on 8,080 benchmark images. With uncropped images as input, the same crop-trained classifier reached 0.627{+/-}0.039, and crops that kept the surrounding background outperformed background-masked crops (0.867 versus 0.760). With identical detector-cropped input, Swin-B outperformed convolutional baselines (0.863 versus 0.718-0.813), and its advantage over ResNet50 persisted across three training configurations. In LODO, macro-F1 on the held-out dataset ranged from 0.59 to 0.91, revealing source-specific variation not fully covered by the remaining datasets. On Phase-2, macro-F1 was 0.769{+/-}0.002. Two hematologists independently reviewed all 205 blast- or promyelocyte-related model-benchmark disagreements and gave the same verdict on 73 crops (35.6%): 21 model right, 43 model wrong, 9 ambiguous. Conclusions: The proposed two-stage pipeline achieved strong cross-dataset WBC classification performance. Context-preserving cropping was essential for the crop-trained classifier, and the LODO findings support representing the same classes across diverse sources when developing robust WBC classifiers.

title: HGCF/LGCF classification from (Mavrich and Hatfull, 2017) is explained by heterogeneity in pairwise ANI rather than by intrinsic evolutionary modes
abstract: Mavrich and Hatfull proposed that phages could be separated into two broad evolutionary modes (high gene-content flux or HGCF; and low gene-content flux or LGCF) according to the rate at which their gene content changes relative to nucleotide sequence divergence. In their analysis, HGCF phages appeared to gain and lose genes substantially faster relative to genome divergence than LGCF phages and were particularly associated with temperate phages. However, as the analysis represents a comparison between two phage genomes, the difference between the two groups identified in their study (HGCF/LGCF) should not be interpreted as a property of either phage (such as their lifestyle) as they suggest. Instead, it should be explained by a property inherent to the comparison such as the organization of the shared regions between both genomes. Indeed, the two groups identified in the original study reflect differences in the ANI (average nucleotide identity) and coverage of aligned regions between pairs of genomes and is independent from the gene-content similarity central to the original interpretation. More fundamentally, we show that the k-mer based genomic similarity used in the original study (namely Mash) is biased towards short regions of very high nucleotide identity, which exaggerates the differences described previously. This is particularly important for phage genomes which are often mosaic: closely related regions can alternate with more divergent or unrelated regions, and the number, length and identity of these regions can differ markedly between genome pairs.

title: Evaluating the Nanopore Inosine Model for ADAR-Dependent A-to-I RNA Editing Detection
abstract: Oxford Nanopore direct RNA sequencing (dRNA-seq) reads native RNA molecules, and its basecaller now includes models that detect RNA modifications directly, among them inosine, the product of adenosine-to-inosine (A-to-I) editing by ADAR enzymes. These models are increasingly used, but how reliably they detect modifications in biological samples has rarely been tested. We evaluated the Dorado inosine model in a mouse macrophage cell line, comparing wild-type cells with ADAR1-knockout cells and in vitro transcribed RNA, before and after an inflammatory stimulus that increases editing. As a reference, we used the editing sites identified by Illumina sequencing of the same cells. We assessed whether the model distinguishes edited from unedited RNA, which negative control is needed to identify editing sites, how many reference sites are recovered, and why sites are missed. The confidence of the Nanopore inosine model alone was not sufficient to identify editing, and a matched ADAR-deficient control was essential. Even with this control, detection was limited by sequencing depth, by low editing levels and by basecalling errors at edited positions. Nanopore sequencing can detect A-to-I editing, but its inosine calls require an ADAR-deficient control and sufficient depth, and should be confirmed by an orthogonal method.

title: Fast draft assemblies using locally consistent parsing
abstract: Recent improvements in long-read sequencing accuracy, particularly the introduction of PacBio HiFi reads, have created new opportunities for more efficient sequence representations in genome assembly. In particular, variations of de Bruijn graphs (dBG), such as sparse dBG and minimizer-space dBG, provide efficient representations of sequences and have enabled genome assemblers to leverage the high accuracy of long-read data while maintaining low memory usage and fast analysis times. Locally consistent parsing (LCP) is another technique for compact sequence representation that partitions a string into nearly uniform, highly distinctive substrings in a consistent manner. In this work, we combine ideas from minimizer-space assembly and LCP to achieve a significant speedup in HiFi long-read assembly. Specifically, we define a locally consistent de Bruijn Graph (lcDBG), in which string partitions serve as the graph's building blocks. We introduce Gallifrey, a rapid PacBio HiFi assembler that outperforms the fastest existing tool, rust-mdbg, by >6x in runtime while requiring 2x less memory, assembling a human genome in under one minute on a standard laptop, while generating assemblies with comparable contiguity. Code for Gallifrey is freely available at https://github.com/BilkentCompGen/gallifrey.

title: SingloCell: an open and accessible web platform for multimodal single-cell data exploration
abstract: Single-cell research is transforming biology and medicine, offering unprecedented insight into health and disease. Yet, the true potential of single-cell data can only be realized when datasets are open, easy to interact with, and accessible to all. We introduce SingloCell (https://singlocell.openscience.mcgill.ca/), an intuitive multimodal single-cell web platform built on three principles: accessibility, interactivity and traceability. SingloCell provides free browser-based access to single-cell datasets and supports user submission of suspension-based transcriptomics, proteomics, chromatin accessibility (ATAC-derived gene activity matrices), immune receptor (BCR, TCR) and multi-omics modalities, as well as spatial datasets. This enables researchers, clinicians, educators, and the broader community to explore high-dimensional datasets without programming expertise. Users can explore and analyse data in real time using tools for differential gene expression, functional enrichment, and pathway visualisation, while also examining pre-computed analyses such as pseudotime trajectories and cell-cell interactions. Datasets can be shared publicly or via unlisted links, and analytical workflows are documented through downloadable receipts.

title: Somatic mutation detection from non-malignant liver tissues using cell-free DNA
abstract: Somatic mutations accumulate in the liver during aging, yet their role in chronic liver disease (CLD) remains unclear due to the difficulty of obtaining liver tissue for analysis. Here, we demonstrate that circulating cell-free DNA (cfDNA) can be used as a minimally invasive tool to detect liver-derived somatic mutations in patients with CLD. Using ultra-deep targeted duplex sequencing, we show that CLD patients have a higher mutation burden in CLD-associated somatic mutation (CASM) genes compared to healthy individuals. Recurrent driver mutations, including CHD4, INSR, and GPAM, were detected in both liver tissue and cfDNA, with distinct mutational patterns linked to disease etiology: INSR mutations were enriched in metabolic-dysfunction associated steatotic liver disease, while GPAM mutations were associated with alcohol-related liver disease. Liver transplantation led to a significant reduction in CASM mutation burden in cfDNA, providing strong evidence for the diseased-liver origin of these mutations. These findings establish cfDNA analysis as a scalable and noninvasive platform for investigating somatic evolution in non-malignant tissues, offering new opportunities for molecular stratification, longitudinal monitoring, and early detection of CLD progression.

title: Convergence of Independently Established Oncogenes in a Combined Breast and Ovarian Cancer Model: Hub Gene Validation and identification of potential Food-Derived therapeutics.
abstract: Breast and ovarian cancers share molecular alterations that may reveal common therapeutic targets. Here, we integrated six Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) datasets to identify shared transcriptional changes across the two cancers. Independent differential expression analysis followed by direction-specific intersection identified 396 shared differentially expressed genes (DEGs), comprising 192 upregulated and 204 downregulated genes. Protein-protein interaction analysis prioritized ten hub genes: AURKA, AURKB, BCL2, BIRC5, CCNA2, CDK1, FOXO1, KIF11, PTEN, and TOP2A. Functional enrichment highlighted cell-cycle regulation, mitotic spindle organization, and p53-associated signalling. Independent expression assessment using GEPIA2 identified seven hub genes significantly upregulated in both cancers, while FOXO1 was downregulated. Regulatory network analysis further identified candidate transcription factors and miRNAs potentially associated with these hubs. For therapeutic exploration, a 70,478-compound FooDB library was progressively filtered to 233 candidates using physicochemical, structural-alert, machine-learning-based bioactivity, and ADMET criteria. Molecular docking against eight selected druggable hubs, followed by decoy benchmarking and 100-ns molecular dynamics simulations, prioritized three complexes: CDK1-artonin L, AURKB-taraxacin, and KIF11-L-thyronine. CDK1-artonin L demonstrated the strongest overall computational support, whereas the AURKB and KIF11 complexes showed differing levels of binding and energetic evidence. This study provides an integrated multi-cohort framework for identifying shared molecular hubs in breast and ovarian cancer and prioritizing food-derived compounds for further investigation. The findings nominate CDK1, AURKB, and KIF11 for experimental evaluation.

title: Disentangling within-cell-type heterogeneity from transcript contamination in imaging-based spatial transcriptomics
abstract: Recent advances in imaging-based spatial transcriptomics have enabled high-resolution characterization of gene expression and cellular organization in situ. Resolving within-cell-type heterogeneity is essential for understanding how cellular states relate to tissue function and disease. However, imperfect cell segmentation and RNA spillover can contaminate cell-level expression profiles, obscuring intrinsic expression patterns and generating spurious variation. Existing decontamination methods can struggle to distinguish intrinsic variation from contamination when both are inferred from spatial measurements alone, and may suppress genuine state-associated signals when within-cell-type heterogeneity is not explicitly modeled. Here we present Dancer, a reference-guided probabilistic framework that disentangles within-cell-type heterogeneity from transcript contamination by combining cell-type-specific gene programs learned from single-cell data with explicit modeling of intrinsic expression, neighboring-cell contamination and background RNA. Across multiple human tumor datasets with varying gene compositions and panel sizes, Dancer improves cell-type separation and expression specificity while preserving identity-associated signals, achieving superior overall performance in benchmark comparisons. Inferred gene program activities reveal within-cell-type heterogeneity in the form of distinct cellular states and continuous spatial gradients associated with local tissue environments, while reference-guided panel expansion extends molecular characterization beyond the measured genes. Together, Dancer supports accurate transcript decontamination and more faithful interpretation of cellular heterogeneity within its native tissue context.

title: Multi-omics causal deep learning reveals regulatory structure while interventions refine perturbation predictions
abstract: Inferring gene regulation from single-cell data is difficult because observational measurements cannot distinguish correlation from causation and access to perturbational data, especially with multiple modalities, remains limited. Here we present the Cross-Modal Causal Variational Autoencoder (CMC-VAE), which learns a network linking genes and proteins (gene-gene, protein-protein and gene-protein) in the latent space and maps each connection back onto measured features. Trained on 809,130 observational CITE-seq profiles, CMC-VAE recovers co-expression, transcription factor regulons and immune signalling programs, and learns a sparse cross-modal map enriched for transcript-protein cognate pairs. On three CRISPR screens used during development, it ranks knockout-responsive genes better than correlation and latent-VAE baselines. Fitted to a screen's unperturbed control cells, without perturbation labels, the model translates measured knockout RNA responses into protein responses better than a correlation map and cognate transcripts. The direction of gene-to-gene regulation, however, is not recovered from observational data. On the CITE-seq screens, fine-tuning only the latent network improves held-out response correlation, mainly by learning a response shared across knockouts. On larger Perturb-seq screens, with about 1,000 training perturbations, fine-tuning the latent network learns gene-specific effects that transfer to held-out genes, more so than a gene-level causal model fine-tuned on the same cells, and in simulation, such interventions also restore edge orientations that observational training leaves unresolved.

title: Measuring Cell Type Resolved Aging Through Long-Read Sequencing
abstract: Epigenetic clocks based on bulk blood DNA methylation are powerful tools for quantifying biological aging, but bulk measurements conflate cell-autonomous epigenetic changes with age-related shifts in blood cell composition. Here, we develop LongReadClock, a set of cell-type-resolved epigenetic aging clocks constructed from cohort-scale long-read whole-genome sequencing of bulk blood without physical cell sorting. Individual sequencing reads were classified using seven target-specific blood-cell models using methylation-based log-likelihood-ratio scoring against a purified-cell atlas. LongReadClock achieved mean absolute errors of 2.8-5.7 years on held-out samples across bulk blood and digitally resolved cell types. Covariate-adjusted analyses identified associations that differed across cell types, including lower mean epigenetic age deviation (EAD) in males in B-cell and NK-cells, associations of systolic blood pressure and resting heart rate with myeloid EAD, and higher NK-cell EAD in participants with asthma. A Fisher-information screen was used to prioritize age-informative genomic windows and to explore read-level methylation patterns at the ELOVL2 locus. These results support cell-type-resolved epigenetic age inference from cohort-scale long-read methylation data from standard bulk blood samples.

title: Distinctive fragmentation of circulating DNA from chromosome Y and its alteration in cancer
abstract: Circulating cell-free DNA (cirDNA) fragmentation reflects chromatin organization and represents a promising source of cancer biomarkers. Here, we characterized the fragmentation patterns and nucleosome occupancy of Y chromosome (chrY) cirDNA in healthy individuals and cancer patients. In healthy males, we found that the shorter chrY-derived cirDNA fragments predominantly originate from heterochromatic regions. We also observed substantially lower nucleosome occupancy on chrY than on all other chromosomes, a finding independently supported by micrococcal nuclease digestion data. Remarkably, in patients with colorectal, pancreatic, lung and prostate cancer, the chrY-specific enrichment of shorter fragments was markedly attenuated, contrasting with the increased fragmentation usually observed in cancer when chromosome specificity is disregarded. We reproduced these observations in an independent local cohort of healthy and colorectal cancer patients. We could exploit ratios of short (100-147 bp) to long (147-200 bp) fragments between chrY and other chromosomes to discriminate healthy males from patients with colorectal, pancreatic, and lung cancers with AUCs above 0.98. Autosomes 19, 17, and 22 also displayed atypical fragment patterns, different from chrY and associated with gene density. This last observation was confirmed in females.

title: In silico pipeline for identification of targets of plastic-derived chemicals
abstract: Plastic pollution is a growing global health concern, yet the specific human protein targets mediating the toxic effects of plastic-derived chemicals (PDCs) remain largely unknown. Here, we present an integrative in silico pipeline that combines transcriptomic data with structural bioinformatics to identify putative human plastic-derived targets. Through comparative analysis with their canonical ligands, we identified 27 potential targets showing global binding energies comparable to endogenous ligands (-5.26 vs -5.60 kcal/mol), and six cases in which plastic-derived compounds performed better. Chemical similarity analysis revealed very low structural resemblance between PDCs and canonical ligands, indicating that PDCs do not act as structural mimetics but instead exploit different interactions within the same binding cavities. In a proof-of-concept case, we showed that Deoxyribonuclease I (DNase I) binds BP2 with higher affinity than its canonical ligand PO-3 (median -5.85 vs -2.55 kcal/mol). It also forms hydrogen bonds with Asn192 and {pi}-stacking interactions with the catalytic histidine His274, a pattern conserved in bovine DNase I. Experimental validation confirmed that BP2 at 10- M inhibits DNA hydrolysis by 21.5% in bovine DNase I (p-value < 0.01) and 23.2% in recombinant human DNase I (p-value < 0.001). Our work establishes a robust, transferable computational framework for identifying protein targets of environmental contaminants and reveals that PDCs engage their targets through novel non-mimetic binding modes, with structural patterns that can be conserved across species. These findings may have significant implications for the safety assessment of plastic additives.

title: High prevalence and diversity of nematodes associated with Europe's most destructive forest pest, revealed by off-target genomic data
abstract: We know very little about the biotic interactions of most species on our planet, including many organisms that play a crucial role in ecosystem networks. One highly cost-effective way of reconstructing these networks is to analyse the rapidly growing collections of high-throughput sequencing datasets. In this study, we examine a large whole-genome resequencing dataset for the spruce bark beetle (Ips typographus), one of Europe's most destructive forest pests, to determine the diversity and distribution of associated organisms that such datasets can reveal. We found that from among metagenomic datasets for 312 adult beetles from across the species' European range, 69% contained small subunit ribosomal RNA (SSU rRNA) reads from other eukaryotic organisms, most often nematodes. Among 13 rRNA-reconstructed nematode species, Contortylenchus sp. and Micoletzkya sp. were the most prevalent taxa across the European populations. Frequently, nematode DNA comprised a large proportion of the sequencing libraries, suggesting a significant impact on the host. Mitochondrial genes reconstructed for many of these beetles provided additional phylogenetic resolution, although the reconstruction success varied. Overall, our results demonstrate potential for reconstructing the key biological associations using sequencing data originally generated for a different purpose, highlighting a path towards comprehensive survey of interactions likely to substantially influence the population dynamics of ecologically significant species.

title: BioSensor-X: A Coverage-Aware Evidence-Integration and Benchmarking Framework for Transcription-Factor Prioritization in Microbial Biosensor Engineering
abstract: Transcription-factor (TF) prioritization in microbial biosensor engineering requires integration of heterogeneous molecular and regulatory evidence, yet benchmark-associated performance may be influenced by candidate coverage, annotation density, and information-flow structure. BioSensor-X was developed as a leakage-controlled, coverage-aware framework for evaluating heterogeneous transcriptomic and regulatory evidence for Escherichia coli TF prioritization. Six transcriptomic datasets were processed, of which three contributed candidate instances, yielding 360 candidate contexts representing 60 TFs. The framework integrated transcriptional responsiveness, regulatory specificity, regulon size as an annotation-density proxy, and curated regulatory evidence using discovery-only standardization, prespecified equal weighting, and TF-level maximum aggregation. Performance was evaluated using mutually exclusive TF-level DEVELOPMENT and LOCKED TEST partitions with family-aware stratification, while candidate coverage was assessed separately from conditional ranking performance. Of 12 LOCKED TEST TFs, five were represented in the discovery candidate universe, corresponding to 41.7% coverage. The primary BioSensor-X score achieved a conditional AUROC of 0.5782 (95% bootstrap CI, 0.3308-0.8109), with 1/5 TFs recovered in the Top-10 and 2/5 in the Top-20. The regulon-size/annotation-density component achieved an AUROC of 0.7945 (95% bootstrap CI, 0.6655-0.9055). The integrated framework retained a measurable benchmark-associated ranking signal, while the results also indicated that annotation structure contributed substantially to benchmark discrimination. These findings support the value of separating candidate coverage from conditional ranking performance and explicitly accounting for annotation-density-associated effects when evaluating TF prioritization frameworks.

title: Structural clustering of paired αβ T-cell receptor repertoires recovers antigen-specific convergence beyond sequence similarity
abstract: T-cell receptor (TCR) antigen recognition depends on the three-dimensional geometry of the paired {beta} complementarity-determining regions (CDRs), which primary sequence does not fully capture. Most repertoire-clustering methods group receptors by CDR3 motifs, sequence distance or V-J gene usage, and may miss receptors that differ in sequence but adopt similar loop conformations. We present SPACE-TCR (Structural Profiling of Alpha-Beta Clonotypes by Epitope), which stratifies predicted paired {beta} backbone models by CDR length, aligns them on conserved framework anchors and clusters them by C RMSD across the CDRs. On an independently curated benchmark of 4,779 paired CD8 TCRs spanning 367 epitopes, 94.6% of SPACE-TCR clusters at the focal 0.75 [A] threshold had purity [≥] 0.9, close to ClusTCR (97.3%), while clustering more than twice as many unique CDR3{beta} (10.4% versus 4.7%); every method that clustered more did so at markedly lower purity. SPACE-TCR had the lowest polyspecificity (5.4%), and 22.7% of its high-purity clusters were sequence-diverse or sequence-unrelated, categories rarely recovered by the evaluated CDR3{beta}-similarity methods. With increasing unannotated repertoire background, it kept higher purity than the evaluated sequence-based methods across all available comparisons (30.4% at 89.2% noise, compared with 15.0% for TCRMatch). Paired structural clustering therefore complements sequence-based analysis, recovering convergent receptor families that sequence criteria miss.

title: Pharmacogenomic diversity at tuberculosis-treatment loci across African populations: phased haplotypes, regulatory architecture and NAT2 acetylator inference
abstract: Background: Tuberculosis imposes a major public-health burden in Africa, while variation in isoniazid and rifampicin disposition creates opportunities for improved pharmacotherapy. The population architecture of extended, phased pharmacogenomic backgrounds remains less well characterized than individual marker frequencies. Methods: We analyzed high-coverage, phased GRCh38 genomes from 661 unrelated individuals sampled from five continental-African and two African-diaspora populations at NAT2, SLCO1B1, CES2, HLA-B, NR1I2 and UGT1A1. We integrated frequency differentiation, reduced phased signatures, linkage disequilibrium, functional annotation and NAT2 core-allele inference with individual-clustered permutation tests. Results: The six loci contributed 17,223 annotated variant records and 276 entries in a capped frequency-differentiation register. Exact NAT2 core-definition matching was achieved for 1,321/1,322 chromosomes (99.92%), and determinate genotype-inferred acetylator categories for 620/661 individuals (93.80%). Among the sampled continental-African populations, 35-site noncore background distributions differed within NAT2 *5 (BH-adjusted q=0.000100), *4 (q=0.024733) and *6 (q=0.000350) groups. Distinct phased and linkage architectures also characterized transporter, hydrolysis, regulatory and HLA-B genomic regions. Conclusion: African population-associated variation extends beyond commonly used pharmacogenetic allele definitions. The observed NAT2 backgrounds and complementary locus signatures provide a foundation for targeted molecular studies and prospective pharmacokinetic validation that could inform future population-responsive TB treatment research.

title: Full-length transcript architecture reveals RNA fate and regulatory state
abstract: Pervasive transcription generates diverse RNAs, including promoter-upstream transcripts (PROMPTs), coding and non-coding transcripts from protein-coding loci, and enhancer RNAs. How their full-length architectures relate to RNA fate remains poorly understood. Using ultra-deep sequencing of polyadenylated and non-polyadenylated capped RNAs from mouse embryonic stem cells, we show that nuclear exosome surveillance of PROMPTs is associated with transcript length and sequence composition. We show that for most protein-coding genes, capped transcripts are dominated by cytosolic 3'[->]5' degradation intermediates or premature transcription termination products rather than full-length mRNAs. The relative abundance of intact mRNAs, cytosolic degradation intermediates and prematurely terminated transcripts varies between genes and is associated with gene architecture, expression level and biological function. Finally, we identify a class of convergently transcribed enhancers enriched for Polycomb repressive complex 2-associated proteins and poised enhancer features, with an increased propensity for activation during differentiation. Full-length transcript architecture thus reveals RNA fate and regulatory state.

title: GlycanPUG: WURCS-Based Heterogeneous Graph Pretraining for Structurally Ambiguous Glycans
abstract: Background: Glycans orchestrate diverse biological processes, yet they remain underrepresented in computational biology compared to proteins and nucleic acids. Although WURCS 2.0 provides a machine-readable structural representation that preserves uncertainty, the evaluated IUPAC-based deterministic workflow processes 43.1% of the GlyCosmos-derived cohort examined here, motivating approaches that retain structural ambiguity. Methods: To overcome this limitation, GlycanPUG (Probabilistic Uncertainty-aware Graph) was introduced as a pretrained graph model for glycan representation learning. By leveraging WURCS 2.0, GlycanPUG represents candidate linkages and substituent attachments using weighted edges and uncertainty attributes within a heterogeneous graph framework. A 4-layer Heterogeneous Graph Neural Network with a dedicated node pre-enhancement module aggregates edge features weighted by the assigned edge weights, enabling representation of supported structurally ambiguous glycans without selecting a single resolved structure. The model is pretrained on a preprocessed subset of the GlyTouCan1 repository, which contained 253,596 entries before filtering. After excluding entries linked to downstream tasks and applying sequential structural filtering, 167,020 samples remained and were used for pretraining. Pretraining comprised nine self-supervised tasks. Results: Benchmarking on the GlycanML dataset demonstrates that GlycanPUG shows competitive performance relative to GlycanGT across multi-label taxonomy classification and binary immunogenicity prediction. Crucially, on datasets natively containing structural uncertainties (GlyCosmos, GlyConnect), GlycanPUG effectively processes additional structurally ambiguous entries, achieving 83.5% processable coverage across all glycans from all biological sources in GlyCosmos, with taxonomic classification performance (e.g., mean macro F1 of 0.7376 for Domain). Ablation of the node pre-enhancement module reduces macro F1, and post-hoc analysis identifies rank-dependent associations between structural uncertainty and prediction errors. All results reported above are averaged over ten independent random seeds (1-10). Conclusions: GlycanPUG broadens the set of glycans that can be represented while retaining supported structural ambiguities.

title: PathwayTheme: identifying and attributing pathway-level axes of variation in omics data
abstract: Exploring gene expression datasets often involves delineating principal axes of variation corresponding to either biological or technical variables. Principal component analysis (PCA) is typically employed as it uses all genes, reflecting global relationships between samples. Existing tools decompose gene expression first and interpret components afterwards. However, gene-level components are sensitive to sparsity and difficult to relate directly to biology, signals carried by low-variance components are easily overlooked, and differential pathway analysis is usually performed separately, on thresholded gene lists. PathwayTheme addresses these limitations by reversing the order of operations: per-sample pathway scores are generated first and then decomposed by PCA, so that each component is defined by pathways and can be tested directly against biological and technical variables. PathwayTheme further incorporates a statistical framework for supervised differential pathway enrichment that does not require thresholded gene lists, with Gene Ontology results summarised into themes. Applied to a published paediatric cancer cohort, PathwayTheme separated technical from biological axes and identified components distinguishing sample types, diagnoses and genetic subgroups, including rare groups represented by low-variance components.

title: CheekAI: An explainable, deep learning epigenetic aging clock based on lifestyle and health epigenetic biomarker proxies
abstract: The human methylome is poorly understood and, as such, the vast majority of epigenetic aging clocks are unexplainable black boxes. To address this, we created CheekAI, a robust deep learning model that uses lifestyle and health epigenetic biomarker proxies (EBPs) to predict age. Trained using a longitudinal dataset of 25,400 adult buccal DNA methylation samples derived from 14,716 distinct adults, we used principal components and multi-objective optimization to produce a clock that is explainable, reproducible, responsive, and accurate. The Pearson correlation with chronological age is 0.969, the mean absolute error is 2.49 years, and the intraclass correlation coefficient across 679 replicate pairs is 0.990. CheekAI was significantly associated with a plethora of lifestyle and health variables, including resting heart rate, omega-3 intake, ultra-processed food intake, daily step count, resistance training, and time spent in nature. When applied to external saliva and buccal datasets, CheekAI significantly captured a variety of signals, including smoking and oesophageal cancer. CheekAI was also significantly reduced by a multifactorial lifestyle intervention and this reduction was driven by improvements in dietary and metabolic EBPs. This novel artificial intelligence model represents the first instance of a buccal epigenetic aging clock that utilizes EBPs to offer interpretability and actionability.

title: Diversity of Environmental and Genome-Associated Eukaryotic Circular Rep-Encoding Single-Stranded DNA Viruses
abstract: Circular Rep-encoding single-stranded (CRESS) DNA viruses are widespread across diverse environments, yet their genomic diversity, evolutionary relationships, and associations with eukaryotic hosts remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated the evolutionary diversity of CRESS DNA viruses by integrating replication-associated protein (Rep) sequences from environmental viral metagenomes, publicly available viral references, and endogenous viral elements (EVEs) identified in fungal and algal genomes. Genome-wide screening revealed numerous EVEs distributed across diverse fungal and algal lineages, highlighting the potential historical associations between CRESS DNA viruses and eukaryotic hosts. Phylogenetic analyses revealed considerable diversity among CRESS DNA viruses, including sequences that could not be assigned to currently recognized viral families. Yet, several of these unclassified sequences formed well-supported monophyletic clades, suggesting that existing taxonomic classifications may require further revision. Furthermore, phylogenetic relationships within and among established viral families suggest that existing taxonomic boundaries may not fully capture the evolutionary diversity of these viruses. The phylogenetic placement of fungal and algal EVEs alongside environmental and reference viral sequences further provides insights into the evolutionary relationships between CRESS DNA viruses and eukaryotic genomes. Collectively, our findings expand the known evolutionary diversity of CRESS DNA viruses, identify distinct viral lineages requiring further taxonomic evaluation, and provide a framework for investigating their genomic evolution, taxonomic relationships, and associations with eukaryotic hosts.

title: Large-scale analyses of short open reading frames yield few if any novel human genes
abstract: Recent efforts to discover new protein-coding genes in the human genome have yielded a large number of short open reading frames supported by limited experimental evidence supporting translational activity in fragmented parts of those sequences. We examined the 19 highest-confidence predictions made by the TransCODE Consortium, and found that three of them were previously known and thus not novel, while the other 16 could be explained by mechanisms that do not require the assertion of a novel human protein. In several cases, the alternative explanations for the other 16 had already been published. We also analyzed the other 118 predictions and found that most of these, too, could be explained without positing the existence of novel proteins. Our findings show that in the search for new human genes, evidence of transcription and translation can almost always be explained by known mechanisms, and that the predictions of the TransCODE Consortium likely do not include any novel genes.

title: Divergent immune trajectories distinguish resistance and susceptibility to bacterial leaf streak in wheat
abstract: Bacterial leaf streak (BLS) is an increasingly important disease affecting several cereal crops. The mechanisms linking quantitative trait loci for resistance to downstream immune response against BLS in wheat remain poorly understood. Here, we developed a chromosome-scale genome assembly of the BLS resistant cultivar Boost. With de novo annotation of Boost and Timstein (susceptible cultivar) assemblies, we established a cultivar-resolved framework for dissecting BLS resistance. Both cultivars encoded highly similar immune receptor repertoires, but the major resistance locus, QBls.fcu-3B.1, comprised a divergent receptor kinase haplotype with extensive structural variations, divergent tandem receptor arrays, and constitutively elevated expression of multiple receptor kinases in the resistant cultivar. Candidate receptor kinases in Boost exhibited conserved intracellular kinase domains but substantial divergence among extracellular recognition domains relative to their syntenic homologs in Timstein. Dual reference transcriptome analyses at 24, 48, and 96 hours after inoculation (HAI) revealing contrasting immune trajectories in resistant and susceptible cultivars. Boost progressed through a focused signaling transition at 48 HAI, followed by coordinated activation of several defense modules, such as antimicrobial metabolism, cell wall reinforcement, transcriptional regulation, and immune homeostasis. In contrast, the susceptible cultivar underwent coordinated repression of these defense-related modules together with chromatin-associated transcriptional changes and induction of host transcriptional machinery during disease establishment. Our findings suggest that quantitative resistance to BLS is associated not simply with immune receptor composition, but also with constitutive immune surveillance and temporal coordination of downstream defense, providing a putative mechanistic framework linking natural genomic variations to quantitative BLS resistance in wheat.

title: The 'near T2T' Canton-S assembly is inconsistent with other Canton-S genomes
abstract: Canton-S is among the most widely used Drosophila melanogaster strains, underlying substantial community infrastructure, including serving as a wild-type strain for: genetics studies; studying phenotypes, especially in behavioral studies; and complex trait mapping studies among many others. The recent 'near T2T' assembly of Canton-S (LIU et al.) is presented as delivering modern sequencing and assembly quality to the Drosophila community via this important strain. I find that this assembly is inconsistent with three other independently sequenced Canton-S genome assemblies on a magnitude comparable to differences between distinct strains, raising concerns about its genetic identity that the community should consider when choosing whether to adopt it as a resource.

title: Clonal landscape of human nephrons
abstract: The nephron is a highly compartmentalized structure, where distinct patterns of somatic mosaicism may be established and contribute to altered kidney functions with aging. Here we show extensive remodeling of aged nephrons by mosaic clones using integrated sequencing of >1,000 microdissected samples collected from anatomically distinct nephron segments. Striking differences were observed across segments. Proximal tubules exhibited markedly higher mutation burdens with mutational signatures characteristic of clear cell renal cell carcinoma and larger clonal expansion than other segments. Cancer-related mutations were observed only infrequently and largely limited to proximal tubules, while copy number abnormalities were quite common, most frequently involving chromosomes 18, 10, 7, X, 22, 3 and 9, in a segment-specific manner. Clone size appears to depend more on cell turnover than on driver events. Particularly, in collecting ducts, numerous clones independently acquiring chromosome 18 loss evolved over years and ultimately replaced 15-47% of collecting duct cells in aged donors despite minimal increase in their clone size, likely reflecting strong fitness advantage of chromosome 18-deficient clones under slow tissue turnover. Chromosome 18-deficient cells significantly correlated with fibrosis and showed reduced expression of chromosome 18 genes, including those involved in sodium handling (NEDD4L) and TGF-{beta} signaling (SMAD2/4/7). In line with this, GSEA of chromosome 18-deficient cells revealed enhanced hallmark pathways overlapping those associated with acute kidney injury that are related to TGF-{beta} signaling and epithelial-mesenchymal transition, and inflammatory responses. These findings illustrate how nephrons are remodeled with aging, providing insights into the role of somatic remodelling in altered kidney structures and functions with aging.

title: BiocPy: A Framework for Cross-Platform Genomic Data andMethods Interoperability
abstract: Bioconductor provides standardized data structures and statistical methods for high-throughput genomic analysis in R, whereas Python has become a primary environment for machine learning, image analysis, and general-purpose data science. Combining tools across both ecosystems often requires ad-hoc file conversions or embedded language runtimes that can lose metadata, introduce maintenance overhead, or lead to subtle differences in downstream results. Here, we present BiocPy, a collection of Python packages that support cross-language genomic workflows through three complementary layers: (1) native Python implementations of Bioconductor's core data structures; (2) lossless data exchange via direct reading and writing of serialized R (.rds) objects and the language-neutral ArtifactDB format for persistent, multi-stage pipelines; and (3) a cross-platform method development paradigm built on shared C++ libraries wrapped across R, Python, and WebAssembly to support identical statistical analyses across environments. All packages in the BiocPy ecosystem are published to the Python Package Index (PyPI) with source code hosted at [https://github.com/BiocPy].

title: Deciphering Molecular Language for Spectral Interpretation with a Foundation Model Pretrained on Repository-Wide Metabolomics Data
abstract: In-depth, scalable structural interpretation of tandem mass spectra from diverse biological tissues and environmental samples is essential for understanding the molecular diversity of cellular environments and the metabolic architecture of living systems. Although community-driven resources such as GNPS and MassIVE have aggregated massive volumes of tandem mass spectra spanning a wide range of organisms, clinical cohorts and environmental surveys, modeling and interpreting this exponentially expanding spectral corpus to distill molecular information and derive meaningful biological insights poses a fundamental challenge for established computational methods. Here we present UltraMS, a dual-polarity foundation model tailored to decipher the molecular language latent in tandem mass spectra through large-scale pretraining on more than 160 million spectra encompassing both positive and negative ion modes. Our findings illustrate that UltraMS is capable of effectively decoding the chemical semantics of molecules underlying mass spectra via self-supervised learning, achieving superior performance across a variety of downstream tasks, including elemental detection, molecular identification, molecular property profiling, and metabolic landscape characterization. Remarkably, UltraMS enables conducting molecular identification with fine-grained spectral interpretability, simultaneously elucidating molecular structures from untargeted MS/MS spectra and providing peak-by-peak substructural attributions via annotation transfer. Deployed on a clinical cohort of human plaque samples, UltraMS demonstrates significant potential in discovering previously unrecognized phenotype-linked metabolites supported by structurally grounded fragment-ion formation pathways, while effectively correcting likely misannotated clinical markers. Furthermore, building on the structure-aware spectral representations learned by UltraMS, we construct UltraAtlas, a chemical-property-resolved map that organizes millions of experimental spectra into a unified coordinate system, enabling millisecond-scale molecular profiling and offering practical guidance for exploratory navigation across vast chemical space. Applied to human scalp metabolomics, UltraAtlas effectively captures distinct metabolic variations across individuals, highlighting phenotype-specific chemical signatures while shedding light on the chemical niches of the resident microbiome. Together, UltraMS and UltraAtlas constitute a generalizable framework for structural elucidation and biological discovery from tandem mass spectra, empowering the comprehensive exploration of the largely undeciphered metabolomes across different domains of life.

title: FiberTron enables regulatory variant effect prediction and testing from multi-omic long reads of a single sample
abstract: State-of-the-art sequence-to-function models are trained on large compendia of public data to predict regulatory activity across hundreds of cell types. However, they are not designed to interpret individual genomes, effects in under-sampled cell types, or provide a comprehensive view of how genetic variation influences complex diseases. Here we show that a single sample profiled with Fiber-seq and Nanopore direct RNA-seq contains enough information to train such a model from scratch. FiberTron, a 12M parameter convolutional-transformer model, takes 524 kb of reference sequence and predicts CpG methylation, chromatin accessibility and strand-specific transcript coverage at base-pair resolution (median Pearson's r of 0.85-0.97 on held-out chromosomes). Trained in under a day on a single four-GPU node, our HG002 model performs on par with models such as AlphaGenome on dsQTL and eQTL variant effect prediction tasks, despite being over an order of magnitude smaller. As training uses reference sequence only, each sample's phased multi-omic long reads remain available to test its variant-effect predictions. FiberTron recapitulates OAS1 splicing variation associated with COVID-19 risk, recovers 79% of allele-specific accessibility variants in a melanoma line, identifies oncogenic TERT promoter and TAL1 enhancer mutations, and predicts EWSR1::ATF1 fusion transcript expression and its unique chromatin imprint in a rare clear cell sarcoma patient sample. Lightweight single-sample training brings base-resolution interpretation of non-coding variation within reach of individual laboratories.

title: Annotated reference genome for the Critically Endangered, paleoendemic Bermuda skink (Plestiodon longirostris)
abstract: Skinks, one of the largest vertebrate families with over 1,500 described species, are represented by only 19 publicly available chromosome-level genome assemblies. Here, we present the first whole-genome assembly of the Bermuda skink, Plestiodon longirostris, a Critically Endangered, evolutionarily distinct, and endemic species. We conducted a de novo genome assembly using Oxford Nanopore Technology long reads, followed by reference-guided scaffolding against the five-lined skink Plestiodon fasciatus and Gilberts skink Plestiodon gilberti genomes. We generated a 1.496 Gb assembly with 2,579 scaffold contigs over 500 bp in length, a scaffold N50 of 224.1 Mb, with 98.7% Benchmarking Universal Single-Copy Orthologs (BUSCO) completeness score and 94.8% of gene annotations transferred from the P. fasciatus annotated genome. Repetitive elements comprised 48.37% of the genome, including 33.79% unclassified repeats, while 9% of transposable element sequences contained internal stop codons, consistent with other reptile genomes. Synteny analysis revealed strong conservation of macrochromosomes and gene order through the Plestiodon genus, and progressive chromosomal rearrangement with increased phylogenetic distance across the wider skink family. We also present the first mitogenome for the species. These genomic resources will further evolutionary research in the skink family and will facilitate applied conservation genomic approaches in this Critically Endangered species.

title: WildTrust-UAV: uncertainty-aware wildlife detection with privacy-preserving spatial disclosure and verifiable inference provenance
abstract: Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) imagery has made wildlife surveys faster and safer, but a detected animal is not yet a conservation record. Detector confidence scores are often poorly calibrated, exact coordinates of threatened species can expose them to harm, and an observation is rarely tied back to the image, model, and settings that produced it. WildTrust-UAV addresses these three problems in one framework. It pairs a YOLO11 detector with stochastic-view uncertainty estimation, temperature scaling fitted on validation data, a selective gateway that accepts, defers, or rejects each detection, role-based disclosure of animal locations, and a provenance record that hashes the source image, model, configuration, prediction, uncertainty, timestamp, and nonce. Records are aggregated in a Merkle tree and signed with Ed25519 so that any observation can be verified independently. We report three evaluations on the public WAID dataset. In the detection experiment, two YOLO11n runs reached mAP@0.50 of 0.901 and 0.903 and mAP@0.50:0.95 of 0.527 on a 2,000-image held-out test set. In a separate reliability experiment on 122,720 test detections, temperature scaling reduced expected calibration error from 0.0715 to 0.0179 and the Brier score from 0.0353 to 0.0222. Composite uncertainty identified erroneous detections with an AUROC of 0.904, although confidence alone did better (0.992). Deferring the least reliable detections lowered selective risk from 0.722 at near-full coverage to 0.610 at 69.9% coverage, so considerable error remains in the candidate set. In the provenance experiment, the verifier rejected all 4,500 tampered submissions across nine attack scenarios and accepted all 500 genuine controls, with batch construction and signing taking 0.1 to 2.5 ms. Location policies used synthetic coordinates, and the ledger is a local prototype. Calibration and verifiable records can thus be added to a UAV detection pipeline at low cost, while combining uncertainty signals does not automatically improve error detection.

title: Beyond profiles: Supervised repeat annotation using protein embeddings
abstract:
by Kaiyu Qiu, Jan Ludwiczak, Andrei N. Lupas, Stanislaw Dunin-Horkawicz 

Protein repeats give rise to diverse protein structures and functions, yet their sequence-based detection is often challenging because individual repeat units can diverge substantially in sequence while retaining similar structures. Most sensitive approaches rely on sequence information directly represented by alignments or derived profiles, thereby limiting flexibility and scalability. Here, we introduce TREAD (Transfer learning-based REpeat Annotation using Protein EmbeDdings), a supervised framework that reformulates repeat detection as a residue-level annotation problem and operates directly on embeddings from protein language models. Instead of constructing explicit probabilistic profiles, TREAD learns repeat-specific features implicitly, enabling residue-resolved scoring and flexible repeat segment extraction. Across complementary benchmarks based on RepeatsDB and Pfam, TREAD consistently matches or outperforms the widely used profile-based tool HMMER, particularly in low-data and high-divergence settings. The model exhibits robustness to score thresholding and demonstrates better generalization to independent test sets, including those containing remotely related families. To illustrate the practical utility of TREAD, we applied it to survey β-propeller proteins across the AlphaFold Database and representative proteomes to generate a comprehensive census of this fold. This analysis highlights extensive propeller diversity, identifies lineage-specific expansion patterns across the tree of life, and suggests previously unrecognized relationships between propellers and other repeat folds. Together, TREAD provides a flexible and scalable alternative to profile-based repeat annotation and establishes a general motif-centric framework for protein sequence annotation.

title: Vascular modelling of peripheral ischaemic disease response
abstract:
by Lachlan Arthur, Michele Carrabba, Paolo Madeddu, Steven McDougall, Vassilis Sboros 

Ischaemic disease presents a significant challenge in medical science due to its widespread manifestations in the body and its tendency to only become overt in its late stages, beyond where current intervention methods are effective. Diseases such as coronary heart disease and peripheral artery disease (PAD) represent leading causes of death and are detrimental to quality of life. Focussing on the latter, PAD incurs an amputation rate of around 25%, largely owing to microvascular disease that prevents tissue recovery even after revascularisation. Current methods for investigating PAD either cannot chart specific vascular determinants, such as with  in vivo  imaging, or deform and remove subjects from longitudinal studies, such as with  ex vivo  tissue sampling. Presented to aid live research, computational modelling can collate information and build models of ischaemia using available information and provide a reasonable approximation of the disease’s chronology and thus support understanding and advance research of PAD. Proposed here, is a 3D  in silico  model of ischaemic disease in the limb using a system of purpose-built platforms. Starting with a real micro-computed tomography image of the murine hindlimb, a realistic vessel bed was generated using vascular graphing software,  ViGiL . From here, the model was realised in a defined pressure gradient via flow-modelling software,  numPTI . With the base model of lower limb arteries, collateral vasculature was generated throughout the vessel space. This provides a bypass system for adaptation post-ischaemia. Upon ischaemic induction, the collateral bed responds to the loss of flow and successfully adapted to recover flow with similar density and distribution of diameters in collateral arterioles ( p >> 0.05). Moreover, a satisfactory flow recovery of 50% was achieved after 6 days, showing that the model can reflect the specific vascular environment in which disease is incited. The proceeds of this study lay the groundwork for truly realistic ischaemic models including moving towards a predictive model than can signify when and where key indicators of PAD manifest.

title: CoEVFold suite: User friendly pipelines to visually represent protein coevolution
abstract:
by Chris L. B. Graham, Liam Cremona, Robin Little, Christopher D. A. Rodrigues 

Multiple sequence alignment (MSA) data underlies current principles in protein folding and protein-protein interaction prediction, from which deep-learning models trained on protein sequence and structure datasets can predict protein structure. However, what is missing are user-friendly tools that enable researchers to identify and visualise coevolution, the principal signal that these MSAs encode. Here we present tools to identify and visualize coevolution, through a pipeline (CoEVFold) that uses basic direct coupling algorithms derived from GREMLIN and an input alignment of sequences from MMseqs2. We also provide notebooks to calculate coevolution with alternative methods such as CCMpred or plmc. The pipeline generates a visual representation of coevolution for a single protein but can also represent coevolution of homomeric or heteromeric protein complexes, as well as coevolution within protein networks. The input for this pipeline can be an amino acid sequence, or protein structures from AlphaFold/RoseTTAFold, the user’s own files or the PDB. Using proteins from well-studied prokaryotic and eukaryotic model systems ( Bacillus subtilis ,  Escherichia coli  and  Saccharomyces cerevisiae),  as well as phage proteins, we show that CoEVFold detects coevolution between proteins known to interact, between protomers of known oligomers, and within known protein complexes. Benchmarked against 18 heteromeric complexes of known structure, the top-ranked inter-protein couplings identified interface contacts with a precision of 0.8 or more in 7 complexes, and CoEVMapper rankings agreed with STRING associations for an  Escherichia coli  cell-wall synthesis network (ROC AUC 0.72–0.74). For homo-oligomers, the top-ranked coevolution pairs not explained by the monomer structure were protomer–protomer contacts in 25% (SpoIIIE) and 47% (MlaD) of cases, against 2% or less expected by chance. The coupling calculation for a ~ 950-residue complex took 114 s with GREMLIN, compared with 116 s for CCMpred and 2,060 s for plmc. Collectively, this suite of tools, named ‘CoEVFold suite’, has broad applicability and provide a useful toolkit to those interested in dissecting protein-protein interactions and networks.

title: Deciphering the replication-division coordination in  E. coli : A unified mathematical framework for systematic model comparison
abstract:
by Alexandre Perrin, Marie Doumic, Meriem El Karoui, Sylvie Méléard 

Despite extensive research, the quantitative principles that govern the coordination between DNA replication and cell division in bacteria remain debated. Multiple theoretical models have been proposed, some postulating that a single regulatory process is sufficient to ensure replication–division coordination, while others argue that two concurrent processes are required for robust control. In this work, we develop a unifying mathematical framework within which models can be consistently formulated, qualitatively analysed and quantitatively compared. This framework also allows us to propose a new double-process model. Through theoretical analysis, we establish the necessary and sufficient conditions under which single-process models can reproduce physiological cell behaviours. Beyond the correlation-based analyses extensively used to date, we further demonstrate within a comprehensive statistical framework that double-process models more accurately recapitulate experimental data across all growth conditions. Specifically, the new model we propose robustly captures the replication-division coordination in every growth regime, thereby providing a foundation for future mechanistic studies.

title: Differential vulnerability of stimulus-locked and persistent gamma oscillations: Implications in schizophrenia
abstract:
by Daniel W. Chung, G. Bard Ermentrout 

Working memory depends on gamma oscillations generated across sensory and prefrontal cortices. In primary visual cortex (V1), stimulus-locked gamma oscillations encode stimulus information, while in prefrontal cortex (PFC), persistent gamma oscillations maintain this information after the stimulus is removed. In schizophrenia (SZ), gamma power is reduced in both V1 and PFC, consistent with deficits in sensory encoding and working memory maintenance. Both oscillation regimes arise from a canonical microcircuit involving pyramidal neurons (PNs) and parvalbumin-expressing interneurons (PVIs). Yet, whether the two regimes are similarly or differentially vulnerable to synaptic alterations within this circuit in SZ remains unknown. To investigate this question, we used a mean-field model of the PN-PVI circuit, in which the two regimes were distinguished by NMDA conductance values reflecting the difference in GluN2B expression between human PFC and V1. We then assessed three synaptic alterations quantified using molecular and structural proxies in postmortem SZ brains: lower excitatory inputs to PVIs (E→I), lower inhibitory inputs to PNs (I→E), and greater variability in E→I strength. Each alteration produced larger gamma power deficits in the persistent regime than in the stimulus-locked regime. Applied together, these alterations interacted synergistically to reduce gamma power, with the persistent regime exhibiting a more pronounced deficit. Bifurcation analyses revealed that this differential vulnerability arises from a wider margin of oscillatory stability in the stimulus-locked regime, and that reduced I→E strength additionally abolished the bistability required for the persistent regime. These findings predict that a larger magnitude of synaptic alteration is required to disrupt gamma oscillations in V1 than in PFC, consistent with postmortem reports of more severe alterations in V1 in SZ. Together, they establish a differential vulnerability model of cortical gamma oscillations in SZ, in which regional differences in oscillatory stability determine how much synaptic alteration is required to disrupt oscillations with distinct dynamics.

title: TRAFIKK: Systematic prediction and mechanistic interpretation of anticancer drug synergies
abstract:
by Marco Fariñas, Viviam Bermúdez, Eirini Tsirvouli, Kristine Lippestad, John Zobolas, Tero Aittokallio, Kaisa Lehti, Åsmund Flobak 

Effective drug combination therapies can improve cancer treatment, yet the mechanistic basis of drug synergy remains poorly understood. Most computational approaches prioritise predictive accuracy over molecular mechanistic interpretability, providing limited insights into how synergistic effects emerge across signalling contexts. We developed Trafikk, a molecular-signalling network-based framework that simulates drug perturbations in cell-line-specific computational models to mirror functional outcomes in experimental combination screens.
