Across two independent large-scale datasets, Trafikk identified synergistic combinations with >77% recall. Functional response predictions revealed both conserved and context-dependent mechanisms. While AKT-MEK co-inhibition consistently disrupted coordinated survival and apoptotic signalling in 742 cell lines, PI3K-BCL2 synergy arose through distinct death programs shaped by cell-context-specific network constraints. Trafikk combines predictive performance with mechanistic interpretability, capturing how and why drug synergy emerges across cellular contexts. Source code, installation instructions and usage tutorial are freely available at https://github.com/druglogics/trafikk.

title: Single-nucleus proteomics reveals proteins regulating LPS-induced nucleocytoplasmic transport in macrophages
abstract:
Background
                      Variation in the proteome configuration of unstimulated cells may be associated with differences in how individual cells respond to stimulation. Multiplexed single-cell proteomics by liquid chromatography mass spectrometry can uncover these associations at high depth and throughput. 
                  
                     Results
                      Here we develop an approach that links proteomic and phenotypic variation across individual cells and nuclei to identify potential regulators of biological processes for targeted validation. We apply this approach to identify regulators of nucleocytoplasmic protein transport in macrophages stimulated with lipopolysaccharide (LPS). We quantify the proteomes of 3,412 individual nuclei across the dynamic response to LPS and associated proteomic variation with differences in transport. Within minutes of stimulation, protein transport in individual nuclei correlates strongly with the abundance of known protein transport regulators, revealing how natural protein variation relates to cellular responses. Simple biophysical constraints, including nuclear pore abundance, partially explain the variation in LPS-induced nucleocytoplasmic transport. We select 16 new potential regulators of protein transport to test by targeted knockdown. The knockdown phenotypes confirm the inferences derived from natural protein and functional variation of single nuclei. 
                  
                     Conclusions
                      By linking proteomic and functional variation among individual nuclei, we identify proteins associated with LPS-induced nucleocytoplasmic transport and prioritize potential regulators for functional validation. This approach should be broadly applicable to discovering protein regulators and enhancing the functional interpretation of single-cell omics data.

title: AURA decomposes spatial gene expression to reveal composition-dependent regulation
abstract: Spatial transcriptomics at single-cell resolution can relate each cell’s expression to its surroundings, yet analyses still depend on predefined domains or niches. We present AURA, a statistical framework that tests and quantifies how a cell type’s gene expression depends on the continuous composition of its local neighborhood, separating this from cell-level transcriptional output and flagging transcript spillover. AURA is calibrated in simulations, scales to millions of cells, and applies to Xenium, CosMx and Visium HD data. Across lymph node, fibrotic lung and cancer, it reveals widespread small composition-dependent effects organized into a few interpretable axes.

title: Multi-institutional harmonization framework for heterogeneous panel-based NGS in precision oncology
abstract:
Background
                      Panel-based NGS is increasingly used in Korea, but heterogeneity in file formats, reference builds, and reporting conventions across institutions constrains secondary use for policy evaluation and translational research. Before consortium-scale data accrue in the newly launched CURE-NGS (Collecting Universal Real-world Evidence of Next-Generation Sequencing Panel in Korea) initiative, a harmonized methodological framework is required to standardize real-world multi-panel NGS outputs and enable comparable evidence generation across institutions. 
                  
                     Methods
                      We implemented an open-source, multi-tier harmonization framework that prioritizes raw VCF as the primary evidentiary layer and supports structured tables containing Human Genome Variation Society (HGVS) expressions and report-derived inputs obtained by manual abstraction or optical character recognition (OCR) as supplementary routes. A unified Python command-line interface and version-pinned Docker images perform input quality control (QC), conservative reference-build inference, explicit target-build selection, reference-aware left alignment, multiallelic decomposition, provenance tracking, VCF-to-MAF transformation, HGVS-to-minimal-MAF construction, and minimal-MAF-to-annotated-MAF generation. Public non-clinical fixtures and automated tests exercise all six components. 
                  
                     Results
                      The public regression suite comprises 108 tests. On the Windows development host, 106 passed and two bcftools-dependent tests were skipped as expected; the corresponding Linux/container tests and all configured code, container, release-lock, and repository-health verification jobs passed. Across 12 public non-clinical technical fixtures, 2,095 of 2,149 unique HGVS-evaluable direct-route variants were recovered by the report-HGVS route, and 2,095 of 2,108 report-route variants matched the direct route. Canonical allele normalization therefore yielded 97.49% sensitivity, 99.38% positive predictive value, 96.90% Jaccard agreement, and 98.43% F1. Matched downstream summaries reproduced the gene-frequency, oncoplot, and MUC16 protein-position patterns across the two routes. 
                  
                     Conclusions
                      This framework provides a practical pre-accrual methodological foundation for CURE-NGS and for multi-institutional harmonization of real-world clinical NGS data in Korea. As CURE-NGS data accumulate, the framework can be iteratively refined, prospectively validated, and extended through continuous reporting, policy-oriented real-world evidence generation, and downstream analytical applications.

title: Integrating MeSH semantics and knowledge graph topology for structure-agnostic drug-drug interaction prediction
abstract:
Background
                 Adverse drug–drug interactions (DDIs) cause preventable hospitalizations, but exhaustive experimental screening of all drug pairs is infeasible. Many computational predictors rely on small-molecule structural representations, limiting their direct applicability to biologic therapeutics. We present a structure-agnostic framework that combines semantic representations derived from Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) with graph-derived topology from a Drug–Target–Protein knowledge graph constructed from DrugBank and UniProt. We further examine how MeSH annotation depth is associated with predictive performance. 
              
                Results
                 In transductive evaluation, latent gated fusion achieved an overall AUROC of 0.988 and improved mean AUROC and F1 over MeSH-only across all six interaction categories. Improvements in AUROC, F1, and precision remained significant after Holm correction for Low-Mid, Mid-Mid, and Mid-Deep interactions, with the largest mean AUROC gain in Low-Mid (+0.0304). In seen–unseen inductive evaluation, each test pair contained one held-out drug and one seen drug, and all DDI edges were excluded from the feature graphs. Fusion achieved an overall AUROC of 0.937, exceeding MeSH-only by 0.045; this improvement remained significant after Holm correction. Mean AUROC gains occurred across all six categories, with recurring improvements in Low–Mid ( + 0.063) and Mid–Mid ( + 0.053) that reached nominal significance, although the inductive category-level evidence remained exploratory. 
              
                Conclusions
                 MeSH annotation depth is associated with systematic variation in DDI prediction performance that aggregate evaluation can obscure. Recurring gains for Low–Mid and Mid–Mid interactions across evaluation settings support the predictive benefit of combining MeSH semantics with graph-derived topology, with additional transductive evidence for Mid–Deep interactions. The framework provides a common, structure-agnostic representation compatible with both small-molecule and biologic therapeutics and supports first-pass DDI prioritization for subsequent expert assessment. 
              
                Clinical trial number
                 Not applicable.

title: ZipAEr: A compressive convolutional autoencoder for high-dimensional spatial omics data at subcellular resolution
abstract:
Background
                      Recent advances in spatial transcriptomics, such as the CosMx Spatial Molecular Imager, enable the detection and quantification of thousands of RNA transcripts at subcellular resolution. While these data offer unprecedented insight, computational analysis remains a significant bottleneck. Current methods typically aggregate transcripts at the cell level, relying on precise cell segmentation—a notoriously difficult task in complex tissues like the brain. Deep learning autoencoders offer a segmentation-free, pixel-level alternative but face a major engineering hurdle: standard convolutional architectures expand channel depth while reducing spatial resolution. When applied to high-plex data, this “channel expansion” creates prohibitive memory requirements that exceed the limits of currently available hardware. 
                  
                     Results
                      To overcome this computational barrier, we introduce ZipAEr, a deep learning framework featuring a novel “dual-compression” architecture that simultaneously reduces dimensionality along both the spatial and channel axes. We validated ZipAEr on the CosMx human frontal cortex dataset—a publicly available resource that provides single-molecule subcellular resolution (20–50 nm) and ultra-high-plex coverage (more than 6,000 genes) in human brain tissue. ZipAEr effectively compressed these high-dimensional data, reducing memory requirements by factors of 195 × to 1,649 × (depending on model depth) while preserving essential biological information. In a downstream classification task identifying  MAPT -positive neurons, a classifier trained on ZipAEr’s latent representations outperformed a baseline model with the same architecture but trained on raw data, with similar accuracy (69% vs. 68%) but substantially higher precision (75% vs. 68%) and specificity (69% vs. 48%). 
                  
                     Conclusions
                      ZipAEr establishes a scalable, segmentation-free framework for pixel-level analysis of high-plex spatial omics data. By resolving the channel-expansion problem, ZipAEr enables researchers to investigate subcellular mechanisms in complex tissues.

title: The MKS1–WRKY12 brake‐and‐release module controls SOS2 de‐repression and salt tolerance in Arabidopsis
abstract:
SUMMARY 
 To adapt to salt stress, plants must rapidly activate ion homeostasis pathways while preventing their unnecessary activation under non-stress conditions. How this balance is achieved at the transcriptional level remains incompletely understood. Here, we identify the WRKY transcription factor WRKY12 as a transcriptional brake that directly represses  SOS2 , a central kinase of the salt overly sensitive pathway, thereby limiting basal pathway activity in Arabidopsis. Loss of  WRKY12  enhances salt tolerance and improves Na + /K +  homeostasis, whereas its overexpression causes hypersensitivity to salinity. Upon salt stress, WRKY12 is rapidly attenuated at both transcript and protein levels, indicating an active de-repression mechanism. We further demonstrate that MKS1 interacts with WRKY12 and antagonizes its function through a dual mechanism, reducing WRKY12 occupancy at the  SOS2  promoter while participating in its proteasome-dependent degradation. Genetic analyses place  MKS1  upstream of  WRKY12  and  SOS2  in regulating salt tolerance. Together, our findings uncover a transcriptional brake-and-release module that enables rapid and robust activation of  SOS2 , providing a mechanistic framework for how plants balance growth and stress adaptation through dynamic transcriptional control.

title: Discovery and Deployment of Herbicide Tolerance in Domesticated Pennycress (Thlaspi arvense L.) to Enable Modern Agronomic Integration
abstract:
ABSTRACT 
 Modern agronomic systems for large-scale oilseed production rely heavily on chemical weed control, presenting a barrier to the adoption of newly domesticated crops that lack herbicide tolerance. Pennycress ( Thlaspi arvense  L.), a domesticated winter oilseed developed to increase land productivity and support sustainable biofuel production, is highly sensitive to commonly used herbicides targeting acetolactate synthase (ALS) and 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase (HPPD). Here, we report complementary strategies for identifying and deploying herbicide-tolerant alleles in pennycress. ALS inhibitor tolerance was identified through Ethyl methanesulfonate (EMS)-derived chemical mutagenesis, whereas HPPD inhibitor tolerance was explored using a microbial-based rational enzyme design platform as proof of concept. Selected alleles were introduced into advanced germplasm via homology-directed repair (HDR) and evaluated across developmental stages. Plants carrying the P187S mutation in the ALS gene exhibited robust tolerance at both seedling and rosette stages without detectable penalties to growth or seed yield. In contrast, the G419A allele in the HPPD gene conferred tolerance to residual herbicide activity when overexpressed but showed limited efficacy when expressed from its native locus, indicating context-dependent functionality. Collectively, this study demonstrates the feasibility of integrating herbicide tolerance into a newly domesticated oilseed crop and highlights the utility of combining mutagenesis-based discovery, rational enzyme engineering, and precision genome editing to support agronomic compatibility and crop deployment.

title: Optimization of the pC‐HSL‐Induced Transcriptional Regulator, Rpa, for Use in Plant Synthetic Biology
abstract:
ABSTRACT 
 Advancements in plant synthetic biology rely on developing genetic parts with reliable and tunable expression levels for regulation of large genetic pathways. A slow design-build-test cycle and vast design space for modifying genetic parts make precise development of plant synthetic biology tools a challenge. In this work, a transcriptional activator derived from  Rhodopseudomonas palustris  and re-tooled to function in plants was optimized for low basal expression and high activated expression upon induction with the ligand  p -Coumaroyl-homoserine lactone. Modifications to the activation domain, nuclear localization signal, DNA operator design, minimal promoter driving the reporter gene, and combinatorial pairings of these modifications resulted in significant variation in the dynamic range of the system. The overall lowest basal expression produced from the tested designs was approximately 30% that of the internal reference gene  elongation factor-1 α  and the greatest activated expression produced was approximately 130-fold induction. Functionality of expression from the optimized activation system was demonstrated in both transient  Nicotiana benthamiana  assays and stably transformed potato, with successful induction observed from a range of concentrations and application methods of  p- Coumaroyl-homoserine lactone.

title: mRNA Decay Mediates Evolution and Biological Functions in Plant Gene Expression
abstract:
ABSTRACT 
 mRNA decay is a key post-transcriptional regulatory mechanism that fine-tunes plant development and stress adaptation through dynamic mRNA stability control, bridging fundamental biology and crop improvement. Current knowledge of mRNA decay mechanisms in plants, largely derived from  Arabidopsis , is poorly generalisable across plant lineages owing to insufficient exploration of other species. Recent advances in high-throughput sequencing have accelerated the discovery of mRNA decay mechanisms. Here, we systematically illustrate its core molecular mechanisms alongside breakthrough advances. We further dissect evolutionary characteristics of highly conserved core components and lineage-specific adaptive variations across eukaryotes. Notably, conserved since the last eukaryotic common ancestor (LECA), this machinery reflects a complex ancestral eukaryote and provides high-resolution phylogenetic markers for reconstructing eukaryotic origins. We also clarify the essential biological roles of mRNA decay in developmental modulation and stress responses. Finally, we propose precision breeding strategies based on mRNA stability regulation to develop high-yielding, climate-resilient crops. This review integrates up-to-date mechanistic evidence and comparative evolutionary perspectives, consolidates consensus findings and sorts out inconsistent research outcomes, and seeks to enrich the fundamental biological understanding of plant mRNA stability modulation.

title: ZmPHO2‐Mediated Phosphorus Homeostasis Modulates PAMP‐Triggered Immunity and Disease Resistance in Maize
abstract:
ABSTRACT 
 Maize production is influenced by both macronutrient-driven growth and resistance to various abiotic and biotic stresses. While phosphorus (P) is essential for maize growth and productivity, its role in maize immunity remains elusive. Here, we characterized a maize lesion mimic mutant,  les33,  which exhibits enhanced resistance to southern corn rust (SCR) and  Curvularia  leaf spot (CLS). Positional cloning indicated that  ZmPHO2 , encoding an E2 ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme involved in P homeostasis, was the causal gene. In  les33 , increased P level was accompanied by upregulated defence-related gene expression and elevated accumulation of phenylalanine-derived salicylic acid, lignin, and flavonoids, establishing a genetic link between P status and immune activation. Consistently, exogenous phosphate (Pi) application activates defence-related gene expression and enhances resistance to SCR and CLS in a hydroponics system. In particular, flg22-triggered defence marker gene expression, phosphorylation of mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK), and burst of reactive oxygen species (ROS) were enhanced by Pi application, indicating a positive role of P in potentiating PAMP-triggered immunity (PTI). Moreover, field trials showed that application of Pi fertilizer improved SCR resistance in a Pi-dose-dependent manner, further supporting a critical role of P in maize immunity. Taken together, this study provides both genetic and agronomic evidence that P primes defence responses, and highlights optimized Pi fertilization as a practical strategy to coordinate growth and immunity in maize production.

title: High‐Contiguity Haplotype‐Resolved Genome Assembly of the Hexaploid Actinidia valvata Rootstock Sheds Light on Waterlogging Resistance Gene
abstract:
ABSTRACT 
 Polyploidisation, creating redundant or diverged copies of the genome, is a major driving force in plant evolution, diversification and environmental adaptation, including for the kiwifruit genus ( Actinidia  Lindl.). We present a high-contiguity, haplotype-resolved genome assembly of the hexaploid  Actinidia valvata  rootstock cultivar ‘Zhongmikangzhen No. 2’ (ZK2), a novel rootstock and the first of its kind to receive Plant Variety Protection in China, exhibiting superior waterlogging tolerance. The assembly, ZK2, contains 174 chromosomes in 6 haplotypes (2 n  = 6 x  = 174), where > 82% of chromosomes per haplotype are telomere-capped at one or both ends, including three haplotypes achieved with 100% telomeric representation. In total, 212 055 protein-coding genes are predicted, or about 35 000 genes per haplotype on average. Our work on comparative genomics, including analyses of TE composition, collinearity, orthologs and phylogenies, strongly reveals an AABBBB subgenome structure derived from ancestral donors  A. polygama  (A1 and A2) and  A. macrosperma  (B1 to B4). Transcriptome analysis showed differential expressions between the homeologs under waterlogging stress, highlighting subgenome-specific regulatory dynamics. A key example involves an ethylene-response factor ( ERF ) gene: when the B1 copy of  ERF  was overexpressed in the kiwifruit transgenic lines, they illustrated an enhanced waterlogging resistance. In addition, this high-quality haplotype-resolved  A. valvata  genome assembly enables functional trait discovery, homeolog-aware genome-wide association studies, and targeted editing of beneficial alleles or homologous gene sets, supporting the breeding of resilient polyploid kiwifruit cultivars and rootstocks. This resource provides a foundation for future research in kiwifruit, particularly for rootstock-mediated crop improvement.

title: Structural Variations Contribute to Subspeciation and Yield Heterosis in Rice
abstract:
ABSTRACT 
 Yield heterosis has been extensively exploited in hybrid breeding, with intersubspecific hybrids often exhibiting the most pronounced effects. However, developing elite hybrids remains a laborious and time-consuming process. The genetic basis of heterosis has been debated for over a century, hindered largely by the lack of high-quality genomes. Here, we assembled genomes for 12 representative  indica , intermediate type and  japonica  rice accessions. Using sequence variants of the  Phr1  gene, we functionally validated two deletions responsible for phenol reaction variation between the subspecies. Comparative genomic analyses revealed extensive sequence variation among these inbred lines and highlighted the pivotal role of structural variants (SVs) in rice subspeciation. Importantly, the number of SVs between parental inbred lines significantly correlated with heterosis across 17 agronomic traits, with distinct correlation patterns for intra- and intersubspecific F 1  hybrids. We identified SVs associated with  S5-ORF5  and  OsBZR1  and validated their function to heterosis for seed setting rate and yield heterosis, respectively, underscoring the importance of SVs in breeding intersubspecific hybrids. The genomic SVs altered gene expression and these transcriptional changes effectively explained the variance in heterosis. Furthermore, translocations outperformed other SVs and their heterozygous haplotypes exhibited heterosis over homozygous ones. Our findings establish SVs as pivotal drivers in subspeciation and highlight the overdominance model for harnessing rice heterosis.

title: Global patterns of cultivated plant diversity and their implications for invasion
abstract:
Euler diagram showing species richness and overlap among the global vascular flora (in white), the global cultivated flora (in blue), and the global naturalized flora (in pink).







Summary

People have cultivated plants for their wide‐ranging services for millennia, introducing thousands of species to new regions through human migration and trade. By increasing the number and abundance of introduced species and selecting for particular traits, cultivation likely promotes the self‐sustained establishment (naturalization) of alien species.
Using a recently collated database of 3050 lists of vascular plant species cultivated around the world, we characterized the global cultivated flora and explored the role of cultivation in naturalization.
The global cultivated flora is highly diverse, comprising about a quarter of all known vascular plant species. Species richness and phylogenetic richness of cultivated plants were highest in temperate, species‐rich regions. Most species were alien to the regions where they were cultivated and were climatically suited to these regions. The majority (84.6%) of species that have naturalized world‐wide are cultivated, and alien cultivated species richness strongly predicted naturalization within regions. This suggests that global regional patterns of naturalization are most directly shaped by the human‐mediated introduction of plants for cultivation.
Our findings provide a broad description of cultivated plant diversity and demonstrate the tight coupling of cultivation and naturalization at the global scale.

Ion pair acceptor electrolyte for high-energy Li-rich batteries
abstract: Abstract Anion-derived inorganic-rich cathode-electrolyte interphases (CEIs) offer a promising solution for high-voltage lithium-ion batteries. However, conventional electrolytes struggle to suppress parasitic side reactions at the high-voltage cathode interface. Herein, a principle for ion pair acceptor electrolyte (IPAE) is proposed utilizing phosphazene-based molecules. Leveraging both anion- π  and ion-dipole interactions, tailored (trifluoroethoxy)pentafluorocyclotriphosphazene (TFPN) interacts moderately with Li +  and anions. These coordinations promote the formation of compact Li⁺-TFPN-anion nano-clusters in the electrolyte and facilitate a uniform, thin CEI during initial charging. The resulting interphase alleviates oxygen evolution and inhibits surface structural degradation, enabling the lithium-rich battery with 80% capacity retention over 1000 cycles. Furthermore, the IPAE enables a high energy density of 514 Wh kg −1  in a Li||LLO pouch cell with stable cycling. This work establishes a general design principle for high-performance electrolytes and an effective interphase engineering strategy for high-energy-density batteries with extended cycle life.

title: Mutation-biased adaptation: The Yampolsky-Stoltzfus model revisited
abstract: Abstract The Yampolsky-Stoltzfus (YS) model provided the first formal demonstration that a bias in the introduction of new mutations can shape the direction of adaptive evolution, even when mutation rates are small relative to selection coefficients. Despite its foundational role, the model has been characterized almost entirely by simulation and closed-form solutions for its central quantity, the probability that a mutationally favored but less-fit genotype fixes ahead of a rarer, fitter alternative, have been available only in the limiting regimes of vanishing mutation supply and infinite population size. Here we derive closed-form approximations for  P   A   across the intermediate regime of finite population size and appreciable mutation supply that lies between these two limits. Under strong selection between the competing mutants, we combine an establishment-probability argument with clonal interference theory to obtain an explicit expression for  P   A   that accounts for both the ongoing input of the mutationally favored mutation and the frequency-dependent establishment probability of its competitor. Under weak selection between competing mutants, we derive a complementary expression based on the fixation of a mixed population under Kimura’s classical formula. Both expressions agree closely with direct simulation of the underlying Wright-Fisher process, recover the known limiting cases, and remain consistent with one another over a substantial intermediate range of parameters. Our work precisely quantifies the weakening influence of mutation bias on adaptation with increasing population size. It thus provides a basis for assessing the strength of mutation bias in empirical data, and contributes to resolving the controversy surrounding this problem.

title: Demonstration of sexual mating and recombination in the fungal pathogen Candida auris
abstract: Abstract  Candida auris  (renamed  Candidozyma auris ) is a multidrug-resistant fungal pathogen designated as a critical global health threat by the World Health Organization. Since its first clinical identification in 2009,  C. auris  has spread across six continents, forming distinct genetic clades. Although the clades were initially separated geographically, they now coexist in several regions, raising the possibility that different clades could recombine and produce new variants. In this study, we demonstrate for the first time that  C. auris  can undergo sexual mating and recombination. We show that haploid clinical isolates of  C. auris,  taken from different clades, can undergo sexual mating to form diploid cells with a single nucleus and the full genomes of both parents. Diploid cells, in turn, readily produce haploid segregants that contain new combinations of the parental chromosomes. Genome sequencing of haploid segregants revealed many instances of recombination, generating hybrid chromosomes with contributions from both parents. These results show definitively that the apparatus for sexual mating, chromosome segregation, and recombination has been preserved in  C. auris  clinical strains, presumably by purifying selection. These observations raise the possibility that new  C. auris  strains with increased drug resistance, virulence, or host range could be generated by these innate capabilities.

title: Fast genomic read alignment with minibwa
abstract: Abstract  Motivation BWA-MEM remains a popular short-read mapper especially for the purpose of variant calling. Several groups have accelerated this algorithm as it has been the performance bottleneck of many current workflows. However, constrained by the original design, these drop-in replacements could only achieve limited speedup. Breaking changes to BWA-MEM are required for further improvement. Results We developed minibwa for aligning short and accurate long reads against a reference genome. It combines BWA-MEM variable-length seeding with minimap2 chaining and base alignment. It speeds up BWA-MEM2 further with additional prefetch for seeding, new heuristics to skip unnecessary mate rescue and reduced effort in highly repetitive regions where reads would anyway be wrongly mapped due to structural changes. Minibwa is about four times as fast as BWA-MEM and over twice as fast as BWA-MEM2 at comparable accuracy. It also natively supports directional bisulfite sequencing data to high mapping accuracy. Availability and implementation  https://github.com/lh3/minibwa

title: Bridging Graph and Pairwise Learning for Gene Regulatory Network Inference from scRNA-seq Data
abstract: Abstract  Motivation Gene regulatory networks (GRNs) capture the underlying interactions through which transcription factors (TFs) regulate genes. Based on gene expression data, existing GRN inference approaches generally fall into two categories: graph-based methods, which model the GRN as a whole graph, and pairwise-based methods, which decompose the GRN into individual TF–target gene pairs for modeling. However, each approach exhibits limitations that are precisely the strengths of its counterpart. Graph-based methods tend to overfit due to their reliance on a single training graph, whereas pairwise-based methods benefit from abundant TF–target training pairs. In contrast, pairwise-based methods overlook the global topological structure, which is essential for comprehensively capturing regulatory mechanisms. Results To address these limitations, we propose  scGPL , an end-to-end unified framework that jointly models global regulatory topology and local interactions.  scGPL  extracts macro-level features from the global regulatory graph and introduces a dynamic, importance-guided subgraph sampling mechanism to capture fine-grained local dependencies. By fusing global representations with subgraph-enhanced local features, our framework bridges the gap between the two paradigms, incorporating essential whole-graph topological dependencies while retaining the data abundance advantage of pairwise methods. Extensive experiments on seven benchmark datasets demonstrate that  scGPL  consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance, with up to 13.7% improvement over the strongest baseline, validating the effectiveness of our integrative design. Availability and implementation The source code is maintained on GitHub ( https://github.com/talent-hang/scGPL ), and the datasets and versioned releases are archived at  https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21608485  for reproducibility.

Redox dialogue: a transkingdom cysteine code at the plant–pathogen interface
abstract: Reactive oxygen species (ROS), nitric oxide (NO), and hydrogen sulfide (H2S) are canonical weapons of plant immunity. We argue that their most consequential role at the plant–pathogen interface is informational: reversible cysteine oxidation—S-sulfenylation, S-nitrosylation, S-persulfidation, and S-glutathionylation—is a chemical alphabet that both kingdoms read. We formalize this as the transkingdom cysteine code (TCC), a heuristic whose grammar comprises signal-generating enzymes, sensor proteins, and erasers on both sides of the interface, and whose candidate memory layer links redox state to chromatin regulation.

abstract: Zeng et al. demonstrate that vagus nerve stimulation alleviates epilepsy by regulating gut microbiota and butyrate production and trafficking via the gut-brain axis. This study clarifies the microbiota-dependent mechanism of vagus nerve stimulation and informs therapeutic target exploration for epilepsy.

title: Drought tolerance-enhancing fungal pathogens reprogram plant cell identity through mRNA turnover
abstract: Subieta et al. find that the fungal pathogen Verticillium deploys the effector TRADE to reprogram plant cell identity. By targeting the mRNA turnover factor VARICOSE and promoting its phosphorylation, TRADE stabilizes transcripts regulating vascular differentiation, triggering the conversion of differentiated plant cells into water-conducting xylem elements.

title: A shared interbacterial membrane underlies mycobacterial cording
abstract: Cording is a century-old mycobacterial virulence trait. CryoET and light microscopy reveal that incomplete cell separation during division generates a shared interbacterial membrane. Membrane sharing provides the mechanistic basis for cording, an explanation for mechanical resilience, and a new picture of the mycomembrane in supracellular architectures distinct from planktonic bacteria.

title: Cardiomyocyte-derived circulating extracellular vesicles enable a non-invasive liquid biopsy of human myocardium
abstract: This study develops an approach to selectively capture cardiomyocyte-derived circulating extracellular vesicles (cardiovesicles) from plasma. Cardiovesicle RNAs dynamically track disease-specific cardiomyocyte transcriptional states and reflect genetic liability for cardiovascular disease, providing a non-invasive window into the molecular state of the human heart, suggesting a path toward personalized cardiovascular medicine.

title: Asymmetric Visible‐to‐Near‐Infrared Absorption Responses of Nickel Dithiolene Complexes Induced by Ambipolar Charge Injection
abstract:
d/π-Conjugated nickel dithiolene complexes exhibit redox-driven multi-step tailoring of their visible-to-near-infrared absorption profiles. The single molecular framework displays asymmetric optical responses, with shifts spanning over 350 nm, depending on the direction of charge injection. This striking asymmetry may originate from the spatially distinct frontier orbitals, namely a metal–ligand delocalized d–π hybridized LUMO and a ligand-localized HOMO.

 
 
 ABSTRACT 
 Potential-induced modulation of visible-to-near-infrared (Vis–NIR) absorption using single-component molecules remains challenging, as conventional extended π-conjugated systems suffer from aggregation-induced poor solubility and elevated HOMO levels that cause ambient chemical degradation. Here, we demonstrate versatile and multi-step optical tailoring using ambipolar d/π-conjugated nickel dithiolene complexes,  Ni(4OR ). In situ spectroelectrochemistry across three redox states reveals highly distinct, asymmetric optical responses spanning >350 nm: electron injection induces a continuous red-shift, whereas hole injection abruptly reconstructs the electronic excitation profile. This striking asymmetry originates from the spatially distinct frontier orbitals—a metal–ligand delocalized d–π hybridized LUMO and a ligand-localized HOMO. Furthermore, to prevent the diffusional dissipation of the generated redox species in solution, this electronic state modulation was extended to the solid phase to realize steady electronic states: a synthetic approach yielded pure, stoichiometric radical anion salts, while solid-state charge-transfer complexation with F 4 TCNQ successfully captured the radical cationic species. Finally, the Ni-to-Pd substitution further narrowed the energy gap to 0.77 eV, shifting the NIR absorption maximum up to 1342 nm. These results demonstrate that our ambipolar molecular system serves as a versatile single-component platform, establishing a powerful paradigm for broad-band absorption tailoring within a single molecule.

title: Targeting the YAP‐BST2 Axis Overcomes Intrinsic Anti‐PD‐1 Resistance in Metastatic Gastric Cancer (Adv. Sci. 65/2026)
abstract:
Targeting BST2 Overcomes Immunotherapy Resistance  
 In their Research Article (DOI:  10.1002/advs.77708 ), Yan Meng, Shi Jiao, Zhaocai Zhou, and co-workers establish a faithful mouse model for clinically refractory signet-ring gastric cancer, whose malignant “magic ring” recapitulates tumor pathology. BST2 emerges as a novel immune checkpoint sustaining myeloid-driven immunosuppression. Antibody blockade–light piercing the tumor's dark shield–dismantles this barrier, reinvigorates anti-tumor immunity, and improves immunotherapy efficacy.

title: OAF Blocks SIAH1‐Mediated Degradation of SCPX, a Therapeutic Strategy for MASLD (Adv. Sci. 65/2026)
abstract:
Therapeutic Strategy for MASLD  
 The cover illustrates OAF (red) shielding SCP2 (green) in the liver. Binding SCP2 sterically blocks SIAH1 (purple) from ubiquitinating and degrading it. This maintains SCP2's lipid transport function, preventing lipid droplet accumulation and reversing fatty liver disease. More details can be found in the Research Article by Shanshan Lai, Cheng Deng, and co-workers (DOI:  10.1002/advs.77451 ).

title: Issue Information: (Adv. Sci. 65/2026)
abstract: Advanced Science, Volume 13, Issue 65, 20 November 2026.

title: SOX30 Facilitates Triple‐Negative Breast Cancer Metastasis via TNFR2–NF‐κB Signaling and Tumor Microenvironment Remodeling (Adv. Sci. 65/2026)
abstract:
SOX30 Facilitates Triple-Negative Breast Cancer Metastasis  
 SOX30 drives triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) metastasis through a dual mechanism: direct activation of the TNFR2/NF-κB signaling cascade and subsequent CCL20-mediated recruitment of tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) into the tumor microenvironment. Combined pharmacological blockade of the CCL20–CCR6 axis and TNFR2 using a CCR6 inhibitor and the TNFR2 inhibitor Etanercept synergistically and significantly suppresses metastasis in vivo, revealing a highly promising dual-targeted therapeutic strategy for TNBC. More details can be found in the Research Article by Pingping Gao, Yi Zhang, Fei Han, Xiaowei Qi, and co-workers (DOI:  10.1002/advs.77690 ).

title: Dual Repression by IPA1 Fine‐Tunes OsbZIP79‐Mediated Salt Tolerance in Rice (Adv. Sci. 65/2026)
abstract:
Breaking Dual Reins: Conquering Salt in Rice  
 Drawing on the Chinese idiom “Mǎ Dào Chéng Gōng” (achieve victory upon the horse's arrival), the cover depicts the wild horse OsbZIP79 snapping IPA1's dual reins at the onset of salt stress, then galloping forward to confer salt tolerance on rice. The pun of “rice” (Dào) replacing “arrive” (Dào) heralds the crop's triumph over salinity. More details can be found in the Research Article by Conghe Zhang, Qingyao Shu, Meng Jiang, and co-workers (DOI:  10.1002/advs.77806 ).

title: Gestational Hypoxia Disrupts Medial Ganglionic Eminence Progenitor Dynamics and Interneuron Development in Schizophrenia (Adv. Sci. 65/2026)
abstract:
Schizophrenia  
 Two lotus leaves depict divergent interneuron development. The left leaf, rooted in a short rhizome in deep mud, represents gestational hypoxia and a shortened progenitor cell cycle. Premature unfurling damages the leaf as it pushes through the mud, while dew droplets symbolize NAC-mediated rescue. More details can be found in the Research Article by Sangmi Chung, Fan Guo, Tao Li, and co-authors (DOI:  10.1002/advs.76936 ).

title: Modular Metamaterials for Adaptable MRI Signal Control: Combining Dipole Array With a New Hexagon‐Based Artificial Dielectrics (Adv. Sci. 65/2026)
abstract:
Modular Metamaterials for Adaptable MRI Signal Control  
 Seeking to improve MRI quality, this cover presents a hexagonally packed artificial dielectric combined with a tunable dipole array for RF field shaping. The thin, flexible platform enables high effective permittivity, reconfigurable responses, and patient-specific RF enhancement across anatomies and imaging conditions. More details can be found in the Research Article by Santosh Kumar Maurya, Ilan Goldberg, and Rita Schmidt (DOI:  10.1002/advs.77378 ).

title: Materials‐based Design and Multi‐Criteria Selection of High‐entropy Alloys for Concentrated Solar Power Plants
abstract:
This study examines high-entropy alloys as advanced materials for improving the durability of thermal energy storage tanks in concentrated solar power plants. Using a database and a multi-criteria selection process, it identifies alloys and coatings with superior mechanical strength, corrosion resistance and wear resistance, whilst highlighting the challenges related to cost and sustainability in scaling up production.

 
 
 ABSTRACT 
 Currently, thermal energy storage (TES) systems are a key component of concentrated solar power (CSP) plants. However, their long-term performance is limited by the degradation of tank materials due to high-temperature corrosion. This study analyses high-entropy alloys (HEAs) as potential candidates for extending the service life of these tanks. For this purpose, a comprehensive database was compiled containing over 1900 materials in bulk and coating forms, gathering data on their physical, mechanical, wear-resistance and corrosion-resistance properties. Using a materials selection approach, three material indexes were proposed for the system: one focused on mechanical strength (M 1 ), another on corrosion resistance (M 2 ), and a third on wear resistance (M 3 ), enabling the selection of materials with optimal overall durability performance (M global ). The results indicated that certain HEAs, in particular the AlCoCrFeNi and CoCrFeNi families, as well as certain deposition techniques (CGS, HVAF, laser cladding), perform better than conventional stainless steels in terms of combined behavior (mechanical, corrosion and wear resistance). However, high costs and dependence on critical raw materials remain obstacles to their industrial implementation. Therefore, strategies are also proposed to produce more sustainable and competitive HEAs, including element substitution, recycling of secondary materials, and reinforcement with industrial by-products. The results demonstrate the potential of database-assisted material selection as a guide for the development of advanced alloys for TES applications.

title: Multiscale superinformation reveals structured organization of genomic sequence features
abstract: Genomic sequence organization varies across spatial scales, but sequence complexity measures are often evaluated at a single resolution. Superinformation (SI), introduced by Bose and Chouhan, measures heterogeneity in local sequence entropy by taking the entropy of the distribution of block-level Shannon entropy values. We characterize SI across 14 Sequence Ontology-defined genomic feature classes in seven species and seven block sizes from 20 to 200 bp. SI profiles were non-increasing for 72 of 86 evaluable species-feature combinations, although this pattern was not universal. Observed SI generally exceeded both a block-count-controlled random null and a species-level GC-controlled null. Associations with mononucleotide entropy, dinucleotide entropy, and GC content were modest, with no individual descriptor explaining more than 10.4% of the observed variation. For the 13 complete feature-level profiles used in geometric analysis, the first two principal components explained 97.859% of the variance, and hierarchical clustering grouped features with similar SI trajectories. We also summarize the profiles using the Characteristic Information Scale and Information Persistence Score. These analyses extend the original superinformation framework to a comparative, multiscale analysis of genomic feature heterogeneity while keeping the interpretation of SI limited to the sequence properties measured here.

title: A stop codon shared by all Gyps vultures, including the three Critically Endangered species of South Asia, lies in a coding exon of the bird gene CYP2C45
abstract: Veterinary diclofenac devastated three South Asian Gyps vultures, but the basis of their sensitivity is unclear. A stop codon reported in a Cape vulture P450 gene, described as CYP2C19 in a retained intron, was re-examined with public data: 45 genome assemblies, raw reads of seven Gyps birds and a liver transcriptome. The gene is the bird CYP2C45, without a one-to-one human orthologue. The stop (codon 338, CGA[->]TGA) lies in coding exon 7; the intron is spliced normally, the mRNA carries the stop, and the truncated protein lacks the haem-binding cysteine. The stop was found in all eight living Gyps species, homozygous wherever testable, and in none of 27 other raptors, including two killed by diclofenac. It arose once, 1.5-10.6 million years ago on the Gyps stem, and the gene has since evolved near-neutrally. This genus-wide loss marks Gyps vulnerability but cannot explain diclofenac deaths in other raptors.

title: TrailMix: Mixture Proportion and Placement Estimation of Ancient Hominin mtDNA Samples using a Pangenomic Reference
abstract: Hominin mitochondrial DNA extracted from sediments or ancient environments is sometimes a mixture of multiple contributing sources. Researchers must subsequently computationally identify from which mitochondrial lineages the DNA sequences comes (e.g. Denisovan vs. modern human superhaplogroup) and ideally, quantify their abundance. Bioinformatics approaches described in the literature to achieve this involve in-house scripts or heuristics applied to tools designed for other datasets. However, such approaches have neither been fully tested nor do they provide credible intervals on model parameters. To address this, we introduce TrailMix, a C++ program for estimating contributing mixture proportions as well as individual source placements on the hominin mitochondrial tree for ancient environmental DNA. Using a pangenome reference graph to mitigate reference-related bias, TrailMix works well to accurately deconvolve mixtures of multiple mitochondrial lineages and place each contributor within its respective phylogenetic context. Crucially, it allows users to place minor contributing sources on the tree even on ancestral nodes without needing to reach consensus in the presence of multiple sources. TrailMix is part of the vgan suite of tools and is available at https://github.com/grenaud/vgan.

title: Genomic foundation models and complementary variant-scoring strategies in LGMD-associated genes: architecture, adaptation, and sequence context
abstract: Genomic foundation models learn representations from DNA sequence, although their usefulness for variant classification depends on the architecture and downstream evaluation procedure. We compared six genomic foundation models using 6,960 ClinVar single-nucleotide variants from ten limb-girdle muscular dystrophy (LGMD)-associated genes, with 4,866 variants assigned to training and 2,094 to held-out testing. The analyses included frozen alternate-minus-reference embeddings at 101, 201 and 501 bp, supervised adaptation at 101 bp, and gene-held-out downstream classifier training. GPN-Star V100 and AlphaGenome Atlas AVI were evaluated separately using their native scores. At 101 bp, frozen Evo2 achieved the highest discrimination among the six foundation models (MCC 0.644; AUROC 0.879; AUPRC 0.818). Supervised adaptation increased MCC for three architectures and reduced it for the remaining three. Extending sequence context to 501 bp improved all three primary metrics in five of six frozen architectures, with Evo2 reaching an MCC of 0.864, AUROC of 0.964 and AUPRC of 0.952. Evo2 also led the frozen gene-held-out readouts (pooled MCC 0.641; AUROC 0.852; AUPRC 0.789). GPN-Star V100 and AVI achieved MCC values of 0.929 and 0.938, respectively, using distinct biological inputs and scoring procedures. The number of variants misclassified across all evaluated configurations decreased from five under the original 101-bp readouts to one after including longer contexts and native scores. An exploratory HGVS-category control identified substantial annotation-associated structure in the benchmark labels. The findings characterize classification performance against aggregate ClinVar labels within LGMD-associated genes. Disease-specific pathogenicity and clinical diagnostic utility remain untested.

title: deeprok: highly accurate prokaryotic gene prediction through deep learning and overlap-aware decoding
abstract: Prokaryotic gene prediction is often considered solved, yet widely used tools still disagree on many genes, chiefly short genes and translation starts. We present deeprok, an ab initio prokaryotic gene prediction method that combines a base-level neural network with an overlap-aware decoder, and refines start-site predictions with a self-trained neural ranker. On four curated genomes distant from its training data, deeprok made 10-18% fewer exact-match errors than Prodigal and GeneMarkS-2, and on 2,925 experimentally verified starts it made 21-41% fewer start errors. Furthermore, deeprok's base-level architecture reveals lineage-specific translation initiation signals. These results show that per-base deep learning combined with overlap-aware decoding can improve prokaryotic gene prediction, especially for resolving translation starts.

title: Zero-shot virtual knock-out rankings do not recover causal genes from observational single-cell data
abstract: Background: Virtual knock-out methods rank genes by the change predicted after deleting one gene in silico and nominate targets without perturbation data. That use assumes the ranking reflects the causal consequence of removal; we tested it for three zero-shot methods in four configurations under one criterion. Results: We compared scTenifoldKnk (R and Python), CellOracle and Geneformer on 438 real, 3,585 synthetic and 330 DepMap knock-outs. Top-20 lists of different knock-outs overlapped by a median of 12 to 14 of 20, against 0.08 by chance. Displacement followed out-degree (R^2 = 0.825; 0.852 with six further features). Decoupling causal effect from topology left criterion value and grade unchanged (36 of 36 RED). For scTenifoldKnk, the ranking showed no evidence of recovery above chance where causal genes were planted (AUROC 0.538 and 0.528 in the two constructions). CellOracle's displacement showed no detectable relation to the data-built network (rho = -0.212, P = 0.556). Geneformer's shift tracked token coverage inconsistently (+0.41, +0.40, -0.27). Against DepMap essentiality, scTenifoldKnk's Python implementation (scTenifoldpy 0.5.1) reached AUROC 0.459 (95% CI 0.357-0.566), not distinguishable from chance; detection rate reached 0.588 (95% CI 0.497-0.677). Conclusions: For scTenifoldKnk and CellOracle, the ranking reports network properties, not the causal consequence of removal. No measured structural feature accounted for more than a small fraction of Geneformer's shift. Detection rate, needing no network, gained +0.129 (95% CI 0.0017-0.2543; 97.6% of resamples positive) over the tool.

title: How predictable is an individual's DNA methylation?
abstract: DNA methylation is largely shared among individuals of the same cell type, yet at specific genomic sites it differs substantially between individuals. Methods that predict methylation are usually evaluated by their accuracy over all sites. Because methylation at most sites is shared, this accuracy cannot show whether a method predicts an individual's methylation where individuals differ. We present individual-level methylation prediction at sites where individuals differ as a new challenge. Given the reference genome sequence, the methylation of other individuals of the same cell type, and measurements at some sites of a target individual, but not the individual's genotype, the task is to predict the target individual's methylation class (unmethylated, intermediate, or methylated) at the remaining sites. We evaluate predictions separately at sites with low and high variation across individuals. We compare four approaches: the average of other individuals, a sequence model (the DNA language model Nucleotide Transformer) fine-tuned on other individuals' methylation, the same model further fine-tuned on the target individual's measurements, and a local class-average approach using the target individual's nearby training-site class labels. Across 32 individuals from six human cell types, the average of other individuals matched or slightly exceeded both sequence models at sites with low variation among individuals. At the most variable sites, the average of other individuals performed worse than a random predictor that assigns classes at the observed class frequencies, whereas both sequence models performed substantially better than the average. Both sequence models also achieved higher mean weighted F1 than the local class-average approach. Fine-tuning on the target individual's measurements improved predictions more inside regions where other individuals show bimodal methylation (a mix of methylated and unmethylated DNA molecules within one sample) than outside them. Among the most variable sites, it also improved predictions at CpG islands for 25 of the 32 individuals. We conclude that individual-level methylation prediction is a distinct problem that is particularly challenging at sites where individuals differ, and that the benefit of an individual's own measurements is concentrated in genomic contexts identifiable from other individuals' methylation and genomic annotations.

title: BASIN: Background-Anchored Signal Normalization with Integrated Quality Control for CUT&RUN and CUT&Tag
abstract: Quantitative comparison of CUT&RUN and CUT&Tag datasets is complicated when a perturbation changes the global abundance of the profiled chromatin feature or when there is substantial variability between replicates. Read-depth normalization removes global differences by design, whereas exogenous spike-in normalization can introduce substantial technical variability. We developed Background-Anchored SIgnal Normalization (BASIN), an endogenous-reference framework that exploits recurrent, peak-like background in IgG controls as a quantitative internal reference. BASIN Anchor Regions (BARs) act as reproducible read sinks whose representation rises as specific signal falls, allowing global differences to be inferred from the balance between specific and nonspecific reads. BASIN comprises three pipelines: OVERTURE identifies and evaluates BAR panels, HARMONY derives and applies robust sample-specific scale factors from trimmed BAR signal, and CODA determines whether the assumptions supporting normalization are satisfied. BASIN provides a validated, ready-to-use universal BAR panel for Drosophila melanogaster, and the OVERTURE pipeline enables BAR panel development in other organisms. We tested BASIN against independent expectations and compared its performance with spike-in normalization. BASIN remained quantitatively stable across a >100-fold cell-input titration and detected global depletion of H3K36me3 in Set2 mutants that read-depth normalization concealed. BASIN also preserved expected H3K9me3 differences even when target signal overlapped anchor regions. Applied to a variety of profiling experiments, CODA distinguished normalization failures arising from both biological and technical causes. BASIN thus converts reproducible background from a nuisance signal into an internal reference standard, enabling spike-in-free quantification of global chromatin changes while providing an explicit framework to test when and why that normalization can or cannot be trusted.

title: Cortical neurons accumulate point mutations at similar rates in mice and humans
abstract: Across vertebrate species, it has long been known that germline mutation rates per year are inversely proportional to reproductive ages. A similar pattern was recently reported in mammals for mutations in colonic epithelium, leading to speculation that this inter-species scaling may apply to many cell types. We tested whether a similar relationship holds in postmitotic cells, by estimating point mutation rates in mouse cortical neurons from PacBio HiFi circular consensus sequencing data. Our analysis revealed a significant effect of age on the number of point mutations, of 25.9 mutations per diploid genome per year (95% CI: [17.7, 34.1]). This rate is comparable to the one reported for human neurons, indicating that somatic rates need not scale with lifespan. Our findings further demonstrate that a readily available sequencing method can be used to reliably identify somatic mutations at single-cell resolution.

title: Deciphering state bridges via a single-cell large language model
abstract: Large-scale single-cell transcriptomic data provide a new avenue for precision medicine by uncovering cellular heterogeneity. However, systematic comparison of remodeling patterns across various biological states remains unavailable. Here, we first developed a computational framework based on a foundation model of single cell biology, Universal Cell Embedding (UCE), to harmonize annotations comprising 36 cell types. Based on an integrated dataset of single cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) with 8,789 human samples comprising more than 59 million cells or nuclei across 614 biological states, we then embedded each state with a 36-dimensional vector in a unified space of cell-composition change and further deciphered states bridges by analyzing the relationships among the 614 state vectors. As a result, 22,161 significant bridges (P < 0.05) between the 614 states were revealed. Moreover, we successfully identified a number of well-known bridges such as bridge between Alzheimer's disease and Parkinson's disease (P = 2.21e-15), suggesting the effectiveness of the proposed framework. More importantly, we uncovered a number of new bridges. Furthermore, analyses of the number of changed cell types (NCC) and Shannon entropy revealed heterogeneous and tissue-dependent patterns of cellular composition remodeling. This study provides a new strategy for identifying disease associations and potential therapeutic relationships by deciphering bridges between biological states from scRNA-seq landscape.

title: Genomic Characterisation of the Irish Traditional BoRiabhach Cattle Breed
abstract: The BoRiabhach is a highly endangered traditional landrace cattle breed in Ireland with a culturally significant history. The Irish Gaelic word "riabhach" means "streaked", "striped", or "brindled", and a distinctive brindle coat colour pattern is characteristic of the BoRiabhach breed. The breed had declined to about 20 animals by 2016 and has no systematic pedigree. Despite conservation efforts that have increased the population to an estimated 70 animals, the breed remains one of Europe's most critically endangered livestock genetic resources. We present the first genomic characterisation of the BoRiabhach breed, using Illumina BovineSNP50 genotypes of 84 BoRiabhach animals and 688 cattle from 28 European comparator breeds. Using model-based clustering, we identified a BoRiabhach-specific ancestry component. Only 28 animals carried more than 50% of this component, which we term "high-BRBH"; the remaining 56 showed extensive introgression, chiefly from Limousin and Holstein, which explains the breed's high observed heterozygosity. Phylogenetic analysis placed the high-BRBH cohort with British Shorthorn and Lincoln Red within a British-Irish clade, distinct from Kerry and Dexter, and recovered a Limousin-to-BoRiabhach migration edge. This high-BRBH core group exhibited the lowest effective population size (Ne) of any adequately sampled breed and consists of closely related animals: 34% of pairs within the core were second-degree relatives or closer. Conservation of the BoRiabhach must therefore balance breed distinctiveness with genetic diversity. We recommend genotyping all extant animals, recording genomic ancestry at registration, managing mating based on genomic relatedness as well as ancestry, and cryopreserving germplasm from the high-BRBH core population.

title: Identification of eukaryotes as a bycatch in global microbiome data
abstract: Eukaryotes shape microbiomes as macroscopic hosts, microscopic community members, and food sources, yet the diversity and ecological significance of microbial eukaryotes remain poorly resolved. Here, we present metaEukaryome, an organelle genome-centered framework for detection of eukaryotes in metagenomic data that leverages mitochondrial and plastid sequences as robust signatures of presence. Applying metaEukaryome to 75,727 metagenomic samples collected across the globe reveals strong environment-specific patterns in the prevalence of detected eukaryotes. Integrating eukaryotic and prokaryotic profiles further reveals recurrent cross-domain co-occurrence and symbiosis in the human gut. In particular, Blastocystis is associated with metabolically reduced, uncultured bacterial clades, including Candidatus Borkfalkia and CAG-345, whose DNA and RNA are detected in a Blastocystis culture previously reported as axenic. Their complementary metabolic repertoires further support a candidate symbiotic relationship. These findings imply that more novel (endo-)symbionts of gut protists can be discovered by reanalysing existing data.

title: Unsupervised tensor integration of hippocampal and colonic multi-omics reveals enteric neural signatures in cognitive aging
abstract: Background: Molecular changes in peripheral tissues may provide insights into cognitive aging, but identifying relevant genes without using behavioral outcomes for feature selection remains challenging. Results: We applied tensor decomposition-based unsupervised feature extraction to publicly available hippocampal and colonic transcriptomic and promoter DNA methylation profiles from mice across five age groups. A tensor comprising tissue, molecular modality, age group, biological replicate, and gene dimensions was constructed using 16,080 shared genes. Higher-order singular value decomposition identified a component with a monotonic age pattern, shared tissue contributions, and opposing transcriptomic and methylation contributions. This component yielded 1,577 selected genes without using cognitive scores for feature selection. The corresponding colonic methylation score correlated with overall cognition (r=0.589; Benjamini--Hochberg-adjusted P=9.87 x10-7), although no significant associations remained after age adjustment. The selected genes were enriched for enteric neuronal and glial markers derived from a published single-cell atlas, with 5.10-fold and 4.65-fold enrichment, respectively. Comparison with the broadest available Boruta-selected gene set identified only 64 overlapping genes, leaving 1,513 genes selected exclusively by the tensor approach in this comparison. These remaining genes retained significant enrichment for synaptic processes and enteric neuronal and glial signatures using library-specific backgrounds. Conclusions: Unsupervised tensor integration recovered an aging-associated relationship between colonic methylation and cognition while identifying a largely distinct set of functionally coherent candidate genes. These findings complement supervised feature selection and provide candidates for investigating enteric neural involvement in cognitive aging, without establishing an age-independent association or a causal gut-to-brain mechanism.

title: The IGVF Catalog Knowledge Graph
abstract: The Impact of Genomic Variation on Function (IGVF) consortium is systematically characterizing how genomic variation influences regulatory elements, gene expression, and human phenotypes through thousands of experimental mapping and perturbation datasets alongside predictive models. To synthesize these diverse results into quantitative relationships and situate them within established biological knowledge, we developed the IGVF Catalog, a large-scale knowledge graph. Implemented in ArangoDB using schema-validated JSON records. Version 1.3 encompasses nearly 3 billion nodes across 14 entity types (including variants, coding variants, genomic elements, genes, transcripts, proteins, pathways, and ontology graphs for biosamples and phenotypes) connected by more than 8.6 billion edges across 31 relationship types. Edges encode statistical significance, effect sizes, source provenance, and biological context via ontology-linked hyperedges. The Catalog integrates 657 IGVF datasets spanning non-coding reporter and CRISPR perturbation screens (MPRA, STARR-seq, Perturb-seq), coding variant assays (VAMP-seq, SGE, MAVE, DUAL-IPA), and predictive models (scE2G, SEMVAR, cV2F, TLAND, and BlueSTARR), unified with extensive public context including GENCODE annotations, FAVOR and dbSNP variants, TopLD linkage disequilibrium, GWAS, QTLs, and protein interactions. Users can interrogate the Catalog through a web portal (https://igvf.catalog.org) Python and R clients, an OpenAPI-documented API featuring 86 endpoints supporting identifier and genomic-region queries, and a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server enabling agent-assisted querying with large language models. We demonstrate the Catalog's utility for mechanistic interpretation across three case studies: resolving a FOXA1-dependent enhancer variant (rs11257655) regulating CAMK1D at a type 2 diabetes locus, distinguishing coding (GCKR rs1260326) and regulatory (HNF1A rs1169289) mechanisms for liver traits, and linking vascular CRISPRi-perturbed elements to CDKN2A/CDKN2B and NOS3 in coronary artery disease. Updated quarterly with open data and software, the IGVF Catalog provides a scalable resource for variant-to-function discovery.

title: SCOPE: Gaussian-regularized graph learning for enzyme catalytic residue prediction
abstract: Accurate identification of catalytic residues is central to understanding enzyme mechanisms and engineering biocatalysts, yet annotation remains challenging because experimentally validated sites are sparse. Here, we present SCOPE, a graph learning framework for catalytic residue prediction that integrates evolutionary, physicochemical, and three-dimensional structural information at the residue level. SCOPE represents enzymes as residue-level structural graphs and incorporates a Gaussian auxiliary training objective that aggregates structure-aware representations along sequence order. Evaluations across five benchmark datasets, CATH family-disjoint retraining and the external CataloDB benchmark assess predictive performance and generalization. Structural analyses associate complete catalytic-residue recovery with compact active-site arrangements. We further validated SCOPE prospectively across four enzymes using site-directed mutagenesis and activity assays, confirming multiple predicted residues as functionally important. These results support SCOPE as a framework for catalytic residue annotation and prioritizing functional sites for experimental investigation.

title: Transposon-driven pervasive genome restructuring and regulatory evolution in early-diverging Holomycota
abstract: Early-diverging non-Dikarya fungi showcase major evolutionary transitions in the fungal kingdom, share features with other eukaryotic clades and bacteria, and include pathogens of significant concern. These lineages contain some of the most reduced and expanded genome architectures of the fungal kingdom and have adopted unique DNA methylation systems. Yet, the evolutionary trajectory of early-diverging non-Dikarya fungi remains poorly understood. A key driver is thought to be transposable elements, which shape genomic plasticity, organization and regulation. Here, we perform a comprehensive comparative analysis across the Holomycota to chart drivers of early fungal evolution. We demonstrate that contrasting transposon dynamics directly shape genomic diversity across these lineages, fueling extensive protein domain expansions through widespread co-option. This heterogeneous landscape is regulated by a multi-layered epigenetic network impacting chromatin configuration, and we reveal a distinct transcriptional activation role for adenine methylation over specific transposons. Beyond driving functional innovation, mobile elements serve as a source of regulatory diversification, providing transcription factor binding sites at key chromosomal features. Furthermore, synteny tracking uncovers multiple whole-genome duplication events across Mucoromycotina, where DNA transposons preferentially accumulate at duplication breakpoints and undergo rapid inactivation. Strikingly, we also show that horizontal transposon transfers frequently cross deep evolutionary boundaries, including cross-kingdom exchanges with protists. Together, our findings illuminate key drivers of genome architecture in non-Dikarya fungi and reshape our understanding of genome dynamics across the fungal kingdom.

title: Dependence-Aware Conformal Prediction for 3D Uncertainty Quantification in Molecular Docking
abstract: Molecular docking plays a critical role in drug discovery by predicting three-dimensional (3D) binding poses of small molecules within proteins. However, docking predictions can contain substantial positional errors, making reliable uncertainty quantification essential. Conformal prediction (CP) provides a principled framework for uncertainty quantification, yet constructing compact 3D prediction regions with reliable joint coverage remains challenging due to heterogeneous atomic errors, dependence among spatial coordinates, and distribution shifts. We develop a dependence-aware CP framework for molecular docking that leverages a shared graph neural network (GNN) to estimate adaptive, asymmetric uncertainty intervals using local atomic and global molecular information. Copula-based joint calibration accounts for dependence among coordinate-wise nonconformity scores to construct compact 3D prediction boxes. We further introduce density ratio estimation (DRE) to adapt calibration under distribution shift. Experiments across three docking methods demonstrate that our approach reduces median prediction-box volumes by 37.40%, 95.00%, and 39.16% for AutoDock Vina, Protenix, and MedusaGraph, respectively, compared with a state-of-the-art CP baseline, while achieving empirical joint coverage close to the 90% target. Under the Molecular Group Split and controlled distribution shifts, DRE further reduces coverage deviations, highlighting the potential of dependence-aware and shift-adaptive calibration for reliable 3D molecular docking uncertainty quantification.

title: Genomics of the diversification of Heliconius cydno (Lepidoptera: Nymphalidae) in northern South America: geographic and phenotypic patterns
abstract: The interplay between natural selection, gene flow, and geography is a key driver of population differentiation. This study investigates their influence on the recent adaptive radiation of Heliconius cydno, a mimetic and aposematic butterfly with striking variation in wing color pattern across its distribution in Central and northern South America. The genetic basis of this phenotypic diversity has a modular architecture, whereby a few key genes and cis-regulatory elements control differences among morphotypes. Using whole-genome sequences from 133 individuals representing all subspecies of H. cydno, we investigated (1) the role of Andean orogeny in its diversification and (2) the genetic basis of the variation in the hindwing white submarginal band, which to date, had remained unknown. First, we found that five of the fourteen described subspecies correspond to distinct monophyletic lineages and well-defined genetic clusters that originated in northwestern South America and later expanded into Central America and the Colombian inter-Andean valleys. Second, we observed signatures of genetic structure that were consistent with geographic patterns, particularly those associated with the inter-Andean region and Gorgona Island. Third, we identified ivory:mir-193 as the locus underlying variation in the white submarginal band on the hindwing. We also detected evidence of introgression suggesting that this trait was likely transferred from H. cydno to H. melpomene, contributing to the establishment of a novel mimicry ring with H. erato. Altogether, these findings highlight the roles of geography, genomic architecture, and introgression in the diversification of H. cydno.

title: NanoHIV-DR: a Nextflow workflow for consensus and read level HIV-1 drug resistance profiling from Oxford Nanopore sequencing
abstract: Oxford Nanopore sequencing offers a rapid and portable approach for HIV-1 drug resistance (HIVDR) genotyping, but analysis of the resulting long-read data requires multiple bioinformatics steps and currently available nanopore workflows are limited. We developed NanoHIV-DR, a Nextflow-based workflow that streamlines the analysis of Oxford Nanopore sequencing data and generation of HIVDR reports. NanoHIV-DR processes raw POD5 files through basecalling, demultiplexing, host-read removal, quality filtering, read alignment and consensus generation, before identifying resistance-associated mutations and interpreting predicted drug susceptibility. The workflow provides two complementary approaches to HIVDR analysis: consensus-based resistance interpretation using Sierra and read-level detection of resistance-associated variants, enabling mutations below the consensus level to be identified and quantified. Outputs are integrated with clinical metadata to generate human-readable HIVDR reports. NanoHIV-DR provides a reproducible and accessible workflow for Nanopore-based HIVDR analysis with reduced bioinformatics expertise and manual processing for translating long-read sequencing data into interpretable resistance profiles.

title: Population-level learning of non-additive effects enables accurate and efficient prediction of combinatorial perturbation responses
abstract: Combinatorial perturbations are widely used to study genetic interactions and to develop drug combinations, but the number of possible combinations grows quadratically with the number of perturbations, and only a small fraction can be measured in a screen experiment. Despite their growing sophistication, deep-learning and foundation models often fail to outperform a simple additive baseline based on measured single-perturbation responses. This suggests a simpler approach that builds on these measurements and directly learns deviations from additivity at the population level. We therefore developed GAIN, a lightweight model that implements these principles by predicting the pseudobulk response to a combination as the sum of its two single-perturbation responses and a learned interaction term. Across three single-cell datasets of genetic and drug combinations, GAIN corrected deviations from additivity and outperformed the additive model and cell-level methods across generalization settings and metrics, while training 3- to 64-fold faster. Applied to a combinatorial CRISPR screen of leukemia differentiation regulators, GAIN revealed synergy between key regulators of the differentiation block and genes that restrain differentiation but have little effect alone. It also revealed dampening by the histone chaperone FACT, which supports the induction of differentiation genes. These results establish population-level modeling of the deviation from additivity as a simple, accurate and scalable approach to predicting combination responses.

title: Machine learning prediction of antimicrobial resistance in respiratory metagenomes
abstract: Background: Targeted therapy for patients with suspected respiratory infections traditionally requires bacterial culture followed by phenotypic antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST), a process that can take up to 5 days. In acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), delays in identifying the causative pathogen and its resistance profile may be especially harmful because patients are critically ill and often receive broad-spectrum empiric antibiotics. The growing burden of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) further complicates clinical decision-making by reducing effective treatment options and increasing the risk of inadequate initial therapy. Culture-free, AI-driven computational metagenomic strategies have the potential to drastically shorten this window, enabling more rapid targeted therapy prescription. To show the feasibility of such approaches, we develop a proof-of-concept framework based on clinical metagenomics. Methods: We simulated respiratory metagenomes using real-world bacterial genomes with associated antimicrobial susceptibility phenotypes. Each simulated metagenome contained a fixed commensal background and one clinically important respiratory pathogen, Acinetobacter baumannii, Klebsiella pneumoniae, or Pseudomonas aeruginosa, at 5% or 10% bacterial read abundance. Realistic reads were simulated for Oxford Nanopore, PacBio, and Illumina sequencing platforms. Random Forest (RF) classifiers were trained and evaluated using five-fold, strain-grouped cross-validation with fold-specific {chi}2-ranked 13-mer features. ResFinder and KARGA were included as reference-based metagenomics benchmarks and evaluated using the same five held-out folds across the three sequencing platforms and two pathogen-abundance conditions. Results: RF performance varied substantially across species, antibiotics, and sequencing platforms. The strongest and most consistent results were observed for K. pneumoniae, with accuracy reaching approximately 0.96 for ceftazidime, 0.93 for amikacin, and 0.92 for ciprofloxacin. Performance for P. aeruginosa was more heterogeneous: long-read models performed well for amikacin, reaching 0.89 with PacBio and 0.88 with Nanopore, whereas Illumina performed substantially better for ciprofloxacin, ceftazidime, and levofloxacin, reaching accuracies of approximately 0.87, 0.77, and 0.70, respectively. Across most organism-antibiotic combinations, RF accuracy was numerically higher than the classification accuracies obtained with KARGA and ResFinder, which generally remained near 0.50. Increasing pathogen abundance from 5% to 10% and increasing the number of selected features from 2,500 to 5,000 generally produced modest improvements in classification accuracy, although the magnitude of improvement varied across organism-antibiotic combinations and sequencing platforms.
