Conclusions: Genome-wide k-mer machine learning can recover phenotype-associated antimicrobial resistance signals from simulated respiratory metagenomes, although performance depends strongly on the organism, antibiotic, and sequencing platform. These results represent a simulation-based proof of concept.

title: The Impact of Germ Layer Origin on the Ageing Transcriptome
abstract: Ageing is accompanied by widespread changes in gene expression, yet whether these changes share any common organisation across groups of tissues remains unclear. Adult tissues arise from three embryonic germ layers (ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm), so shared developmental lineage could influence how tissues age. Using bulk RNA-seq data from 24 GTEx tissues, we estimated age effects in each tissue with limma-voom and combined them within each germ layer by random-effects meta-analysis. Endoderm had the most significant age-associated genes (4,805), followed by mesoderm (4,520) and ectoderm (1,744), but this order reversed for genes with consistent effects across tissues of the same germ layer. These consistent genes were largely germ layer specific, although mesoderm and endoderm shared more than expected by chance. Ageing profiles were significantly more similar between tissues from the same germ layer than between tissues from different germ layers. Germ layer origin also explained 13.6% of the variation in tissue ageing profiles. Co-expression networks of ageing were organised differently in each germ layer, and 43% of enriched biological processes were specific to one germ layer. However, after grouping related processes, most functional themes were shared by all three, and genes shared between modules of different germ layers were enriched mainly for immune processes. Together, these results indicate that germ layer origin leaves a small but detectable imprint on transcriptomic ageing. However, tissue-specific and shared immune programmes are also prominent.

title: Effects of sequence splitting and negative-set selection on antimicrobial peptide prediction
abstract: Sequence partitioning and negative-set selection determine the prediction problem posed by an antimicrobial peptide (AMP) benchmark. We quantified their effects using a DRAMP 5.0 audit, controlled comparisons with frozen ESM-2 classifiers and additional benchmark configurations. On DRAMP, random splitting increased Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) from 0.718 under cluster-disjoint splitting to 0.932. This difference of 0.214 exceeded the gains from the architectural additions tested, and 75.6% of randomly assigned test sequences shared a homology cluster with training sequences. Across three additional dataset configurations, random-minus-cluster MCC differences ranged from -0.04634 to +0.05682, showing that the magnitude and direction of the split effect depended on benchmark composition. With the fitted classifiers and APD6 positives held fixed, replacing DRAMP test negatives with external hard negatives reduced the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve from 0.9833 to 0.9018 (paired difference 0.08149, bootstrap 95% CI 0.07196 to 0.09181). These comparisons quantify substantial sensitivity to evaluation design and show why split effects require assessment within each benchmark. AMPBenchAudit provides the audited records, split assignments and evaluation code needed to examine this sensitivity and interpret model comparisons under explicit test conditions.

title: Transpiling reproducibility: Multi-language implementation for the St. Nicolas House Analysis algorithm using Fusion
abstract: The integration of tools written in different programming languages is common in bioinformatics pipelines. When extending these tools, developers are required to either manually port the code or use wrapper libraries, which incurs a substantial "translation tax" on developer time. Transpilers have emerged as a potential solution, enabling the generation of algorithm implementations in multiple languages from a single source code base. However, it remains essential to establish whether transpiled code preserves both functional correctness and stochastic reproducibility across language ecosystems. In this case study, we investigated whether the Fusion language and its fut transpiler could produce functionally identical, stochastically reproducible, and high-performing code for the St. Nicolas House Analysis (SNHA) algorithm across multiple target languages. The SNHA algorithm was implemented once in Fusion and transpiled to nine target programming languages. The generated code was evaluated against reference R, Python, and Julia implementations using the clinical birthwt dataset and a 26-variable synthetic benchmark dataset evaluated over 1,000 bootstrap iterations. All nine transpiled outputs produced identical network structures to the original R implementation. With the deterministic Xorshift*64 pseudo-random number generator integrated into the algorithm, all languages generated identical bootstrapped datasets and adjacency matrices. Runtimes and memory usage spanned more than two orders of magnitude: the transpiled Python implementation achieved an 8.5-fold speedup and an 8.8-fold reduction in peak memory relative to reference Python, while compiled targets (C, C++) achieved speedups exceeding 160-fold and memory reductions up to 36-fold. These findings demonstrate that modern transpilers can eliminate cross-ecosystem translation tax while guaranteeing cross-language reproducibility in computational biology.

title: Plasma electrolyte changes can modulate post-repolarisation refractoriness in the human atrium
abstract: Changes in plasma Na+, K+ and Ca2+ levels are common in patients with chronic kidney disease or gastrointestinal disorders, or in those taking certain medications, and may promote atrial fibrillation or impair drug-induced cardioversion. Post-repolarisation refractoriness (PRR) is an established mechanism by which antiarrhythmic drugs suppress tachyarrhythmias. We investigated how changes in extracellular Na+, K+ and Ca2+ concentrations ([Na+]o, [K+]o, [Ca2+]o) modulate ionic currents and PRR in healthy and fibrotic human atrial tissue. We used a multi-scale computational framework comprising an isolated atrial myocyte, a one-dimensional atrial tissue strand, and a virtual cohort of 14 left atrial digital twins, combined with Gaussian process emulators and variance-based global sensitivity analysis. Changes in [K+]o strongly modulated PRR by altering the inward rectifier K+ current (IK1), shifting the resting potential and thereby regulating Na+-current availability. In contrast, [Na+]o had only a weak effect on PRR, mediated primarily through the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger, and [Ca2+]o had a negligible effect. Tissue PRR was more sensitive to electrolyte changes than myocyte PRR, reflecting electrolyte-dependent alterations in the safety factor for action potential propagation. Changes in [K+]o also substantially affected arrhythmia vulnerability, increasing inducibility and prolonging rhythm disturbances. We conclude that extracellular K+ is the principal plasma electrolyte determinant of atrial PRR and arrhythmia burden, acting primarily through IK1. Monitoring and maintaining serum K+ within the normal range may be important for managing atrial arrhythmia risk.

title: Integrating CRISPRi perturbation responses and transcription-factor binding priors for regulatory network inference in triple-negative breast cancer
abstract: Triple-Negative Breast Cancer (TNBC) represents an aggressive breast cancer subtype that lacks actionable cell-surface receptors, restricting frontline systemic management to cytotoxic chemotherapy. While recent functional epigenomics shows that TNBC progression is governed by non-coding regulatory remodeling at distal super-enhancers, conventional Gene Regulatory Network (GRN) inference methods rely on observational transcriptomic co-expression, which suffers from technical dropouts and confounding correlations that inflate false discoveries (>30%). Here, we present an interventional network inference framework that integrates large-scale single-cell CRISPR-interference perturbation sequencing (Perturb-seq; GSE224986, 95,678 cells across 11,975 sgRNAs) with ENCODE Factorbook ChIP-seq physical transcription factor binding priors across 819 somatic mutation-associated enhancer loci in human TNBC (MDA-MB-231). Our pipeline reconstructed a tripartite network yielding 5,935 physical TF-enhancer edges, 383,757 functional enhancer-gene edges, and 542,760 unique TF-target gene functional pairs across 372 active enhancers. Topological centrality prioritized master transcriptional drivers governing TNBC oncogenic signaling, including CTCF, POLR2A, EP300, JUND, MYC, and FOS, which regulate Hallmark programs for Epithelial-Mesenchymal Transition (p = 1.2 x 10-9) and cell cycle progression. Explainable machine learning (SHAP TreeExplainer) revealed non-linear, thresholded transactivation dynamics for AP-1 and MYC. Quantitative benchmarking against held-out CRISPRi ground truth demonstrated strong discriminatory accuracy (AUROC = 0.8999, AUPRC = 0.8745, Precision = 90.13%, FDR = 9.87%), substantially outperforming GENIE3 (AUPRC = 0.6323, FDR = 35.73%) and co-expression correlation (AUPRC = 0.6814). In silico-simulated driver feature silencing correlated with experimental responses (R2 = 0.473, p < 10-122), and master driver signatures significantly stratified overall survival in the METABRIC (n = 320) and TCGA-BRCA (n = 160; p [≤] 0.019) cohorts. Finally, in silico perturbation modeling indicated that multi-target epigenetic combinations achieved 93% topological disruption of oncogenic regulatory connectivity, nominating prioritized candidate circuits for experimental validation.

title: Predicted templates improve the prediction of antibody-antigen structures by AlphaFold 3 and Boltz-2
abstract: Motivation: In spite of the much improved protein structure prediction methods, the success rate remains low for antibody-antigen complexes. While this can be improved by computationally demanding massive sampling, results are still much poorer than for most other types of protein-protein interactions. In principle, improvement can be achieved by using templates that are close enough to the native structure of the complex, but these are generally not available for antibody-antigen complexes. Results: We explore the use of templates, generated by the computationally inexpensive rigid body docking program PIPER. Applied to a leakage-free antibody-antigen benchmark set, standard AlphaFold 3 with 1000 random seeds yields acceptable or better models as the top predictions for 56.2% of complexes. Adding the PIPER generated templates in the unmasked version of AlphaFold 3 either increases the success rate to 63.4%, or reaches the same 56.2% success rate in about 200 runs. The template-based approach similarly improves antibody-antigen prediction by Boltz-2. This result demonstrates that the space explored by the ML based approach can be expanded by adding templates prepared by traditional docking, compensating for the lack of evolutionary relationship and the limited availability of training data. Availability and Implementation: The ClusPro server (https://cluspro.bu.edu/login.php) containing the PIPER program is free for non-commercial applications and the program is available by request (https://www.vajdalab.org/). All other study data are included in the article and/or supporting information.

title: Evolutionary constraints on mitochondrial bioenergetics are reshaped in cancer
abstract: Mitochondrial DNA encodes thirteen subunits of the oxidative phosphorylation system, many of which are subject to strong purifying selection in humans. In cancer this selection is relaxed, which is usually read as a weakening of the inherited filter. Comparing somatic variants from 8,886 tumours with population variation using a unified analytical framework and a dataset-specific mutational null, we show that the tumour filter has a different shape. ATP synthase, the least constrained complex in the germline, becomes the most constrained in tumours, an inversion that holds within the tumour data alone and is not explained by the measurement ceiling. Holding residue position fixed, the germline avoids substitutions that change side-chain charge at the proton-loading sites of complex I, as does the human phylogeny, and around the haems of complex III, whereas tumours no longer distinguish them. Damage at the redox centres of complexes III and IV is tolerated mainly at low variant allele fraction, including within single cohorts, and tumours retain constraint on the electron-tunnelling medium of complex IV. At a complex I proton bridge, density-functional calculations separate substitutions that retune the transfer potential from those that abolish it, and a gated-tunnelling model predicts that removing the charge of one tumour-mutated residue changes the rate far more than the kinetic isotope effect.

title: siGMA: Modeling Label Noise and Heterogeneity in siRNA Efficacy Prediction
abstract: Small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) have emerged as a powerful class of therapeutics, yet identifying viable candidates remains costly and labour-intensive given the vast combination space that must be screened. This challenge is compounded by the need for chemical modifications, which are essential to mitigate off-target effects and enhance serum stability but frequently come at the expense of baseline knockdown efficacy. As a result, siRNA design requires careful, iterative optimization, further expanding the experimental burden and rendering exhaustive screening impractical. Computational prediction offers a compelling alternative, enabling rapid, low-cost identification of promising candidates prior to wet-lab validation. In this work we present siGMA, a heteroscedastic multimodal predictive model that integrates sequence, chemical, structural, and experimental information to predict the silencing efficacy of chemically modified siRNAs. Modelling in this domain is constrained by two principal obstacles: the scarcity of experimental data and the substantial noise arising from protocol heterogeneity across publicly available datasets. We therefore propose a model that quantifies predictive uncertainty rather than issuing confident mispredictions. We calibrated the model against such noise using a combined aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty prediction. The resulting model yielded well-calibrated estimates of predictive variability on held-out folds across datasets and outperformed current state-of-the-art approaches across noisy cross-dataset conditions, including previously unseen chemical modifications and target sequences. This demonstrates our model's ability to rank better than the baselines while rendering the noise ceiling measurable. This provides a scalable framework that could accelerate the therapeutic siRNA development pipeline while reducing the need for exhaustive empirical screening.

title: A2Holo: Dual-Stream Flow Matching of 3D Structure and a Protein Language Model for Conformational Transition Prediction
abstract: Modelling a ligand-bound holo conformation from a ligand-free apo conformation is essential in structure-based drug discovery. We present A2Holo, which casts apo-to-holo prediction as flow matching between two experimental structures rather than generation from noise. It transplants the dual-stream joint attention of in-context image generation to residue-aligned protein language model embeddings and structure. Without ligand conditioning or stochastic sampling, A2Holo's single deterministic trajectory reaches a median C RMSD of 0.809 [A] on the D3PM benchmark, the lowest among existing methods. Its TM-score exceeds even the best of 10 samples from every stochastic baseline on at least 144 of 150 pairs. Beyond performance, we directly measure the transplanted multimodal mechanism itself. Because sequence and structure are residue-aligned, its joint attention can be measured at residue resolution and tested for reproducibility across independently trained model variants. Within the structure stream, the attention a residue receives recovers moving residues better than the attention it emits, and this asymmetry is learned. A2Holo demonstrates a successful multimodal transplant from in-context image generation to protein conformational change, with strong deterministic apo-to-holo prediction. It also provides a quantitative account of how that mechanism organises residue-aligned sequence and structure around the residues that move.

title: Machine Learning-based Transcriptomic Data Analysis of Long COVID Patients: Generating Hypotheses for Molecular Signatures
abstract: Introduction: Long COVID (LC) remains a global public-health challenge, affecting an estimated 10-30% of COVID-19-survivors. Machine learning (ML) can help identify molecular features associated with LC. Human ion channels (HICs), that regulate immune-cell signaling and cellular homeostasis, may contribute to LC-associated processes and offer insights into relevant pathways and potential drug-repurposing candidates. Methodology: RNA-seq data from COVID-19-recovered and LC patients across six datasets were integrated, preprocessed, and corrected for batch effects. Supervised ML models were evaluated using leave-one-batch-out validation, with SHAP identifying features across validation folds. Functional enrichment, host-host and host-viral protein-protein interaction analyses were performed, followed by drug interaction analysis of potential HICs within the resulting interactome. Results: A support vector classifier with an RBF kernel achieved a mean-AUC of 0.664 across six validation folds. SHAP analysis of the three selected folds (AUC = 0.722, 0.836, and 0.817) identified 225, 153, and 241 genes, respectively. Functional enrichment highlighted pathways including histidine metabolism and TNF signaling. Among the 613 genes identified across these folds, 9 were HICs and 39 were immune signaling-related genes (ISGs), whose protein-protein interaction analysis revealed a pharmacologically relevant interactome. Furthermore, four HICs including CLCN3, KCNQ3, RYR1, and ZACN interacted with 30 approved drugs. Conclusion: ML-based analysis of integrated RNA-seq data identified HICs and ISGs associated with LC, while functional enrichment and PPI analyses provided insights into their potential biological relevance. Drug interaction analysis further highlighted candidate HIC-targeting drugs for future investigation in LC management. This computational framework provides preliminary, hypothesis-generating insights to guide future research.

title: Large populations from few founders: founder-aware likelihoods for inferring cell proliferation rates
abstract: Gaussian approximations to demographic noise are usually justified by large numbers of cells. In populations described by branching processes, however, a large population descended from few founders is not approximately Gaussian. A culture grown from few cells can contain thousands of cells yet retain large, skewed variation from its earliest divisions, deaths, and phenotypic switches. A random establishment amplitude, the limit of the population size divided by its exponential growth factor, summarizes this variation. We propose a founder-aware likelihood for cell cultures observed at an endpoint. Given the establishment amplitude, it approximates the remaining demographic fluctuations by a Gaussian distribution and then averages over the distribution of the amplitude. Its conditional Gaussian approximation requires a large population rather than many founders, and the likelihood approaches a single Gaussian distribution as the founder count grows. We compare it with a population Gaussian likelihood developed for many-founder cultures, using a pure-birth (Yule) process, whose cell-count distribution is known exactly, and exact simulations of a two-type process with division, death, and reversible switching. With one founder per culture, the founder-aware likelihood estimates rates more accurately than the population Gaussian likelihood, and its confidence sets are longer but have coverage close to the nominal level. With 50 founders per culture, the two likelihoods perform comparably. Founder-aware likelihoods thus suit clonal and other few-founder experiments.

title: gutenTAG: A MALDI-IHC processing and quality control tool
abstract: Coupling of immunohistochemistry with MALDI mass spectroscopy (MALDI-IHC) enables targeted spatial analysis of proteins through the use of photocleavable mass tags. Upwards of 100 proteins can be imaged in a single run due to the high multiplexing power of this technology. Coupled with mass shifts in MALDI-IHC data, this scalability creates a challenge for users, as there are currently no dedicated software tools for MALDI-IHC data processing. Here we introduce gutenTAG, an open-source processing and quality control tool specifically designed for MALDI-IHC. gutenTAG uses a novel strategy based on grouping clusters of m/z bins originating from the same molecular species into single entities termed metapeaks. This strategy is robust to mass shift, generating ion images that capture the full signal of peaks corresponding to each mass tag while minimizing noise. Furthermore, we show that the metapeak strategy can be adapted to alternative open-source tools to facilitate their use in targeted imaging applications.

title: Non-invasive detection of tissue clonal mosaicism in chronic disease
abstract: Liquid biopsy has transformed our ability to non-invasively interrogate the somatic genome, but its reach has been largely confined to fetal genetics in prenatal testing and tumor genetics in cancer. Clonal mosaicism (CM) pervades non-malignant solid tissues, where somatic driver mutations expand under specific selective pressures and may shape the course of chronic illness. Access to this biology has been limited to invasive tissue biopsies, restricting the field to small cohorts and single time points, and has precluded large-scale, clinically-linked analyses. Here, ultra-sensitive cell-free DNA (cfDNA) sequencing of patients with chronic liver disease revealed genome-wide somatic variants from matched liver biopsies at plasma fractions comparable to those of cancers (10^-4 - 10^-5), with signal corresponding to variants from spatially and phylogenetically related clones. A biopsy-naive targeted panel detected pathogenic variants in chronic liver disease driver genes in 81.5% patients with chronic liver disease, undetectable in controls, with stage-specific enrichment of ACVR2A in early disease and clearance of liver-derived signal following transplant. Extending the framework to inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), we detect clonal expansions of IBD driver genes in active ulcerative colitis, and observe greater detection in patients with pancolitis versus more localized disease. Together, these results open a new domain for cfDNA genetics beyond cancer and prenatal genetics, the non-invasive interrogation of somatic evolution in chronic disease, and establish a framework for the large-cohort, longitudinal, clinically linked studies of solid-tissue CM that has been inaccessible to the field.

title: SpliceVarMech: A causal generative framework for mechanistic interpretation of non-canonical splicing variants
abstract: Non-canonical splicing variants occur beyond the conserved dinucleotides flanking splice junctions and are difficult to interpret because disruption scores alone do not explain splice outcomes or quantify uncertainty. We have developed SpliceVarMech, a causal generative framework in which a dual-stream encoder compares the wild-type and mutant sequences and conditional discrete sequence diffusion generates candidate splice outcomes. We then apply Bayesian causal inference to estimate posterior disruption probabilities with 95% credible intervals. The framework reports the predicted splice mechanism together with sequence attribution maps and an exploratory mapping to clinical evidence labels. On a gold-standard cohort of experimentally validated variants from male infertility genes, Bayesian leave-one-out cross-validation on 31 variants yielded an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 1.000. We benchmarked 16 individual splice prediction tools on the same cohort, where the highest-performing tool, SpliceAI, achieved 0.619 on its 30 scored variants. Ablation experiments showed that removing individual components reduced discrimination, and a separate evaluation on 54 variants supported the contribution of fine-tuning. In a cross-domain assessment, fine-tuning on BRCA1 saturation genome editing data increased discrimination from 0.722 to 0.840 on 203 held-out variants without architectural modification. We assessed in-sample calibration, and held-out validation remains necessary. These results support further evaluation of paired-sequence generative modeling and Bayesian inference for mechanistic interpretation of splicing variants across disease contexts.

title: The IGVF Data Portal: a repository for insights into genome function
abstract: The Impact of Genomic Variation on Function (IGVF) Consortium has utilized a wide variety of assays and computational methods to study how genomic variation impacts function. To support the collaborative efforts of labs within IGVF, and to share the results of these efforts, the IGVF Data Administration and Coordination Center (DACC) has developed a data portal (https://data.igvf.org/) that serves as the repository for all results from the IGVF Consortium and as the source of results that have been integrated into the IGVF knowledge graph. Data generated by the IGVF Consortium, which has reached over 240 terabytes as of November 2026, can be publicly accessed via web browser, or programmatically via API, as well as via agentic tools. Here, we provide a summary of the available IGVF data and an overview of the design of the IGVF Data Portal.

title: LPMOcat: an interactive database for comparative structural analysis of lytic polysaccharide monooxygenases
abstract: LPMOcat is a comprehensive resource of 161 characterised lytic polysaccharide monooxygenases (LPMOs) from all eight CAZy families, in which an automated pipeline integrates data from public databases and, based on a structural alignment, annotates common structural features of LPMOs (e.g. histidine brace, second-sphere residues, loop regions), and calculates per-residue properties (e.g. flexibility, hydrophobicity, hole-hopping pathways). The web application summarises all the gathered information in plots integrated with a similarity tree and allows users to filter the catalogue and compare any set of LPMOs to investigate their structure-function relationships.

title: Statistical analysis of residue contact energies reveals folding determinants of ion channels
abstract:
by Svetlana I. Tarnovskaya, Boris S. Zhorov, Denis B. Tikhonov 

Tetrameric and pseudo-tetrameric cationic channels, which are targeted by many drugs and toxins, play key roles in the cell physiology and pathophysiology. This diverse superfamily of P-loop channels includes but is not limited to voltage-gated potassium, sodium and calcium channels, TRP channels, and ionotropic glutamate receptors. In hundreds of crystal and cryoEM structures of P-loop channels, the general folding is rather similar but subfamily-specific structural details vary greatly. The latter underlie atomic mechanisms of ion selectivity, gating, sensitivity to drugs and toxins, and dysfunction of thousands disease-associated variants. Understanding these mechanisms may benefit from comparative analyses of multiple structures. Here, we propose a statistical method to reveal structural determinants of folding in related proteins, which involves clustering of residue-residue contact energies. We applied the method to a pH-gated potassium channel KcsA and a voltage-gated sodium channel NavAb. Twenty 3D-aligned experimental structures of each channel with universal residue labels were downloaded from database www.plic3da.com and Monte Carlo energy minimized. Residue contact energies clustered in the multidimensional space of contacts automatically discriminated open vs. closed states of KcsA, and wild-type vs. chimeric structures of NavAb. We found and analyzed specific contacts that underlie structural peculiarities. The proposed approach may help detecting folding peculiarities and their structural determinants between subfamilies of P-loop channels, within individual subfamilies, and could be adapted to other proteins.

title: Multi-model forecasting of respiratory disease activity in Germany during the 2024–2025 season
abstract:
by Johannes Bracher, Daniel Wolffram, Rodrigo Amaral Lind, Nils Bardeck, Micha Böhm, Seba Contreras, Philipp Dönges, Felix Günther, Rolf Kaiser, Jan van de Kassteele, Alexander Kuhlmann, Berit Lange, Barbora Němcová, Viola Priesemann, Ulrich Reinacher, Isti Rodiah, Frank Sandmann, the RESPINOW Study Group , Melanie Schienle 

Respiratory diseases cause considerable morbidity in autumn and winter and are a priority in public health monitoring. In Germany, they are subject to a number of surveillance systems, including both pathogen-specific and syndromic indicators. In this paper we present a collaborative multi-target and multi-model real-time forecasting system rolled out during the 2024/25 season, and discuss differences to earlier efforts carried out during the COVID-19 pandemic. We focus on general practitioner consultations for acute respiratory infections (ARI) and hospitalizations for severe acute respiratory infections (SARI), where a total of eight models were run to generate nowcasts and forecasts. In addition, we consider confirmed cases of seasonal influenza and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) where one forecasting model each was available. As all indicators were subject to retrospective revisions, forecasting models were combined with a nowcasting step. For the SARI and ARI indicators, we combined the available models into an ensemble and conducted detailed quantitative evaluations. Nowcasts overall showed convincing performance, even though for some models Christmas break effects led to an upward bias in early January. Forecasts were overall well-calibrated and most models outperformed simple benchmark models. When taking into account age-stratified targets, most observed performance differences to a persistence baseline were statistically significant. Anticipating the peak timing and magnitude, however, proved to be challenging, with many models predicting too flat curves with a too early turnaround (e.g., in late January rather than mid-February for SARI). The combined ensemble forecast was among the best-performing approaches, but unlike in previous related projects did not consistently outperform individual models. We conclude by discussing learnings on the organization of collaborative forecasting projects in post-COVID-19 times.

title: AlphaFold models of host-pathogen interactions elucidate the prevalence and structural modes of molecular mimicry
abstract:
by Delora Baptista, Lidia Gomez-Lucas, Jürgen Jänes, Nevan J. Krogan, Maria João Amorim, Ylva Ivarsson, Pedro Beltrao 

Pathogens exploit host cellular machinery through protein-protein interactions (PPIs), often using molecular mimicry to hijack host cellular processes. While there have been thousands of host-pathogen PPIs determined to date, the lack of structural information for these impedes the study of the prevalence of molecular mimicry and convergent evolution of protein interaction interfaces. To address this, we benchmarked AlphaFold2 and 3 for prediction of structures of host-pathogen interactions observing that accurate models can be retrieved when ranking by modelling confidence, despite an overall low performance. We predicted structures for 6,782 pathogen-human PPIs yielding 803 models of higher confidence. Most pathogen proteins interacting with a common human protein are predicted to do so via the same interface, suggesting a high degree of convergent evolution of protein interaction interfaces. When comparing structural models from host-pathogen and host-host interactions, we observe that a majority of pathogen proteins are predicted to target existing human PPI interfaces. We categorized instances of mimicry into different modes, occurring at different frequencies: 1) via the same domain family (least common); 2) via a similar structural motif; and 3) via a similar linear peptide (most common). We selected examples of linear peptide interactions for binding assay testing, confirming 8 out of 12 predicted interfaces, including 3 viral linear peptide interactions. This validates AlphaFold’s ability to model some host-pathogen interactions and the mechanisms underlying molecular mimicry. This work showcases the value of large-scale structural modelling to study convergent evolution of host-pathogen interactions and how molecular mimicry may contribute to infection or host defense.

title: Large-scale analysis of AlphaFold structures reveals organism-specific physicochemical signatures
abstract:
by Michael J. Stam, Diego A. Oyarzún, Nadanai Laohakunakorn, Christopher W. Wood 

Recent advancements in protein structure prediction methods have ushered in a new era of abundant and accurate structural data, providing opportunities to analyse proteins at a scale that has not been possible before. Here we performed a large-scale analysis of physicochemical properties across 373,779 confident AlphaFold structures. Our analysis revealed systematic variation between proteins from different organisms to such an extent that major features of the tree of life could be recovered from these data. Surprisingly, this relationship persisted even when we restricted our analysis to eukaryotic, cytosolic proteins and proteins from single AlphaFold Database Foldseek clusters. Given the strong functional constraints on protein chemistry, this finding is unexpected and suggests that protein structures have organism-specific physicochemical signatures, which might reveal evolutionary constraints imposed by the cellular environment and could have significant implications for the design and engineering of novel proteins.

title: FOXK2 lactylation drives sorafenib resistance in hepatocellular carcinoma by activating fatty acid oxidation
abstract:
Background
                      Sorafenib resistance is a major clinical challenge in advanced hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). However, the underlying mechanisms remain incompletely understood. This study investigates the role of FOXK2 protein lactylation in driving sorafenib resistance and elucidates the associated molecular mechanisms. 
                  
                     Results
                      We identify K300 lactylation of FOXK2 as a key metabolic–epigenetic switch that sustains sorafenib resistance by rewiring fatty acid β-oxidation (FAO). Mechanistically, lactate-derived K300 lactylation, catalyzed by KAT3B and reversed by SIRT1, enhances the DNA-binding capacity of FOXK2, leading to the transcriptional activation of FAO enzymes, particularly ACSL4, and thereby supporting energy production in drug-resistant cells. Accordingly, inhibition of FOXK2 lactylation sensitizes HCC cells to sorafenib in both cell-based and animal models. Clinically, elevated FOXK2-K300 lactylation in tumors from patients with HCC correlates with a poor therapeutic response and unfavorable survival outcomes. 
                  
                     Conclusions
                      The FOXK2 lactylation–FAO axis is a critical regulator of sorafenib resistance in HCC. Targeting FOXK2-K300 lactylation represents a promising strategy for overcoming resistance and improving treatment outcomes.

title: The structure-specific endonuclease HIGLE contributes to TONSOKU-mediated DNA repair during replication in  Arabidopsis thaliana
abstract:
Background
                      Faithful genome replication requires coordinated recognition and processing of DNA replication intermediates. In plants, the DNA repair factor TONSOKU (TSK/TONSL) promotes replication-associated DNA repair through recognition of H3.1K27me0-marked chromatin. However, the downstream factors that execute DNA processing remain unknown. 
                  
                     Results
                      We identify the structure-specific endonuclease HYL1 INTERACTING GIY-YIG LIKE ENDONUCLEASE (HIGLE), a plant SLX1-like endonuclease, as a TSK-interacting factor. TSK interacts with the GIY-YIG-containing N-terminal region of HIGLE through a previously uncharacterized region. Disruption of this interaction impairs TSK-mediated tolerance to genotoxic stress. Biochemical analyses show that TSK enhances HIGLE nuclease activity toward replication-fork and Holliday-junction substrates while reducing HIGLE self-association. Loss of HIGLE causes hypersensitivity to DNA damage and increased genome instability. Single-cell transcriptomics and EdU incorporation assays reveal defects in S-phase progression in both  tsk  and  higle  mutants under genotoxic stress. Genetic analyses indicate overlapping functions of HIGLE and RAD51 during DNA repair and reveal an additional role for HIGLE in DNA polymerase θ-mediated end joining in  atxr5/6  mutants lacking H3.1K27me1. In this context, HIGLE promotes repair of aberrant DNA intermediates but also contributes to heterochromatic DNA amplification and transcriptional reactivation. 
                  
                     Conclusions
                      These findings identify HIGLE as a TSK-recruited structure-specific endonuclease that connects chromatin-based recognition of replicative chromatin with processing of DNA repair intermediates. The TSK-HIGLE pathway safeguards genome stability during replication, while its outcomes become context dependent when H3.1K27me1 is depleted.

title: Benchmarking of haplotype- and clone-specific detection callers of complex copy number alterations in single-cell DNA sequencing with HCDSIM and HCBench
abstract:
Background
                      Single-cell DNA sequencing enables high-resolution characterization of somatic copy number alterations, yet accurately detecting haplotype-, cell/clone-, and locus-specific copy number alterations (hcCNAs) remains challenging. Complex hcCNA events, characterized by coordinated hcCNA changes affecting multiple haplotypes, clonal populations, or genomic loci, are pervasive in cancer and constitute important mechanisms underlying intratumor heterogeneity and tumor evolution. 
                  
                     Results
                      We present HCDSIM, a single-cell genomics simulator that models complex hcCNA events during clonal evolution, and HCBench, a benchmarking framework with simulation-based and real-data concordance modules. We evaluate five leading callers at 5 Mb and 100 kb resolution across sequencing coverage, clone structures, and clone ratios in simulation. CHISEL provides the best overall performance in hcCNA detection at 5 Mb but fails to correctly phase over half of the allelically imbalanced bins. SIGNALS exhibits the strongest clone detection among retained cells but poor hcCNA inference and limited phasing. Alleloscope achieves moderate clone recovery but low hcCNA accuracy. SEACON performs relatively well for deletions at 5 Mb, whereas CNRein performs best in inferring clone structure, evolution, and deletions at 100 kb. Simulations further demonstrate that caller rankings are generally stable across tree topologies and clone proportions, with task-specific exceptions. On real data, however, callers are highly discordant on three low-coverage single-cell DNA sequencing datasets. 
                  
                     Conclusions
                      These findings highlight the critical need for improved algorithms targeting complex hcCNA detection. HCDSIM and HCBench provide a robust foundation for developing and evaluating next-generation hcCNA callers.

title: G2PT: a genotype–phenotype transformer to assess and explain polygenic risk
abstract: Genome-wide association studies have linked millions of genetic variants to biomedical phenotypes, but their utility has been limited by lack of mechanistic understanding and widespread epistatic interactions. Here, we introduce the Genotype-to-Phenotype Transformer (G2PT), a framework for modeling hierarchical information flow among variants, genes, multigenic systems, and phenotypes. We train G2PT to model the genetics of metabolic traits including insulin resistance, LDL and type 2 diabetes. G2PT predicts these traits with accuracy comparable to best-in-class methods, demonstrates transferability across cohorts, and captures epistatic effects. This work positions hierarchical graph transformers as a next-generation approach to polygenic risk interpretation.

title: SPARC: sparsity-aware structural consistency for single-cell RNA-seq imputation
abstract:
Background
                      Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data are characterized by substantial sparsity, while most existing imputation approaches prioritize expression reconstruction accuracy. However, downstream tasks such as clustering and trajectory inference rely on preserving intercellular structural relationships, and the existing reconstruction-centered objectives may not adequately reflect structure-level requirements. This study investigates whether integrating structural information into the imputation objective improves structural consistency across varying sparsity levels. 
                  
                     Results
                      We introduce a sparsity-aware framework SPARC that augments a reconstruction-based objective with auxiliary structural constraints, and explicitly models intercellular relationships during optimization. The proposed method SPARC is evaluated on ten public scRNA-seq datasets under controlled missingness settings to assess robustness across different sparsity levels. Experimental results show that reconstruction errors are better than or comparable to representative baselines across missing ratios, with SPARC achieving the lowest RMSE on 9 of the 10 evaluated datasets under the 20% masking condition. Moreover, the increase in reconstruction error across masking levels (10%–30%) remains comparable to or slower than that of competing approaches, suggesting stable performance under increasing sparsity. Reconstruction accuracy and clustering consistency do not exhibit a stable monotonic relationship. The data also suggests that expression recovery alone does not reliably predict downstream structural performance. In downstream clustering analysis, SPARC achieves the highest ARI on 7 datasets while maintaining stable performance across five independent masking simulations. Trajectory analyses further suggest that group-level connectivity patterns remain largely preserved under the proposed objective formulation. 
                  
                     Conclusion
                      These findings offer insight into objective function design for single-cell imputation, and demonstrate that incorporating structural signals provides a controlled adjustment that aligns reconstruction optimization with downstream structural evaluation in sparsity settings.

title: pSLiM: Clustering of protein language model embeddings enables hypothesis‑driven identification and prioritization of short protein motifs
abstract:
Background
                      Canonical short linear motifs and other conserved motifs are compact sequence elements that mediate diverse protein functions through interactions with proteins, ligands, and nucleic acids. Their short length, sequence degeneracy, and weak evolutionary conservation complicate identification and functional annotation. We developed pSLiM, an analysis framework based on unsupervised clustering that uses motif-level embeddings from pretrained protein language models to organize and prioritize candidate motifs within a user-defined hypothesis space. 
                  
                     Results
                      pSLiM identifies candidate motif instances from regular expressions or user-specified residue ranges, aggregates residue embeddings into motif-level vectors, and applies dimensionality reduction and density-based clustering without relying on sequence similarity or labeled training data. We evaluated pSLiM on three  Arabidopsis thaliana  case studies representing a subtilisin-like serine proteinase recognition motif, a transcriptional repression motif, and an EF-hand-associated metal-binding motif. For each case study, the gene-level Jaccard index quantified cluster overlap with case-specific reference gene sets and was used to prioritize clusters containing biologically validated motif instances. The analyses grouped validated subtilisin recognition motifs, separated transcriptional repression motif subclasses, and recovered EF-hand-associated motifs. The biological relevance of the prioritized clusters was further supported by complementary evidence from Gene Ontology term enrichment, gene co-expression patterns, and predicted metal-binding activity. 
                  
                     Conclusions
                      Motif-level protein language model embeddings provide a flexible and interpretable approach for exploring short protein motifs within user-defined candidate spaces. pSLiM complements sequence-based searches by supporting candidate annotation and hypothesis development, while functional assignments require experimental validation.

title: A hybrid framework for uncertainty quantification in partially observed dynamic biological systems
abstract:
Background
                      Mechanistic ordinary differential equation (ODE) models are widely used in systems biology, but uncertainty quantification (UQ) remains difficult when only a subset of state variables is experimentally observed. Existing Bayesian and likelihood-based approaches can be computationally demanding for nonlinear, weakly identifiable, or high-dimensional systems. 
                  
                     Results
                      We present a framework, and its corresponding software CUQDyn1_Plus, for UQ in partially observed ODE systems. Our method combines leave-one-out jackknife+-style empirical calibration for observed states with sensitivity-based Gaussian uncertainty propagation for hidden states. The software supports global parameter estimation, covariance propagation, bootstrap trajectory uncertainty and simulation-based calibration. It also facilitates comparison with Bayesian workflows, automated reporting, and reproducibility diagnostics. Validation on six benchmark systems shows accurate behavior in well-conditioned cases and model-dependent degradation under nonlinearity, weak identifiability, or global branch-switching non-identifiability. 
                  
                     Conclusions
                      CUQDyn1_Plus provides a practical and computationally efficient UQ workflow for systems biology models with observed and latent states. Its diagnostic outputs help identify when local Gaussian propagation is reliable and when uncertainty bands should be interpreted cautiously, making it a useful complement to fully Bayesian workflows.

title: A CpG score-based gene set enrichment test for analysis of DNA methylation data with a hierarchical structure
abstract:
Background
                      DNA methylation is a key epigenetic modification that regulates gene expression and plays a crucial role in disease progression and carcinogenesis. Although numerous statistical methods have been developed to identify differentially methylated CpG sites and genes, most are not designed to detect disease-associated gene sets or regulatory pathways. Furthermore, DNA methylation data exhibit a three-level hierarchical structure consisting of CpG sites, genes, and genetic pathways, rendering conventional gene set testing methods inapplicable. 
                  
                     Results
                      We propose a CpG score-based gene set enrichment test that captures both mean and variance signals by quantifying the association strength of individual CpG sites and aggregating them into gene-level scores. Fast gene set enrichment analysis is then performed using these scores to identify disease-associated pathways. In addition, we introduce a plug-in weighting scheme that incorporates prior biological network information into the computation of gene-level scores. Simulation studies demonstrate that the proposed method substantially improves detection power when either mean or variance signals are present. We further apply the proposed approach to DNA methylation data from The Cancer Genome Atlas Breast Invasive Carcinoma (TCGA-BRCA) cohort and identify biologically meaningful pathways that are missed by conventional gene set testing methods. 
                  
                     Conclusions
                      The proposed CpG score-based gene set test quantifies the significance of individual CpG sites and integrates these signals into gene-level scores for gene set enrichment analysis. By improving robustness, flexibility, and interpretability, the proposed framework provides a versatile approach for investigating gene regulation and disease mechanisms using epigenome-wide DNA methylation data.

title: The long non‐coding RNA lncWOX5 modulates auxin‐responsive adventitious root formation in poplar
abstract:
Significance Statement 
 The poplar lncRNA  lncWOX5  contributes to the modulation of auxin-responsive adventitious root formation, with its loss accelerating root emergence and increasing root formation.
 
 The poplar lncRNA  lncWOX5  contributes to the quantitative modulation of auxin-responsive developmental output during adventitious root formation. Genetic and transcriptomic evidence links  lncWOX5  with the neighbouring  PeWOX5a  and broader auxin-associated transcription, providing insight into how lncRNAs may contribute to regenerative responses in woody plants. 
 
 SUMMARY 
 Adventitious root (AR) formation requires coordinated auxin signaling and developmental reprogramming, yet how the magnitude and timing of this response are modulated remains incompletely understood. Here, we investigated the function of the poplar ( Populus deltoides  ×  P .  euramericana , clone ‘Nanlin 895’) long non-coding RNA (lncRNA)  lncWOX5  using CRISPR/Cas9-mediated loss-of-function analyses together with previously reported gain-of-function evidence. Independent  lncWOX5  knockout lines showed accelerated AR emergence and increased AR formation, accompanied by altered auxin-responsive phenotypes and increased expression of the neighbouring WOX gene  PeWOX5a . Actinomycin D (ActD) treatment indicated that reduced  lncWOX5  transcript stability contributes to its lower steady-state abundance in the edited lines. The reciprocal responses of  PeWOX5a  in knockout and overexpression backgrounds support an inverse association between  lncWOX5  and  PeWOX5a  expression. Transcriptome profiling of knockout roots revealed broader changes in auxin-associated transcription, which were further supported by temporal expression analyses following auxin treatment. Together, these findings indicate that  lncWOX5  contributes to the quantitative modulation of auxin-responsive developmental output during AR formation and identify  PeWOX5a  as a candidate gene associated with this response. This study highlights an lncRNA-associated regulatory layer that contributes to the quantitative modulation of root regeneration in poplar.

title: Maxime Trasser‐Durand
abstract: Maxime Trasser‐Durand, Ecology, Society and Evolution Laboratory (ESE, CNRS/Université Paris‐Saclay, France).

title: MdEF‐Tu‐associated translational reprogramming modulates apple disease resistance through the MdGAPC2–autophagy pathway
abstract:
A proposed working model linking MdEF-Tu-associated translational reprogramming to MdGAPC2-mediated autophagy modulation.
 
 
 Summary 
 
Elongation factor-Tu (EF-Tu) is a central component of the ribosomal translation machinery, and the ribosome-associated regulatory environment is an important determinant for translational control. However, the molecular mechanisms involving plant EF-Tu in immune-associated translational regulation remain largely unexplored.
We show that apple EF-Tu (MdEF-Tu) associates with the ribosomal proteins MdRPL28 and MdRPS8 and modulates global translational activity during  Valsa mali  ( V. mali ) infection. Transcriptome and translatome analyses reveal widespread translational reprogramming. Polysome profiling and ribosome fractionation analyses show that altered MdEF-Tu abundance affects the translational output of  MdGAPC2 , which encodes a cytosolic glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase.
MdGAPC2 interacts with the autophagy-related protein MdATG3a and interferes with autophagy. Notably, the  V. mali  effector Vm1G-1794 stabilizes MdEF-Tu, sustaining an MdEF-Tu-associated translational response involving MdGAPC2, thereby promoting autophagy suppression and compromising apple disease resistance.
Collectively, our findings uncover a regulatory process linking MdEF-Tu-associated translational reprogramming to MdGAPC2-mediated autophagy during the apple immune response and reveal how  V. mali  hijacks this process to facilitate infection. This work provides novel insights into the autophagy modulation during the interaction between plants and pathogens.

title: A CPK28‐GS2 phosphorylation switch uncouples nitrogen‐promoted growth from disease susceptibility
abstract:
Working model of CPK28-GS2 phosphorylation-mediated nitrate-induced susceptibility to  Ralstonia solanacearum .
 
 
 Summary 
 
Nitrogen fertilization underpins global crop yields, but it paradoxically increases plant vulnerability to pathogens, a phenomenon known as nitrogen-induced susceptibility (NIS). This phenomenon has been repeatedly observed in both field and laboratory studies; however, the underlying molecular mechanism remains elusive.
Here, we show that the nitrogen assimilation gene  glutamine synthetase 2  ( GS2 ) plays a central role in NIS in tomato. Genetic analyses revealed that GS2 promotes both biomass accumulation and susceptibility to  Ralstonia solanacearum . Using immunoprecipitation-mass spectrometry (IP-MS), we identified the calcium-dependent protein kinase CPK28 as an interactor of GS2.
CPK28 phosphorylates GS2 at serine 334 in a nitrate-dependent manner, and this modification alters GS2 subcellular localization and is associated with perturbation of the phenylpropanoid pathway. Consequently, lignin deposition is reduced, leading to enhanced bacterial wilt susceptibility. Notably, a phospho-dead GS2 S334A variant abolished NIS without impairing growth.
These findings uncover a post-translational switch that uncouples nitrogen-promoted growth from disease susceptibility, thereby offering a framework to achieve agronomic productivity with ecological sustainability.

title: Broadening the lens: chemical defense and the molecular resolution of the root economics space
abstract: New Phytologist, EarlyView.

title: Monoterpenoid indole alkaloid biosynthesis reshaped by a scaffold protein
abstract: This commentary discusses two recent studies that identified and characterized a scaffold protein from  Catharanthus roseus  involved in the biosynthesis and regulation of monoterpenoid indole alkaloids. This protein emerges as a promising factor for enhancing the heterologous production of geissoschizine-derived alkaloids.

title: Solar assisted lithium recovery from brines: challenges and opportunities for integrated system
abstract: Abstract The rapid projected increases in demand for batteries over the upcoming decades requires a large expansion of lithium production capacity. While hard rock mining currently dominates the worldwide production, brines hold over 60% of global lithium reserves. Lithium production from brines is hampered by low lithium concentrations and high concentrations of other interfering ions such as magnesium. This review comprehensively analyzes integrated solar evaporation methods for capturing the lithium in brines. By firstly reviewing the conventional solar evaporation-chemical precipitation method, a currently commercialized technique, we identify several key challenges, including long timescales, large environmental impacts, and issues capturing lithium in some brine chemistries which prevents it from being applied in more places. A promising strategy to address these challenges is integrating interfacial solar evaporation with adsorption materials. This integration presents several advantages, such as producing both high evaporation and lithium adsorption rates and separating lithium from interfering ions. However, a key issue that needs careful evaluation is scaling taking place on the evaporative surface over time, which can cause significant drops in evaporative flux, thereby lowering the effectiveness of this integrated method. Several anti-scaling technologies have been reported, among which integrated membrane and solar evaporation systems demonstrate excellent potential in maintaining long-term performance of high evaporation and lithium capture rates. Ultimately, integrating interfacial solar evaporation with adsorption/membrane processes has the potential to provide a versatile and sustainable method for capturing lithium from brines with complex compositions.

title: Molecular regulation and recurrent evolution of fungal bet-hedging conidiation
abstract: Abstract Bet-hedging (BH) mitigates risk in fluctuating environments by promoting phenotypic diversity within a single genotype. Fungi exhibit remarkable phenotypic plasticity, such as conidiation polymorphism. Here, we show that entomopathogenic  Metarhizium  species produce either monomorphic or dimorphic conidia, which exhibit marked size variation to support different BH strategies. The large cylindrical and small ovoid conidia produced by the same species possess complementary advantages that facilitate adaptation to different conditions. Large conidia are heavily pigmented, ultraviolet-resistant, and highly virulent, whereas small conidia, produced either on separate phialides or atop large ones, germinate faster and resist bacteria better. These complementary traits represent a classic, yet previously unsuspected, diversified BH strategy. Mechanistic analysis revealed distinct gene expression patterns between morphotypes, leading to the identification of a transcription factor and a lipid-droplet surface protein that play key roles in governing dimorphic conidiation and pigmentation. Phylogenomic reconstruction revealed that later-diverging species reverted to an ancestral, monomorphic medium-spore state, indicating a recurrence of the conservative BH strategy. Pairwise experimental evolution confirmed that monomorphic populations have a fitness advantage under fluctuating ultraviolet irradiation. Our findings establish the BH mechanism in conidiation and reveal evolutionary experimentation with reversion across fungal speciation.

title: Photothermal-driven CO2 hydrogenation to methanol on an integrated Au–MoS2–TiO2 catalyst
abstract: Abstract Light-driven CO 2  hydrogenation to methanol is constrained by insufficient broadband light utilization and inefficient CO 2  activation. Herein, we achieve highly efficient photothermal hydrogenation of CO 2  to methanol on an integrated Au–MoS 2 –TiO 2  catalyst, in which MoS 2  is anchored on TiO 2  to form an intimate interface, and Au nanoparticles (NPs) are deposited on MoS 2 –TiO 2 . We demonstrate that the MoS 2 –TiO 2  interface induces the formation of few-layered MoS 2  and transfers electrons from TiO 2  to MoS 2 . MoS 2  serves as the primary active phase for CO 2  hydrogenation, while Au NPs enhance photo-to-heat conversion via the localized surface plasmon resonance (LSPR) effect, thereby collectively facilitating CO 2  activation under mild reaction conditions. Under photothermal conditions at 120°C in a continuous-flow reactor, the catalyst achieves 13.4% CO 2  conversion with 84.7% methanol selectivity, and maintains stable performance over 400 hours without observable deactivation, underscoring it among the most competitive photothermal catalysts for CO 2  hydrogenation to methanol.

title: Room temperature giant in-plane anomalous Hall effect in TbMn6Sn6
abstract: Abstract The anomalous Hall effect is the transverse voltage response in the presence of out-of-plane magnetization or non-zero Berry curvature, which, traditionally, is modulated by an out-of-plane magnetic field. Here we demonstrate a giant in-plane anomalous Hall effect (AHE) induced by coplanar magnetic fields in the quantum magnet TbMn 6 Sn 6  at room temperature. The very large Hall conductivity arises in response to an applied in-plane magnetic field and results from the tilting of the ferrimagnetic axis of the Mn and Tb moments to the out of plane direction. With the in-plane magnetic field aligning the ferrimagnetic axis, the Berry curvature induced giant anomalous Hall effect is observed. Further, we show that the in-plane field induced AHE is more pronounced below the temperature induced spin reorientation, showing a 2π periodicity in angular dependent measurements. Unlike the in-plane Hall effect previously observed primarily at low temperatures, the AHE we observe here represents the largest room-temperature response reported in a single material. Our results reveal strong coupling between an in-plane magnetic field and out-of-plane Berry curvature, enabling new opportunities to engineer spintronic and quantum device responses at practical operating temperatures.

title: Nucleophile–electrophile chemistry produces a stable interphase for long-Life anode-Less lithium metal batteries
abstract: Abstract Anode-less lithium (Li) metal batteries (ALLMBs) represent the optimal cell architecture for maximizing energy density, yet their practical viability is severely hindered by poor cycling life. This limitation stems from the unstable solid-electrolyte interphase (SEI), which drives continuous parasitic reactions with Li metal and induces severe interfacial degradation. Here we report a nucleophile–electrophile bridging strategy to construct a robust, passivating SEI that enables long-term stable cycling of ALLMBs. By leveraging a nucleophilic substitution mechanism, electron-rich organic species derived from the solvent, acting as nucleophiles, are covalently bridged by electron-deficient, boron-centred electrophiles derived from the anion. This molecular-level integration overcomes the inherent fragility of the SEI organic phase, generating mechanically robust oligoborates that resist interfacial degradation, along with lithium fluoride (LiF) nanocrystals nucleated in-situ to facilitate rapid Li +  transport. The resulting oligoborate–LiF hybrid SEI enables highly reversible Li plating/stripping and remarkably extends the ALLMB cycling life by 12-fold, maintaining 80% capacity over 300 cycles. The superior cyclability is maintained even under stringent practical conditions (high cathode loading, lean electrolyte supply, and pouch-cell operation). This work establishes a fundamentally new paradigm in interphase engineering, paving the way for high-energy, reliable ALLMBs.

title: Nanocatalytic modulation of thrombin-ferroptosis axis for efficient intervention of ischemic stroke
abstract: Abstract Ischemic stroke represents a leading cause of global mortality. Current therapeutic strategies, including recombinant tissue plasminogen activator and mechanical thrombectomy, are constrained by suboptimal recanalization, high recurrence rates, and reperfusion injury. In this work, we initially identified elevated intrathrombotic thrombin as a critical mediator of fibrinolytic resistance and a driver of ferroptosis-related neuronal injury following stroke. To specifically target this thrombin dysregulation, we designed ultrasmall tungsten-based polyoxometalate (W-POM) nanodots capable of penetrating the blood-brain barrier. In addition to their specific reactive oxygen species-scavenging capability, W-POM nanodots primarily modulate thrombin activity and attenuate its pathological signaling. In both thrombin-induced and ischemia-reperfusion injury models, W-POM nanodots significantly improve neurological outcomes by directly suppressing thrombin activity and inhibiting thrombin-driven ferroptosis. Furthermore, W-POM nanodots remodel the thrombotic microenvironment and reduce neuroinflammation, thereby conferring robust neuroprotection. This study highlights the thrombin-ferroptosis pathway as a key mechanistic axis in stroke and introduces a nanotherapeutic platform for targeted thrombin modulation in ischemic stroke therapy.

title: The protein phosphatase 2A catalytic subunit Pph22 partners with Tap42 and Rrd2 to control viability and virulence in Cryptococcus neoformans
abstract: Abstract Protein phosphatase 2A regulates eukaryotic signaling, but the function of its associated regulators remains poorly understood in the human fungal pathogen  Cryptococcus neoformans . Here, we used affinity purification coupled with mass spectrometry and identified 81 candidate proteins associated with the catalytic subunit Pph22, including the scaffold subunit Tpd3, the regulator Tap42, and the protein phosphatase methylesterase 1. Conditional-expression and meiotic spore analyses supported an essential role for  TAP42  in viability. We identified CNAG_05505 as the Rrd2 ortholog and detected an interaction between Rrd2 and Pph22 in a yeast two-hybrid assay. Deletion of  RRD2  impaired thermotolerance, altered responses to multiple stresses and antifungal agents, reduced melanin and capsule production, delayed sexual development, and inhibited titan cell formation. Mutants also displayed altered cell wall staining and reduced expression of genes involved in chitin synthesis and deacetylation.  RRD2  deletion increased basal Hog1 phosphorylation, whereas  PPH22  overexpression reduced it. Double-mutant analysis revealed phenotype-dependent genetic interactions between  RRD2  and  HOG1 . Although  RRD2  deletion did not significantly alter overall survival in the  Drosophila  infection assay, it markedly attenuated virulence in mice: all mutant-infected mice survived the 70-day observation period, and fungal burdens were reduced across multiple organs at 21 days post-infection. These findings distinguish the essential contribution of Tap42 from the broad roles of Rrd2 in stress adaptation, morphogenesis, cell surface organization, and mammalian virulence, extending the functional analysis of the cryptococcal protein phosphatase 2A regulatory network.

title: Genetic architectures of floral pigment and patterning in hybrid monkeyflowers
abstract: Abstract Coloration in living organisms varies in hue, saturation, and pattern. Here we use genetic mapping to investigate all three elements in monkeyflowers  Mimulus luteus  var.  variegatus  and  M. cupreus , whose flower petals differ in both yellow carotenoid and magenta cyanidin (anthocyanin) pigmentation and whose hybrids exhibit anthocyanin pattern variation not seen in either parent. We report two QTLs associated with carotenoid intensity, and show that lighter yellow petals accumulate relatively high proportions of beta-carotene at the expense of downstream carotenoids. We propose that the derived loss of carotenoid saturation in  M. l. variegatus  is due to a function-reducing mutation in a  Beta-Carotene Hydroxylase  candidate gene, possibly coupled with a reduction in the availability of carotenoid-storing chromoplasts influenced by the  ORANGE  candidate gene. We next identify five QTLs associated with the spatial patterning of anthocyanin pigment. Two QTLs, 9b and 23, each contain genes in the anthocyanin-activating subgroup of the  MYB  family. We hypothesize that  MYB5a/NEGAN , at QTL-9b, activates spot formation in hybrids as part of a Turing-type reaction-diffusion system, while a MYB at QTL-23 activates solid, non-Turing-type anthocyanin pigmentation and may also be able to activate the  variegatus  allele of  MYB5a/NEGAN . In addition to the apparently stochastic placement of most spots (consistent with a Turing mechanism), some pattern aspects – such as spots at the petal tips – appear to conform to a positional specification model in which spot location is predetermined. Collectively, this work begins to identify how combinations of yellow and red hues, shifts in carotenoid intensity, and two cryptic patterning systems all contribute to the complexity of color divergence between two close relatives.

title: Seeing through hypoxia: an oxygen-independent fluorescent reporter reveals ferritin regulation and mitochondrial remodeling in Caenorhabditis elegans
abstract: Abstract GFP-like fluorescent proteins, including GFP, mCherry, and their derivatives, have transformed in vivo biology but require molecular oxygen for chromophore maturation, potentially decoupling fluorescence from protein abundance under hypoxia. Here, we developed  Ce FbFP, a  Caenorhabditis elegans -optimized flavin-binding fluorescent protein (FbFP) that matures independently of oxygen, and benchmarked it against mCherry using matched reporters driven by the ferritin gene  ftn-1  promoter. Both reporters detected  ftn-1  induction at 0.5% O 2 , but  Ce FbFP produced a larger, more reproducible fold induction and remained robust at 0.2% O 2 . Following hypoxia, 2 h of reoxygenation at 21% O 2  increased mCherry fluorescence 4.5-fold despite declining mCherry protein abundance, demonstrating that oxygen-dependent maturation can drive fluorescence and reporter abundance in opposite directions; by contrast,  Ce FbFP fluorescence and protein abundance remained concordant. Using  Ce FbFP, we found that pathogenic bacteria and hydrogen sulfide regulate  ftn-1  differentially during hypoxia and that  ftn-1 , unlike the related ferritin gene  ftn-2 , is required for hypoxic survival. Mitochondrially targeted  Ce FbFP revealed reduced mitochondrial area and perimeter and increased network fragmentation in animals maintained chronically at 0.5% O 2 , without the reoxygenation that GFP-like reporters require—itself an acute mitochondrial stimulus. To our knowledge, this is the first use of an FbFP as a transcriptional reporter in an intact metazoan during prolonged hypoxia. By eliminating the oxygen dependence of reporter fluorescence,  Ce FbFP overcomes a fundamental limitation of GFP-like proteins and enables faithful interrogation of iron homeostasis, H 2 S responses, host–pathogen interactions, and mitochondrial adaptation in living animals under sustained low oxygen.

title: GLAND: Resolving small and non-continuous tissue domains via a hybrid attention mechanism
abstract: Abstract  Motivation Recent advances in spatial transcriptomic technology provide unprecedented insights into tissue architecture by enabling high-throughput gene expression profiling with the corresponding spatial context. While identifying spatial domains is a prerequisite for understanding tissue heterogeneity and functional organization, current computational methods often fail to resolve non-continuous or small domains that, despite their biological significance, exhibit complex spatial distribution. Results We present GLAND, a deep learning framework with a hybrid attention mechanism designed to capture multi-scale spatial dependencies. GLAND utilizes a spatial outlier detection strategy to refine the spatial graph, coupled with a hybrid encoder that simultaneously captures long-range biological similarity and localized spatial continuity. Comprehensive benchmarking across 39 slices and 7 spatial transcriptomic platforms demonstrates that GLAND achieves superior performance in identifying not only traditional continuous spatial domains but also non-continuous and small domains. Within the complex tumor microenvironment, GLAND accurately resolves non-continuous tumor regions and small lymphoid aggregates. Its learned spot embeddings bridge spatial gaps by preserving the transcriptomic identity of tumor domains across distal locations, facilitating a unified characterization of heterogeneous tissue landscapes. Availability and implementation GLAND is freely available at  https://github.com/CSUBioGroup/GLAND . All data have been deposited to Zenodo at  https://zenodo.org/records/18756215 . Supplementary information Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

title: GSP: a multi-scale metric for evaluation of 3D RNA structure predictions
abstract: Abstract  Motivation Accurate prediction of RNA 3D structures remains a central challenge in structural bioinformatics, necessitating reliable measures to quantify similarity between predicted models and experimentally determined reference structures. Currently, many scoring functions are available to assess different aspects of the tertiary structures of biomolecules. On the one hand, global measures average local irregularities, so that structures with distortions in different regions might generally be considered structurally similar. On the other hand, local conformational measures focus on specific inter-residue interactions and often fail to capture the broader topological context. Thus, there is a lack of methods capable of comprehensively assessing structural discrepancies across various spatial scales. Results To address this gap, we introduce Geometric Spherical Precision (GSP), a novel multi-scale score that assesses the quality of 3D RNA and RNP complex predictions. It integrates multiple partial scores computed from local geometric agreements into a single, easy-to-read, normalized score for ranking these predictions. We demonstrate that GSP reliably identifies models with comparable overall deviations, while maintaining strong agreement with global measures. These properties make it a useful tool for benchmarking and comparing 3D RNA structures and RNP complexes. Availability and Implementation The GSP script and evaluation results against state-of-the-art measures on the RNA-Puzzles and CASP15 datasets are available at  https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19608328 . Supplementary information Supplementary data are available at  Bioinformatics  online.

title: BioBatchNet: A Dual-Encoder Framework for Robust Batch Effect Correction in Imaging Mass Cytometry
abstract: Abstract  Motivation Imaging Mass Cytometry (IMC) is a cutting-edge technology for analysing spatially resolved protein expression at the single-cell level. However, its downstream analyses are often hindered by batch effects, which introduce systematic biases and obscure biological variations. Existing correction methods, largely developed for scRNA-seq data, face challenges in adapting to IMC data due to differences in data characteristics. Moreover, these methods struggle to achieve precise control, leading to either over-correction by removing critical biological information, or under-correction by leaving residual batch effects. Furthermore, IMC data often feature overlapping cell populations, complicating clustering and downstream analysis. These challenges underscore the need for a robust and controllable batch effect correction approach tailored to IMC data. Results We present BioBatchNet, a dual-encoder framework utilising adversarial training to explicitly disentangle batch-specific and biological signals. BioBatchNet enables controllable batch effect correction, balancing correction with preservation of biological variation. We evaluated BioBatchNet on three IMC datasets, where it outperformed seven benchmarking methods with robustness in both correction and biological signal conservation. Additionally, we developed a Constrained-Pairwise-Clustering (CPC) method, which employs constrained pairs to improve clustering performance, even in datasets with overlapping cell populations. To validate its generalisability, we adapted BioBatchNet for scRNA-seq datasets by altering the data likelihood from Gaussian to Zero-Inflated Negative Binomial distribution. This adapted version achieved competitive performance across four scRNA-seq datasets, obtaining the highest overall score on three of them. These results demonstrate BioBatchNet’s generalisability and robustness in correcting batch effects across diverse single-cell datasets and underscore its potential for large-scale biological analyses. Availability and Implementation The source code is available at  https://github.com/UoM-HealthAI/BioBatchNet , with an archived snapshot on Zenodo (DOI:  https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18783840 ).

title: SpatialMuSC: Spatial Graph-Conditioned Diffusion Refinement for Robust Spatial Multi-Omics Integration
abstract: Abstract  Motivation Emerging spatial multi-omics technologies enable the simultaneous profiling of multiple molecular layers within the same tissue section, offering new opportunities to interrogate tissue organization in its native spatial context. However, sequencing-derived spatial multi-omics data are often affected by intrinsic perturbations, such as technical noise, missing values, sparsity and measurement bias. These perturbations make existing methods that mainly use spatial graphs for neighborhood aggregation insufficient to recover continuous tissue-region structures, while unconstrained representation learning may propagate noisy associations and lead to fragmented spatial domains. Results We present SpatialMuSC, a robust spatial multi-omics integration framework centering on spatial graph-conditioned diffusion refinement and perturbation-invariant fusion consistency. SpatialMuSC introduces spatial topology as conditional information into the latent diffusion process, enabling spatial adjacency to guide neighborhood aggregation, spatial structure propagation and graph-aware denoising of latent states. Perturbation-invariant fusion consistency further encourages stable multi-omic fusion under perturbed observations. We evaluate SpatialMuSC on diverse spatial multi-omics datasets across different tissues and sequencing platforms, including 10x Visium, Stereo-CITE-seq, SPOTS and spatial epigenome–transcriptome data. Across these benchmarks, SpatialMuSC consistently outperforms ten state-of-the-art methods in spatial domain identification and tissue-structure preservation. Ablation analyses confirm the contributions of graph-conditioned diffusion refinement and perturbation-invariant fusion consistency, rather than post hoc graph smoothing or graph propagation alone. In particular, SpatialMuSC effectively distinguishes adjacent tissue regions, preserves block-wise smoothness and layered architectures, and shows more stable performance in missing-observation stress tests, while hippocampal marker, enrichment, and paired RNA–ATAC analyses identify a GCL-associated neuronal program and a TTR-associated accessibility feature in a choroid plexus-enriched domain. Availability and Implementation The source code is available at  https://github.com/CSUBioGroup/SpatialMuSC . Supplementary Information Supplementary data are available online.

title: Ambient Drying Enabled Energy Efficient Fabrication of Skin‐Free Aerogel Evaporators for High‐Performance Interfacial Solar Evaporation
abstract:
