This approach preserves classification accuracy while improving calibration and resolving continuous pathway activities across individual cells. Importantly, intermediate scores primarily reflect ambiguity in cellular response states rather than insufficient model knowledge. Applied to engineered and natural tissues, the calibrated model successfully recovered graded activities. These results establish combinatorial perturbation screens as a self-calibrating framework for decoding graded cellular responses.

title: SOUR Disentangles Heritable and Microenvironmental Contributions to Intratumoral Heterogeneity in Spatial Lineage Tracing Data
abstract: Intratumoral heterogeneity is hypothesized to be a major contributor to treatment resistance, yet the processes that generate it remain only partially understood. New technologies enable measurement of gene expression in individual tumor cells while also determining where the cells are located within a tumor and how they are related through cell division. A central question for such data is how much gene expression differences reflect characteristics passed from parent cells to their descendants, rather than influences from their local surroundings. Distinguishing these influences is challenging because closely related cells often reside near one another. Existing methods examine the relationship between gene expression and each of these factors separately, and can therefore incorrectly attribute spatial effects to ancestry or inherited effects to spatial location. Here, we present SOUR, a statistical method that uses both cell ancestry and spatial location to estimate their respective contributions to differences in gene expression. Using simulated data and two spatial lineage tracing datasets, we demonstrate that SOUR can estimate the separate contributions of cell ancestry and spatial location to variation in gene expression, while substantially reducing the confounding observed with existing approaches.

title: PhageLysClass: Evidence-aware classification of phage lytic proteins using protein language models
abstract: Phage lytic proteins are promising antibacterial and biotechnological candidates, yet uncertain annotations, modular architectures, and class imbalance complicate sequence-based classification. We developed PhageLysClass, an evidence-aware framework for recognizing lytic proteins and distinguishing Endolysins, Depolymerases, and virion-associated lytic enzymes. From 442,329 unique phage sequences, including 11,867 evidence-supported positives, we defined distinct candidate non-target, unlabeled, and challenge populations. Seven supervised and two positive-unlabeled tasks were evaluated across factorial redundancy and train-test homology conditions, yielding 2,240 and 768 experiments, respectively. Redundancy reduction influenced generalization more strongly than homology separation, with non-additive interactions between them. ESM2-T30 consistently outperformed alternative representations and supported a hierarchical classifier achieving approximately 0.89 MCC under strict R30/S30 conditions in the selected, pre-refitting benchmark. Applied without retraining to 77,897 sequences across three collections, PhageLysClass combined predictions with physicochemical and geometric contextualization, highlighting Depolymerase-like candidates among structurally ambiguous proteins while distinguishing reference-supported assignments from extrapolation.

title: Single-cell study of the FCG rat model and cross-species comparison reveal stronger gene regulation by sex chromosome complement in the medial septum
abstract: Sex differences are prominent in neuropsychiatric, neurological, and neurodegenerative conditions. While both gonads (ovaries vs. testes) and sex chromosome complement (SCC; XX vs. XY) contribute to sex differences, these effects are hard to differentiate in humans and gonadal contributions have been considered dominant in the brain. The four core genotypes (FCG) mouse model distinguishes between SCC and gonadal effects but whether findings are conserved across species remains unclear. Here, we present the first application of the novel FCG-derived rat model to explore cell-type-specific sex differences in the medial septum (MS), which shows robust structural sex differences, and convergence/divergence between species. Differential gene expression, pathway, transcription factor, and gene regulatory network analyses show dominant SCC effects and concordant gonadal effects on gene and network regulation in rat MS cell types. Comparison between the FCG rat and mouse models find convergence across species on the dominance of the SCC in regulating gene expression in concert with gonadal effects in the MS, despite divergence in individual sex-biased genes. In both species, the sex-biased, cell-type-specific MS genes and networks are associated with diverse diseases relevant to MS functions, such as anxiety, Alzheimers Disease, epilepsy, and schizophrenia, that can be targeted by proposed therapeutic candidates. Our cross-species investigation identifies a conserved dominance of SCC effects in sex-biased gene expression in the MS, thereby challenging the classical gonad-centric view of sexual differentiation in the brain and highlighting the MS as an important region for the study of sex differences driven by the sex chromosome complement.

title: Modelling Phenotypic Assay Noise for Multivariable Biomarker Discovery using Deep Neural Networks
abstract: Accurately predicting cancer drug response remains a major challenge in precision oncology. Although some therapies are guided by clinically-approved biomarkers, these markers often yield limited predictive value and are unavailable for many drugs. Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning approaches trained on large-scale cancer cell line pharmacogenomic screens offer a promising route to more comprehensive response prediction, yet they generally assume that phenotypic readouts are measured without error. This assumption is problematic because viability-based drug response assays are inherently noisy, potentially causing models to learn experimental artefacts rather than biologically meaningful determinants of sensitivity. Here, we show that phenotypic measurement noise is present in four widely used cancer cell line screening datasets and introduce Deep Concordance Index Networks (DeepCINET), a deep learning framework that explicitly accounts for this noise. Across datasets, incorporating this noise-aware ranking strategy improves generalization across experimental conditions and to previously unseen samples. DeepCINET outperforms baseline models in multiple settings, with particularly notable gains in prioritizing the most drug-sensitive cell lines. Together, these results establish phenotypic assay noise as a critical and previously overlooked source of error in drug response modelling and provide a principled framework for noise-aware multivariable biomarker discovery.

title: Replicate libraries set the noise floor for cell-state claims in cross-sectional single-cell data: an empirical audit in drug-tolerant EGFR-mutant PC9 cells
abstract: Claims that drug-tolerant cancer cells occupy stable states rest on single-cell snapshots with one sequencing library per condition, where a difference between conditions cannot be separated from a difference between libraries. No standard says how far a contrast must exceed replicate-library variation. We contribute a replicate-referenced framework: a distance ratio expressing a contrast as a multiple of the distance between replicate libraries of one condition, and a library-level permutation test giving exact p values by relabelling whole libraries. In simulations, single-library tests and a split-half reference rejected a true null in 99 to 100% of runs, and Harmony followed by a cell-level test did so in 12 to 32% with structured library effects. With four libraries per arm, the library-level test held false positives at 3 to 5% in every setting. In public osimertinib-treated PC9 data with two libraries per condition (GSE150949), halves of one library were indistinguishable, replicate libraries separated at 59 to 93% accuracy, and contrasts between times in drug and sort gates exceeded replicate distance 4.5- to 51-fold. In Drop-seq erlotinib data with one library per condition (GSE149383), two libraries of the same condition separated more readily (93.3%) than withdrawn and re-treated cells (88.5%). Cross-sectional contrasts should be reported as multiples of replicate-library distance and, with four or more libraries per arm, tested by library-level permutation. Cells moved away from the untreated profile and stayed away, but the data do not support attractor-style inference, nor do they show that tolerant states are not bistable.

title: MSGFLEX: An optimized end-to-end pipeline for proteomics and metaproteomics analysis built on MS-GF+ with a dedicated rescoring model XPECTRA
abstract: Mass spectrometry-based proteomics workflows often face competing demands between identification sensitivity, false discovery rate (FDR) control, and computational scalability, particularly for metaproteomic datasets that require searching large and complex sequence databases. Here, we present MSGFLEX, an integrated end-to-end workflow that combines database searching, machine-learning based rescoring, and peptide-to-protein quantitative inference. MSGFLEX integrates three components: SPARX handles raw file conversion, and MS-GF+ database searching; XPECTRA is a cross-validated XGBoost ensemble that rescores peptide-spectrum matches by combining ensemble predictions with MS-GF+ search evidence through noisy-OR fusion model. QUANTIX provides protein quantification through multiple protein rollup strategies. Across four benchmarking datasets, XPECTRA consistently increased peptide and protein identifications relative to Percolator, MS2Rescore, and MSBooster. On a human gut metaproteome dataset, XPECTRA achieved the largest effect size among all methods evaluated (Cohen's d = 0.95; p < 0.0005). SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP)-based analysis indicated that XPECTRA learned consistent relationships from spectral and physicochemical features. Database partitioning does not introduce detectable bias in peptide identification or FDR estimation, while QUANTIX's DWrollup provides the most accurate recovery of known protein abundance changes in a ground-truth spike-in benchmark. Together, these results establish MSGFLEX as a scalable and interpretable framework for mass-spectrometry based proteomics and metaproteomics.

title: Systematic inference of biological relatedness across the global ancient DNA record
abstract: The rapidly expanding scale of ancient DNA data creates an increasing need for high-performance software methods. One area for such improvement is the inference of pairwise biological relatedness, a prominent aspect of many ancient DNA studies. We present fastpmr, a fast and memory-efficient method for biological relatedness inference based on the computation of pairwise mismatch rates. We demonstrate that fastpmr can achieve over 1000x speed-up over READv2, a widely used relatedness-inference method. We leverage this performance to investigate relatedness at the scale of the global ancient DNA record. Analyzing biological relatedness across all pairs in the Allen Ancient DNA Resource (n = 19,118 ancient and 23,089 total samples) recapitulates human evolutionary history and identifies previously unknown genetic duplicates and likely sample mix-ups, demonstrating fastpmr's utility for ancient DNA analysis and quality control at scale.

title: MDQ: A DockQ-Inspired Scoring Function for Assessing Interface Similarity and Clustering in Molecular Dynamics
abstract: Assessing the similarity between protein-protein interfaces is essential for evaluating docking models, yet widely used metrics such as DockQ rely on a single native reference structure and yield asymmetric scores, making them unsuitable for molecular dynamics (MD) trajectories where no reference exists and frame-to-frame comparisons are required. Here, we introduce the MDQ, a fully symmetric reformulation of DockQ designed for MD trajectory analysis. MDQ replaces the fraction of native contacts with the Fraction of Shared Contacts (FSC), and redefines interface and ligand RMSD as weighted variants that penalize low atomic overlap between compared frames. The score can be used to follow structure/contacts convergence of an interface along a trajectory. And it is inverted to produce a true distance metric ranging from 0 (identical interfaces) to 1 (distinct interfaces), directly compatible with distance-based clustering. Applied to two benchmark complexes, Ail-Vitronectin and TGFBR1-FKBP12, MDQ heatmaps reveal global interface stability alongside subtle conformational rearrangements, while DBSCAN and hierarchical clustering of the MDQ distance matrix identifies representative conformational states. Then non-bonding interaction found in clusters were identified by MICLOT software. MDQ thus provides a robust and frame-to-frame symmetric framework for monitoring protein-protein interface conformational and interaction heterogeneity throughout MD simulations.

title: Curated annotations locate biological concepts in protein language models from layers to neurons
abstract: Interpretability methods describe what a network has learned, yet their claims are rarely tested against model-independent ground truth. We argue that proteins are an ideal modality for interpretability since curators annotate functional sites residue by residue. Across three ESMC protein language models (300M-6B parameters), we show that conclusions depend on where models are read, how concepts are decoded, which units are examined, and how they are scored. Concepts become linearly readable along depth long before erasure impairs masked-token prediction, and 20-fold scaling shifts concept depth more than peak score. Most of a nonlinear probe's lead over a linear one reflects fitting and readout shape rather than nonlinear encoding. Over whole proteins, saturated metrics render feed-forward neurons indistinguishable from random rotations. At annotated residues, dual-signed neuron poles identify 2.5-5.4 times as many concepts as rotations without training, though sparse autoencoders identify more. Without held-out validation, however, shuffled annotations label nearly every latent, and causal reliance emerges in neuron groups rather than single poles. Reading selected intra-block states exposes binding and active sites that stream probes read poorly and lifts a simple probe 5% above the best published MCC on a leakage-controlled interaction benchmark. We recommend reading a model directly against annotation, scoring units where they fire with a measure that is not saturated, and training a dictionary only where it adds coverage.

title: VEGABrain: a Visualizer of Enriched Gene Analysis for the developing human brain
abstract: RNA sequencing datasets are widely reused resources in developmental neuroscience, yet inspecting them spatially remains unclear and difficult. Here, we present VEGABrain, an openly accessible web tool that renders bulk RNA-seq onto brain cortical and subcortical atlas surfaces across five human developmental windows spanning the first trimester to adulthood. Beyond single-gene maps, VEGABrain contributes a composite per-region enrichment layer using single-sample gene set enrichment analysis (ssGSEA) scores precomputed for [~]19,000 gene sets drawn from Gene Ontology, Reactome, KEGG, BioCarta, the Human Phenotype Ontology and the MSigDB hallmark collection, and aggregated to a score for every gene set, developmental window and brain region. Furthermore, VEGABrain allows users to submit a custom gene list and obtain its ssGSEA map across development, computed on demand. VEGABrain is open source and requires no installation, offering easy-to-query expression throughout development and brain areas.

title: A site-resolved post-translational modification framework for drug-response analysis
abstract: Post-translational modifications (PTMs) regulate protein activity and treatment-associated signalling, providing functional information that can connect drug-response estimates with candidate pharmacodynamic measurements. Assessing this information requires a framework that determines its contribution beyond fixed molecular features while retaining the identity of the modified sites underlying model predictions. We developed the PTM Biological Dynamics Layer (PTM-BDL), which integrates typed PTM states with protein sequence, structure-derived and drug chemical features to predict log-transformed half-maximal inhibitory concentration and resistance while providing site-level interpretation through integrated gradients. Retrospective evaluation used source-derived and propagated PTM profiles across biologically distinct BCR-ABL, HDAC/EP300 and EGFR/ERBB2 settings, yielding internal areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROCs) between 0.785 and 0.946. Retraining demonstrated a consistent incremental contribution from PTM inputs in K562/CML, with a mean AUROC increase of 0.0268 and positive gains in all five folds, alongside more modest incremental gains in HeLa/HDAC and EGFR/ERBB2. Within K562/CML, CRKL Y207 and STAT5A Y694 retained the leading attribution ranks for their proteins across three seeds, while greater PTM attribution in dasatinib than in cytotoxic drug contexts identified a focused setting for pharmacodynamic investigation. These findings support context-dependent use of PTM information and connect predictive assessment with prioritisation of individual sites, providing a basis for targeted pharmacodynamic measurements and independent experimental validation.

title: SNP2Cluster-Py: A pathogen-agnostic, context-aware framework for Core SNP and transmission-cluster analysis
abstract: Whole-genome sequencing enables high-resolution identification of genetically related pathogen isolates, but genomic similarity alone does not establish epidemiologically meaningful transmission. We developed SNP2Cluster-Py, an open-source Python framework that separates context-aware Core SNP clustering from the subsequent application of epidemiological and temporal criteria. The software accepts a precomputed pairwise Core SNP-distance matrix and user-configured metadata and supports analysis of all eligible isolates in a single context, as well as sequence-type, geographical, epidemiological and ordered composite contexts. Within each context, authoritative Core clusters are defined as connected components of an SNP-threshold graph; K-means assignments and silhouette widths are retained as exploratory diagnostics only. We evaluated the workflow using 172 Klebsiella pneumoniae isolates from six neonatal-surveillance hospitals in South Africa, a focused 36-isolate single-hospital subset from the same surveillance dataset, and 168 Streptococcus pneumoniae carriage isolates from Ghana. In the full K. pneumoniae dataset, ST-only analysis assigned 141 isolates to Core SNP clusters, whereas Facility + ST analysis assigned 134, demonstrating how facility stratification can remove cross-facility genomic connections. In the single-hospital subset, both contexts assigned 30 of 36 isolates to five Core clusters, and Facility analysis retained 23 isolates in four temporally compatible clusters. In the pneumococcal dataset, ST-context analysis assigned 114 isolates to 38 Core clusters, which were characterised across sampling locations and time through Community analysis. SNP2Cluster-Py therefore provides a reproducible framework for adapting genomic clustering to specific surveillance questions while maintaining a clear distinction between genomic relatedness, analytically inferred transmission clusters and confirmed direct transmission. SNP2Cluster-Py v1.1.2 is available under the Apache License 2.0 through GitHub and Zenodo.

title: Improving Target-Adverse Event Association Prediction via Inverse Node Frequency Transformation to Mitigate Knowledge Graph Topological Bias
abstract: Motivation: Identifying significant associations between therapeutic protein targets and adverse events (AEs) is a critical component of drug safety assessment. To accelerate the process, machine learning methods have been developed to predict these associations as edges in network data integrating molecular interactions and other key biomedical knowledge. However, these networks often suffer from topological imbalances where a minority of "hub" nodes determine the predictive signal. This "topological" or "degree bias" can lead to poor performance on novel or understudied targets where safety inference is most needed. Results: We introduce Inverse Node Frequency (INF), a generally applicable node degree-based approach for mitigating topological bias. Employing an enriched biomedical knowledge graph and our own carefully curated target-adverse event associations, we apply INF as a normalisation procedure on a class of graph-derived features called metapaths and evaluate their resulting target-AE association prediction performance. Our results demonstrate that INF significantly improves the true positive rate (TPR/recall) for low-degree targets compared to the untransformed metapath features as well as a popular established normalisation method, while also achieving highly competitive hits@k, a ranking-based metric for knowledge graph-based inference. We also evaluated INF on an external set of target-AE associations never before used for modelling, on which INF also showed superior resilience compared to the two benchmarks.

title: NeuroSim: a clinically informed multi-disorder EEG simulator with personalized pattern injection and AI-driven neurological modeling
abstract: Deep learning for electroencephalography (EEG) based neurodiagnostics is constrained by the limited availability of labeled clinical recordings. Datasets covering Alzheimers disease (AD), Parkinsons disease (PD), schizophrenia (SCZ), epilepsy (EPI), and frontotemporal dementia (FTD) are scarce, demographically narrow, and heterogeneous across acquisition sites, while privacy requirements restrict data sharing. Existing EEG simulators typically address a single disorder or trade biological interpretability for statistical fidelity. This study presents NeuroSim, a simulation framework that generates synthetic multichannel EEG with user-controlled injection of disease-specific patterns across five disorders and multiple severity levels. A physiologically motivated baseline generator produces band-limited rhythms, event-related potentials, artifacts, and hierarchical subject-level and trial-level variability. Disease patterns are introduced through region-specific and severity-specific spectral modulation that encodes established biomarkers, including posterior alpha suppression in AD, motor beta enhancement in PD, and spike-wave discharges in EPI. An interactive interface exposes montage, sampling rate, duration, artifacts, stimuli, affected regions, and severity, and exports signals with reproducible metadata. The simulated signals reproduced the expected biomarker directionality under spectral, topographic, and multivariate statistical analysis. A convolutional-attention classifier trained on simulated data reached 95.3 to 96.8 percent hold-out accuracy, and post hoc explainability analyses produced class-separable embeddings with attributions concentrated on pathophysiologically expected electrodes. Application of the analysis pipeline to recordings from the Temple University Hospital EEG Corpus confirmed compatibility with heterogeneous clinical data. In subject-level augmentation experiments on real clinical EEG, supplementing real training data with NeuroSim samples increased classification accuracy from 91.6 to 94.5 percent for AD versus healthy controls and from 90.9 to 94.0 percent for PD versus healthy controls, exceeding the improvement obtained with conventional signal-level augmentation. NeuroSim is released as open-source software to support augmentation, benchmarking, and explainable artificial intelligence in neurological diagnostics.

title: Evaluating cell-free RNA extraction platforms for RNA liquid biopsy via nanopore sequencing
abstract: RNA liquid biopsies provide systemic insights into health and disease by profiling cell-free RNAs (cfRNAs) secreted into the circulation. While cfRNAs are thought to be short or fragmented, recent efforts using long-read nanopore sequencing have found that thousands of longer, full-length cfRNAs are highly abundant in plasma. However, cfRNA extraction methods have not been rigorously evaluated to assess reproducibility, cfRNA length, and transcriptome complexity. Here we show that extraction workflow is a major source of variation by comparing identical plasma samples across three different cfRNA extraction platforms. While these platforms recover comparable quantities of cfRNA, we perform nanopore sequencing to show that they differ in their cfRNA composition based on read-length distribution and biotype representation. Principal component analysis and hierarchical clustering of variable protein-coding and repeat-derived cfRNAs show that samples tend to cluster based on extraction platform. Robust detection of specific biotypes is contingent on extraction platform, as evidenced by significant enrichment of Alu element- and long noncoding RNA (lncRNA)-derived cfRNAs in some but not all methodologies. Our results reveal that cfRNA extraction platforms influence the composition and complexity of downstream libraries, highlighting the importance of selecting the right platform for profiling disease-relevant biomarkers in RNA liquid biopsy studies.

title: Tissue-specific mucociliary regulatory programs in the healthy human endocervix and ectocervix
abstract: The cervix is a dynamic mucosal barrier in the female reproductive tract that balances inflammatory and anti inflammatory functions to regulate physiologically critical functions, including pregnancy, sperm transport, fertility, and protection of the upper reproductive tract from infection. Despite its central role in reproduction, the cellular and transcriptional organization of the healthy human cervix remains incompletely characterized, including how clinical sampling methods influence the epithelial populations recovered and how cervical mucociliary programs compare with those of pulmonary epithelium. We performed single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNAseq) on paired Tischler punch biopsy and endocervical curettage (ECC) samples from four healthy, exogenous hormone-naive donors to generate a dedicated transcriptomic map of the healthy human cervix followed by an integrative computational analysis framework combining differential expression, functional enrichment, cell to cell communication, cross-tissue mapping, and regulon activity inference. This approach identified ten cell types spanning epithelial, stromal, vascular, and immune cell populations and found that sampling method strongly influenced cellular composition and transcriptional state as Tischler punch biopsy preferentially recovered basal and suprabasal epithelial populations, whereas ECC enriched for secretory and ciliated epithelial cell types. Cross-tissue comparison with publicly available healthy lung epithelial transcriptomics dataset revealed conserved mucociliary cell types alongside tissue-divergent transcriptional programs, including distinct regulation of ion transport and mucin associated genes. Together, these findings demonstrate the importance of sampling modality in resolving cervical epithelial heterogeneity, and reveal tissue-specialized mucociliary regulatory programs underlying cervical mucus biology and fertility regulation.

title: scPACE: A Personalized Autoencoder for Cell Evolution in Single-Cell Transcriptomics
abstract: Single-cell studies increasingly profile large cohorts of individuals, measuring thousands of cells in each donor. These datasets contain information at two levels: variation among individual cells and among donors. Analyzing both levels requires methods that can learn cellular representations, infer cell and donor states, and account for cell types that may be missing in some donors. Existing methods partially address these tasks. We introduce scPACE, a hierarchical personalized variational autoencoder handling these tasks. scPACE learns a cell representation, a cell state, and then aggregates cells within each type of cell to infer a donor state. It also imputes missing cell types with confidence estimates. Across simulated cohorts and a developing mouse visual-cortex dataset, scPACE recovered held-out cell and donor states accurately while achieving efficient cell-type imputation and representation. scPACE provides a unified framework for learning phenotypes across cellular and donor scales in cohort-scale single-cell transcriptomics.

title: RR3DD 2.0: an expanded database for RNA three-dimensional structure classification
abstract: RNA performs diverse biological functions by folding into specific 3D structures, which are often more conserved than their sequences. Systematic classification of RNA 3D structures is fundamental to understanding structure-function relationships. We previously established RR3DD, the first classification database based on global 3D structural similarity. However, its version 1.0 contained data only up to July 2021 and can no longer reflect the rapidly growing RNA structure space since then. Here, we present RR3DD 2.0. Starting from the 7,466 PDB-format chains in 1.0, we incorporated 8,298 newly released or updated chains, expanding the dataset to 15,764 chains. Pairwise structural similarity (RMscore) was calculated using RMalign, and all chains were re-clustered to yield 1,042 clusters. Compared with 1.0, 2.0 not only increases sampling density but also identifies 342 new clusters. Notably, Cluster-891 and Cluster-899 correspond to the ROOL RNA and GOLLD RNA families, marking the first inclusion of these large structured bacterial ncRNAs into a global classification framework. Mapping the clusters to Rfam annotated 6,388 chains (40.5%) across 154 families. A single cluster can correspond to one or several Rfam families, indicating that global structure classification and sequence family classification are complementary. RR3DD 2.0 provides an updated web interface.

title: CELL-X: A Single-Cell Transcriptomics Framework for Cell-Type and Disease-State Prioritization of Type 2 Diabetes Risk Genes
abstract: Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified hundreds of loci associated with Type 2 Diabetes (T2D), yet pinpointing specific causal genes and their relevant cellular contexts remains a critical bottleneck. To address this gap, we developed CELL-X, a novel computational framework systematically integrating fine-mapped genetic evidence with high-resolution single-cell transcriptomics and disease progression dynamics. Utilizing a custom out-of-memory processing engine, we analyzed an integrated human pancreatic islet atlas of 245,878 cells without forced data downsampling. We evaluated 37 genetically supported T2D candidate genes, quantifying cell-type relevance via a max-scaled Cell Relevance Score (CRS). Disease-associated transcriptional dynamics were subsequently incorporated using a Disease Relevance Score (DRS) based on heterogeneous expression shifts across normal, prediabetic, and T2D metabolic states. CELL-X successfully identified beta cells as the dominant disease-relevant cellular context and prioritized established causal genes, including SLC30A8, GLIS3, GCK, and TCF7L2. Validation against a 30-gene benchmark demonstrated exceptional target recovery and significant metabolic pathway enrichment. Furthermore, rigorous statistical null modeling confirmed this prioritization is driven by true biological variance rather than background transcriptomic noise. Ultimately, CELL-X provides a highly scalable, robust framework for generating biologically informed hypotheses in complex polygenic disease research.

title: Learning RNA secondary structure from chemical probing with MXfold2
abstract: Training RNA secondary structure predictors is limited by scarce reference annotations, even as chemical probing produces abundant nucleotide-level measurements. These measurements inform pairing states without identifying base-pairing partners. Here we extend MXfold2, which combines neural and thermodynamic folding scores, to learn from probing profiles and predict RNA secondary structures from sequence alone. We introduce three training objectives. One learns from probing-assisted target structures. The other two use implicit maximum-likelihood estimation to pass surrogate gradients from reactivity-ranking and likelihood losses through discrete folding. Simulations, RNAgym measurements and external structural tests show improved chemical agreement and gains in exact base-pair prediction when chemical supervision is combined with structural pretraining and replay. Probing profiles can thus broaden the range of RNAs that inform sequence-only structure prediction, including RNA populations with few complete structure annotations.

title: Pangenome-guided interpretation of k-mer GWAS inCapsicum
abstract: Agronomic trait diversity in Capsicum is shaped by sequence variation that it is not always captured by SNPs called against a single reference genome. Reference-free k-mer GWAS can detect variants beyond SNPs, but significant k-mers are difficult to interpret as they lack genomic coordinates and annotation. In this study, we developed a pangenome-guided workflow to localize significant k-mers in a graph-based Capsicum pangenome. The workflow connects significant k-mers, identified through k-mer GWAS, to genomic positions, their annotations and homology groups. We applied this approach to a metabolite dataset of 343 C. annuum accessions, focusing on the cases of capsaicinoids and specific aroma compounds. For capsaicinoid content, our workflow provided insight in the haplotype composition of the sequenced accessions in the Pun1 locus and the genomic variations contributing to pungency. In the case of dehydroxylinalool oxide, the analysis identified that the haplotype associated to high phenotypes contained an extra terpene synthase (TPS). And last, the production of -ylangene seems to be influenced by a 2 Mb inversion on chromosome 9, right next to a terpene synthase gene. Integrating k-mer GWAS with graph-pangenome localization improves the interpretation of k-mer association signals in complex plant genomes. This workflow can help identify structural variation, haplotypes and candidate loci relevant for trait/metabolic diversity and future breeding applications.

title: Identification of seven candidate structured noncoding RNA motifs in protists by comparative genomics
abstract: Protists represent a highly diverse assemblage of predominantly unicellular eukaryotes, including protozoa, algae, and slime molds. Their essential roles in global ecosystems, along with their significance as human parasites, underscore the need for a deeper understanding of their conserved genetic elements. In this study, we employed an integrated computational approach combining CMfinder and R-scape to systematically identify and evaluate structured non-coding RNA (ncRNA) motifs across protist genomes. Through rigorous assessment and functional annotation, we report seven conserved structured ncRNAs that are likely functional RNA motifs involved in regulating the synthesis of the carbon fixation protein ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate carboxylase/oxygenase (RuBisCO), the light-harvesting and transfer protein phycocyanin, subunits of photosystems I and II, as well as mRNA splicing regulation. Notably, we also identified a structured ncRNA motif that may possess a dual function, capable of bidirectionally regulating the photosystem genes psaI and psbJ simultaneously. Our findings provide valuable insights into the diversity and functional significance of structured ncRNAs in microbial eukaryotes.

title: Cross-Species Dynamics of Transposable Elements in Aging Female Visceral Adipose Tissues
abstract: Transposable elements (TEs) make up nearly half of mammalian genomes and are increasingly implicated in genomic instability, cellular stress responses, aging, and age-related disease. Recent past research has highlighted their significant involvement in disease models such as cancer and Alzheimer's disease (AD), though much remains to be unraveled regarding these genomic insertions. In this study, we explore the involvement of TEs in aging female mouse and human visceral adipose tissue (VAT) using 10x single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) data analyzed with the computational tool SoloTE. By assessing the TE-annotated snRNA-seq count matrix using Seurat, we found that retrotransposons-specifically short interspersed nuclear elements (SINEs) and long interspersed nuclear elements (LINEs) on chromosomes 1 and 19-are significantly upregulated in aging female human VAT and in potential senescent cells (CDKN1A^+). Although changes in mouse VAT were less pronounced, long terminal repeats (LTRs) were predominant in aging mouse cells. Furthermore, analysis of upregulated features in aging and CDKN1A^+ female human VAT cells revealed that LINE and SINE TEs embedded within specific gene loci-most notably CUX1, SOD2, C3, NAMPT, ALDH1A3, IL6, and the non-coding RNA LOC105375913-exhibit a positive regulatory relationship with their host genes. Specifically, higher TE expression may directly upregulate host gene expression (e.g., C3 TEs driving C3 upregulation). Consistently ranking at the top of differentially expressed feature lists, these TEs act as potential drivers of aging and cellular senescence in female human VAT and can be plausible targets without risk of disruption of multiple biological systems.

title: Mapping Senescence Landscapes in Metabolic Liver Disease Progression
abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) affects more than 30% of the population, often progressing from reversible steatosis to irreversible fibrosis and cirrhosis. Although cellular senescence is implicated in driving MASLD, the evidence in human tissue and the mechanism are lacking. Here, we apply spatial transcriptomics and scRNAseq to human liver samples spanning healthy to fibrotic disease to address these knowledge gaps. Using a combination of cell stress, cell cycle arrest, extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling, and inflammatory genes, senescent microenvironments termed "SenSpots" were identified by Visium transcriptomics that predominantly localized to portal tracts and fibrotic septa across all specimens. Functional profiling revealed a fundamental phenotypic divergence: SenSpots in healthy liver displayed a physiological wound-healing and tissue-development program, whereas SenSpots in fibrotic tissue expressed genes related to inflammation, stress, and ECM-disassembly. Spatial deconvolution and network expansion analyses demonstrated that SenSpots act as epicenters for TGF-{beta}, NOTCH, complement, and ECM-reorganization signaling, which spreads into the surrounding tissue microenvironment as disease advances. Furthermore, scRNAseq data validated the Visium results and identified a previously unappreciated population of senescent Schwann cells in the diseased liver niche. These findings map the spatial origination and paracrine propagation of pathological senescence and identify senotypes associated with liver fibrosis.

title: Ionic condition-dependent allostery shapes ribosomal dynamics
abstract:
by Danis Yangaliev, Gürol M. Süel, S. Banu Ozkan 

Ionic composition is a key determinant of ribosomal RNA structure and function. Metal cations such as potassium (K + ) and magnesium (Mg 2+ ) stabilize rRNA architecture. While certain positions in the ribosome are strictly occupied by either potassium or magnesium for distinct structural or functional reasons, their broader role in modulating ribosomal dynamics remains poorly understood. Here, we use microsecond-scale coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations of the bacterial 70S ribosome to examine how ionic composition affects structural flexibility and long-range communication. We compare a native ribosome with experimentally resolved ions to two variants: a magnesium-enriched model, in which K +  ions are replaced with Mg 2+ , and a hydrated magnesium model. While these substitutions do not aim to reproduce physiological ionic conditions, they provide a controlled framework to isolate the physical effects of ion identity on ribosomal dynamics. Increasing magnesium content reduces ionic and backbone mobility and enhances rigidity within the ribosomal core. Dynamic Flexibility Index analysis shows that these changes extend beyond local coordination sites, producing flexibility shifts at distances exceeding 30 Å. Dynamic Coupling Index analysis further reveals that ionic perturbations reshape long-range communication pathways. Functionally important regions, including the L1 and L7/12 stalks, exhibit distinct, ion-dependent responses, while the L10–L11 region shows enhanced long-range coupling under varying ionic conditions. These results demonstrate that ionic composition modulates both local stability and global ribosomal dynamics, with implications for translational efficiency and fidelity.

title: A hybrid mixture approach for clustering and characterizing biomedical data
abstract:
by Kazeem A. Kareem, Fan Dai 

Model-based clustering (MBC) is widely used for identifying latent groups and characterizing heterogeneous structures in biomedical data. However, modern biomedical studies often generate datasets with large sample sizes and many variables, for which standard MBC approaches can be difficult to fit reliably and efficiently. Mixture of factor analyzers (MFA) addresses part of this challenge by representing high-dimensional covariance structures through a few underlying factors, thereby reducing the covariance dimensionality. However, current estimation methods for MFA are often computationally impractical for massive data due to the slow convergence of nested EM-type algorithms. Moreover, many existing implementations require a common number of latent factors across clusters, limiting their ability to capture group-specific structures. We propose a hybrid matrix-free computational scheme for accurate and efficient estimation of Gaussian mixture of factor analyzers, which avoids explicit construction or storage of large covariance matrices. We further develop a generalized version that allows different clusters to have varying numbers of factors, providing additional flexibility for group-specific characterization. Simulation studies show that the proposed approach achieves substantially faster convergence than the existing method, especially in high-dimensional settings, while preserving high clustering and estimation accuracy. Applications to the Wisconsin breast cancer dataset, a lymphoma gene-expression dataset, and a human brain single-cell RNA sequencing dataset demonstrate accurate identification of benign/malignant breast tumors, lymphoma subtypes, and neuronal and astrocytic cell populations. The fitted factor-loading structures reveal biologically meaningful differences in nuclear morphology for breast tumors, with malignant samples showing stronger irregularity-related variation, group-specific gene-expression heterogeneity among the three lymphoma subtypes, and distinct patterns of transcriptional variation between neurons and astrocytes, with neuronal variation reflecting a broader set of coordinated transcriptional directions and astrocytic variation concentrated in a more compact latent structure.

title: Inferring population-level physiologically based model parameters for sleep in infancy and young childhood
abstract:
by Lachlan Webb, Andrew J. K. Phillips, James A. Roberts 

The sleep patterns of infants and young children differ from adult sleep patterns, with longer duration and multiple bouts per 24 hours. There is also considerable heterogeneity in infant sleep, both between individuals and within individuals across development. While mathematical models have been used to understand the mechanisms that regulate adult sleep, the development of sleep from infancy through early childhood has remained largely unexplored. Here we used an established mathematical model for adult sleep regulation to investigate how the underlying mechanisms of sleep mature from ages 1 month to 5 years, and identify a basis for inter-individual differences at each age. Using a Bayesian approach to estimate joint distributions of model parameters at different ages, we found that: (i) decreases in the rate of accumulation of sleep homeostatic pressure captured the reduction in sleep duration across development; while (ii) increases in the time scale of the sleep homeostatic drive captured the consolidation of sleep into fewer sleep bouts per day across development. In terms of inter-individual differences, we found larger spread in the parameters within the earlier stages of infancy ( 24-h) cycles. These results establish plausible, population-level trajectories in physiological parameters underpinning maturation of sleep regulation through infancy and early childhood.

title: Rollout models of human planning with exact action probabilities
abstract:
by Jeroen Olieslagers, Wei Ji Ma 

One proposed mechanism for human planning is the mental simulation, or “rollout,” of potential action sequences to evaluate future outcomes. While rollout-based models have seen great success in artificial intelligence, cognitive models that describe how people use rollouts remain scarce, in part because they are difficult to fit to behavioral data. Existing methods rely on computationally intensive simulations that result in approximate, noisy estimates of latent planning parameters. We introduce ROSETTE (Rollouts with Stochastic Early Termination and Tractable Estimation), a rollout-based model for finite goal-directed tasks with absorbing goals that provides analytically tractable, simulation-free model fitting. ROSETTE treats planning as a sequence of mental simulations formalized as an absorbing Markov chain. The model deterministically accumulates analytically computed expected rollout evidence and performs a variable number of policy-update cycles. We fit ROSETTE to data from human participants in two multi-step planning tasks and found that it well accounted for a rich set of summary statistics of behavior. By making this specific class of absorbing-goal rollout models tractable, our framework provides a testable account of how people may simulate and evaluate possible futures.

title: Simulation-guided design of exotendons to reduce the energetic cost of running
abstract:
by Jon Stingel, Nicholas Bianco, Carmichael Ong, Steve Collins, Scott Delp, Jennifer Hicks 

A passive device that attaches to the feet, called an exotendon, can reduce the energetic cost of running at moderate speeds, but its efficacy and optimal design parameters at higher speeds are unknown. Identifying optimal parameters at new speeds experimentally would require many experimental trials with different exotendon designs, which is challenging for participants at higher running speeds. We developed a muscle-driven simulation framework to predict the effect of various exotendon designs on the energetic cost of running at an experimentally untested speed (4 m/s). We used these predictions to select four designs, which we evaluated experimentally as users ran at this speed. The framework correctly predicted that an exotendon that reduced energetic cost at 2.7 m/s would also reduce energetic cost at 4 m/s (10% predicted vs. 5.7% measured) and that a short, stiff exotendon and a long, compliant exotendon would not significantly reduce energetic cost. However, exotendon parameters predicted by the simulation to maximize energetic savings did not significantly reduce energetic cost when evaluated experimentally. There was variability between participants in both the magnitude of maximum energy savings and the exotendon condition associated with those savings. In a 5-km time trial performed with and without the exotendon condition that elicited the largest energy savings for each participant during the experiment, we observed a lower average heart rate (-3.9 ± 3.8 beats/min;  P  = 0.03; mean ± standard deviation) and increased cadence (15.9 ± 9.6 steps/min;  P  = 0.002) when participants ran with the exotendon but did not observe a statistically significant difference in finishing time (-13.5 ± 24.6 sec;  P  = 0.3). These results demonstrate exotendons can reduce energetic cost across multiple running speeds and that predictive simulations provide a framework for guiding experiments to evaluate assistive device designs.

title: Pupil dynamics reflect uncertainty-driven adjustments of probability learning
abstract:
by Aaron Greenhouse-Tucknott, Cedric Foucault, Anne Buot, Florent Meyniel 

Adaptive learning in dynamic environments depends on the brain’s ability to represent and respond to uncertainty. Changes in arousal-mediated pupil diameter provide insight into the neural basis of this process. Prior work has focused on magnitude-based inference tasks and revealed that learning is primarily influenced by the detection of change points and the corresponding modulation of arousal. In comparison, the role of arousal systems in learning contexts where changes are harder to detect, such as in probability learning, remains poorly understood. Here, we combined pupillometry with a probability learning task in which human participants estimated a hidden generative probability of stimuli that changed abruptly and unpredictably. A Bayesian ideal observer model was used to estimate trial-by-trial learning rates and two uncertainty-associated factors: change point probability (the probability that the generative process has abruptly changed) and prior uncertainty (about the current beliefs on this generative process). In line with normative theory, participants relied on prior uncertainty to adjust learning rates. Pupil analyses revealed temporally distinct representations of uncertainty, with phasic dilations tracking change point probability and tonic pupil dilations tracking prior uncertainty. Mediation analyses further indicated that both phasic and tonic pupil signals partially carried the effects of change point probability and prior uncertainty on learning, respectively. Critically, high tonic arousal weakened the coupling between phasic pupil responses and change point probability, accompanied by a reduced influence of change point probability on learning. Together, our results demonstrate that probability learning in a dynamic environment is underpinned by computationally rational integration of latent uncertainty factors and its contribution to belief updating,regulated through arousal-associated responses.

title: Korea10K integrates 10,239 whole genomes with multiomic and clinical health information as a Korean reference dataset
abstract:
Background
                      Large-scale genome projects have advanced the characterization of human genetic diversity. However, the lack of deeply sequenced, multiomic resources representing the Korean population has limited systematic evaluation of population-specific variation and its functional and translational impact. 
                  
                     Results
                      We present Korea10K, a population-scale multiomic resource comprising 10,239 high-depth whole genomes (mean coverage 30 ×) with integrated molecular and phenotypic data. Analysis of 9,000 unrelated individuals enables near-complete discovery of ultra-rare variants (allele count > 2 and allele frequency ≤ 0.0005) and supports the construction of a high-resolution, population-specific imputation panel. Koreans exhibit pronounced autosomal genetic homogeneity together with a narrow Y-chromosomal and  HLA-A  allelic spectrum and comparatively deep mitochondrial lineage diversity, consistent with long-term demographic continuity. We further identify 16.4 million variants that alter CpG dinucleotide context, revealing widespread sequence-driven modulation of the genomic CG landscape. Notably, CG-eliminating variants generate loss of methylation signal and disrupt CpG probe targets in widely used methylation arrays, introducing a systematic source of bias in epigenome-wide association studies and epigenetic clock estimation. 
                  
                     Conclusions
                      Korea10K establishes a high-resolution genomic and multiomic reference for the Korean population and reveals a previously unrecognized interaction between genetic variation and epigenomic measurement. This resource provides a foundation for precision medicine and highlights the need for ancestry-aware interpretation of molecular data.

title: Genetic dissection of kernel dehydration traits in maize using a recombinant inbred line population: key loci and candidate genes
abstract:
SUMMARY 
 High kernel moisture content (KMC) at harvest impedes mechanized harvesting of maize and increases production costs. As a complex trait influenced by both genetic and environmental factors, kernel moisture dynamics can be quantified using three key metrics: KMC, kernel dehydration rate (KDR), and area under the dry-down curve (AUDDC). Here, we evaluated the dynamic changes of kernel moisture across five consecutive stages in a KD recombinant inbred line population across five environments. KMC was measured every 5 days from 34 to 58 days after pollination (DAP), and KDR and AUDDC were calculated based on these measurements. Quantitative trait locus (QTL) mapping identified 100 non-redundant QTLs, mainly located at distal chromosomal regions. Of these, we prioritized environmentally stable QTLs and 9 high-confidence pleiotropic candidate regions controlling all 3 kernel dehydration traits, alongside trait-specific loci unique to KMC (11), KDR (28), and AUDDC (4). Meanwhile, combined with RNA-seq data and published literature, we further identified 982 genes differentially expressed between the parental lines at the late stage of kernel development within these 100 QTL intervals. The colocalization of our QTLs with meta-QTLs (11 for GDR and 34 for GWC) revealed 13 high-confidence conserved genomic regions, among which 2 prioritized candidate genes ( Zm00001d002455  and  Zm00001d005798 ) were identified. Our study integrated QTL mapping, genome-wide association studies, and transcriptomic analysis to identify high-confidence pleiotropic QTLs and key candidate genes regulating maize kernel moisture, revealing the genetic architecture of moisture dynamics and supporting the breeding of fast-dehydrating maize varieties.

title: Cracking vacuolar fumarate and malate transport shows its function in Arabidopsis metabolism and growth
abstract:
Vacuolar malate and fumarate transport is integrated in Arabidopsis cell metabolism.
 
 
 Summary 
 
Malate and fumarate constitute a significant transient carbon stock that is dynamically synthesised during the photoperiod. These organic acids are diurnally stored and remobilised from the vacuole, and they have a key role in cellular metabolic regulation. This function is well known in C 4  and Crassulacean acid metabolism plants. However, in C 3  species, the majority of terrestrial plants, the importance of vacuolar accumulation/release and its influence on plant growth is still an open question.
We addressed this issue by generating multiple knockout mutants in  Arabidopsis thaliana  lacking vacuolar anion channels of the aluminium-activated malate transporter (ALMT) family ( At ALMT4,  At ALMT5 and  At ALMT9) to impair malate and fumarate transport to the vacuole.
In these mutants, reducing vacuolar transport of malate and fumarate in mesophyll cells leads to a dramatic growth impairment. Metabolic and fluxomic analyses revealed that vacuolar malate and fumarate transport influences plant carbon and nitrogen metabolism as well as cellular pH and ionic homeostasis.
In conclusion, our results show that the transport of organic acids like malate and fumarate across the vacuolar membrane is important for plant growth in a C 3  plant too. These results establish the importance of the vacuolar pools of malate and fumarate in plant metabolism.

title: The rice peptide OsWIH2 intercepts a planthopper‐specific salivary protein SP4 to confer resistance and growth enhancement
abstract:
Interaction between the BPH salivary protein SP4 and the rice peptide  Os WIH2.
 
 
 Summary 
 
The brown planthopper (BPH),  Nilaparvata lugens  (Hemiptera: Delphacidae), is a major pest responsible for substantial yield losses in rice production throughout East and Southeast Asia. Although planthopper-specific salivary proteins are known to play critical adaptive roles during feeding, the molecular interactions between these proteins and rice remain poorly understood.
A yeast two-hybrid screen of eight planthopper-specific salivary proteins (SP1–SP8) revealed a direct interaction between SP4 and  Os WIH2, a cysteine-rich small rice peptide that can be significantly upregulated in response to BPH infestation. Constitutive overexpression of  SP4  resulted in growth retardation in rice plants.  OsWIH2  overexpression significantly enhanced BPH resistance, as evidenced by feeding deficiency, reduced honeydew excretion, impaired nymph survival and development, and decreased fecundity. The resistance of  OsWIH2 -overexpressing rice lines to BPH was further confirmed in both pot and field trials. Metabolomic analyses indicated that  Os WIH2 activates salicylic acid-dependent defense signaling without leading to significant accumulation of jasmonic acid.
 OsWIH2 -overexpressing plants displayed improved growth, along with increased grain size and weight.
This study reveals that  Os WIH2 confers dual benefits of planthopper resistance and improved plant growth and grain yield, providing valuable genetic resources for molecular breeding of rice cultivars.

title: The chloroplast CLP chaperone–protease system controls the steady‐state abundance of the singlet oxygen sensors EXECUTER 1 and 2
abstract:
Working model of EX1,2 protein homeostasis.
 
 
 Summary 
 
The chloroplast Caseinolytic Protease (CLP) chaperone–protease is essential for chloroplast biogenesis. CLP substrate selection is aided by the N-recognin CLPS1 and CLPF adaptors. They interact with each other and the CLPC1 chaperone, but their specific functions are poorly understood.
We employed  in vivo  CLPC1 substrate trapping in Arabidopsis by expressing a  35S:CLPC1-TRAP-STREPII  transgene in wild-type (WT),  clpf, clps1,  and  clpfclps1  to test the consequences of the loss of these adaptors on CLPC1-trapped proteins. Immunoblotting and protein half-life experiments were carried out for identified CLP substrates.
Expression of the  35S:CLPC1-TRAP-STREPII  in  clps1cpf  was embryo lethal. CLPF was trapped at a reduced level in  clps1 , supporting CLPS–CLPF interactions. Chloroplast  1 O 2  sensor EXECUTER1 (EX1) was trapped in WT and  clps1  but not significantly in  clpf . Steady-state protein accumulation of EX1 and its homolog EX2 increased 30-fold in the CLPC1-TRAP lines and  clpr2-1 , but not in  clpf  or  clps1 .  In planta  experiments showed that the half-life of EX1 is c. threefold longer in  clpc1-1  than in WT, but EX1 half-life was unaffected in  clpf .
We conclude that the CLP system plays a key role in EX1,2 homeostasis by keeping their intra-chloroplast concentrations low through continuous degradation, upstream of their  1 O 2  signaling function.

title: Coordinated immune, chloroplast and chemical defences underpin BYDV and aphid resistance in barley carrying a Ryd4Hb introgression
abstract:
Candidate defence metabolites identified by integrated multi-omics reduce  Rhopalosiphum padi  survival in artificial diet assays.
 
 
 Summary 
 
Barley yellow dwarf virus (BYDV), transmitted by the bird cherry-oat aphid ( Rhopalosiphum padi  L.), is among the most damaging diseases of barley ( Hordeum vulgare ), but the mechanisms underlying resistance to both the virus and its vector remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated resistance in the barley hybrid SY Kestrel, carrying an  H. bulbosum -derived  Ryd4 
 
    Hb 
  introgression.
We integrated aphid behavioural and electrophysiological assays, virus quantification, Chl fluorescence, transcriptomics, metabolomics and small RNA profiling. Functional assays evaluated the effects of candidate defence metabolites on aphid survival.
SY Kestrel exhibited constitutive volatile-mediated antixenosis, postsettlement antibiosis involving impaired phloem feeding, reduced aphid fitness and suppression of BYDV establishment. Multi-omics analyses revealed coordinated immune, chloroplast and metabolic responses associated with resistance. Maintenance of photosystem II function during viruliferous aphid challenge was accompanied by reprogramming of α-linolenic acid-derived oxylipin metabolism, while metabolites associated with phenylpropanoid and amino acid metabolism reduced aphid survival.
These findings identify multiple barriers to aphid-mediated BYDV transmission in SY Kestrel, encompassing vector deterrence, disruption of compatible phloem feeding and postinoculation host defence. Our results distinguish core  Ryd4 
 
    Hb 
 -associated resistance from additional defence phenotypes associated with the larger introgressed genetic background and provide a mechanistic framework for breeding durable resistance to aphid-transmitted cereal viruses.

title: Daidzin, an allelochemical from Pueraria, inhibits root growth by targeting COP1
abstract:
Daidzin is an allelopathic chemical produced by invasive species of the genus Pueraria, which includes kudzu. Daidzin inhibits root growth by promoting accumulation of the light signaling regulator COP1 in the nucleus and reducing HY5 abundance, while triggering oxidative stress, autophagy, and changes in developmental gene expression.
  
 ABSTRACT 
 The invasive North American plant  Pueraria  employs allelopathy as a key strategy to outcompete native vegetation, leading to biodiversity loss. The isoflavonoid daidzin has been implicated as a major allelochemical, yet the molecular mechanisms underlying its phytotoxicity, particularly under light conditions favorable to  Pueraria , remain poorly understood. In this study, we demonstrate that daidzin inhibits  Arabidopsis thaliana  root and hypocotyl elongation in a light-enhanced manner. Through a chemical-genetic screen, we identified CONSTITUTIVE PHOTOMORPHOGENIC 1 (COP1), a central regulator of light signaling, as a key mediator of this process.  COP1  mutants exhibited significantly enhanced resistance to daidzin, whereas  COP1 -overexpressing lines showed hypersensitivity. Using confocal imaging and immunoblotting analysis, we observed that daidzin promotes COP1 nuclear accumulation, increases total COP1 protein levels, and reduces the abundance of its downstream substrate HY5 in a COP1-dependent manner.  In vitro  assays, including CETSA and MST, confirmed a direct interaction between daidzin and COP1, with a dissociation constant ( K 
 d ) of 2.39 μM. Molecular docking indicated that daidzin binds primarily to the WD40 domain of COP1. Transcriptome analysis of daidzin-treated roots revealed extensive COP1-dependent transcriptional reprogramming, with significant enrichment in autophagy and oxidative stress pathways, alongside suppression of root developmental programs. Physiological and biochemical assays confirmed that daidzin induces reactive oxygen species accumulation and autophagic activity in wild-type roots, whereas these responses were absent or attenuated in  cop1  mutants. Our findings elucidate a mechanism whereby an invasive plant exploits a conserved light regulator through its allelochemical, revealing how chemical interference integrates with environmental cues to drive invasion. These findings provide molecular insights crucial for ecological risk assessment and potential herbicide development.

title: T2T‐guided EPFL9 editing: Stepwise stomatal‐density reductions in Populus “Beilinxiongzhu 1”
abstract: Guided by the first complete genome of the elite poplar cultivar ‘Beilinxiongzhu 1’, editing the stomatal development gene  EPFL9  reduced the density of leaf pores and water loss while improving water use efficiency under drought.

title: Fluorescent END-BINDING 1b fusions alter cortical microtubule array architecture independently of pattern specification in Arabidopsis thaliana
abstract: Abstract Microtubules in flowering plants play a central role in morphogenesis by creating array patterns at the cell cortex that guide cellulose deposition into the cell wall. Fluorescent END-BINDING 1b (EB1b) fusions preferentially label growing microtubule plus-ends and are used extensively to assess microtubule growth polarity in imaging studies. Here, we use a variety of fluorescent EB1b fusion lines, shown to produce growth phenotypes, as perturbative probes to ask how changes to the plant cortical cytoskeleton affect changes in epidermal hypocotyl cells. EB1b fusion lines showed a range of gain-of-function effects on microtubule polymerization, the distribution of growing plus-ends, and axial growth phenotypes in different organs. Substantial differences in polymerization rate and plus-end density did not alter the frequency of cortical array pattern types observed in light-grown hypocotyls or prevent transverse patterning after brassinosteroid induction. Common differences were discovered in lines showing growth phenotypes for the spatial distribution of growth trajectories across the cell face, despite the absence of correlation between EB1b fusion construction and growth phenotype. We found that transitioning to a transverse pattern produced a significant and sustained downward shift in polymerization rate and plus-end density in all lines. These quantitative observations indicate that longitudinal and transverse cortical arrays exhibit distinct microtubule dynamics states and suggest that the underlying array architecture contributes to morphogenesis, independently of array pattern specification.

title: Defective HIV DNA genomes provide ancestral relevance critical for phylogenetic inference of reservoir dynamics
abstract: Abstract During the course of infection, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) persists in anatomical sanctuary and reservoir sites that lack necessary sensitivity to antiretroviral therapy. Curative advancements rely heavily on targeting these sites, though the precise contribution of each to viral persistence remains ill-supported through current sequencing and sequence analysis strategies. As a prime example, the vast replication-defective genomic landscape that comprises the HIV DNA population targeted for sequencing is often discarded, despite providing key information regarding competent ancestry that can be used to improve viral population dynamic inferences. Here, we describe the application of single-cell DNA sequencing to blood and lymph node samples from a treatment-interrupted S[imian]IV-infected animal model and evaluation of the contribution of genome coverage and inclusion on phylogenetic resolution and phyloanatomic inference. Findings from this study point to incomplete genomes as a significant source of phylogenetic information on reservoir dynamics during therapy.

title: Unexpected genetic and metabolic interactions between the SOS and OxyR stress responses in Escherichia coli
abstract: Abstract  Escherichia coli  employs stress responses to maintain homeostasis and mitigate harmful impacts on cellular and genomic integrity. Two key systems managing tolerance to unfavorable conditions include the DNA damage-inducible SOS response and the oxidative stress-inducible OxyR response. Recently, we demonstrated that simultaneous activation of these two systems resulted in the suppression of the SOS-associated hypermutability, suggesting that these systems when co-induced may yield new regulatory features. To further investigate these systems individually and jointly we used whole-transcriptome sequencing and proteomics to assess the underlying gene and protein networks. We used  E. coli  K-12 strain MG1655 and its derivatives carrying the  recA730  and  oxyR2  c  alleles that yield constitutive expression of the SOS and OxyR systems, respectively. Our findings indicate the genetic scope of these systems to be significantly broader than previously reported, revealing scores of differentially expressed genes not formerly classified as part of the systems (143 in the  recA730  and 248 in the  oxyR2  c  strain). A key finding was that the constitutive co-expression of the two systems led to a broad suppression of genes of both systems. Importantly, a novel group of 137 genes not belonging to either individual system proved differentially expressed under co-activation conditions, which was further corroborated by proteomic data. Overall, the data suggest that SOS-induced cells may be preoccupied with aerobic energy producing activities, while OxyR-induced cells are focused on energy-conserving reactions, biofilm formation and reducing motility. Under co-activating conditions a compromise might be reached that represents a further adaptive mechanism to support survival under multi-stress conditions.

title: Small RNA-mediated genome silencing in Caenorhabditis elegans promotes telomere stability in the absence of telomerase
abstract: Abstract We previously found that small RNAs with perfect homology to (TTAGGC) n  telomere repeats are very rare. Here we use long read sequencing to reveal that most N2 wild type  C. elegans  strains have few telomere mutations at 5’ ends of telomeres, where the telomeric lncRNA TERRA is transcribed. Therefore, telomere mutations cannot explain the absence of perfect small RNAs to (TTAGGC) n  telomere repeats. We show that the heterochromatin mark H3K9me2 is enriched at  C. elegans  sub-telomeres and that the HP1 protein HPL-2 that binds H3K9me2 promotes telomere stability in the absence of telomerase. Small RNA silencing can promote H3K9 methylation, and telomere stability in the absence of telomerase requires germ granule proteins MUT-7 and MUT-14 that promote small RNA biogenesis and also WAGO-1 and HRDE-1 Argonaute proteins that bind subtelomeric small RNAs. Loss of telomerase induced biogenesis of small RNAs from the subtelomeric 5’ end of the telomeric lncRNA TERRA but not from telomere repeats of TERRA. Loss of both telomerase and small RNA-mediated genome silencing induced TERRA expression, telomere damage and accelerated sterility. We propose that small RNA-mediated heterochromatin formation and telomerase function redundantly to repress a form of telomeric DNA damage that is coupled to TERRA expression and subtelomeric small RNA biogenesis. However, telomere repeats of TERRA strongly resisted RNA-dependent RNA polymerase activity in telomerase mutants, revealing an exceptional quality of telomere repeat RNA.

title: Met4All: a dockerised Shiny application for DNA methylation array analysis, visualization and reporting
abstract: Abstract  Motivation DNA methylation profiling is widely used for tumour classification, biomarker discovery and the identification of molecular subgroups. However, routine analysis of Infinium methylation-array data typically requires combining multiple R packages and custom scripts for preprocessing, quality control and downstream interpretation. Results We developed Met4All (Methylation For All), a dockerised Shiny application for integrated analysis of Infinium HumanMethylation450K, EPIC and EPIC v2 array data. Met4All accepts both raw IDAT files and precomputed beta matrices, enabling either end-to-end preprocessing or direct downstream analysis within the same interface. It integrates automated quality control, normalisation, dimensionality reduction (MDS, PCA, UMAP), consensus heatmaps, global methylation profiling, two-group differential methylation analysis, gene-set enrichment testing and copy-number analysis. Structure discovery relies on unsupervised learning (UMAP with graph-based community detection, and consensus clustering); no supervised classification or model-based feature selection is implemented. Outputs are exportable as publication-ready plots and tables for use in downstream workflows. In a systematic comparison against nine representative tools, Met4All was the only one to make all 17 assessed criteria available within a single graphical interface, although individual criteria are supported by several of the frameworks compared. The framework has already supported published methylation studies and is illustrated here on independent public data. Met4All provides an accessible and reproducible environment for integrated methylation-array analysis without requiring extensive bioinformatics expertise. Availability Met4All is implemented in R as a dockerised Shiny application. Source code, Docker configuration files and documentation are available at  https://github.com/gcampof/Met4All , and the version described here is archived at Zenodo (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23265674). Supplementary information Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

title: pyGENIE: A Python library for programmatic access and mutational analysis of AACR Project GENIE
abstract: Abstract  Motivation As of today, AACR Project GENIE has completed 19 data releases since its launch in 2015. The latest release includes more than 268 000 samples from nearly 250 000 patients, and as of February 2026, over 1730 scientific journal articles have cited Project GENIE data. Despite its scale and scientific impact, programmatic analysis of GENIE data often still requires researchers to work directly with complex flat files and develop custom data integration workflows. Results Here we present pyGENIE, a Python package that provides a unified API for accessing GENIE flat files, performing clinical and genomic queries, computing tumor mutational burden, and integrating with leading mutational signature analysis tools including SigProfiler and SigMA. Following a data-as-a-service paradigm, pyGENIE returns all results as native pandas DataFrames, enabling seamless integration with machine learning and visualization libraries. Applied to a lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) case study, pyGENIE reproduces known mutation frequencies, co-mutation patterns, and mutational signatures while reducing the required codebase by approximately an order of magnitude. Availability pyGENIE is freely available at  https://github.com/gersteinlab/pyGENIE  under the MIT License, archived at  https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21981945 , and can be installed from PyPI using pip install pygenie-sdk. Supplementary information Supplementary data are available at  Bioinformatics  online.

title: RNAcomp2D: a web tool to execute multiple methods and visually compare predictions of RNA secondary structure
abstract: Abstract  Motivation Ribonucleic acids (RNAs) are involved in many important biological processes. In particular, non-coding RNAs are crucial regulators of cellular processes, playing a significant role in gene expression. RNA secondary structure is key to infer their specific function and for understanding how they interact with other molecules. Many computational models have been developed in the last decade to predict the secondary structure, achieving increasingly higher success rates. However, each new method has its own input-output interface, programming language, computational requirements and, sometimes, a dedicated server to run the model or just a source code in a repository. Thus, nowadays it is very hard to obtain predictions from multiple methods and compare them at once. A unified interface is urgently needed, which allows accessing several methods at the same time, visualizing and comparing predictions among them, and also with a reference structure when available. Results We introduce here RNAcomp2D, a web-based tool that allows users to enter an RNA sequence, or select one from RNAcentral, and obtain predictions of RNA secondary structures using several state-of-the-art methods. Both classical thermodynamic methods and the latest deep learning models are packaged in containers and accessible in an unified website. All the predictions, and the reference structure if available, are shown at the same time in a single graphical interface. Moreover, as new models continue to be developed, this tool is designed to be scalable, allowing the addition of more prediction methods in the future. Availability Web server is available at  https://sinc.unl.edu.ar/web-demo/rnacomp2d/ . Data and source code are available at  https://github.com/sinc-lab/RNAcomp2D  Supplementary information Supplementary data are available at  Bioinformatics  online.

title: ABAQS: A comprehensive scoring method for assessing genome annotation quality
abstract: Abstract  Motivation As genome resources continue to expand, estimating the accuracy and completeness of genome annotations (e.g., gene and protein models) becomes essential to ensure quality of downstream analyses and applications. It becomes critical in comparative genomic analysis to select genomes with comparable qualities of assembly and annotation. Without careful scrutiny, inconsistencies in annotation quality can undermine downstream studies. Results We have developed Accuracy-Based Annotation Quality Score (ABAQS), a novel method to comprehensively assess genome annotation quality. ABAQS evaluates multiple factors, including genome completeness, gene model validity, and protein profile accuracy, providing a more complete picture of annotation quality than metrics like BUSCO and PSAURON. We applied ABAQS to 1700+ eukaryotic fungal and algal genomes and showed its robustness and effectiveness in evaluating genome annotation quality, making it a valuable tool for researchers working with genomic data. Availability ABAQS software is available at  https://github.com/mycocosm-lbl/abaqs . It requires Java SDK version > =21 and Maven. We also provide a Docker image on DockerHub. Supplementary information Supplementary data are available at  Bioinformatics  online.
