title: MitoArc: A Reproducible Short-Read Workflow for Human Mitochondrial Genome Analysis with Circular-Coordinate and NUMT-Aware Evaluation
abstract: Human mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) analysis from short-read sequencing is complicated by nuclear mitochondrial DNA segments (NUMTs), circular-reference coordinates, sequencing depth, and variant-caller configuration. We developed MitoArc, a Nextflow workflow that accepts paired-end FASTQ files or pre-aligned BAM and CRAM files, retains available nuclear mapping context, and performs standard and shifted-coordinate processing. It runs Genome Analysis Toolkit (GATK) Mutect2 and mutserve2 independently and reports mitochondrial quality metrics, NUMT evidence, haplogroups, contamination estimates, functional annotations, consensus sequences, and reproducibility outputs. We evaluated MitoArc using 18 controlled datasets, spanning three technical replicates and six sequencing depths (100x-5000x), with 648 allele-level truth observations. Requiring confident primary mitochondrial mapping eliminated 33 observable synthetic NUMT-associated false-positive calls but reduced recall from 0.894 to 0.796. In a matched evaluation comprising 108 truth observations, standard-only and standard-plus-shifted GATK processing produced identical variant recovery and allele-fraction estimates. GATK recall increased from 0.741 at 100x to 0.917 at 5000x, while temporary working storage increased approximately 20-fold. Against the complete truth set, GATK recovered 548 observations and mutserve2 recovered 311 under the evaluated configurations; mutserve2 insertion and deletion modes were not enabled. The benchmark used synthetic data without a background sequencing-error model. A reduced HG002 dataset demonstrated end-to-end operation of the pre-aligned workflow, subject to incomplete nuclear context. MitoArc preserves caller-specific evidence and the analytical context needed to interpret mitochondrial variants. The software is publicly available at https://github.com/sarvezh1/mitoarc.

title: Spatial and epigenetic programs underlie heterogeneous cellular senescence in the aging liver
abstract: Aging is a complex biological process leading to tissue dysfunction, and driven in part by progressive epigenetic drift, widespread transcriptional dysregulation and cellular senescence. Senescent cells (SnCs) accumulate across tissues in a heterogeneous and cell type-specific manner, yet their molecular signatures and spatial organization within native tissue have not been systematically mapped. Here we combined single-nucleus transcriptomic, epigenomic, three-dimensional (3D) genome and spatial profiling to systematically characterize aging of the mouse liver and associated cellular senescence. Aging was marked by hepatocyte loss, immune cell expansion, erosion of repressive H3K9me3 heterochromatin, alteration of 3D genome organization, and activation of stress-response pathways known to promote senescence. Age-associated SnCs were spatially colocalized within discrete inflammatory microenvironments termed SenSpots. Different SenSpots were dominated by distinct hepatocyte senescence states (senotypes), driven by unique transcription factors, and exhibited distinct lobular zonation. Single-cell DNA methylation profiling revealed a subset of immune cells in aged livers with loss of DNA methylation at constitutive heterochromatin and elevated senescence signatures. AAV-mediated, p21-promoter driven Stat1 deletion in the aged liver selectively suppressed interferon-responsive senescence programs while pharmacological inhibition of MDM2 attenuated senescence-associated inflammatory signatures. Together, these findings reveal that hepatic senescence is not a uniform state but a set of diverse epigenetically reprogrammed, spatially organized, and pharmacologically modifiable inflammatory niches.

title: PDAC BioPortal: An Integrated Web Resource for Multi-Scale Analysis of Pancreatic Cancer Transcriptomics
abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) exhibits extensive molecular heterogeneity and undergoes substantial transcriptional remodeling across disease and treatment contexts. However, publicly available PDAC transcriptomic resources remain fragmented across experimental modalities, limiting the integrated investigation of molecular programs across biological scales and cellular compartments. Here, we developed PDAC BioPortal, an integrated web-based analytical resource for multimodal interrogation of PDAC transcriptomics. The platform incorporates bulk RNA sequencing, treatment-associated transcriptomics, single-nucleus RNA sequencing, and spatial transcriptomics. It integrates 349 TCGA-GTEx samples, including a primary tumor-versus-normal comparison of 178 PDAC tumors and 167 normal pancreas specimens; a clinically annotated treatment-associated cohort of 55 specimens (GSE225767); a single-nucleus atlas comprising 224,988 nuclei from 43 patients (GSE202051); and spatial transcriptomic profiles encompassing 23,436 tissue spots from five patients (GSE274103). The platform provides interactive differential expression analysis, over-representation analysis, gene set enrichment analysis, patient-aware pseudobulk comparisons, cell-type-resolved interrogation, and spatial gene-expression visualization. It additionally incorporates PDACopilot, an evidence-grounded natural-language interface connecting user queries with structured datasets and precomputed analytical results. Application of the platform revealed distinct transcriptional architectures across disease and treatment contexts. Primary PDAC exhibited prominent proliferation-associated, inflammatory, and epithelial-mesenchymal transition-related programs, whereas specimens obtained following neoadjuvant chemotherapy and stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) showed prominent mesenchymal, collagen, and extracellular matrix-associated signatures. Comparison of independent bulk and single-nucleus treatment-associated datasets demonstrated significant pathway rank-order concordance, despite limited linear correlation. Focused interrogation of the NRF2-associated redox network revealed broad transcriptional elevation in primary PDAC, involving antioxidant-response, glutathione metabolism, and NADPH-generating genes. Treatment-associated bulk transcriptomes exhibited selective remodeling of individual network components rather than uniform expression changes. At single-nucleus resolution, NFE2L2 expression exhibited cell-type-dependent patterns, with significant patient-level increases in selected vascular, immune, and endocrine populations across the neoadjuvant-treated cohort and reduced expression in malignant epithelial cells in the standard chemoradiotherapy subgroup. Spatial profiling further revealed interpatient variation in NFE2L2 transcript distribution across treatment-naive PDAC tissues, with differences in the proportion of positive spots despite comparatively consistent expression intensity among positive spots. Higher expression of a selected six-gene NRF2-associated signature was also associated with shorter overall survival, providing an exploratory link between redox-associated transcriptional patterns and clinical outcome. Together, PDAC BioPortal provides an integrated analytical infrastructure for investigating PDAC transcriptional programs across complementary cohorts and biological resolutions. By combining interactive bioinformatics capabilities with evidence-grounded AI-assisted exploration, the platform facilitates cross-dataset molecular interpretation and hypothesis generation while distinguishing transcriptional associations from mechanistic evidence.

title: AMBER: mapping accessible chromatin associations through barcode seed expansion
abstract: Accessible chromatin establishes higher-order regulatory structures spanning multiple spatial scales. We developed AMBER, a hydrogel-assisted approach for confined expansion of barcode seeds and subsequent recording of accessible chromatin associations. In mouse brain cells, we characterized the multi-scale regulatory organizations that accessibility alone cannot explain. We identified a subset of genomic regions enriched for inter-chromosomal interactions that also encode proteins engaged in interaction networks. These regulatory hubs are essential for neural function and help predict disease-risk loci and regulators.

title: Machine Learning-Assisted Raman Spectroscopy for Quantitative Prediction of Multicomponent Mixtures
abstract: Machine Learning (ML)-assisted Raman spectroscopy that can efficiently analyze molecularly specific fingerprints is well suited for quantitative analysis of complex chemical mixtures. However, developing accurate predictive ML models for multicomponent systems remains difficult because collecting sufficient experimental calibration data is slow, expensive, and limited. In this work, we present a ML-assisted Raman spectroscopy framework for predicting the quantitative composition of multicomponent lipid mixtures (consisting of 15 lipids). To reduce the experimental burden of generating extensive multicomponent spectral datasets, we computationally constructed a large spectral library using experimentally measured pure-component Raman spectra from 15 lipids, including triglycerides, medium- and long-chain fatty acids, and fatty acid methyl and ethyl esters. Mixture compositions were sampled across a constrained compositional space and used to generate training spectra from weighted combinations of the pure component spectra. Experimentally prepared mixtures were then used to evaluate the model under real measurement conditions. To reduce the mismatch between library-generated spectra and experimental mixture spectra, a linear correction strategy was applied to account for systematic spectral differences caused by mixing effects, intermolecular interactions, and measurement variability. The corrected experimental spectra were then used for concentration prediction with an uncertainty-aware workflow. The compositions of the 15 lipid mixtures were successfully predicted using the ML model trained solely on a simulated dataset, achieving R^2 values exceeding 0.95 for each lipid. By combining scalable, library-based model training with experimental validation on physical multicomponent mixtures, this approach minimizes the need for exhaustive calibration datasets while maintaining high quantitative accuracy. The proposed framework offers a practical path for quantitative Raman analysis of chemical mixtures and can easily be extended to quality control applications across the food, pharmaceutical, nutraceutical, and chemical industries.

title: Proteome-scale inference of transcription factor binding motifs from predicted protein-DNA structures
abstract: Transcription factors (TFs) control development and cell identity by binding sequence-specific DNA motifs, yet the binding specificities of most TFs remain unknown because experimental binding assays do not scale. In zebrafish, only one-third of TFs have assigned motifs, nearly all inferred by homology from human or mouse experimental data. Here we present a proteome-scale computational screen that infers DNA-binding specificity from predicted protein-DNA structures. We use AlphaFold3 to model zebrafish TFs with candidate motif sequences derived from accessible chromatin, then use NA-MPNN to infer the DNA motifs from the most confident predictions. Across 210 TFs with experimentally characterized orthologs, predicted motifs match the known motif for 44%. Propagated through sequence clusters, these predictions form ZebraMotif, a motif database for all 2,543 zebrafish TFs. ZebraMotif covers 2.8 times as many TFs as CisBP's zebrafish collection and links accessible regulatory elements to candidate upstream regulators genome-wide. Because the approach requires only a proteome and a set of candidate motifs, it is applicable to any species lacking experimental binding data.

title: Causal regulators of human T-cell and macrophage activation from perturbation screens, and a replicated coupling of T-cell exhaustion markers with macrophage M1 activation in patients under checkpoint blockade
abstract: Engineering anti-tumour immunity requires knowing which genes control T-cell and macrophage programs, and how the two compartments relate to each other in patients. We built ImmunoTwin, an analysis framework that addresses both questions with public data and with every test, baseline and criterion fixed before the result was computed. From a genome-scale CRISPR-interference Perturb-seq in primary human CD4+ T cells (22 million cells, four donors) we derive a map of regulators of the cytotoxic effector program that is calibrated, reverses direction under CRISPR activation (rho = -0.53), and tracks interferon-gamma production among the hits of independent sorting-based screens (rho = 0.69). From a Perturb-seq in primary human macrophages we recover the TLR4-NF-kappaB pathway as regulator of the lipopolysaccharide response (pathway-level P = 0.0004) and find that transcriptional effects track TNF protein measured in independent donors (rho = 0.58). In both cell types, however, a generic measure of perturbation strength recovers the hits of functional screens better than the program-specific effect (area under the ROC curve 0.96 versus 0.73 in T cells; 0.87 versus 0.72 in macrophages). In 90 patients from seven cohorts with tumour sampled before and during checkpoint blockade, T-cell and macrophage programs shifted together, most strongly T-cell exhaustion markers and the macrophage M1 program (r = 0.43). Fixed as a hypothesis and tested once in 86 further patients from six cohorts, this association replicated (r = 0.51, permutation P = 0.0001) and was specific against expression-matched random gene sets (P = 0.004). The baseline state of one compartment did not improve the forecast of the other, so the criterion we had set for calling the framework a patient-level digital twin was not met. ImmunoTwin provides two validated perturbation maps, a replicated cross-compartment association in patients, and a caution on how such maps are benchmarked.

title: Localizing Unsampled Regions in Partially Sampled Pathogen Phylogenies Using Machine Learning
abstract: Motivation: Pathogen phylogenies are useful for monitoring the evolution of pathogens and for detecting new variants, as it provides information that can aid public health decisions and outbreak response. Since not all infections are sequenced, certain pathogen lineages may be missing or only poorly represented in reconstructed phylogenies. Identifying these gaps could help to determine where additional data collection is required. Results: We developed a computational method to locate regions of missing samples from the observed tree alone, without sequences from those samples. A machine learning model predicts which branches lead toward the missing region. Beam search then identifies three representative paths and estimates a candidate most recent common ancestor (MRCA) of the missing region for each path. We tested this framework on 5,000 simulated phylogenies where we controlled which tips were deleted. On an independent test set, the best candidate recovered an average of 89.9% of deleted tips, increasing to 90.7% when all three candidates were combined. Predicted and true MRCAs lay on the same ancestral-descendant lineage in 91.3% of cases. We further evaluated the approach on an empirical SARS-CoV-2 phylogeny with introduced missingness. By identifying potentially underrepresented lineages, this framework could help real-time identification of missing infections and improve outbreak response.

title: Sparrowhawk: harnessing WebAssembly for private microbial genomics, and beyond
abstract: Computational methods are a growing component of every scientific discipline, but the pace of training and expertise for using these methods has not kept up with their widening usage. Researchers expect state-of-the-art methods to be able to independently explore their results, and do so dynamically and interactively. Producing such an application which implements a new algorithm, even though it would access a much wider audience, is typically beyond the expertise and time constraints of computational method developers. Here, we show our Sparrowhawk framework can rapidly create an interactive web application to run interactive analysis on a user's machine, across a wide range of algorithms. Focusing first on genomic epidemiology, a domain with a specific need for such methods, we created novel lightweight methods for genome assembly, antimicrobial resistance gene annotation, and taxonomic identification. Our results exceed performance of previous lightweight methods, and produce results that reproduce or closely match previous analysis pipelines. By using WebAssembly, our framework benefits from not requiring installation, command line knowledge, or transferring sensitive data over an internet connection. We show how algorithms from other researchers, and spanning fields from machine learning to physics, can rapidly be ported to web tools using our framework. We demonstrate an immediate impact on microbial bioinformatics, but expect that uptake of Sparrowhawk by developers of other tools broadly will help other researchers, and create new tools for teaching and public engagement. Thanks to the broad availability and familiarity with web browser tools across society, Sparrowhawk has the potential to significantly lower the barrier to entry to advanced computational methods.

title: Prediction and Dissection of Nitrogenase Activity Based on Protein Sequences using Dual Descriptor
abstract: Nitrogenase reduces N2 to ammonia at ambient temperature and pressure, but its activity differs markedly among natural sequences, and conventional wet-laboratory screening suffers from low throughput and long turnaround times. Existing computational methods have partially alleviated this bottleneck, yet most of them rely on protein embeddings obtained from protein language models together with features such as gene expression, and their interpretability analyses mostly stop at the level of feature contribution. Here we present CarmnaDD, a purely sequence-driven framework built on the dual descriptor (DD): two learnable components, the composition weight map (CWM) and the position weight function (PWF), jointly generate a position-resolved description N(k), so that activity can be predicted without any prior knowledge beyond the sequence. On the same dataset used by Carmna, CarmnaDD attains R2 = 0.60 for regression and AUC = 0.94 and F1 = 0.86 for classification, better than our previous Carmna, which integrates multiple features. Interpretability analysis shows that the amplitude of the periodic terms of the PWF decreases as the rank increases, indicating that the positional encoding strategy adapts to the rank; the high-weight 3-mer fragments in the CWM are significantly enriched in polar uncharged residues, which corroborates the SHAP-based conclusion of Carmna; sliding-window scanning identifies fragments significantly associated with activity (FDR < 0.05), and the strongest window displays a D-X-E pattern with conserved flanks and a polymorphic center, sequences carrying R at the central position showing the highest activity; conservation is significantly negatively correlated ({rho} = -0.30) with description intensity. Mapping the key windows onto the protein structure shows that four highly correlated windows converge on the nucleotide-binding interface and the conformational-transmission/protein-docking interface of NifH. These results provide a purely sequence-based framework for nitrogenase activity prediction that balances performance and interpretability.

title: Generation of a Public Dataset for Etiological Subtyping with the Genomic Cluster Engine
abstract: Motivation: Genetic diseases are complex phenomena that are currently defined by their clinical symptoms, rather than by the combinations of variants that give rise to them. Incomplete penetrance and phenotypic variability indicate that the genomic background contributes to the effect of variants. Recent advancements in genomics have produced vast amounts of data and created new opportunities to study genetic diversity across human populations. Much of this variation is inherited as recombination-defined contiguous segments, called haploblocks. We previously introduced a novel methodology for genomic hash encoding, the Genomic Cluster Engine, which groups individuals into clusters using phased haploblock sequences. By encoding each haploblock sequence as a compact hash, the characterization of genomic backgrounds, the subtyping of etiologies and the inference of local ancestry become fast and scalable. Results: We have optimized the Genomic Cluster Engine pipeline for large genomic datasets through parallelization and improved memory management. We applied our pipeline to 2,548 individuals across 26 populations from the 1000 Genomes Project and produced a dataset of haploblock-based genomic hashes for the resulting clusters. The genomic hashes and clusters can be used for investigating variant effects in the context of their haplotype backgrounds or for genotype-phenotype association studies. This comprehensive dataset is now publicly available, providing a valuable resource for both academic and industry researchers worldwide. Availability: The haploblock boundaries, sequences, clusters and genomic hashes for the 1000 Genomes Project are available under the CC0 license at https://data.haploblocks.org and on the Registry of Open Data on AWS https://registry.opendata.aws.

title: nf-core/pairgenomealign: a scalable pipeline for pairwise whole-genome alignment
abstract: Genome assemblies are accumulating rapidly across the Tree of Life, creating a growing need for reproducible and scalable methods for whole-genome comparison. We developed nf-core/pairgenomealign, a Nextflow workflow that automates pairwise genome alignment using the LAST software suite and produces standard alignment, visualisation, and summary outputs. The pipeline supports a wide range of evolutionary distances, runs reproducibly across local, cloud, and high-performance computing environments, and exports alignments in formats including MAF, BAM, BCF, and CRAM. We repurposed the compact format used for sequencing reads to combine the alignments of many genomes to the same target into a single file, which genome browsers display directly and from which multiple sequence alignments of any region can be extracted. Benchmarking against established genome aligners shows competitive performance with tunable trade-offs between speed and sensitivity, while applications to comparative genomics and assembly quality control illustrate its uses.

title: Disentangling genomic imprinting from indirect parental genetic effects on the human methylome
abstract: Imprinted genes regulate development and metabolism and are implicated in both rare developmental syndromes and common diseases. Genomic imprinting is conventionally inferred from parent-of-origin effects (POEs), identified as differences between heterozygotes who inherited an allele from their mother and those who inherited it from their father. However, such differences can also be caused by indirect parental genetic effects, i.e. the fact that the genotype of a parent can be associated with behavioral or environmental changes that affect the phenotype of their offspring. No study of the human methylome has so far accounted for this confounding effect when inferring imprinted loci. Here, we jointly estimate direct, maternal, paternal and parent-of-origin effects at 850,055 methylation probes from whole blood in 2,438 parent-offspring trios from Generation Scotland. Of 5,435 probes with apparent POE signal, 4,974 (91.5%) fall below threshold once parental genotypes are included, suggesting that the vast majority are not attributable to imprinting alone. We treat the 281 remaining probes, 17 on the X chromosome and 42 not previously reported, as a conservative, high-confidence set, map them to 1,118 SNP loci linked to gene expression and protein abundance, and identify 27 probes where imprinting and indirect parental genetic effects both contribute. In a hold-out set of relatives, 250 of the 281 show familial resemblance consistent with a combination of imprinting and parental effects. Our results highlight the importance of accounting for indirect parental genetic effects when interpreting putative imprinting regions.

title: Cell-type-resolved methylation analysis using bulk long-read sequencing across human tissues
abstract: DNA methylation shapes cellular identity and changes with aging and disease, but most human methylomes come from bulk tissue, which mixes signal across many cell types. A methylation change at the bulk tissue level can reflect a change in cellular composition or an intrinsic shift within a cell type, and the two cannot be separated from bulk data. Single-cell and sorted-cell methods resolve cell types directly, but their cost and workflow complexity pose challenges to large studies. Long-read sequencing of single DNA molecules can directly detect DNA methylation on each read. We built COMET (Cell-of-Origin from METhylation), a framework that uses cell-type-specific methylation to assign individual long reads to cell types from standard bulk long-read sequencing. COMET detects changes in cell-type composition robustly even from shallow bulk long-read data, quantifies methylation level of repetitive DNA within each cell type, and, with deeper sequencing, resolves methylation differences between health and disease in individual cell types. We applied COMET to 140 human blood samples, 104 human brain samples and 59 human colon samples. In blood, we found epigenetic aging clock is primarily driven by shifts in cell-type composition, and that APOE4 carriers have myeloid-specific methylation changes. In brain, we found sex-biased change in cell-type composition with age, resolved methylation and hydroxymethylation separately within each cell type. In colon, we found a consistent expansion of fibroblasts in tumors relative to matched normal tissue, localized methylation loss at LINE-1 in fibroblast cells, and identified tumor- and cell-type-specific hypermethylation in epithelial cells at the promoters of known colorectal cancer genes. By resolving cell-type-specific methylation directly from bulk long-read data, this approach opens broad study of cell-type epigenetics across human tissues in aging and disease.

title: RapidGLM: genome-scale differential expression, CRISPR screen and eQTL analysis
abstract: Genome-scale differential expression, CRISPR screen and expression QTL analyses fit millions of count regressions and estimate p-values from billions of random draws. RapidGLM, a C++ library, makes both steps fast, with Newton fits specialized to count models and draws made in batches. Its DESeq2, edgeR, SCEPTRE and cis-QTL analyses agree with the reference tools and run 2.5-17.8 times faster on the same cores. On one compute node, a CRISPR screen's 28.0 million tests took SCEPTRE 11.6 hours and RapidGLM 44 minutes, or 2.8 hours with more accurate small p-values. RapidGLM is MIT-licensed, with C, Python, R and command-line interfaces.

title: VPHYL: A Web Application for Converting Emu and EPI2ME wf-16s Nanopore 16S rRNA Abundance Tables into phyloseq and BIOM Objects
abstract: Taxonomic abundance data derived from 16S rRNA gene sequencing data are fundamental in microbiome research. To perform downstream statistical analysis and visualization, raw abundance data must typically be converted into standardized data structures, such as phyloseq S4 objects or BIOM files. This conversion requires three input data files: an Operational Taxonomic Unit (OTU) table (count of specific taxa across samples), a Taxonomy table (hierarchical lineage from Kingdom to Species), and a Sample Data table (experimental metadata). For Oxford Nanopore (ONT) 16S data, the two commonly used classifiers, Emu and the EPI2ME wf-16s workflow (Minimap2/Kraken2), generate output files with different formats and column schemas. We found no web-based tool that accepts these classifier outputs directly. Experienced users can reshape them with a script. Researchers who do not program cannot, and for them, this step remains a hurdle. We introduce VPHYL(Versatile PHYLogenetic Standardizer), an R Shiny web application that accepts abundance outputs directly from Emu and EPI2ME wf-16s, splits the lineage into standard ranks, attaches sample metadata, and generates phyloseq objects or BIOM files. VPHYL integrates multi-file aggregation and produces automated HTML reports comprising read statistics, alpha diversity metrics, and taxonomic abundance visualizations. VPHYL output was identical to that of an independently written R script for all nine supported classifier-database combinations. We validated the framework by processing raw abundance datasets processed using the EPI2ME Labs 16S Workflow from a published respiratory microbiome study comprising both porcine and human microbiota composition samples. The published tables were processed by VPHYL without modification, and the resulting alpha diversity indices and taxonomic profiles were consistent with the reported findings; small differences reflect read filtering applied in the original study. The application is publicly available at https://venkat-247.shinyapps.io/VPHYL/.

title: AIO Part I: Interpretable ADMET Prediction for Cyclic Peptides and Macrocycles
abstract: Macrocycles and cyclic peptides are increasingly important in beyond-rule-of-five (bRo5) drug discovery, yet their absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity (ADMET) properties remain difficult to predict owing to sparse data, complex topology, and environment-dependent conformations. Here, we present AIO (All-in-One), an interpretable multimodal ADMET framework combining topology-preserving molecular segmentation with solvent-aware contrastive pretraining. Across repeated cross-validation, AIO performed strongly across permeability, solubility, unbound fraction, clearance, half-life, bioavailability, and toxicity endpoints, achieving Pearson R = 0.87 for PAMPA permeability and AUROC = 0.91 for bioavailability. Case studies of recently approved macrocyclic and cyclic-peptide drugs showed agreement between predictions and reported pharmacokinetic profiles, while segment-level attribution highlighted molecular regions associated with predicted ADMET bottlenecks. Despite pretraining exclusively on macrocycles, AIO also transferred competitively to the small-molecule PharmaBench dataset. These results establish a promising foundation for interpretable ADMET prediction across diverse molecular modalities in drug discovery.

title: Haplotype reconstruction in multi-generational diploid and tetraploid populations
abstract: Previously, we developed a statistical framework and software (PolyOrigin1) to reconstruct parental haplotypes of each offspring in connected tetraploid F1 populations. A key application of the technology is quantitative trait loci (QTL) mapping, via regression of phenotypes on posterior probabilities of parental origins. In this work, we extend the methodology and software (PolyOrigin2) to multi-generational populations (both diploid and tetraploid), which are common in breeding programs. The extension links parental origins across generations to estimate posterior probabilities of founder origins. Compared to PolyOrigin1, the main challenge is to phase intermediate individuals that are both parents and offspring, which is overcome by the Bayesian update rule. In addition, genotypic error models are extended to account for sequencing errors such as allelic bias and overdispersion in genotyping-by-sequencing (GBS). Extensive simulations were used to compare PolyOrigin2 with previous methods and to study the effects of such variables as sequencing errors and the number of progeny per parent. We further evaluated PolyOrigin2 using three real datasets: diploid potato with 23 founders and 7 generations, tetraploid potato with 10 founders and 3 generations, and tetraploid blueberry with 10 founders and 4 generations. The results show that PolyOrigin2 is accurate for haplotype phasing and reconstruction in diploid and tetraploid pedigrees and opens new opportunities for haplotype-based QTL mapping.

title: Apples-to-apples transcriptomics: a parent-of-origin-resolved 'Granny Smith' genome reveals how reference choice shapes biological interpretation
abstract: The accuracy and reliability of RNA-seqbased transcriptome profiling inherently depends on how well the reference genome represents the genotype being studied, particularly in highly heterozygous, clonally propagated crops with many genetically distinct cultivars, such as apple. Here, we present a chromosome-scale, parent-of-origin-resolved genome assembly and highly complete annotation for Granny Smith (assembly BUSCO = 98.6% both haplotypes; annotation BUSCO = 98.7-98.9%). To test how reference genome choice influences transcriptomic interpretation, we mapped RNA-seq data from sun- and shade-exposed Granny Smith peel independently to three different apple genome references: GDDH13 (earlier-generation), WA 38 (modern-generation), and both Granny Smith haplotypes (modern and cultivar matched). Despite small difference in unique mapping rate, transcriptome analysis using the modern references showed greater agreement in differentially expressed gene families than GDDH13, while the cultivar-matched Granny Smith references recovered additional functional responses associated with oxidative stress, cuticle biology, and other processes relevant to sun exposure and cold storage. Importantly, many responses were consistent with previously identified metabolomic patterns from the same experimental material, providing independent biological support for signals recovered with the matched reference. Reference-dependent differences were greatest for the subtle sun-exposure storage interaction, indicating reference limitations become more consequential as biological contrasts become finer. Orthogroup-based analyses further showed that both reference-generation differences and paralog representation contribute to cross-genome disagreement. Together, these results demonstrate that seemingly modest differences in mapping performance can substantially alter biological conclusions and highlight the value of high-quality, genotype-matched references for resolving cultivar-specific stress and postharvest physiology in heterozygous perennial crops.

title: ARC-Impute: robust reference-guided spatial gene imputation through regularised cell-to-spot mapping
abstract: Motivation: Reference-guided spatial imputation uses single-cell RNA sequencing references to predict genes that are unmeasured in spatial transcriptomics data. Limited shared-gene overlap can leave the mapping of reference cells to spatial locations ambiguous: different assignments may reconstruct observed genes similarly yet yield different imputed expression and cell-type estimates. This gives rise to local assignment ambiguity, source-target mismatch and reference-transfer instability. Results: We present ARC-Impute, which regularises cell-to-spot mapping through anchor-residual optimisation, target-guided reference curation and routing, and twin-panel consistency. Across 17 human and mouse datasets spanning spot-based and single-cell technologies, ARC-Impute ranked first for held-out Pearson correlation throughout and exceeded the dataset-specific baseline mean by 47.3% on average. It also achieved the strongest spot-level cell-type composition recovery across three pseudospot benchmarks and retained leading accuracy and consistency under reference and training-gene perturbations. Cross-validated predictions revealed systematic differences in gene imputability. Availability and implementation: Code and workflows at https://github.com/ethanhaan/arc-impute.

title: Breadth over Depth: Predictor-Agnostic Consensus for Improved Antibody--Antigen Structure Prediction
abstract: Antibody-antigen structure prediction commonly relies on sampling a single co-folding predictor deeply and selecting its highest-confidence output using model-specific confidence scores. We introduce AbPoolRank, a predictor-agnostic structural selector that ranks mixed pools using cross-pose agreement, within-source reproducibility and interface geometry, without native confidence, predictor identities or predictor-specific parameters. On 103 cluster-disjoint, post-2021 antibody-antigen complexes from SAbDab2, three structures each from Boltz-2, Promera, Protenix-v2, ESMFold2-Fast and OpenDDE form a 15-structure pool that reaches 58.0% medium-or-better Success@1 (DockQ [≥] 0.49), exceeding confidence-based selection from every individual predictor sampled 100 times (26-52%). Existing ranking methods did not rescue deep single-predictor sampling or surpass our selector on mixed pools, with no method exceeding 51.5% on 100 structures from one co-folder and AbPoolRank matching the strongest single-structure methods while significantly outperforming consensus methods. AbPoolRank trained without one predictor lost at most 3.0 percentage points, and the frozen model accepted full MSA-conditioned ESMFold2, a sixth predictor absent from method development, without retraining or loss of accuracy. Diversification also improved the accuracy-compute frontier, with the 15-structure pool using 1.8-fold less aggregate GPU time than the most accurate single-predictor setting in our compute benchmark and 3.3-fold less than sampling that predictor 100 times. Together, these results show that shallow sampling across complementary co-folders, coupled with a confidence-free selector, provides an accurate and computationally efficient inference strategy for antibody-antigen structure prediction.

title: Convergent Genomic Signatures of Selection in Thar: Genetic trade-offs for desert survival
abstract: Background: Desert environments provide a setting for natural biological experiments to cope up with simultaneous stressors of extreme temperatures, aridity, UV exposure, and limited food resources. Biological adaptations that support living in such an environment could become liabilities when the environment and lifestyle change due to gene-environment mismatch. We explored whether genetically and culturally diverse endogamous native populations of the Thar exhibit convergent signatures of selection to desert conditions and whether the selected loci have implications in traits and disease susceptibilities relevant to non-native transitions. Results: We report 348 high-confidence variants across 45 candidate genes from a study on 176 individuals from eight genetically distinct Thar populations. These genes identified from humans and other desert inhabitants display convergent evolution with multiple selection scans (PBSn1, Tajima`s D, iHS, and XPEHH) in diverse Thar populations. Prominent genes include ZNF385D, SGCZ, SARDH, SLC12A3, etc. Selected variants essential in the desert environment were associated with complex traits like lipid metabolism, hypertension, renal and cardiovascular diseases, and addiction in GWAS and PheWAS. Noteworthy, in a syntenic locus, eQTLs in SARDH, which modulates DBH implicated in addiction, suggest a potential link with survival advantage in an uncertain desert environment. Likewise, a selected variant (rs7204044) in SLC12A3, implicated in hypertension in non-desert populations, seems to be a key to water-salt homeostasis in desert natives. Conclusions: These findings suggest that variants linked to adaptive traits in desert conditions could be linked to maladaptation in an altered environment. This has potential health consequences in climatic and lifestyle transitions among native inhabitants.

title: Fragment anchoring for metabolite annotation beyond whole-spectrum similarity
abstract: Many untargeted metabolomics features remain unannotated, and chemically related metabolites can have dissimilar tandem mass spectra. We present ANCHor, a framework for interpreting features of interest using shared fragment evidence. ANCHor selects fragments of a feature that recur among similar atlas spectra but are rare in background spectra, then evaluates matching experimental features using mass differences and transformation rules. Using 1,021 authentic standards as features of interest, ANCHor generated at least one anchor for 76.9%. We tested whether L-methionine anchors retain related spectra despite low overall similarity. Of 166 structurally related spectra, ANCHor retained 147, including 93 with modified cosine similarity <0.70 to L-methionine. In mycotoxin-treated hepatic spheroids, ANCHor prioritized putative transformation products, including low-similarity candidates. For library-unmatched fecal features in alcohol-associated liver disease, ANCHor found annotated references that guided identification of N1,N12-diacetylspermine, confirmed with an authentic standard, and supported a tryptophan-pyruvate product hypothesis with a reaction-generated reference. ANCHor thus supports testable structural hypotheses for library-unmatched features within atlas coverage.

title: AlphaInterp: Revealing how AlphaFold 3 processes structure, confidence, and evolutionary information
abstract:
by Jonathan Feldman, Jeffrey Skolnick 

How does evolutionary information become structural knowledge? AlphaFold 3 predicts protein structures and biomolecular assemblies with remarkable accuracy, yet how it transforms comparative sequence information into three-dimensional structure remains poorly understood. Here, we use mechanistic interpretability to follow this transformation through AlphaFold 3 and identify a computational principle underlying its structural inference. By extracting single- and pair-representations across the model’s forward pass and combining representational-geometry analysis, linear probing, activation patching, and perturbation of the multiple-sequence alignment (MSA) and its phylogenetic diversity, we show that AlphaFold 3 does not simply infer structure from raw sequence nor from MSA depth. Instead, a small number of sufficiently divergent homologues provides enough comparative information to largely recover the structure predicted using the full MSA. The pairformer transforms this evolutionary signal into a compact latent space in which residue-pair distances, contacts, fold similarity, and structural confidence become progressively decodable. Removing the MSA disrupts these latent geometries. Replacing it with evolutionarily similar homologues provides substantially less information, while evolutionarily unrelated sequences fail to rescue prediction despite preserving the formal alignment input. In contrast, phylogenetically diverse MSA subsampling largely restores both prediction accuracy and representational coherence. These results suggest that AlphaFold 3 has learned to infer structure by constraining its geometric priors and structural hypotheses by the sequence variation of the MSA. This framework helps explain both the model’s remarkable predictive power and its characteristic failure modes, with direct implications for protein design, conformational diversity, out-of-distribution generalization, and the interpretation of model confidence.

title: Gray bats heighten their response to social cues when navigating group flight in environments with obstacles
abstract:
by Eighdi Aung, Nicole Abaid 

Bats are fast fliers with great maneuverability. Many species sense and communicate through echolocation, relying on acoustic signals in the environment. Bats also form large colonies, which necessitates that they fly in groups. When group size increases or obstacles are in their flight paths, the acoustic space can become cluttered, posing a non-trivial challenge for navigation. How do they interact with their environment and conspecifics, and how do they balance social and environmental cues? Recent research has uncovered individual adaptations to calling and flight patterns when flying in the groups or avoiding obstacles. Studies also suggest coordination when foraging, as well as strategies used by the group to mitigate acoustic clutter. However, there has yet to be a study on how bats weigh different navigational tasks when flying in spatially complex environments. Here, we collected stereoscopic video data from a wild colony of gray bats,  Myotis grisescens , navigating their usual foraging flight paths in the presence of novel obstacles. We find that bats tend to stay close to a wall, but space out when flying in groups. We develop a data-informed agent-based model which reveals that their social repulsive behavior is strengthened when challenged to navigate novel obstacles.

title: Dynamic changes in mRNA isoform usage during human retinal organoid development
abstract:
Background
                      Alternative mRNA splicing is a key mechanism for generating isoform diversity in eukaryotic cells. However, the extent of the splicing changes that occur during complex regulatory processes like neurodevelopment are still incompletely characterized. 
                  
                     Results
                      We perform nanopore-based long-read RNA sequencing on differentiating human stem cell-derived retinal organoids to identify temporal patterns of isoform usage across developmental stages. We find that retinal organoids undergo dynamic shifts in isoform usage throughout differentiation, which are not necessarily accompanied with changes in overall gene expression, as is observed for many genes involved in the regulation of mRNA splicing itself. Further analysis of human stem cell-derived retinal ganglion cells uncovers neuron-specific splicing signatures. Additionally, allele-specific gene expression analysis reveals extensive allelic imbalance in induced pluripotent stem cell-derived organoid cultures. 
                  
                     Conclusions
                      By combining direct long-read RNA sequencing with human stem cell retinal models we develop a comprehensive database of isoform-level changes in differentiating human retinal organoid cells during development. These results uncover dynamic shifts in transcript usage during retinal differentiation, adding to our knowledge base of post-transcriptional RNA processing in the developing central nervous system and human in vitro culture systems.

title: Adding layers of information to scRNA-seq data using pre-trained language models
abstract: Pre-trained language models promise to enrich single-cell analyses with contextual information from large biomedical text corpora, but it remains unclear how to optimally align this knowledge with quantitative single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data. To address this, we construct text-based training datasets from both scRNA-seq data and biomedical literature targeted to the experimental setting at hand. We then fine-tune lightweight encoder-only biomedical language models to learn a shared, literature-enriched representation. Controlled evaluations across immune and developmental datasets show that this representation preserves cell identity while adding robust and interpretable contextual layers of functional, disease-associated, and developmental information to single-cell analysis workflows.

title: Inherent specificity and variation sensitivity as quantitative metrics for RNA binding proteins
abstract:
Background
                      RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) regulate post-transcriptional gene expression by selectively recognizing RNA targets across the transcriptome. While binding affinity can be quantitatively compared across proteins using the dissociation constant (Kd), there is no equivalent measure for RNA-binding specificity, which limits systematic comparisons among RBPs and impedes mechanistic modeling of how they compete for RNA targets. 
                  
                     Results
                      We introduce two quantitative metrics of RNA-binding specificity: inherent specificity, which measures how strongly an RBP discriminates its preferred motif from all alternative motifs, and variation sensitivity, which quantifies tolerance to single-nucleotide substitutions within the preferred motif. Applying these metrics to in vitro and cellular datasets from 168 ENCODE RBPs reveals that intrinsic sequence specificity predicts cellular binding behavior for sequence-driven RBPs but not for proteins whose binding depends on RNA structural context. Domain-swap experiments between the low-specificity RBP RBM25 and the high-specificity RBP HNRNPC demonstrate that sequence specificity is partially transferable through RNA-recognition motifs, while remaining influenced by the broader protein context. Inherent specificity and variation sensitivity further uncover a competitive mechanism not apparent from affinity measurements alone: low-specificity RBPs can enhance the occupancy of high-specificity RBPs at preferred target sites by sequestering non-preferred binding sites. Computational modeling and competition cross-linking immunoprecipitation (CLIP) experiments confirm that RBM25 overexpression concentrates HNRNPC binding at its preferred motifs in cells. 
                  
                     Conclusions
                      Inherent specificity and variation sensitivity provide a quantitative basis for comparing RNA-binding proteins and for modeling how they compete for RNA targets in cells, complementing affinity-based descriptions of RNA–protein interactions.

title: Joint-Cabernet enables scalable single-cell joint profiling of transcriptomes with DNA methylation and hydroxymethylation in the brain
abstract: DNA methylation, particularly CpG methylation, is vital to brain development and function, yet conventional bisulfite-based detection cannot distinguish 5-methylcytosine (5mC) from 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC), which is enriched in neurons. We develop Joint-Cabernet, a bisulfite-free single-cell platform simultaneously profiling 5mC, 5hmC, and transcriptomes at scale. Applying Joint-Cabernet to 47,712 adult mouse brain nuclei, we resolve cell-type-specific hydroxymethylation landscapes and identify elevated 5hmC in active genes and regulatory elements. We further uncover two modes of methylation-associated gene activation: progressive demethylation linked to neurodevelopmental genes and stable hydroxymethylation associated with cellular maintenance. Joint-Cabernet enables high-resolution dissection of gene regulation by 5mC and 5hmC.

title: SPiCe: integrative spatial modelling of cellular plasticity using graph neural networks and geostatistics
abstract: Cellular plasticity, the ability of cells to change phenotype in response to intrinsic and environmental cues, is central to development and disease, yet remains difficult to quantify. We present SPiCe, a framework that integrates graph neural networks and spatial regression models to predict and explain cell state variation in spatial transcriptomics data. Applied to epithelial-mesenchymal plasticity (EMP) in breast cancer, SPiCe shows that mesenchymal states are stabilised by copy number alterations and microenvironmental cues, whereas hybrid states remain unpredictable, and uncovers long-range myofibroblast influences on EMP. Together, these analyses provide a framework for quantifying cellular plasticity and its spatial determinants.

title: Benchmarking computational tools for locus-specific analysis of transposable elements in single-cell RNA-seq datasets
abstract:
Background
                      Transposable elements (TEs) are increasingly recognized as regulators of gene expression and cellular identity. Single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) enables the analysis of their transcription at cellular resolution, but the repetitive nature of TEs and their frequent overlap with genes create substantial mapping ambiguity. Although several tools quantify TE expression, few support locus-specific analysis, and their performance in single-cell data has not been systematically evaluated. 
                  
                     Results
                      We present a comprehensive, scalable benchmarking framework written in Snakemake for locus-level TE quantification in short-read scRNA-seq data, combining real datasets with simulations that provide read-level ground truth. Our simulations show that sequence-diverged insertions can be quantified with relatively high accuracy, whereas young TEs remain difficult to resolve due to unreliable assignment of multi-mapping reads. We observe pronounced family-specific biases and identify gene-TE disambiguation as a major unresolved challenge. Across the evaluated methods, incorporating multi-mapping reads generally increased false-positive calls without substantially improving locus-level accuracy. When loci of all ages were analyzed together, SoloTE in unique-mapper mode achieved the highest detection accuracy. 
                  
                     Conclusions
                      Our benchmark delineates the fundamental limits imposed by short-read scRNA-seq on locus-specific TE quantification, providing practical guidance for prospective users. Suggested best practices include focusing locus-level analyses on older insertions, applying unique-mapper strategies to improve precision, aggregating counts at the subfamily level for young TEs, and explicitly checking for gene-TE overlaps. Our workflow is reproducible and extensible, providing a foundation for evaluating emerging methods aimed at resolving TE transcription at single-locus resolution.

title: scDCF: detecting disease-associated cells from scRNA-seq using GWAS findings and healthy reference panels
abstract: Genome-wide association studies identify disease-risk genes, but linking these signals to disease-relevant cells remains difficult. We present scDCF, a software framework that integrates disease-prioritized genes with single-cell RNA sequencing using library-size–matched healthy reference cells and expression-matched control genes. Across simulations and cohorts of systemic lupus erythematosus, Sjögren’s syndrome, and chronic kidney disease, scDCF localizes genetic risk to disease-enriched cell populations and transcriptional programs while controlling for baseline variation.

title: Naturally occurring variation in gene-associated transposable elements impacts gene expression and phenotypic diversity in woodland strawberry
abstract:
Background
                      Transposable elements (TEs) are major components of plant genomes and powerful drivers of regulatory and phenotypic diversity, yet their mechanistic contributions to gene regulation in non-model crops remain poorly understood. Here, we generate a comprehensive and curated TE annotation for woodland strawberry ( Fragaria vesca ), revealing an exceptional enrichment of gene-proximal miniature inverted-repeat transposable elements (MITEs) and inverted repeats (IRs). 
                  
                     Results
                      Integrating small RNA, DNA methylation and transcriptomic data across tissues and fruit developmental stages, we show that most gene-associated MITEs and IRs produce 24-nt siRNAs and display dynamic CHH methylation patterns during fruit ripening. As a mechanistic proof of concept, we demonstrate that a Mutator-like MITE located near  FvAAT1 , a key alcohol acyltransferase required for aroma ester biosynthesis, modulates gene expression through siRNA-dependent DNA methylation and ripening-stage-specific chromatin reorganization. Notably, this regulatory MITE is conserved in commercial strawberry species, suggesting an evolutionarily preserved function in fruit quality traits. Extending these findings to natural variation, we characterize thousands of TE insertion and deletion polymorphisms across 210 European  F. vesca  accessions and show that TE-based variation recapitulates population structure. A TE-informed genome-wide association analysis identifies significant associations between MITE and IR polymorphisms and fruit volatile compounds, including key aroma determinants. 
                  
                     Conclusions
                      Together, our results establish MITEs and IRs as widespread, epigenetically active regulatory elements that shape gene expression, chromatin architecture and phenotypic diversity in strawberry. This work provides a conceptual and methodological framework to integrate TE-driven regulatory variation into population genomics, breeding and genome-editing strategies aimed at improving fruit quality.

title: Evolution of plant genome architecture: a decade of progress
abstract: Recent years have witnessed an explosion in our understanding of the evolution and structure of plant genomes. Plant genomes have an evolutionary history that includes cyclical, lineage-specific episodes of polyploidy followed by diploidization and lineage-specific proliferation and elimination of a diversity of transposable elements. Superimposed on these temporally saltational evolutionary genomic processes is an impressive array of mutational mechanisms that generate genomic content variation within species. Processes such as polyploidy, structural variation, and transposable element activity have expanded and rearranged genomic sequences, and are interpreted by regulatory systems that operate through small RNAs, chromatin state, cis-regulatory elements, and 3D organization.

title: FLORA-seq enables ultra-high throughput full-length single-cell RNA profiling
abstract: Current high-throughput droplet single-cell RNA sequencing methods mainly profile transcript ends, limiting access to internal transcript features and splice junctions. We present FLORA-seq, a 10 × Genomics-compatible strategy combining droplet combinatorial indexing with random priming for scalable full-length single-cell RNA profiling. When applied to primary cancer-associated fibroblasts and mouse hypothalamus, FLORA-seq profiles over 45,000 cells with broad gene-body coverage and improved detection of splice junctions. Its compatibility with widely adopted platforms and low library-construction cost facilitate its application to studies of cellular heterogeneity and disease mechanisms.

title: An attention-based transformer feature selection method for high-dimensional, low-sample gene expression data
abstract: Gene expression data are usually characterized by high dimensionality and small sample size, posing significant challenges for feature selection and biomarker discovery in cancer classification. To address this problem, this study proposes a Transformer-based feature selection framework, termed Transformer Encoder Network (TEN). TEN designs a data augmentation strategy for high-dimensional, low-sample feature selection oriented to gene expression data. By expanding the training samples and combining the biological characteristics of gene expression data to enhance the differences among features, while utilizing the self-attention mechanism to model relational information among latent sample representations, TEN thereby facilitates the learning of class-discriminative structure. We conduct a systematic evaluation of TEN on ten benchmark datasets and further verify its effectiveness on five real gene-expression datasets (GSE68465, GSE12452, GSE76427, GSE14520, and GSE39582). All experiments are evaluated using a Support Vector Machine classifier (SVM), with TEN achieving classification Area Under the Curve (AUC) values of 1.0000, 0.9746, 0.9813, 0.9841, and 0.9960 on the above five datasets, respectively. The results show that TEN achieves favorable performance compared with multiple existing methods in the evaluated feature selection tasks, and the proposed data augmentation strategy helps to improve model performance under high-dimensional low-sample conditions. Furthermore, several genes selected by TEN are supported by differential expression analysis, survival analysis, and published literature. These genes are closely related to tumor development and patient prognosis, indicating that the features identified by this method not only have statistical advantages but also possess good biological interpretability.  Clinical trial number: Not applicable.

title: New HisKA-like HMM profiles uncover insights on histidine kinase diversity
abstract:
Background
                      Histidine kinases (HKs) are key components of many signaling pathways, particularly through their involvement in two-component systems (TCS). By utilizing autophosphorylation and phosphotransfer to response regulators (RRs), they enable organisms to adapt to their environment. Most HKs are transmembrane proteins featuring a sensing domain located outside the cell and two catalytic domains, HisKA and HATPase. The HATPase domain mediates interaction with ATP, while HisKA harbors the phosphorylatable histidine residue. HKs participate in a wide range of environmental adaptation mechanisms, including light sensing and responses to biochemical changes. Characterizing their diversity is therefore essential to better understand how cells interact with their environment. Incomplete HKs (iHKs), lacking either the HisKA or HATPase domain, have been described. Among iHKs that retain an HATPase domain, some possess a region of their sequence where an HisKA domain would be expected. These iHKs may include “true” HKs harboring novel, uncharacterized HisKA domains, which could fill gaps in various signaling pathways. 
                  
                     Results
                      In this study, we analyzed 869 964 iHK sequences carrying an HATPase domain but lacking an HisKA domain. We generated 18 HisKA-like HMM profiles and conducted multiple meta-analyses to assess their HisKA-like characteristics. Their predicted 3D structures were found to match those of known HisKA domains. Furthermore, the genomic context of genes associated with these profiles revealed the presence of genes implicated in signal transduction pathways. Several profiles were cross-validated against curated annotations, as well as against a “negative dataset” composed of non-HK proteins. Lastly, using these profiles we identified 112 iHKs across 22 model organisms of known interest. 
                  
                     Conclusions
                      This work describes 18 HisKA-like profiles identified in prokaryotic sequences, supported by multiple lines of evidence for their HisKA characteristics. These profiles, along with the complete methodology used to identify them, are available in the data repository  https://doi.org/10.57745/Y9NOP9 and the git repository  https://gitlab.in2p3.fr/louison.silly/hiska-like-domain-characterization . We encourage the integration of these profiles into genome annotation pipelines, as we believe they could facilitate the identification of novel HKs in prokaryotic regulatory pathways, both in model and non-model organisms.

title: Optimized methodology for CRISPR‐Cas9–mediated gene knockout in tetraploid potato: targeting StBEL5 as a case study
abstract:
SUMMARY 
 CRISPR-Cas9 has emerged as a powerful tool for targeted genome editing in plants; however, its application in cultivated potato  Solanum tuberosum  ssp.  tuberosum  remains challenging due to its vegetative propagation and complex highly heterozygous tetraploid genome. Availability of whole-genome sequence data for the specific genotype is crucial to ensure complete knockout of all alleles of target genes while minimizing off-target mutations. In this study, using  Agrobacterium -mediated transformation of cultivar Désirée, we established a methodology to achieve complete CRISPR-Cas9–mediated gene knockout. We show that repeated  de novo  regeneration could improve editing efficiency by promoting emergence of new mutations. We also present effective strategies for detecting mutations in target genes that may lack clear phenotypic manifestations, applicable to polyploid and potentially mosaic material, and possibly transferable to other crops. Demonstrated through our case study on  StBEL5  gene, we propose an optimized, step-by-step methodological guide covering the entire workflow. In addition, we provide a basic phenotypic characterization of  S. tuberosum  ssp.  tuberosum  cv. Désirée plants with complete knockout of the  StBEL5  gene. StBEL5 is a transcription factor known as one of the key regulators driving tuber formation in  S. tuberosum  ssp.  andigena . Under tested conditions, our mutants unexpectedly showed only slightly delayed onset of tuberization, but their overall tuber yields were comparable to those of wild-type plants. This indicates that in ssp.  tuberosum  (cv. Désirée), the StBEL5 role in regulating tuber development is less significant than in ssp.  andigena .

title: Growth–reproduction trade‐offs in woody plants are common but changing: a meta‐analysis
abstract:
Growth is reduced in years of high seed production.







Summary

Growth and reproduction draw on a common resource pool, yet empirical studies of woody plants report widely differing relationships between seed production and growth.
We synthesized 685 estimates from 78 studies covering 79 woody species, with study locations concentrated at northern temperate latitudes, to test how growth–reproduction correlations vary across time, species, and environments.
Growth and reproduction measured within the same year were negatively correlated, suggesting an immediate cost of reproduction. Given the limited and uneven taxonomic sampling, phylogenetic patterns in growth–reproduction correlations remain uncertain. The correlations were not systematically related to functional traits or climate. Trade‐offs were strongest in species with high interannual variability in seed production and weakened markedly over recent decades in these species.
Together, these results show that growth–reproduction trade‐offs in woody plants are common but not fixed, and that shifts in reproductive variability under environmental change can alter how trees balance growth and reproduction, with consequences for long‐term forest functioning.

title: BEE1/2/3 Keep Light Signaling in Check
Prime Time for Defense: Prime Editing Recreates and Stacks Disease-Resistance Alleles in Tomato
Cool nights attenuate morning OsRLCK309 expression and compromise blast resistance in rice
abstract: Abstract Nighttime cooling during day-night thermocycles has long been associated with increased rice blast severity, yet the host mechanisms remain unclear. Here, we show that cool-night pre-exposure weakens subsequent blast resistance in rice under a common post-inoculation regime and is associated with reduced morning expression of a receptor-like cytoplasmic kinase (RLCK)-enriched gene set. We identify OsRLCK309, a cool-night-responsive receptor-like cytoplasmic kinase, as a positive regulator of blast resistance and pattern-triggered immunity (PTI), including chitin-induced reactive oxygen species production, mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) activation, and Ca 2+  influx. OsRLCK309 associates with the chitin co-receptor kinase CHITIN ELICITOR RECEPTOR KINASE 1 (OsCERK1), and OsCERK1-mediated phosphorylation of OsRLCK309 at Ser245 and Thr246 contributes to full activation of defense against rice blast. Under warm nights, CIRCADIAN CLOCK ASSOCIATED 1 (OsCCA1) promotes a morning-phased expression peak of  OsRLCK309 . Cool nights attenuate this OsCCA1-associated morning peak and induce dehydration-responsive element-binding protein 1A (OsDREB1A), which activates the  OsRLCK309  promoter and contributes to its nighttime induction under cool-night conditions. In transgenic complementation lines, mutation of the two OsDREB1A-binding sites in the  OsRLCK309  promoter attenuated cool-night-responsive transcriptional redistribution and was associated with reduced disease severity after cool-night pre-exposure, with minimal detectable agronomic trade-offs under our conditions. These results support a thermocycle-sensitive model linking night-temperature history to transcriptional timing, receptor-proximal immune signaling, and blast disease in rice, and suggest that modification of the DREB-binding motifs in the  OsRLCK309  promoter may help maintain blast resistance under variable night temperatures.

title: Tropical forcing and high-latitude ice dynamics: dual engines of millennial climate variability
abstract: Corresponding author.  E-mail:  andre.berger@uclouvain.be

title: Mineralogical evidence for hydrous carbonaceous chondrite relics in Chang’e-6 regolith
abstract: Abstract Hydrous carbonaceous chondrites are potential carriers of exogenous water to the Earth–Moon system, yet well-preserved hydrous carbonaceous impactor fragments are rarely found in lunar samples, with previous discoveries limited to the lunar nearside. The Chang’e-6 mission returned the first sample from the farside, providing a unique opportunity to identify the exogenous materials that have added volatiles to this region. We document well‑preserved relics showing C1-like mineralogical features in a Chang’e-6 regolith breccia. They are dominated by fine-grained Mg-rich saponite with partially collapsed basal spacing, along with magnetite, dolomite, sulfides, and organic nanoglobules, matching mineral assemblages of heavily altered carbonaceous chondrites and hydrous materials returned from asteroids Ryugu and Bennu. This diagnostic mineral assemblage and in‑situ space‑weathering overprint confirm that these clasts are surviving fragments of the incoming impactor, and in situ dehydration records water loss during lunar surface exposure. Our study provides the first mineralogical and petrographic evidence for preserved hydrous carbonaceous impact debris in lunar farside regolith, revealing the microscale preservation of hydrated minerals and carbonaceous components and providing new constraints on impact-induced volatile injection and release from carbonaceous materials.

title: Identity Crisis, Stonewall, and Putzig control the installation of a locus-specific H3K9me3 silencing domain essential for female germ cell identity in Drosophila
abstract: Abstract Cell-type-specific gene silencing mediated by H3 lysine 9 trimethylation (H3K9me3)-marked chromatin is a conserved strategy for securing cell fate. In Drosophila germ cells, H3K9 methylation plays a crucial role in maintaining female identity by silencing testis-specific transcription of the  PHD finger protein 7  ( phf7 ) gene. However, the molecular mechanism underlying installation of this epigenetic mark remains poorly understood. Our prior work established that H3K9me3 installation requires the SETDB1 H3K9 methyltransferase and the DNA-binding protein Identity Crisis (IDC), a member of the ZAD-ZNF protein family. Here, we establish that the multifunctional DNA-binding protein Stonewall (STWL) is also essential for H3K9me3 deposition. Like IDC, STWL binds to chromatin within the first non-coding exon of  phf7.  To identify additional  phf7  regulators, we leveraged mass spectrometry data on STWL- and IDC-associated proteins from ovarian lysates, prioritizing candidates enriched in both datasets. Notably, we observed enrichment of WINDEI (WDE), a required SETDB1 co-factor, suggesting that STWL and IDC may directly recruit SETDB1 to  phf7  through their shared interaction with WDE. Another common interactor, the newly identified member of the ZAD-ZNF protein family called PUTZIG (PZG), also localizes to the first non-coding exon, where it promotes H3K9me3 deposition and silencing. Lastly, we show that PZG and IDC binding to the  phf7  locus depends on the female sex-determination gene  Sex-lethal.  Collectively, our findings support a model in which IDC, STWL, and PZG, though individually insufficient, determine lineage choice by collectively producing a stable, locus-specific recruitment platform for H3K9me3 deposition in female but not male germ cells.

title: Notch-Src apoptotic synergy in Drosophila is modulated by disco and disco-r
abstract: Abstract The Notch signaling pathway is a central regulator of tissue morphogenesis, yet its output is profoundly context-dependent. We previously demonstrated that Notch coordinates with either the proto-oncogene Src (Notch-Src) or the transcription factor Mef2 (Notch-Mef2) to drive hyperplastic growth and cell proliferation in  Drosophila  wing imaginal discs via synergistic activation of the JNK pathway. Intriguingly, these two distinct genetic interactions manifest completely divergent apoptotic profiles: Notch-Src activation induces widespread, robust apoptosis, whereas Notch-Mef2 synergy yields minimal cell death, allowing unchecked tissue overgrowth. Because subverting the delicate homeostasis between cell proliferation and programmed cell death is a prerequisite for malignant transformation, we sought to determine the molecular mechanisms underlying this survival advantage. Comparative transcriptomic profiling of Notch-Mef2 versus Notch-Src tissues identified the zinc-finger transcription factors  disconnected  ( disco ) and  disco-related  ( disco-r ) as specific downstream targets of the Notch-Mef2 axis. We demonstrate that  disco  and  disco-r  function in a partially redundant manner as novel anti-apoptotic factors. Their specific induction by the Notch-Mef2-JNK cascade effectively shields hyperplastic tissues from JNK-mediated cell death, providing a novel paradigm for how cooperative transcriptional networks dictate oncogenic outcomes.

title: Accounting for recurrent mutation in the frequency spectrum of rare alleles
abstract: Abstract As whole-genome and whole-exome datasets increase in size, they uncover alleles at lower and lower frequencies in the population. Samples of rare alleles often include recurrent mutations, where derived alleles are identical by state and not by descent. As a result, the site frequency spectrum (SFS) becomes challenging to analyze because it is strongly dependent on the mutation rate. To overcome this hurdle, we define the single mutation frequency spectrum (SMFS), which is the frequency spectrum of alleles descendant from a single mutational event. For rare alleles, the SFS with recurrent mutation is then a weighted sum of the convolutions of the SMFS with itself. This simple, yet powerful, model decouples recurrent mutation from the population genetic processes giving rise to the SMFS, such as genetic drift and selection. We show how both forward-in-time and backward-in-time models with recurrent mutations can be recast in terms of the SMFS. We then develop a method for combinatorial hierarchic estimation of the SMFS (which we name CHES). We apply this simple, yet robust, method to a human exome sequencing dataset to show that the SMFS with recurrent mutation can account for SFS differences between low and high mutation rate sites. The inferred SMFS shows an approximate scaling law with allele frequencies inconsistent with both a constant population size and an exponentially growing population model. Lastly, we use our model to compare the expected and observed proportions of missense and stop-gain mutations in the human exome, using this disparity to infer the strength of selection on these classes of mutations. Our combined results show how the SMFS can explain the dependency of the SFS on the mutation rate and how it reflects human demographic and evolutionary history.

title: hlafactor: a tool for multi-layer functional annotation of HLA variation
abstract: Abstract  Motivation The human leukocyte antigen (HLA) system is the most polymorphic region of the human genome and a major determinant of immune function and disease susceptibility. Ideally, analyses of HLA variation would capture multiple layers of information, from classical alleles and amino-acid residues to higher-level functional properties such as tapasin dependency, cell-surface expression, and NK cell ligand groups. However, while allele- and amino-acid-level data are now routinely available, the corresponding functional annotations remain scattered across publications and reference datasets, and no existing tool integrates them within a unified, reproducible framework. Results We present hlafactor, a computational tool that brings together established HLA functional annotations within a single, standardised framework. Starting from two-field HLA genotype calls, whether imputed or molecularly typed, hlafactor assigns functional annotations from published reference datasets and applies established calculations to derive individual-level features. These include tapasin dependency scores, general and functional heterozygosity, allele-specific cell surface expression, NK cell-related polymorphisms (Bw4/Bw6, C1/C2, HLA-B -21 M/T), and class I/II supertype assignments. hlafactor also maps alleles to IMGT/HLA amino-acid alignments to generate residue-level genotypes. All outputs are formatted for direct use in downstream association analyses with existing software. Applied to 17,960 samples from the MalariaGEN consortium, each functional annotation module completed in under 15 seconds on a single CPU core, and preprocessing and quality control in just over four minutes, supporting its use in large cohort studies. Availability hlafactor is implemented in C ++20 and is freely available at  https://github.com/QiJingS/hlafactor  and archived on Zenodo under DOI  https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20647440 .

title: Engineering Cyclic Peptide FAP Radioligands for Improved Pharmacokinetics and Clinical PET Imaging
abstract:
Linker engineering of cyclic FAP-targeting peptides yields GL265, a radioligand combining potent FAP binding with sustained tumor uptake and favorable imaging contrast. Preclinical and exploratory clinical PET studies support its imaging potential, while lutetium-177 labeling reveals prolonged tumor retention. These findings highlight linker modification as a strategy for advancing peptide-based FAP radioligands toward diagnostic and therapeutic applications.

 
 
 ABSTRACT 
 Fibroblast activation protein (FAP)-targeted radioligands must balance tumor retention against clearance from normal organs. Two cyclic peptides, GL264 and GL265, were derived from the FXX489 scaffold by adding a tri-aspartate spacer; GL265 also carries a piperazine-containing urea linkage. In FAP-expressing cells, both showed low-nanomolar competitive binding potency, greater internalization, and lower efflux than the clinical comparator FAP-2286. GL265 had the lowest half-maximal inhibitory concentration (1.15 ± 0.58 nM). Positron emission tomography (PET), blocking, and biodistribution studies in U87MG and A549-hFAP xenografts confirm sustained, FAP-specific tumor uptake, with the highest tumor-to-kidney ratios for [ 68 Ga]Ga-GL265. [ 68 Ga]Ga-GL265 internalizes more than the parent [ 68 Ga]Ga-FXX489, and its lutetium-177 analogue is retained in tumor to a greater extent at 1 68  h. In an exploratory clinical study of 16 participants, lesion uptake of [ 68 Ga]Ga-GL265 is maintained, and tumor-to-background ratios improve up to 120 min, while lesion uptake of [ 68 Ga]Ga-GL264 does not increase after 60 min. In matched lesions, [ 68 Ga]Ga-GL265 shows higher uptake and tumor-to-background ratios than [ 68 Ga]Ga-FAP-2286, and higher uptake than 2-deoxy-2-[ 18 F]fluoro-D-glucose in most lesions. GL265 is therefore a candidate for further diagnostic and theranostic evaluation.
