Recently developed high phylogenetic resolution fluorescence in situ hybridization (HiPR-FISH) is an image-based mapping technology that provides spatial microbiome data at single-cell resolution, which allows for visualizing and quantifying spatial arrangement of microbial cells. Despite the growing availability of such data, no methods have been tailored to studying spatial dysbiosis in image-based microbiome data. Results: Here we introduce MiSA (Microbiome Spatial Aberration), the first statistical framework for identifying disease-associated spatial dysbiosis and the individual taxa that may contribute to it, based on differing degrees of clustering or regularity, i.e., microbial cells being more aggregated or more evenly spaced than expected under complete spatial randomness, between diagnostic groups. In simulations based on a real dataset, MiSA was robust across diverse and noisy spatial configurations, achieving substantially higher statistical power than a method borrowed from spatial proteomics, while controlling type I error at both the individual-taxon and community levels. When applied to an oral biofilm study, MiSA detected peri-implant mucositis-associated spatial dysbiosis at the community level and identified five taxa as potential contributors, including Actinomyces, which showed increased clustering in mucositis. Conclusions: MiSA is a powerful and robust framework for identifying spatial dysbiosis and the contributing taxa in image-based microbiome data, offering new insights into the spatial organization of microbial communities in disease.

title: Dynamics of somatic L1 retrotransposition in the human brain
abstract: The sole source of genomic diversity in the human brain caused by autonomous retrotransposition is facilitated by the long interspersed nuclear element-1 (L1). However, assessing the rate, timing and source elements of this event has been challenging due to the lack of technologies that capture of L1s at sufficient scale in single cells. Here, we introduce LUSTRE, a single-cell assay that enables mapping L1 sites without whole-genome amplification, and profile ~17,600 neurons from the dentate gyrus, cortex, cerebellum of the adult human brain. We report the presence of somatic L1s that define related lineages and conservatively estimate a validation-adjusted rate of 0.1-0.3 somatic events per neuron. Our analyses further indicate two distinct waves of retrotransposition during development and combined with the variability in their polyA tract lengths across single nuclei, suggest the formation of lineage hierarchies marked by new somatic retrotransposition events and cell divisions. Mapping the origin of L1s through 3'-transduction events identify the rare source L1s that are responsible for the majority of retrotransposition events. These results uncover the dynamics of L1-driven somatic mosaicism and establish L1s as endogenous recorders of cellular and lineage history in human tissues.

title: A large-scale multi-omics study of cortical miRNA dysregulation in Alzheimer's disease
abstract: MicroRNAs regulate gene expression, but their roles in Alzheimer's disease pathology and downstream molecular changes remain incompletely characterized. We integrated cortical small RNA-sequencing data from seven datasets across six postmortem cohorts comprising 1,738 individuals with transcriptomic, proteomic, genetic, and single-nucleus data. Meta-analysis of 405 microRNAs identified 16 associated with advanced and four with intermediate neurofibrillary tangle pathology, with miR-132-3p significant in both comparisons. Five microRNAs (miR-132-3p, miR-212-3p, miR-212-5p, miR-146b-5p, miR-3200-3p) showed evidence of mediating associations between target mRNA and protein expression and tau pathology. Consensus co-expression network analysis linked the miR-132/212 family to opposing neuronal/synaptic and oligodendrocyte/myelination-related programmes. Mediated targets were enriched among tau-associated differentially expressed genes across glial cell types, particularly astrocytes. Inferred cell-type regulatory networks further highlighted miR-132-3p and miR-146b as recurrent hubs. These findings prioritize a restricted set of cortical microRNAs and associated neuronal and glial molecular programmes for mechanistic investigation in Alzheimer's disease.

title: Stress granule transcript contrasts between colorectal cancer compartments depend on scoring and depth
abstract: Stress granule (SG) gene-set scores summarize transcription associated with stress-response machinery, but their stability across scoring definitions is uncertain. We compared fibroblast-epithelial expression contrasts for four fixed SG lists in two colorectal cancer single-cell cohorts containing 195,527 cells from 85 donors. Analyses used donor pairing, gene-wise standardized expression, within-cell ranks and raw-count pseudobulk summaries, with tissue and sequencing-depth sensitivities. At least 20 tumor cells per compartment were available for 15 and 29 paired donors. Pseudobulk SG-A contrasts were negative in both cohorts: median differences in mean log2 counts per million were -0.383 (95% confidence interval -0.493 to -0.319) and -0.493 (-0.614 to -0.384). Rank-based SG-B contrasts were also negative in both cohorts. In a post hoc comparison using identical depth-retained cells and weights, the second cohort had positive gene-Z estimates and negative rank-based estimates; the positive estimates did not meet the eight-test false-discovery threshold. Spatial comparisons depended on the fibroblast reference subtype, and the CosMx panel measured only 11 of 27 SG-B genes. RNA-protein correlations varied across genes, while organoid depletion calls were more frequent for selected translation-associated members than for the four core members. These findings establish reproducible relative-expression contrasts under specified definitions and show that their direction can change across scoring and depth conditions. Reporting the scoring definition, retained donor population, depth sensitivity and gene coverage together identifies the contrasts that reproduce and provides a defined basis for testing their relationship to SG formation.

title: BiomedCAT: Biomedical Context Analysis Tool for Supporting Mechanistic Hypothesis Generation via User-defined Contextual Subgraph Extraction
abstract: Researchers formulate mechanistic hypotheses in slides and figures long before they write them as text, yet knowledge-graph (KG) tools expect a query in the vocabulary of the graph. We present BiomedCAT, an open-source workflow that turns biomedical slides into a subgraph of the RTX-KG2c knowledge graph shaped by the user's research profile, on a laptop and without sending the documents out. A small vision-language model describes each slide; a 4-billion-parameter agent types the terms into the classes of the Biolink model; an existence gate removes invented entities; identifiers are retrieved from Translator services or from a local table and selected, never generated, by a judge model; and a profile-weighted two-hop expansion builds the context graph. On a synthetic Biolink typing benchmark whose labels were audited by an expert, the local agent reaches 0.71 accuracy on 517 non-ambiguous mentions, 4 points below Claude Opus 5 (0.75), level with DeepSeek-V4-Flash (0.69) and above open-weight models of 24 and 31 billion parameters; the audit also showed that 55% of the generated labels were wrong or ambiguous. On expert-annotated slide decks, the reading stage recovers 81 to 94% of the explicit terms of the English deck, less on French decks, and linking assigns the expert identifier to 65% of the found terms online and 26% in the fully local mode. A one-slide run takes 33 to 42 minutes, with peaks of 9.8~GB of system RAM above idle and 5.3~GB of GPU memory. In a facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy (FSHD) case, three slides that each draw one pathway from DUX4 at a different biological scale give graphs that overlap by 7 to 15% of their nodes, each recovering its own pathway's expected nodes, and expose sourced paths from DUX4, such as a DUX4--HMGB1 interaction from IntAct. Of 21 compounds tested in FSHD, seven, including every agent that targets DUX4, are absent from RTX-KG2c, which bounds what a graph-based approach can propose. BiomedCAT lets a researcher set a working hypothesis against curated knowledge, with every edge traceable to its source.

title: LipidRT: leveraging retention time coherence for robust lipid annotation in reversed-phase LC-MS-based lipidomics
abstract: MS/MS data alone is often insufficient for confident lipid identification, while existing retention time (RT)-based methods, despite their promise, have limited applicability. We present LipidRT, an R-based Shiny application that uses RT coherence to validate, refine and expand lipid annotations in untargeted RPLC-HRMS lipidomics in a dataset-specific, software-agnostic manner. By exploiting conserved chromatographic elution relationships as structural constraints and excluding RT-inconsistent annotations from model fitting, LipidRT improves annotation confidence, coverage and consistency while minimizing manual curation.

title: Target-enrichment sequencing reveals intergenotypic reassortment of infectious salmon anaemia virus in Atlantic Canada
abstract: Infectious salmon anaemia virus (ISAV) causes severe disease and substantial economic losses in farmed Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar). The virus has an eight-segment, negative-sense single-stranded RNA (ssRNA) genome and is divided into European and North American genotypes. Despite their co-circulation in locations such as the Atlantic coast of Canada, reassortment between these genotypes has never been observed. However, routine diagnostic and sequence-based surveillance often target individual genome segments and may therefore fail to identify reassortant viruses or accurately resolve their genomic ancestry. In this study, we developed a probe panel targeting both genotypes and applied Oxford Nanopore sequencing to 37 ISAV-positive samples collected from 14 farm sites in the Bay of Fundy, New Brunswick, Canada. Twenty-seven samples yielded 29 consensus genomes, including separate viral consensuses recovered from two mixed infections. Segment-specific phylogenies identified 24 viruses with a previously unreported intergenotypic genomic constellation comprising a European-genotype segment 3 and North American-genotype segments 1, 2 and 4 - 8. Their consistent monophyletic clustering across segment-specific phylogenies supports a single ancestral reassortment event followed by onward circulation of the reassortant lineage. A time-scaled phylogeny of segment 3 estimated the posterior mean time to the most recent common ancestor (tMRCA) of the sampled reassortant cluster as September 2016 (95% HPD: March 2013-June 2019), indicating that this segment 3 lineage pre-dated its first sampling in 2021. Five additional viruses represented several distinct EU-genotype lineages. To our knowledge, this is the first documented reassortment between the European and North American ISAV genotypes. These findings identify an intergenotypic reassortant lineage detected across multiple farms in the Bay of Fundy and demonstrate the value of whole-genome sequencing for detecting reassortment, mixed infections and epidemiologically relevant viral diversity.

title: HARICOT: De Novo Assembly of Raw Nanopore Signals using Fuzzy de Bruijn Graphs
abstract: Nanopore sequencing enables reading long nucleotide sequences by measuring characteristic changes in ionic current as molecules pass through a nanopore. These current measurements, known as raw signals, can be analyzed without translating them into bases (i.e., without basecalling), which provides fast and resource-efficient genome analysis. Prior work, Rawsamble, enables finding overlaps between raw nanopore signals, without basecalling them, and generating assemblies from these overlaps with off-the-shelf assemblers such as miniasm. Constructing assemblies directly from raw signals can substantially reduce redundancy and fragmentation in signal datasets, which is useful for many downstream tasks such as constructing non-redundant and accurate basecalled reads from assembled signals. However, existing overlap-based signal assembly strategies suffer from limited scalability and resolution mainly due to using off-the-shelf assemblers (e.g., miniasm) that are designed for basecalled sequences. While scalability and performance limitations can be addressed by existing de Bruijn graph approaches to assembly, their reliance on exact matches makes these methods too sensitive to the inherently noisy raw nanopore signals. To improve assembly of raw signals using de Bruijn graph approaches, we present HARICOT, a mechanism that constructs assemblies from raw nanopore signals by utilizing fuzzy de Bruijn graphs and Hough-transform-based overlap detection to robustly tolerate errors and noise in raw nanopore signals. Our evaluations on various genomes of different sizes show that HARICOT significantly improves assembly contiguity and quality compared to Rawsamble, helping close the gap to popular assembly tools such as Flye or wtdbg2 operating on nucleotide sequences. At the same time, performance remains comparable to these assemblers, without requiring additional basecalling. We discuss that assembling raw nanopore signals before basecalling enables future work in various ways such as building these de Bruijn graphs in a streaming way and assembly-aware basecalling techniques that can basecall assembly graphs for accurate and redundancy-resolved basecalling. HARICOT is available at https://github.com/STORMgroup/HARICOT . We also provide the scripts to fully reproduce our results on our GitHub page.

title: SPIDER: Contextualizing Biomedical Knowledge for Evidence-Grounded Scientific Reasoning
abstract: Aggregated relations in biomedical knowledge graphs can obscure evidence and study conditions, complicating the distinction between scientific disagreement and contextual differences. Here we introduce SPIDER, a multi-agent framework grounding biomedical relations in literature evidence and extracting study conditions for interpretation. Applied to a graph integrating 48 databases and ontologies, SPIDER analyzed 1.95 million PubMed abstracts, adding 2.31 million previously unrepresented, literature-supported entity pairs to construct SPIDER-KG. Daily updates incorporate relations and evidence from newly indexed PubMed records. Across 89,937 evidence-supported comparisons of potentially incompatible relations, SPIDER classified 79.0% as contextual differences, and 6.1% as genuine disagreement, achieving 80.3% macro-F1 averaged across both categories against expert annotations. On SPIDER-Bench and four biomedical reasoning benchmarks, SPIDER-KG improved large language models' interpretation of evidence-supported biomedical relationships. Retrospective analysis of newly reported gene--disease relationships further demonstrated how evidence-linked knowledge can contextualize emerging discoveries. SPIDER-KG provides a reusable, incrementally extensible evidence layer for biomedical reasoning.

title: Breedbase: An Integrated Breeding Informatics System with Statistical Analysis and Decision-Support Tools
abstract: Breeding programs are becoming increasingly data-intensive, digital and collaborative. One-stop digital breeding ecosystems, in which data storage, field workflow tools, statistical analysis and breeding decision-support tools are seamlessly integrated, are increasingly important. Breedbase (https://breedbase.org) is one of the few open-source platforms that integrate these functionalities within a single system. It provides tools for phenotypic data quality control, descriptive, inferential and predictive statistical analyses. Integrated into the database are tools for single-trial analysis of variance (ANOVA), linear mixed modeling, stability analysis, correlation analysis, principal component analysis, k-means and hierarchical clustering, kinship and inbreeding analysis, genome-wide association study (GWAS), and genomic prediction. Input data and outputs from these analysis tools are visualized in interactive plots and are also available in text files for downloading and sharing. By persisting analysis datasets in the database and applying standardized and automated data preprocessing and analysis workflows, Breedbase is designed to improve efficiency, help maintain data integrity, and support reproducible analyses that can be readily shared among collaborators. Breedbase is open-source software, containerized using Docker, and available for self-hosting or cloud hosting and management by the Mueller lab.

title: Evaluation depth reshapes method rankings in proteomic co-abundance network inference
abstract: Network inference from quantitative proteomics is usually benchmarked at a single, arbitrarily chosen number of top-ranked edges, so the influence of evaluation depth has not, to our knowledge, been systematically tested. We compared five strategies (random forest with bootstrap selection-frequency filtering, WGCNA, GENIE3, Spearman correlation and context likelihood of relatedness) across seven proteomic datasets from four quantification platforms, using harmonised preprocessing and Precision@K, the fraction of a method's K top-ranked protein pairs present in a pooled reference of curated protein associations (STRING, BioGRID and CORUM). Method rankings changed with depth. In all six datasets that allow an equal-depth comparison, the leading method at K = 50 differed from the leader at K = 2,000, and 18 of 24 pairwise comparisons involving the filtered random forest reversed somewhere along the depth range, although seven of these reversals rested on differences of at most 0.02 in precision and each network was inferred only once. No method dominated. Relative to the same random forest without filtering, the selection-frequency filter was associated with small differences (+0.006 to +0.036 in Precision@500 in six of six equal-depth datasets; mixed at shallower depths) that cannot be separated from its 20- to 50-fold greater number of fitted trees. Prospective testing on independent datasets gave one qualified replication, one non-replication and one non-evaluable dataset. We recommend reporting precision trajectories across depths rather than single-threshold comparisons.

title: Computable Genomes: A Layered Computational Framework for Non-Coding DNA and Cellular Behavior
abstract: Genome-wide association studies have catalogued tens of thousands of trait-associated loci, most of them in non-coding DNA, yet for most loci the path from nucleotide to phenotype remains correlational. We propose a layered computational decomposition of the genome as a complement to data-driven approaches: sequence as formal language, sequence as information-bearing signal, mobile elements as runtime, compilation to interaction networks through thermodynamic and rule-based models, and execution as cellular and multicellular dynamics. Each layer is defined by its inputs, outputs and formalisms, and we set out where the frame breaks down, including the looseness of algorithmic-information estimates, the triviality of universality results and the failure of string grammars at the chromatin level. Synthetic-biology platforms serve as tests of whether the layers compose, and genomic foundation models and the AlphaGenome Atlas, which predicts effects for all nine billion possible single-nucleotide variants, serve as oracles whose coverage and limits we map onto the framework. We state five falsifiable predictions and test the first, that sequence compressibility carries information about regulatory function beyond composition and conservation, on 38,556 single-nucleotide variants from a saturation-mutagenesis reporter assay of 21 regulatory elements. In a pooled model, local compressibility is associated with measured effect size (standardized {beta} = -0.030, p = 0.0014). The association roughly halves under full control for base composition, loses significance when composition, motif and noise adjustments are combined under locus-level inference (wild cluster bootstrap p = 0.11), and averages zero within loci (random-effects {beta} = -0.0003, p = 0.90). The prediction is therefore not supported at the variant level in these data, which bound the effect a genome-wide test should expect. The argument is not that the genome "is" a program, but that treating it as one supplies formal tools whose predictions can be checked.

title: Learning spatial cellular state through 3D reconstruction of the cell
abstract: Subcellular-resolution spatial transcriptomics localizes individual RNA transcripts within cells with high-precision. Existing methods for identifying spatially organized cell populations rely on cellular niches defined by neighboring cells, leaving open whether such populations can be identified from individual-cell representations alone. Moreover, representations that jointly capture transcript identity and three-dimensional (3D) spatial organization have not been systematically learned or biologically evaluated. Here we present a representation learning framework that models each cell as a gene-annotated point cloud of transcripts and trains a rotation-equivariant neural network to reconstruct 3D cell shape, yielding spatially informed transcript embeddings. We further aggregate these embeddings into a cell-state representation that summarizes transcript-level spatial patterns. Our framework outperforms existing point-cloud-based 3D reconstruction methods on cell-shape reconstruction. In MERFISH human uterine cancer, combining the learned embeddings with gene expression improved prediction of CD45RO protein intensity over both gene expression alone and niche-based embeddings. Applied to MERFISH human liver cancer and Xenium human lung datasets, our framework identified distinct spatial patterns between cell populations, including spatially organized subpopulations marked by disease-associated gene expression and patterns associated with pathological tissue structures. Together, these results show that learning transcript representations through 3D cell reconstruction provides a novel approach to capture cell-state heterogeneity and biologically relevant spatial organization in subcellular spatial transcriptomics.

title: A statistical framework to identify gene-gene interactions underlying multiple dichotomous phenotypes from genotype data
abstract:
by Siru Wang, Xuhui Zhu, Yu Li, Gengjie Jia 

Identifying gene-gene (G × G) interactions across multiple dichotomous phenotypes is challenging due to the extreme sparsity of SNP-derived interaction matrices and the reduced statistical power associated with binary outcomes. Existing G × G association methods are restricted to either single or multiple continuous phenotypes. Here we introduce GiMat (Gene Interaction and Multiple-phenotype Association Test), a statistical framework that extends multivariate kernel regression to model G × G interactions jointly across dichotomous phenotypes, while explicitly capturing homogeneous and heterogeneous interaction effects. Extensive simulations demonstrate that GiMat controls type I error conservatively and adapts power flexibly to different types of relationships between interaction effects and phenotypes. Applied to type 2 diabetes and hypertension comorbidity in the UK Biobank, GiMat identified four previously unreported G × G interaction pairs associated with both phenotypes. This scalable framework enables robust discovery of complex genetic interactions underlying multiple correlated phenotypes.

title: Aging out of the blue: Region-specific epigenetic clock calibration for a blue zone with the DNAm SuperLearner
abstract:
by Nolan Gunter, Andres Cardenas, Michael Kobor, Nicole Gladish, Julie MacIsaac, Kristy Dever, David Rehkopf, William Dow, Luis Rosero-Bixby, Alan Hubbard 

Epigenetic clocks estimate biological age from DNA methylation patterns at CpG sites, providing robust predictions of mortality and morbidity risk. “Blue zones,” regions of exceptional longevity, offer a unique opportunity to investigate how biological aging diverges from chronological age. However, standard clocks are typically trained on large, heterogeneous datasets, reflecting average population trends rather than region-specific dynamics. Using data from the Costa Rican Longevity and Healthy Aging Study (CRELES), we profiled DNA methylation from residents of the Nicoya blue zone ( n  = 206) and a reference population in other parts of Costa Rica ( n  = 875). We propose training a  SuperLearner , an ensemble machine learning approach, on the non-Nicoyan Costa Ricans to optimize predictive performance across existing clocks and flexible machine learners. By its Oracle property, the  SuperLearner ’s weighted combination of algorithms performs asymptotically as well as the best possible combination of the candidate predictors. We then used this trained model to construct a calibrated hypothesis test comparing Epigenetic Age Acceleration (EAA) distributions between the blue zone region and the reference population. Before calibration or covariate adjustment, estimates for Nicoyans depended heavily on the chosen clock. The SuperLearner placed them about three years younger on average (R¯1=−3.05,95% CI [−3.64,−2.46]), whereas DNAmFitAge placed them almost four years older (R¯1=3.59,95% CI [3.02,4.17]). Mean calibration to non-Nicoyan Costa Ricans made estimates consistent across clocks, with an estimated EAA advantage to approximately two years (Δ^=−1.96,95% CI [−2.56,−1.37]). After age-stratified calibration within 10-year age groups, only a small EAA advantage (Δ^=−0.35,95% CI [−0.64,−0.05]) remained, concentrated among the oldest participants. This approach provides a robust and reproducible framework for estimating longevity in distinct regions when a relevant reference population is available.

title: Storing long-lived memories via molecular error correction: A minimal mathematical model of Crick’s memory switch
abstract:
by John J. Vastola, Tejas Ramdas, Samuel J. Gershman 

Cells store information in part by attaching molecular marks to proteins and DNA. But because marks can be randomly removed (e.g., due to ambient phosphatase activity) and added (e.g., due to ambient kinase activity), information encoding may be poor, and in the worst case marks may only store information on the time scale of molecular turnover. We identify a high-level strategy cells use to maintain encoding fidelity beyond the time scale of turnover—which we call molecular error correction—and find that it closely resembles an underexplored theoretical proposal by Francis Crick. To assess the effectiveness of molecular error correction, we construct and analyze several minimal mathematical models of molecular memory switches. We find that Crick-like error correction provides an efficient way to improve the lifetime of stored memories, especially compared to redundantly encoding information using a large number of molecules, but that it can yield false positives (and hence low information fidelity) when there is ambient marking activity; given these two competing concerns, the optimal level of error correction is moderate rather than arbitrarily high. We also find that combining error correction with redundant encoding can efficiently and robustly produce memories that last between ten and one hundred times longer than the turnover time scale. Our work provides insight regarding how to model and interrogate noisy molecular memory systems, suggests that error correction is a design principle of molecular memory, and quantitatively connects error correction to observable memory time scales.

title: Radiopharmaceutical therapy for metastatic prostate cancer: Insights from mechanistic modeling and  in silico  trials
abstract:
by Matteo Italia, Silvia Bordel-Vozmediano, José García Otero, Gabriel F. Calvo, Víctor M. Pérez-García 

Radiopharmaceutical therapy (RPT) has rapidly evolved into a key precision-oncology modality, with radioligands now approved or in late-stage development for multiple solid tumors, including neuroendocrine and prostate cancers. RPT with [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA (Prostate-Specific Membrane Antigen) has recently been approved as a life-prolonging treatment for metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC), but its clinical use still relies on nonpersonalized, empirically chosen fixed schedules. Here, we develop a mechanistic, patient-personalizable mathematical model simulating mCRPC response and organ-at-risk toxicity during [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA RPT. The model integrates tumor growth dynamics, radiobiological response, and organ-resolved pharmacokinetics inferred from mass data and standardized uptake values obtained from positron emission tomography studies. Parameters were derived from the literature, although the framework allows personalization by fitting to patient-specific data, such as imaging and prostate-specific antigen levels. Analytical threshold analysis identified a critical activity scale governing net tumor control, while simulations of a representative virtual patient (VP) illustrated the model’s coupled tumor and activity dynamics. Global sensitivity analysis identified tumor growth, uptake, and radiosensitivity parameters as key drivers of interpatient variability. Using VP cohorts generated via stochastic parameter sampling, we conducted  in silico  trials and benchmarked the model against published dosimetry and survival data for [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA trials. Convergence testing supported the use of cohorts of 500 VPs for stable population-level estimates. We then explored dosing and scheduling strategies to quantify efficacy–toxicity trade-offs. Consolidated regimens with fewer, higher-activity injections improved overall survival (OS)  in silico  but increased toxicity, especially in kidneys. Cycle length had a weaker influence on OS within a 2–9 week window, while it clearly affected toxicity, whereas excessive delays (> 12 weeks) markedly reduced efficacy. These methodological findings illustrate how mechanistic modeling and  in silico  trials can inform the design and personalization of RPT regimens.

title: Pennycress population genomics reveals a complex global expansion history and local climate-adaptation targets for neodomestication
abstract:
Background
                      Field pennycress ( Thlaspi arvense ) is an emerging winter oilseed crop whose life cycle fits between corn-soybean rotations, yielding animal feed and feedstock for sustainable aviation fuel. 
                  
                     Results
                      Here we analyze the largest pennycress panel assembled to date, 739 natural accessions spanning four continents, combining genome-wide diversity analysis with multi-year field evaluation. Our genomic data support that pennycress originated in Eurasia and likely underwent a complex history involving multiple introductions and admixture. Scans for selective sweeps among populations between Eurasian and North American identify phenology-related genes, including the MADS-Affecting Flowering ( MAF ) transcription factors and the seed-dormancy gene  DELAY OF GERMINATION 1  ( DOG1 ), suggesting possible targets of phenological adaptation. By cross-species climate genome-wide association studies, we detect 10 syntenic peaks, suggesting partly conserved molecular machinery underlying climate adaptation in Arabidopsis and pennycress. Multi-year, multi-location field trials of over 400 accessions in Illinois identify a significant locus associated with green canopy cover, a trait important for biomass, containing a tandem array of Mitochondrial Transcription Termination Factor ( mTERF5 ) genes. Finally, the field trials reveal significant genotype-by-environment interaction, underscoring the need for regional breeding programs. 
                  
                     Conclusions
                      Together, these results document worldwide patterns of genetic variation and candidate climate-adaptive genes that can accelerate the neodomestication of pennycress for cultivation in the midwestern United States.

title: Complex-valued representations of time-series gene expression profiles for network analysis
abstract:
Background
                      Time-series RNA sequencing provides a framework for studying dynamic gene regulation, yet conventional analyses usually represent gene expression profiles as real-valued vectors and quantify similarity using correlation or distance. Inspired by quantum information theory, we present a framework for encoding time-series gene expression profiles as complex-valued vectors comprising amplitude and phase components. 
                  
                     Results
                      We designed multiple encoding models that represent gene expression through the amplitude components of complex-valued vectors, encode temporal differences in the phase components, and extend the phase representation to incorporate the direction of local expression changes. Gene–gene similarity was then quantified using fidelity, which measures the overlap between two encoded vectors. Comparisons of pairwise fidelity values across the encoding models and with conventional correlation measures showed that the models produced related but distinct similarity structures. We then constructed gene–gene networks from pairwise fidelity values and detected communities of genes with similar temporal profiles. Evaluation using simulated time-series RNA-seq datasets showed moderate agreement between detected communities and the ground truth temporal patterns, with no fidelity-based model consistently outperforming weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) or fuzzy c-means clustering across the adjusted Rand index, adjusted mutual information, pairwise F1 score, pairwise precision, and pairwise recall. In real time-series RNA-seq datasets from diverse species and biological contexts, the fidelity-based communities captured major temporal expression programs while differing among encoding m​odels in their ​community structure. Functional annotations provided exploratory biological context, and the major temporal programs broadly overlapped with those identified by WGCNA and fuzzy c-means clustering. As a supplementary proof-of-concept, we simulated SWAP-test circuits on a classical computer to estimate fidelity. Under noise-aware conditions, the simulated fidelity estimates were less accurate and computationally more costly than direct classical computation. 
                  
                     Conclusions
                      Representing time-series gene expression profiles as complex-valued vectors and comparing them using fidelity provides a proof-of-concept framework for temporal transcriptome analysis. The results demonstrate that encoding design changes the temporal relationships emphasized by gene–gene similarity, while not establishing uniform superiority over conventional methods.

title: NeRNA-Web: A web-based platform for structure-aware negative RNA generation and comparative evaluation in ncRNA classification
abstract:
Background
                      Supervised machine learning (ML) is widely used for noncoding RNA (ncRNA) classification; however, model performance is highly dependent on the construction of negative training datasets. Common strategies, such as random or dinucleotide-preserving shuffling, may introduce biases that lead to overestimated performance and reduced generalizability. Despite this, there is currently no standardized and accessible framework for generating and comparing negative RNA datasets. 
                  
                     Results
                      We present NeRNA-Web, a user-friendly web-based platform designed for generating structure-aware negative RNA sequences and conducting comparative evaluations. NeRNA-Web implements the previously developed NeRNA transformation, which incorporates predicted secondary-structure information into an encoded representation to generate transformed negative sequences. In addition to NeRNA-based generation, the platform incorporates several commonly used negative generation methods, such as random shuffling and dinucleotide-preserving shuffling, all within a unified and reproducible pipeline. The platform supports various ncRNA classes, including miRNA, lncRNA, tRNA, and circRNA, and offers visualization and export functionalities for downstream analyses. 
                  
                     Conclusions
                      NeRNA-Web provides an accessible and extensible framework for generating and comparatively characterizing negative RNA datasets using alternative generation strategies. By enabling users to examine and download the generated datasets, the platform facilitates transparent and reproducible negative-data construction for downstream ncRNA research. The observed differences among generation strategies further emphasize the importance of carefully selecting and evaluating negative datasets according to the requirements of the intended downstream analysis.

title: Efficient and generalizable deep attention with weighted residuals for drug-target interaction prediction
abstract: Precise prediction of DTIs (drug-target interactions) is essential for drug repositioning and novel therapeutic development. Despite progress in deep learning and computing power, DTI prediction remains a time-consuming task. And most existing approaches overlook the influence of differentially weighted residual attention mechanisms on model performance, which could hinder their predictive performance. To address these limitations, we present DWRA-DTI (Deep Weighted Residual Attention-DTI), a novel DTI prediction framework that integrates streamlined preprocessing and early stopping strategies to achieve sub-minute inference times without sacrificing accuracy.Specifically, drug and protein feature matrices are encoded into embeddings of a unified dimension using graph convolutional encoders, which are subsequently fused through a weighted residual attention module to capture intricate interaction patterns. The fused representations are then passed into a MLP (Multilayer Perceptron) to predict potential interactions. Our study investigates the impact of varying weights in residual attention through ablation experiments, demonstrating that weighted residual attention effectively enhances model performance. The proposed model achieves outstanding results across multiple datasets, offering a promising approach and valuable insights for advancing current drug-target interaction prediction methods.

title: Pixel-level DNA encoding with codon pattern feature extraction for oral cancer classification using transformer ensembles
abstract:
Background
                      Oral cancer is among the most aggressive cancer types worldwide, and early diagnosis and accurate classification are important for improving diagnosis and patient prognosis. Many oral cancer cases are diagnosed at advanced stages, whereas detection at precancerous stages can contribute to reducing mortality. Therefore, there is a need for effective image-based approaches capable of providing accurate and reliable oral cancer classification. 
                  
                     Methods
                      This study proposes a pixel-level DNA encoding framework with codon-based feature extraction for oral cancer image classification. Each image is transformed into DNA planes using an encoding scheme that considers the first six bits of each pixel and converts them into nucleotide sequences while maintaining run-length and GC-content constraints. Three consecutive nucleotides are grouped to form codons, and probability histograms of the codon patterns are computed to construct feature vectors. These feature vectors are classified using TabPFN, TabTransformer, SAINT, and FT-Transformer, together with an ensemble model. The framework was evaluated on ten publicly accessible datasets comprising four clinical and six histopathological image datasets. 
                  
                     Results
                      On the clinical datasets, the proposed framework achieved 98.90% precision, 98.89% recall, 98.90% F1-score, and 98.90% accuracy. On the histopathological datasets, it achieved 97.49% precision, 98.09% recall, 97.78% F1-score, and 97.99% accuracy. 
                  
                     Conclusion
                      The results demonstrate that the proposed pixel-level DNA encoding and codon-based feature extraction framework provides a robust and accurate approach for oral cancer image classification. The compact codon-derived representation combined with transformer-based ensemble classification shows its potential for analyzing both clinical and histopathological oral cancer images.

title: OsPLT7, a Non‐BBM PLETHORA Factor, Drives Synthetic Apomixis Without Compromising Fertility in Rice
abstract: Plant Biotechnology Journal, EarlyView.

title: A change in sex chromosomes caused by allopolyploidy in a willow lineage triggered new evolutionary changes in descendant species
abstract:
Hypothesis for the sex determination systems and associated sex-determining genes in  Salix  species of the 15ZW clade II.
 
 
 Summary 
 
Polyploidization through hybridization between species with different sex chromosomes is evolutionarily surprising. To understand stable sex-determining systems in such hybrids, we studied a dioecious allotetraploid (4 n ) willow lineage that arose by hybridization between  Salix  species from the  Salix  and  Vetrix  clades.
We generated chromosome-level assemblies for three allotetraploids and one related diploid, characterized their sex-linked regions (SLRs) to infer their evolutionary history, and analyzed mRNA and small RNA (sRNA) expression profiles of candidate sex-determining genes.
Female genome assemblies confirmed that the same two subgenomes contributed to all allotetraploids studied. Both progenitor species have male heterogamety (XY systems), with SLRs on different chromosomes (7 and 15), whereas the allotetraploids have female heterogamety (ZW systems).
Three 4 n  species,  Salix babylonica ,  Salix matsudana , and  Salix chienii , retained Z-SLRs in the former chromosome 15Y pericentromeric location, which carry male-determining partial duplications of the  ARR17  gene, and an inversion between the SLRs arose adjacent to these duplications in their common ancestor. Another 4 n  species,  Salix pentandra , split before these 4 n  species diversified, and the  ARR17  partial duplications are in the chromosome's pseudo-autosomal (recombining) region. We identify a W-linked  ARR22 -like gene and propose it as a candidate sex-determining factor in this species, pending functional testing.

title: From prediction to meaning, from knowledge to practice: revisiting the cis‐regulatory code in plants
abstract:
Schematic overview of how CRMs can be exploited to decode and influence complex traits in plants.
 
 
 Summary 
 Despite major advances in plant genomics, researchers' ability to predict complex trait variation remains limited by an incomplete understanding of the regulatory genome.  Cis -regulatory elements (CREs) and their organisation into  cis -regulatory modules (CRMs) form the building blocks of the regulatory grammar, yet their variability at the intra- and interspecific levels, context dependence, and poor annotation have long hindered their systematic use in plant science. We review how recent progress in deep learning and integrative modelling marks a turning point for deciphering plant regulatory grammar. Moving beyond sequence-centric motif discovery, we highlight the need for plant-oriented, context-aware, and evolution-informed frameworks that explicitly learn and interpret the regulatory grammar. Integrating CRE and CRM predictions into gene regulatory networks, knowledge graphs, and genomic prediction models will be pivotal to bridging regulatory sequences, phenotypes, and environments. Beyond fundamental insight, understanding the  cis -regulatory code opens new avenues for causal variant prioritisation, regulatory engineering, and ultimately regulation-aware precision breeding and agronomic decision-making. Deciphering plant regulatory grammar is therefore both a scientific and a societal priority, with the potential to maximise breeding efficiency and support the development of fine-tuned agronomic management practices.

title: Lanosterol is the biosynthetic precursor of solanoeclepins, root‐secreted hatching factors for potato cyst nematodes
abstract:
Proposed biosynthetic pathway of solanoeclepins and their conversion in soil.







Summary

Solanoeclepins are highly modified triterpenoids secreted from tomato and potato roots that act as potent hatching factors for potato cyst nematodes and are therefore important targets for the development of sustainable control strategies. However, their biosynthetic origin has remained unknown, limiting our understanding of their biological functions and practical exploitation.
In this study, we identified the initial step of solanoeclepin biosynthesis using tomato hairy roots lacking lanosterol synthase, together with chemical complementation and stable isotope feeding experiments using deuterium‐labeled lanosterol to validate its precursor role.
Disruption of lanosterol synthase abolished lanosterol production and greatly reduced solanoeclepin accumulation. Exogenous lanosterol restored solanoeclepin production, and deuterium‐labeled lanosterol was directly incorporated into solanoeclepins, providing definitive evidence that lanosterol is their biosynthetic precursor.
Our results establish the entry point to the solanoeclepin biosynthesis and reveal a previously unrecognized function of plant lanosterol metabolism in the biosynthesis of root‐secreted signaling molecules. These findings provide a foundation for elucidating the complete solanoeclepin biosynthetic pathway, exploring the biological roles of lanosterol‐derived metabolites in plants, and enabling metabolic engineering approaches for sustainable potato cyst nematode control.

title: Mesoscale thylakoid membrane remodelling accompanies photoprotective energy dissipation in diatom algae
abstract:
Photoprotective energy dissipation (qE) in diatoms involves thylakoid membrane thinning and clustering of light-harvesting FCP antenna complexes.
 
 
 Summary 
 
Photosynthetic organisms must rapidly regulate light harvesting to avoid photodamage under intense and fluctuating light, typical of many aquatic environments. However, the structural basis of photoprotective nonphotochemical quenching (qE) remains unresolved across much of the tree of life.
We have combined quantitative Chl fluorescence measurements with transmission and freeze-fracture electron microscopy to define changes in thylakoid membrane organisation during the enhanced qE response of the model pennate diatom  Phaeodactylum tricornutum  grown under different light acclimations.
We show that induction of qE is associated with a coordinated mesoscale reorganisation of the stacked thylakoid membrane in  P. tricornutum , including clustering of light-harvesting antenna complexes and substantial membrane thinning, both of which correlate with the extent of qE across light acclimation states.
Our findings reveal a structural signature of the diatom photoprotective state in  P. tricornutum  and suggest that modulation of thylakoid membrane organisation may represent a general physical mechanism contributing to the regulation of photosynthetic light harvesting in both diatoms and plants.

title: Enigmatic mid‐Cretaceous amber‐preserved flowers with remarkable stellate trichomes show affinities with early‐diverging angiosperms
abstract:
Antiquifloris latifibris  flower from mid-Cretaceous Kachin amber (MB.Pb.2025/0276).
 
 
 Summary 
 
The study of Cretaceous flowers is crucial for elucidating the early evolution and diversification of angiosperms. Approximately 100-million-year-old Kachin amber from Northern Myanmar is well known to preserve flowers in life-like fidelity. Here, we describe new flower inclusions that share a dense indumentum of stellate trichomes and re-evaluate the structure and affinities of similar fossils placed in the genera  Antiquifloris  (magnoliids),  Eophylica  (Rhamnaceae), and  Electrophycus  (green algae).
Using high-resolution X-ray computed tomographic scans of new specimens and data sets provided by previous studies, we applied state-of-the-art phylogenetic analyses in order to place these fossils in the phylogeny of angiosperms.
We demonstrate that all fossils are flowers and share a poorly differentiated perianth and a unicarpellate and uniovulate ovary. Our results also contradict previously suggested systematic affinities and show that the amber inclusions form two distinct clades related to the early-diverging angiosperm lineages Austrobaileyales and Chloranthaceae.
We therefore synonymise  Electrophycus astroplethus  with  Antiquifloris latifibris  and emend the genera  Antiquifloris  and  Eophylica  to accommodate these morphologically distinct fossils. In addition, we describe two new species of  Antiquifloris . Our results are not only more in line with other Early to mid-Cretaceous angiosperm floras but also with previous palaeoenvironmental reconstructions of the Kachin amber forest.

title: Why be deciduous in a tropical savanna climate? Insights from leaf deployment, stem growth and sap flow dynamics
abstract:
Stem increment, sap flow and leaf phenology.







Summary

Savannas are ecosystems with hot and wet summers and warm and dry winters. How and why savanna trees partition their physiological activity through this seasonal cycle is unknown; yet it is important to understand this temporal partitioning in order to anticipate how anthropogenic climatic change will impact the functioning of savannas.
In a South African savanna ecosystem, we examined the temporal pattern of leaf deployment, sap flow and stem increment phenology over three growing seasons for six species.
We found that although the phenologies varied between years, there was a high degree of temporal overlap in leaf, sap flow and stem increment phenology between the six study species. Further, we found that a surprisingly large proportion of days on which the measured soil water potential was sufficient for physiological activity remained unused.
Although our data are consistent with convergent selection for deciduousness, the unused soil water niche we detected suggests that climate should select for evergreen strategies. Possible explanations for the dominance of deciduousness in these savannas relate to the costs of leaf construction coupled with the risk of leaf destruction due to fire and/or foliovory.

title: Genome‐wide comparative diversity uncovers population structure, global distribution, and targets of selection in hexaploid oat
abstract:
Impact of chromosome rearrangements on the population structure of oat landraces.
 
 See also the Commentary on this article by  Guo & Mascher,  252 : 2151–2153.  
 
 Summary 
 
Here, we performed comprehensive genomic analyses aimed at elucidating the population structure, worldwide phylogeography, and breeding selection in cultivated oat.
We utilized 73 261 single-nucleotide polymorphisms from a diverse collection of 920 oat accessions, encompassing 487 landraces and 433 modern cultivars.
Through an examination of spatial and genetic patterns, we identified six genetic groups among landraces. Geographical isolation, founder effects, and chromosomal structural variations were responsible for the observed genetic structure. Phylogeographic reconstruction traced modern cultivars primarily back to the European gene pool, while highlighting the genetic distinctiveness of the East Asian hulless oats and Mediterranean landraces, which represent underutilized reservoirs of diversity. A comparative scan for selection signatures across major breeding regions demonstrated that modern breeding efforts have tapped into only a fraction of the diversity present in landraces, revealing both shared and region-specific selection targets.
This study provides a comprehensive variation map and offers insights into the distribution of genetic diversity in oats. The findings emphasize the importance of leveraging landrace germplasm, particularly from East Asian and Mediterranean origins, to broaden the genetic base of modern oats and guide the development of cultivars with enhanced yield and adaptability.

title: A LINE1‐associated circular RNA circRLn1 modulates apple Alternaria blotch resistance by sequestering mdm‐miR398b to tune ROS homeostasis
abstract:
A circular RNA associated with a LINE transposable element sequesters a microRNA involved in regulating plant antioxidant defenses and helping apples resist Alternaria blotch disease.
  
 ABSTRACT 
 Alternaria blotch causes severe apple yield loss. Circular RNAs (circRNAs) participate in plant stress defense, but their antifungal pathways remain poorly understood. Retrotransposons modulate gene transcription; yet, Long interspersed nuclear element 1 (LINE1)-associated circRNA formation is rarely characterized in fruit trees. We combined circRNA sequencing, RNA pull-down, RNA immunoprecipitation (RIP), fluorescence  in situ  hybridization (FISH), dual-luciferase assays, stable/transient transformation, and pathogen inoculation to dissect the biogenesis of a LINE1-associated circRNA, circRLn1, and its role in apple immunity against Alternaria blotch. circRLn1 overexpression restrained lesion expansion and pathogen growth under  Alternaria alternata  infection. Minigene assays suggest that LINE1-derived intronic inverted repeats promote circRLn1 production. Cytoplasmic circRLn1 may act as a sponge for mdm-miR398b, thereby de-repressing  MdCSD1, MdCSD2  and  MdCCS , elevating copper/zinc superoxide dismutase (Cu/Zn-SOD) activity to balance reactive oxygen species (ROS) and reduce oxidative injury. Functional dependency assays indicate that mdm-miR398b is required for circRLn1-mediated resistance. We identify a LINE1-circRLn1–mdm-miR398b-CSD/CCS regulatory module, revealing a potential retrotransposon-associated circRNA biogenesis pathway contributing to fungal immunity in apple.

title: Unlocking yield potential: TaDL‐B.4‐driven grain weight improvement in post‐Green Revolution wheat
abstract:
The DELLA protein Rht-B1b represses wheat grain development by inhibiting the transcription factor isoform DL-B.4. NEK6-mediated phosphorylation of DL-B.4 relieves this repression, activating  GA20ox3  and increasing gibberellic acid intermediates.  DL-B.4  overexpression and natural variants enhance grain weight without affecting plant height, identifying  DL-B.4  as a key breeding target.

  
 ABSTRACT 
 DELLA proteins repress responses to gibberellins (GAs). The semi-dwarf plant architecture of modern wheat varieties, a hallmark of the Green Revolution, is caused by the  Reduced height-B1b  ( Rht-B1b ) and  Rht-D1b  alleles. Both alleles encode DELLA proteins that repress plant growth and negatively impact grain development, thereby limiting further yield improvements. Here, we demonstrate that Rht-B1b inhibits grain development by suppressing the activity of a specific isoform of the transcription factor DL, DL-B.4. NEK6‑mediated DL-B.4 phosphorylation neutralizes the inhibitory effect of Rht-B1b, thereby upregulating  GA20ox3  expression and GA intermediates in grain. Overexpression and natural variants of DL-B.4 mitigate the adverse effects of Rht-B1b on grain weight without influencing plant height, confirming it as a critical regulatory node. This insight will facilitate further improvements in wheat yield using these modern varieties.

title: The assistant features editor program, nine years on
abstract: Early in 2017,  Plant Physiology  and  The Plant Cell  initiated a new program to provide opportunities for early-career scientists called the Assistant Features Editor (AFE) program. The goal of this program is to support career advancement of early-career plant scientists by providing them with editorial board experience and the opportunity to fine-tune their writing skills. Assistant Features Editors receive formal writing training as well as careful, formative feedback on their drafts by members of the editorial board (as well as other AFEs) as a mentored skill-building activity. Not only do the AFEs gain writing experience and professional exposure, but their summaries bring visibility and accessibility to the highlighted research articles. Additionally, the AFEs are invited to participate in editorial board meetings to get a closer look at how these important bodies function. Several former AFEs have now been invited to serve on the editorial boards in other official capacities.

title: Reexamining the transcriptional landscape of plant specialized metabolism: from a hierarchical to a multi-layered and flatter regulatory model
abstract: Abstract Plant specialized metabolites are essential mediators of adaptation to dynamic environmental conditions, functioning in defense, signaling, and developmental regulation. Traditionally, the regulation of plant specialized metabolism has been conceptualized through a hierarchical framework where global regulators dictate developmental cues which control downstream pathway-specific transcription factors (TFs) to activate individual biosynthetic pathways. In this model, primary metabolism is often considered a disconnected precursor supplier. Emerging genome-wide evidence has increasingly challenged this linear paradigm, revealing an underappreciated level of cross-talk and metabolic coordination.Regulatory networks exist on a quantitative spectrum from the linear hierarchical to highly decentralized flatter networks with extensive connections between both regulatory layers and input signals. This review synthesizes recent advances that suggest a shift in evidence indicating that a better regulatory model for specialized metabolism might be on the decentralized, "flatter" regulatory network architecture end of this spectrum. In this flatter model, individual TFs simultaneously target diverse promoter loci across multiple metabolic layers, while individual enzyme promoters are conversely targeted by a multitude of TFs. This integrated framework is exemplified by developing research spanning diverse classes of specialized metabolites, including glucosinolates, phenylpropanoids, and terpenoids. Focusing on these pathways, we discuss how flat TF networks simultaneously regulate precursor allocation, specialized metabolite production, and stress responsiveness, thereby linking primary and specialized metabolism into cohesive regulatory modules. Collectively, these findings suggest a shift from exclusively hierarchical models toward a flatter and distributed regulatory perspective that better reflects the precise signal-processing capacity and combinatorial control of plant metabolic regulation.

title: High-rate and durable sodium-ion batteries enabled by charge-asymmetric single-atom-energized hard carbon
abstract: Abstract Sodium-ion batteries (SIBs) represent a promising complement to lithium-based systems due to the abundant supply and cost-effectiveness of sodium. However, the widespread adoption of SIBs is practically hindered by the lack of cycling-stable hard-carbon anodes with superior capacity and rate capability. Here, we show a design of high-rate and durable SIB anodes achieved by introducing main-group metal single atoms ( M  SA  = Sb, Bi, Sn) featuring a unique charge-asymmetric N 4 – M  SA –O 2  moiety anchored on nitrogen-doped hard carbon ( M  SA @NC). This designed charge-asymmetric configuration establishes a dynamically evolving atomic interface that adaptively modulates active sites to achieve significant improvements in both Na +  storage kinetics and capacity. The representative Sb SA @NC system demonstrates high specific capacity, improved rate capability and cyclability in both coin and pouch-type cells. Extensive experimental and theoretical analyses reveal that the structural rearrangement of the N 4 –Sb–O 2  moiety during (de)sodiation is highly reversible and energetically favorable, enabling enhanced reversible capacity (422.8 mAh g −1  at 0.1 A g −1 ) and rate capability (207.6 mAh g −1  at 20 A g −1 ) while preserving material integrity. This work offers a promising pathway in advancing high-performing HC anodes for fast-charging and durable SIBs.

title: Single-atom catalyst–Li2O2 interfacial chemistry governs the activity–stability trade-off in Li–O2 batteries
abstract: Abstract Cathode catalysts in aprotic Li–O 2  batteries are commonly judged by their ability to lower charge overpotentials, yet improved catalytic activity often does not lead to durable cycling. Here, we use structurally well-defined M–N 4  single-atom catalysts (SACs) as model cathodes to elucidate the interplay between catalyst activity and battery stability. Integrated experimental and theoretical studies suggest that, although SACs promote Li 2 O 2  oxidation and lower the initial charging overpotential, they also increase the reactivity of discharge-generated Li 2 O 2  toward ether electrolytes, promoting carboxylate accumulation and cathode passivation. On the basis of this mechanistic insight, a localized high-concentration electrolyte is introduced to regulate the catalyst–Li 2 O 2  interfacial chemistry, suppress side reactions, and extend the cycling life from 42 to 398 cycles. This work identifies a previously overlooked trade-off between catalytic activity and battery stability in Li–O 2  batteries and provides a mechanistic foundation for designing stable catalyst/electrolyte interfaces in high-energy electrochemical devices.

title: Paralogs of the Candida albicans TLO gene family form interconnected functional networks with incomplete redundancy
abstract: Abstract Gene duplication typically fails to confer a selective advantage to an organism, prompting their removal from a population. In rare instances that duplication does not incur a fitness cost or enhances fitness, gene families can form through repeating the duplication process. While the function of gene duplicates has been studied in detail, little work has explored how repeated duplication impacts paralog redundancy and may restrict the emergence of new paralogs or novel function. Here, we constructed a panel of single deletion mutants for each of the 14 members of the  Candida albicans   telomere-associated ( TLO ) gene family to test the redundancy in molecular and biological function among paralogs from a lineage-specific expansion. Tlo proteins function as interchangeable subunits of the Mediator transcriptional regulatory complex with the potential to impact global gene expression. Redundancy was the most common outcome, being observed for approximately 90% of the phenotypic assays in strains lacking single  TLO  genes. However, mutants for 12/14 paralogs displayed significant non-redundant functions in phenotypes ranging from carbon utilization to  in vivo  virulence. Double mutants lacking two  TLO  genes produced both positive and negative synergistic phenotypes, suggesting that crosstalk or coordinated regulation is common among paralogs. Together, this study demonstrates that recently emergent paralogs can acquire non-redundant functions despite often retaining redundancy with other gene family members to form a highly interconnected functional network.

title: Nse2 evolves rapidly in Drosophila while preserving essential DNA repair functions
abstract: Abstract Constitutive heterochromatin spans 20–80% of eukaryotic genomes and plays critical roles in transcriptional silencing and genome stability. While heterochromatin functions are well conserved across eukaryotes, the underlying repetitive DNA sequences turn over rapidly across species, and growing evidence suggests that heterochromatin-associated proteins coevolve in response. Whether this paradox extends to one of heterochromatin's most essential functions, the specialized repair of DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) to prevent aberrant recombination between repeats, remains unexplored. Here, we investigate the evolution of genes involved in heterochromatic DSB repair in  Drosophila  and find they have experienced more prevalent adaptive evolution than broadly acting DNA repair genes. In particular, the SMC5/6-complex subunit Nse2, a SUMO-E3 ligase required for heterochromatic DSB repair, has evolved rapidly at the protein sequence level and shows extensive copy number turnover across species. Functional assays demonstrate that, despite substantial amino acid sequence divergence, nearly all tested Nse2 homologs preserve the overall structure of well-annotated domains and Intrinsically Disordered Regions (IDRs) and retain the ability to promote heterochromatic DSB repair in a heterospecific cellular environment. Further, by mutating Nse2 IDRs, we show that their biochemical properties, rather than specific amino acid sequences, are essential for repair. While the primary drivers of the rapid adaptive evolution of heterochromatic repair proteins, and its functional consequences in other cellular contexts, remain to be identified, our findings suggest that this rapid evolution is balanced by selection to maintain the proteins’ biochemical properties essential for genome maintenance, a striking example of functional conservation despite dramatic molecular turbulence.

title: A rarefaction approach to identify local introgression in a three population tree
abstract: Abstract Patterson’s  D  statistic, also known as the ABBA−BABA statistic, is widely used to detect the presence of archaic genome-wide introgression between two non-sister taxa. Patterson’s  D  counts the imbalance between the number of biallelic sites where either the second and third taxa (ABBA site) share the derived allele or the first and third taxa (BABA site) share the derived allele in a four taxa tree. Here, the fourth taxon acts as an outgroup to determine the ancestral allele. When there is no introgression, these counts are expected to be equal, and a discordance between counts suggests introgression from the third taxon into either the first or second. Patterson’s D is limited to the detection of genome-wide introgression and exhibits a high false-positive rate when applied to smaller genomic segments. Here, we present a new method, D STatistic with allelic rarefaction (D*), to address these limitations. D* uses multiple lineages and does not require an outgroup to calculate the imbalance between the number of alleles found exclusively in the second and third taxa and the number of alleles found exclusively in the first and third taxa. D* employs a rarefaction technique to correct for unequal sample size and allows multiallelic sites. We use simulations to show that D* has better precision and recall for detecting introgressed segments of DNA when compared to other methods. We conclude by recovering Denisovan DNA related to immune function in modern-day Papuans.

title: MolEvolvR: A web-app for characterizing proteins using molecular evolution and phylogeny
abstract: Abstract Studying proteins through the lens of evolution can reveal features such as conserved domains, lineage-specific variants, and co-occurring domain architectures in phylogenetic context across all superkingdoms.  MolEvolvR  enables researchers to conduct such evolution-focused studies to generate testable hypotheses about protein function and evolution.  MolEvolvR  is a novel web-app allowing researchers to visualize the molecular evolution of their proteins of interest in a phylogenetic context across the tree of life. It accepts multiple input formats – protein/domain sequences, homologous proteins, or domain scans – and, using a general-purpose computational workflow, returns detailed homolog data and dynamic graphical summaries (e.g., phylogenetic trees, multiple sequence alignments, domain architectures, domain proximity networks, phyletic spreads, co-occurrence patterns across lineages).  MolEvolvR  performs domain-centric searches to capture remote homologs that are missed by full-length searches, integrates domain architecture evolution with phyletic distribution analyses, and provides evolutionary context visualizations that reveal lineage-specific adaptations versus those that are broadly conserved. Thus,  MolEvolvR  is a powerful, easy-to-use web interface for computational protein characterization spanning all superkingdoms. The web-app can be accessed here:  https://jravilab.org/molevolvr .

title: Rapid evolution and functional divergence of the telomerase in monkeyflowers (Mimulus) with a duplicated telomerase RNA
abstract: Abstract Telomeres are maintained by telomerase, where the reverse transcriptase TERT copies a template in the telomerase RNA (TR). How TERT evolves when its RNA partner duplicates and diverges is unknown. In monkeyflowers ( Mimulus ), a TR duplication arose in the ancestor of the Erythranthe group but the derived paralog (TR2) remains functional only in  M. lewisii , whose telomeres consist of two repeat types. Using new genome assemblies, we found that TERT evolved rapidly in the Erythranthe group with the strongest signal in the N-terminal TR-binding domain (TRBD). Most amino acid changes occurred on the ancestral branch carrying the TR duplication. In yeast three-hybrid assays,  M. lewisii  TERT bound both the ancestral (TR1) and derived (TR2) paralogs, whereas TERT from species without a functional TR2 did not bind TR2. Binding of both paralogs required two  M. lewisii -specific residues near the KRxR motif of the TRBD. We developed TRAP NGS  (Telomeric Repeat Amplification Protocol followed by next-generation sequencing) and discovered  M. lewisii  telomerase was more active than that of related species without an increase in TERT expression. In hybrids between  M. lewisii  and  M. verbenaceus , telomeres on  M. verbenaceus  chromosomes acquired  M. lewisii -type repeats and length within one generation. These results suggest that TR duplication can shape the evolution of TERT, enhance the telomerase activity, and alter the telomere composition.

title: Multi-Granularity Cross-Attention Mixture-of-Experts for Protein–Ligand Dissociation Kinetics Prediction
abstract: Abstract  Motivation Drug–target affinity prediction is pivotal in drug discovery. However, most existing computational methods focus primarily on binding affinity and do not explicitly model dissociation kinetics ( K  off ). Accurately predicting  K  off  therefore remains both important and challenging for kinetics-guided drug screening and residence-time optimization. Results To address this challenge, we propose MGCA, a multi-granularity cross-attention framework for  K  off  prediction. MGCA represents proteins using multi-depth ESM2 features and ligands using multi-radius Morgan fingerprints. It integrates these representations through gated expert fusion, low-rank bidirectional cross-attention, and protein-anchored residual fusion. Across the Zhao dissociation-kinetics dataset and the KinetX benchmark, MGCA achieved the lowest mean squared error (MSE) in all warm-start and protein cold-start evaluations. Notably, MGCA reduced protein cold-start MSE by 42.5% and 12.1% relative to the recent kinetics-specific BiCoA-Net model on Zhao and KinetX, respectively. Under matched hardware, MGCA also trained substantially faster than BiCoA-Net and MoE-Kinetic. Ablation and case-study analyses further showed that MGCA effectively integrates protein, ligand, and interaction information, supporting cross-target generalization, within-target compound ranking, and feature-level interpretation. Together, these results establish MGCA as an accurate, efficient, and interpretable framework for protein–ligand dissociation kinetics prediction. Availability and implementation The source code and datasets are available at  https://github.com/CSUBioGroup/MGCA-koff  and  https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22932383 .

title: Cooperative roles of three CrRLK1L family members in regulating plant growth and salt tolerance in Arabidopsis
abstract: Short Summary: The FER cytoplasmic domain, but not its full kinase activity, is required to rescue the dwarfism and salt hypersensitivity of the fer-4 mutant. title: Photo-activated phytochrome A induces DET1-dependent COP1 degradation in mediating far-red light signaling in Arabidopsis
abstract: Short Summary: This study reveals that photo-activated phyA promotes DET1-mediated destabilization of COP1 under far-red-rich conditions, such as shade environments. COP1 facilitates the formation of the phyA−COP1−DET1 complex, while phyA promotes the proteasomal degradation of COP1 possibly by enhancing the COP1−DET1 interaction within this complex. These findings provide new insights into the molecular mechanisms underlying plant acclimation to shade in dense-planting scenarios.

abstract: Using singing to probe pitch perception, McPherson-McNato et al. show that US and Bolivian Amazonian (Tsimane’) listeners both rely on harmonic structure to discriminate pitch changes in noise, revealing shared features of pitch perception. title: Rapid prey capture learning slowly resets activity set points in rat binocular visual cortex
abstract: Leman et al. find that rapid, vision-dependent learning triggers a slow resetting of firing rate set points in visual cortex. This resetting is driven by a homeostatic increase in excitatory drive, and preventing resetting impairs consolidation. Thus, learning can co-opt homeostatic plasticity to reset firing rate setpoints and enhance consolidation.

title: Bdnf mRNA‐LNP Drives Nasal Epithelial BDNF Production and Improves Cognition in Aged and Alzheimer's Disease Mouse Models
abstract:
Intranasal lipid nanoparticles deliver mRNA encoding brain‐derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) to the nasal epithelium, enabling local BDNF delivery to the brain without invasive surgery. Repeated treatment increased brain BDNF, enhanced hippocampal neurogenesis, and improved memory in aged mice and 5xFAD Alzheimer's disease‐model mice, supporting a non‐invasive mRNA platform for neurodegenerative disease therapy.








ABSTRACT
Messenger RNA (mRNA) therapeutics have rapidly emerged as a transformative approach for treating a range of health challenges. Accelerated by the success of mRNA‐lipid nanoparticle (LNP) vaccines during the COVID‐19 pandemic, this platform holds promise beyond immunisation for the transient expression of therapeutic proteins in targeted tissues. Despite this promise, non‐invasive delivery of mRNA‐encoded cargo to the brain remains a challenge, as most peptide drugs do not pass the blood‐brain barrier. Here, we present the development of an intranasal mRNA‐LNP therapeutic that drives production of neurotrophic factors in the nasal epithelium and delivery of the encoded protein to the brain. As a proof of concept, we demonstrate that intranasal delivery of mRNA encoding the neurogenic factor BDNF (Brain Derived Neurotrophic Factor) enhances memory performance in both aged mice and a transgenic mouse model of Alzheimer's disease. This approach offers a promising platform for delivering therapeutic proteins to the brain and opens new avenues for treating age‐related and neurodegenerative disorders.

title: CTCF-anchored cohesin loops are a vertebrate-specific innovation
abstract: Animal genomes are organized into chromatin loops and topologically associating domains. Cohesin drives loop extrusion, and the architectural factor CTCF halts loop-extruding cohesin. CTCF-anchored loops facilitate interactions between distal cis-regulatory elements and regulate gene expression. However, when CTCF acquired its cohesin loop-halting function remains unclear. We performed interspecies domain-swap experiments, replacing the cohesin-interacting N-terminus of mouse CTCF with orthologous sequences from the fruit fly Drosophila (arthropod), Branchiostoma (chordate), and the inshore hagfish (jawless vertebrate). The hagfish N-terminus halted cohesin, whereas the invertebrate CTCF N-termini did not. Consistently, Micro-C maps from hagfish tissues revealed stripes associated with convergently oriented CTCF sites, a characteristic signature of cohesin-loop halting. Notably, cohesin enrichment at promoters and enhancers was more pronounced in hagfish than in jawed vertebrates. Our findings indicate that CTCF-mediated cohesin loop anchoring most likely evolved in the common ancestor of extant vertebrates and was further strengthened in jawed vertebrates.

title: KORUS: probabilistic ancestry inference beyond variant calls
abstract: Ancestry inference typically relies on variant calling and predefined population labels. We present KORUS, a probabilistic framework that infers ancestry from sequencing-derived k-mer representations constructed using ancestry-informative reference variants and encoded in Bloom filters, without requiring explicit variant calls for query genomes. KORUS separates genomic feature representation from ancestry decoding, enabling supervised classification, fractional ancestry inference, and unsupervised population structure discovery within a unified framework. Reference models were constructed from 643 genomes from the 1000 Genomes Project and the Simons Genome Diversity Project. Evaluation on an independent cohort of 22 whole-genome sequencing samples, with comparisons to ntRoot, SNVstory, and ADMIXTURE, showed recovery of continental-scale population structure, with supervised classification accuracy of 72.7-81.8% and ancestry-fraction concordance of R2 = 0.844-0.993 relative to ADMIXTURE and R2 = 0.665-0.983 relative to ntRoot. Ancestry estimates were consistent across alternative k-mer representations. Analyses of ancient human and archaic hominin genomes demonstrated that probabilistic projections quantify affinity to the learned feature space rather than necessarily indicating modern continental ancestry. KORUS provides a unified approach to ancestry inference directly from sequencing-derived representations and is freely available under the GPLv3 license at https://github.com/BirolLab/korus.

title: Pharmacological and genetic access to astrocytic cholesterol programs in human neural cells
abstract: Astrocyte-neuron interactions coordinate cholesterol metabolism, cell adhesion, and synaptic gene expression1,2, and related gene expression programs decline together in schizophrenia3. Whether pharmacological or genetic perturbations can selectively engage components of this coordinated biology was unknown. Here we combine genetically diverse cultures of human stem-cell-derived neurons and astrocytes, pharmacological profiling, genetic association mapping and CRISPR interference to examine these biological programs. In stem-cell-derived astrocyte mono-cultures, the antipsychotic clozapine induced a focused transcriptional response involving cholesterol biosynthesis and export, and drove an increase in intracellular and secreted cholesterol. This response overlapped with the cholesterol-related component of the astrocytic response to neuronal contact seen in neuron-astrocyte co-cultures, but did not extend to synaptic cell-adhesion genes.
