In neuron-astrocyte co-cultures, clozapine also increased neuronal firing. Across individual cell donors, cholesterol-pathway induction by clozapine was broadly shared but varied in magnitude. Gene-expression patterns in untreated donors were associated with differential responses to clozapine and the liver X receptor agonist GW3965. Common genetic variation influenced expression of several cholesterol-related genes, including a clozapine-dependent association of HSD17B7 expression with nearby genetic variants. Independently, repression of LDLR induced coordinated expression of cholesterol-biosynthesis genes in astrocytes that overlapped with astrocyte responses to clozapine and neuronal contact. These findings identify shared cholesterol-related transcriptional responses to pharmacological and genetic perturbations and link common genetic variation to distinct features of cholesterol-pathway responses.

title: Cell-state conditioning predicts the expression response to an unseen stimulus but not stimulus-dependent genetic effects
abstract: Second-generation sequence models can be conditioned on a cell state supplied as a single-cell snapshot rather than selected from a fixed catalogue, but whether that conditioning carries an experimentally applied perturbation has not been tested. We conditioned such a model on interferon-{beta}-stimulated and unstimulated monocytes from a published experiment, using cells disjoint from those providing the measurement, and asked whether the predicted expression response tracks the measured one and whether the same conditioning identifies expression QTL specific to the stimulated state. Predicted and measured responses agree at Spearman {rho} = 0.616 across 119 genes (95% CI 0.486 to 0.716), and at 0.607 after all 119 target genes are deleted from the conditioning input; across fifteen conditions the model's response scales with how much each condition's biology genuinely overlaps the target response (slope 0.73, Pearson 0.92), and a near-neighbour monocyte subset receives 0.295 against a measured overlap of 0.336. For stimulation-specific genetic effects we find no reliable evidence: the pre-specified primary arm moves from p = 0.0019 to 0.443 once both conditions must carry a measurable predicted effect, and the separation localises to the resting-condition baseline. Neither model generation's catalogue contains a perturbed sample, 0 of 4,430 tracks and 0 of 2,799 conditions, although both carry activation-state labels, so the gap is experimental perturbation rather than cell state. Two incidental findings apply beyond this model: credible-set membership mislabels over half of putatively condition-specific loci, and gating a ratio statistic on its larger term manufactures signal.

title: A spatial correlation function approach reveals zonation loss in liver disease
abstract: Spatial transcriptomics measures the expression of hundreds to thousands of genes in each cell together with the cell's position in the tissue. Here we use spatial correlation functions, which describe how the correlation of gene expression between cells decays with distance, to quantify how the spatial organization of gene expression changes in disease. From the correlation function of each gene, or of each pair of genes, we extract two numbers: a susceptibility, which measures how strongly gene expression is correlated between nearby cells, and a correlation length, the distance over which this correlation extends. Both are in physical units and can be compared directly between samples and conditions. We apply the approach to healthy and fibrotic mouse liver using newly generated data, and to healthy and fibrotic human liver using published data. Correlations between gene pairs identify genes of the same hepatocyte zone, and assign a zone to 1,266 genes that are not known zonation markers. The two fibrotic conditions differ: CCl4 injection in mice produces a moderate reorganization in which some genes lose spatial correlation and others gain it, while in human fibrosis almost every measured gene loses it. Changes in spatial correlation are only weakly related to changes in expression level. For instance Cyp2c29 and Pon1 partially lose their spatial correlation in treated mice, although their average expression does not consistently fall. Spatial correlation functions therefore detect changes in tissue organization that measurements of expression level alone miss.

title: Genetic regulation of ALK inhibitor response in diverse human cell types
abstract: Anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK) inhibitors are effective treatments for ALK-positive non-small cell lung cancer but cause diverse adverse events affecting multiple tissues. Genetic variation may contribute to inter-individual differences in susceptibility, but the small number of treated patients limits the power of genetic association studies. Moreover, the diversity of affected tissues and cell types makes functional investigation challenging. We used induced pluripotent stem cells from 49 individuals to generate heterogeneous differentiating cultures (HDCs) containing multiple cell types, treated them with five ALK inhibitors (crizotinib, alectinib, ceritinib, brigatinib, and lorlatinib) for 24 hours, and characterized transcriptional responses using single-cell RNA sequencing. These responses showed cell-type-specific and shared transcriptional effects. Integrating gene expression with individual genotypes, we identified 4,371 expression quantitative trait loci (eQTLs) across 21 cell types, including 2,137 response eQTLs whose regulatory effects differ between untreated and drug-treated cells. These results nominate candidates for future studies of ALK inhibitor toxicity.

title: Vertical transmission and community turnover in seed-borne microbiomes: lessons from an aMAIZEing model system
abstract: The seed microbiome represents a specialized ecological niche, governed by assembly processes that are only partially coupled to the surrounding soil community. While environmental recruitment and vertical transmission from the maternal plant are both recognized sources of seed-associated microorganisms, the mechanisms that determine their relative contributions and whether these contributions shift across generations remain poorly understood. Here, we used long-read metagenomic sequencing to track seed-borne bacterial community dynamics across a founding seed pool and two subsequent generations in two divergent maize (Zea mays L.) varieties exposed to contrasting organic and mineral fertilisation regimes. We recovered 112 medium- or high-quality metagenome-assembled genomes and combined MAG-level taxonomic and functional analyses with genus-level community profiling to characterize persistence and turnover dynamics within the seed microbiome. While soil taxonomic diversity was high, seed-associated communities showed a near-complete compositional disconnect from soil-dominant assemblages taxa, with a persistent Firmicutes core maintained across generations, consistent with vertical transmission. Priority effects remain a possible explanation for these patterns but were not directly tested. Genus-level source attribution suggested greater environmental recruitment under organic fertilization, with more diverse soil communities and a stronger contribution from the preceding seed generation under mineral fertilization. Seed-associated MAGs also carried genes associated with plant growth-promoting potential, although these detections could not be consistently linked to specific transmission routes. In contrast, maize genotype had no detectable effect on seed microbiome composition. Intergenerational persistence and environmental recruitment jointly shape seed-derived communities under contrasting fertilization regimes. Their relative contributions remain inferred from taxonomic overlap, and the effects of microbial source-pool diversity cannot be separated from the accompanying differences in soil chemistry in this design.

title: Sequence-based models predict TF binding with negligible contributions from motif cooperativity
abstract: How transcription factors (TFs) selectively recognize their genomic targets among numerous sites containing similar DNA motifs remains an open question. Cooperative binding at neighboring motif sites is widely considered a key mechanism of TF specificity, yet its genome-wide contribution remains unclear. Machine learning models can now predict TF binding directly from DNA sequence, providing opportunities to investigate its underlying determinants. Here, we leveraged BPNet models trained on ~2,000 ENCODE TF binding profiles to systematically assess motif cooperativity. Although detected at individual loci, cooperativity made a negligible contribution to genome-wide binding predictions. Nevertheless, the models captured differences in binding preferences between TFs with similar motif preferences, even within the same cellular environment. These findings highlight the need to critically assess prevailing assumptions and explore alternative mechanisms underlying selective TF binding.

title: Pharmacophore-Inspired Virtual Receptor: Generating Realistic Peptide Binding Data for Machine Learning
abstract: VReceptor is a virtual receptor simulation framework that generates realistic, sequence-dependent binding data for peptide-based therapeutics. It combines pharmacophore-inspired weighting schemes with amino acid similarity metrics to evaluate peptide design strategies in a controlled environment. Validation using the Prolactin-Releasing Peptide (PrRP) dataset confirms VReceptor's ability to approximate binding behaviours and optimize experimental planning. This framework empowers researchers in computational peptide design and active learning workflows while highlighting areas for further refinement.

title: Pluripotent and differentiated cells display distinct genomic and nuclear landscapes of genome folding variability
abstract: Chromosome folding varies between cells. It is not known whether cell types differ in the extent of folding variability, whether distinct chromosomal regions in the same cell type display different levels of variability, and how folding variability relates to sub-nuclear location and gene expression. We combined two single-cell Hi-C approaches with 3D genome modeling of pseudo-single cells (IGM), DNA FISH, chromosome painting, and single-cell RNA-seq across a five-stage differentiation trajectory from human embryonic stem cells to hepatocyte-like cells. In all cell types folding variability correlates with compartment status, is highest towards the nuclear interior, decreases as a function of radial position in the nucleus, and is the lowest at the periphery. Loci associated with nuclear landmarks such as speckles, and especially the nuclear periphery display more consistent subnuclear positioning in all cell stages. Moreover, pluripotent and differentiated cells display different overall levels of chromosome folding variability: in H1 pluripotent cells the entire genome displays higher folding and positional variability. In contrast, in differentiated cells folding variability is generally lower along the genome and the number of loci that become consistently positioned at the nuclear periphery increases sharply. The two distinct patterns of folding variability were correlated with cell-to-cell gene expression variation: In pluripotent cells gene expression variation is large, pervasive and seen throughout the genome and the nucleus. In differentiated cells cell-to-cell variation in gene expression is much lower and restricted mostly to genes located near the center of the nucleus, consistent with the restricted pattern of chromosome folding variation. These findings reveal two distinct genomic states: pluripotent cells maintain a variably folded, spatially permissive genome and transcriptional plasticity, whereas differentiated cells mature into a spatially deterministic, more consistently folded organization that correlates with more restricted transcriptional programs.

title: The pangenome of the Arctic picoeukaryote Micromonas polaris resolves cryptic ecotypes and identifies a polar-specific gene repertoire
abstract: Micromonas polaris is the dominant picoeukaryote of the Arctic Ocean, where it sustains primary production across habitats from sea ice to open water to the subsurface chlorophyll maximum. How a single species maintains this ecological breadth has remained unclear. Standard phylogenetic markers such as 18S rRNA are nearly invariant within M. polaris and conceal any internal genomic heterogeneity the species may possess. Here we present a pangenome of 14 M. polaris strains spanning the Arctic basin, integrated with Tara Oceans metagenomes, that resolves the species into two diverged ecotypes invisible to 18S rRNA but recovered consistently by prp8, genome-wide SNPs, ANI, and orthogroup-based phylogenies. The two ecotypes coexist sympatrically, with one lineage consistently enriched deeper in the water column across the basin. M. polaris carries 990 polar-specific hierarchical orthogroups absent from temperate Micromonas, organised around one-carbon metabolism, endocytosis, transmembrane transport, and photo-oxidative stress response. Several components show phylogenetic signatures of horizontal acquisition from co-occurring marine taxa. Atlantification is bringing temperate Micromonas into Arctic margins seasonally, but the polar night likely limits their year-round persistence. M. polaris and its polar-specific toolkit appear positioned to persist through the dark season, suggesting Arctic margins will undergo seasonal turnover rather than stable replacement.

title: Air and environmental sampling expand metagenomic viral surveillance in Cambodian pig slaughterhouses
abstract: Surveillance of viruses in swine depends largely on the sampling of individual animals chosen at random, often limiting detection breadth. Environmental sampling has emerged as an alternative strategy, enabling faster, safer and more cost-effective pathogen monitoring at the human-animal interfaces. Across nine visits to two Cambodian slaughterhouses, we applied metagenomic sequencing to air samples (n = 25), faeces (n = 156), wastewater (n = 15), carcass wash water (n = 18), holding-pen swabs (n = 124), slaughter-box swabs (n = 73) and ropes (n = 16), comparing virus composition to pig snout swabs (n = 193). Combined environmental sampling recovered 96.6% of the viral taxa detected in snout swabs, exceeding 90.9% at every visit. Greater viral diversity was consistently captured in the environment, including swine-associated taxa absent from snout swabs and viral RNA associated with avian and human hosts. Air provided the widest coverage of any single environmental sample type and contributed the largest number of independent virus detections that were not recovered from any other environmental sample. Slaughter-box swabs recovered the fewest taxa, showing that visible contamination with swine material did not correlate with greater viral recovery. Overall, this study identifies air as a pivotal core component of any surveillance program. However, pairing air with additional environmental sample types provides the broadest virus coverage and represents the optimal surveillance strategy in swine slaughterhouses.

title: Transferring CRISPRi knockdown responses to new cell lines requires screening part of each line
abstract: Perturb-seq screens measure knockdown responses in one cell line at a time. Models that transfer responses to new lines rarely beat simple averages, and standard metrics often ignore noise. It is unclear how much of a response is shared and what a new line must contribute. We studied CRISPR interference Perturb-seq of essential genes in four human cell lines, using noise ceilings and calibrated metrics. We also introduce CASTER, a set-based model that adapts the transferred mean to the target line. After noise correction, responses correlated at a median of 0.52, highest between the TP53 wild-type lines. With 30% of a line screened, a linear model and CASTER scored 0.84 and 0.80 versus 0.44 for the transferred mean (1 equals a technical duplicate). CASTER led only at 2.5% screened (0.62 versus 0.47) and fell below the transferred mean without a screen. Response size tracked general essentiality more than line-specific dependency.

title: Savant: A Fast, Structure-Free Binding Affinity Predictor For Protein-Ligand Drug Screening
abstract: Protein-ligand binding affinity determines which of many candidate molecules is worth synthesizing and assaying, making it the central measurement in early drug discovery. Binding affinity is commonly expressed as the dissociation constant, an equilibrium measure that indicates how easily a complex separates into its components. AI-based generative chemistry and make-on-demand chemical catalogs now produce molecules faster than rigorous method can evaluate them. Leading computational methods co-fold the complex before scoring the binding affinity between the protein and the ligand, which provides high accuracy but requires a graphics processing unit (GPU) and substantial time for every pair evaluated.Here we present Savant, a machine learning model that estimates the dissociation constant using only the protein's amino acid sequence and the ligand's structure written as a line of text (SMILES). Savant needs no 3-dimensional folded structure, no docking, and no GPU. To test Savant fairly, we built a benchmark designed to prevent any training data to leak into the testing set, drawing only on measurements published after the training data was assembled and on molecules chemically unlike anything the model had seen. On an independent benchmark, Savant ranks ahead of every other 3-dimensional structure-free method.Savant is designed to rank compounds against a single protein, and performs as well as other methods that require a GPU, while running only on a central processing unit (CPU). Thus, Savant can screen libraries of 100,000 compounds in minutes with commodity hardware.

title: Infernal-GPU: accurate E-values and sensitive covariance-model search for structured RNAs
abstract: Covariance models (CMs) find structured RNAs by scoring sequence and base pairing together, and they underlie the Infernal software and the Rfam database. Their dynamic programming is expensive, so Infernal relies on two approximations: E-values are calibrated on a short stretch of random sequence, and fast sequence-only filters decide which parts of a target the CM examines. How much accuracy these approximations cost, and where, is largely unknown, because removing them on CPUs is prohibitively slow. We present Infernal-GPU, a GPU implementation of Infernal's CM dynamic programming that matches Infernal's results. Its key step evaluates the one serial recurrence of CM scoring, the self-loop of insert-left states, as two parallel prefix scans. One GPU calibrates all 4,227 Rfam models overnight, which makes calibrations on ten times more random sequence routine. These longer calibrations show that the E-values distributed with Rfam are off by more than twofold for one model in eight. An exhaustive search reference shows that sequence filters discard remote homologs whose similarity lies almost entirely in base pairing; behind permissive filters, Infernal-GPU recovers them with a third of the CPU work that Infernal needs at the same setting. Infernal-GPU is freely available at https://github.com/void-echo/infernal-gpu and from PyPI, together with Rfam 15.0 recalibrated on ten times more random sequence.

title: Decompose and Recompose: Reference-Centered Multimodal Adaptation of Protein Language Models for Enzyme Turnover Prediction
abstract: Predicting enzyme turnover numbers ($k_{mathrm{cat}}$) from protein sequences and reaction chemistry helps prioritize candidates in virtual screening. Reliable ranking requires distinguishing activity differences between enzyme--reaction pairs. Recent interaction models combine enzyme and chemical information, but two representation challenges remain. First, reactants and products have distinct roles in catalysis: reactants are recognized and transformed, whereas products are formed and released. Yet these models merge the two sides before enzyme interaction, leaving the enzyme's response to each role implicit. Second, enzyme representations produced by cross-attention mix reaction-dependent changes with an enzyme-specific background shared across chemical conditions. This mixture can obscure activity-relevant differences between samples. To address these challenges, we introduce EnzRef, a lightweight multimodal framework that adapts frozen protein language models by decomposing reaction chemistry into reactant and product conditions, expressing each conditioned enzyme response relative to that enzyme's background, and recomposing the responses for activity prediction. Reference-Centered Cross-Attention uses each enzyme's average residue response as an internal reference to expose role-specific conditional deviations. Symmetry-Aware Semantic Recomposition encodes the mean deviation and directed role contrast into a joint activity representation. With 1.72M trainable parameters beyond the frozen encoder, EnzRef achieves state-of-the-art source-domain prediction on CatPred-DB and zero-shot transfer to TurNuP-DB. On unseen enzymes, it improves mean $R^2$ by 19.8% relative to MCKcat, the strongest baseline, without target-domain adaptation.

title: SRAscout: Semantic discovery of public sequencing data through harmonized SRA and BioProject metadata
abstract: The rapid growth of public sequencing data has created great opportunities for data-driven discovery in the life sciences, but it has also made it harder to find relevant datasets. The NCBI Sequence Read Archive (SRA) hosts more than 45 million high-throughput sequencing runs, and the BioProject database, shared by NCBI, the European Nucleotide Archive (ENA) and the DNA Data Bank of Japan, describes the projects behind them. However, their metadata are often incomplete, inconsistently annotated and difficult to search using keywords alone. We present SRAscout, a web-based platform that enables semantic dataset retrieval by integrating SRA run metadata with the corresponding BioProject records. SRAscout collects and indexes metadata for about 714,000 BioProjects, and harmonizes sample attributes such as cell line, tissue, age, sex and treatment into a compact and consistent schema. For semantic embedding, SRAscout employs a biomedical sentence embedding model based on BioBERT, which generates dense vector representations from the title, name, organism and description of each project. Users can search in three modes, with the DOI or PubMed ID of an article, with free text, or with BioProject and SRA study accessions, and SRAscout finds the most related projects in each case. Free-text queries are processed through a hybrid of semantic and full-text search, which finds conceptually relevant studies even when different terms are used to describe the same biology, while exact terms such as gene names are still matched. Structured filters allow refinement by organism, assay type (for example RNA-seq and miRNA-seq), harmonized sample attributes such as tissue, cell type and disease, tag words, and many additional attributes. For each search, users can download a harmonized metadata table and ready-to-use scripts that fetch the sequencing files from ENA. SRAscout also offers a public API for programmatic access. By combining harmonized metadata with context-aware search in a single interface, SRAscout facilitates dataset discovery, meta-analysis and data reuse. The application is freely available at www.srascout.com.

title: Casanovo-TMT: deep learning-based de novo sequencing of TMTpro-labeled peptides and phosphopeptides
abstract: De novo peptide sequencing reads peptides directly from tandem mass spectra, but none of the released deep learning models can sequence peptides labeled with isobaric tags such as TMTpro, which are widely used for multiplexed quantitative proteomics. We extended the residue vocabulary of Casanovo with TMTpro tags and phosphorylation, fine-tuned it on 21 million spectra from our laboratory, most of them TMTpro-labeled, and re-ranked the candidates in the beam by their agreement with the measured precursor mass. The resulting model, Casanovo-TMT, predicted the exact peptidoform for 84.7% of the TMTpro-labeled spectra in our test set and for 87.4 and 79.6% of the spectra in two public global-proteome datasets from other laboratories, whereas the extended vocabulary without fine-tuning gave 0.3%. Discarding the lowest-scoring predictions raised precision to 95% while retaining 81.7% of the test spectra. Casanovo-TMT also predicted the exact peptidoform for 69.2% of the spectra in a public phosphopeptide-enriched dataset and for 66 to 72% of the phosphopeptide spectra in three phosphoproteomic studies from our laboratory that were not used for training. In these studies, it identified numbers of phosphopeptides comparable to or larger than those of database search engines, and proportionally more where database search identified fewer. For the phosphopeptides identified only by Casanovo-TMT, entrapment estimated that more than 90% were correct, and an independent search engine assigned the same sequence to 95 to 98% of the spectra that it identified with confidence. Casanovo-TMT can therefore extend database search in TMTpro-based quantitative proteomics, particularly in studies in which database search identifies few phosphopeptides.

title: Deciphering the genetic bases of canine longevity
abstract: Across dog breeds, the inverse correlation between body size and lifespan is well documented, but its genetic basis remains poorly understood, in part because size and lifespan are confounded at the breed level. Here, we assembled the Cani-DNA discovery cohort of 540 dogs from 27 breeds, with 20 dogs per breed, genotyped by low-pass whole-genome sequencing and imputation. We performed genome-wide association studies (GWAS) of breed-average body weight, breed-median lifespan and individual age at death, and tested the age-at-death loci for replication in the GRLS replication cohort of 3,024 Golden Retrievers. The GWAS of breed-average body weight recovered established body-size loci, confirming that the cohort could detect known associations. Of the 69 breed-weight loci, 30 were shared with breed-median lifespan, and at all of them the allele increasing body weight was associated with shorter lifespan. At the individual level, age at death, with breed-average body weight as a covariate, identified loci distinct from all breed-level loci. Three of them, the CDH4, TSHZ3 and TSC22D2 loci, replicated in the GRLS replication cohort. In humans, CDH4 and TSHZ3 have been implicated in longevity, and the region orthologous to the TSC22D2 locus has been associated with markers of biological ageing. Together, these results identify genetic variation associated with the lifespan of individual dogs beyond breed body size, and support the dog as a model in which genetic leads on ageing can be identified.

title: Efficient genome graphs indexing, querying and visualization with gfaidx and gfaidx-viz
abstract: Genome graphs enable the analysis of genetic variation across many genomes, but exploring individual regions remains computationally demanding. We present gfaidx, a general-purpose indexer giving fast, low-memory access to pangenome, assembly, and de Bruijn graphs in GFA format. It retrieves gene-sized subgraphs and their haplotypes over 100-fold faster than existing tools such as ODGI and vg, and can index human pangenome-scale graphs on a personal computer. The accompanying gfaidx-viz interactively visualizes pre-indexed human pangenomes. Both are freely available at https://github.com/fawaz-dabbaghieh/gfaidx and https://github.com/fawaz-dabbaghieh/gfaidx-viz

title: Brain disorder mechanisms and therapeutic targets identified from developmental, cell-specific gene regulation
abstract: Genetic variation influences brain physiology and disease across cell types and development. We integrated whole-genome sequencing, bulk RNA sequencing, and single-nucleus multiome profiling from 231 human dorsolateral prefrontal cortex donors spanning six postconceptional weeks to 92 years. Across 24 brain-related traits, neurodevelopmental and psychiatric genetic risk was enriched in neuronal transcriptomic and chromatin profiles, whereas neurodegenerative risk was enriched in microglia. Thousands of expression, chromatin accessibility, and splicing quantitative trait loci revealed developmental and cell-type-specific regulatory effects. Colocalization linked multiple sclerosis risk to AHI1 expression in prenatal neurons and problematic alcohol use to GPX1 expression in postnatal glia. Leveraging dynamic cis-regulatory elements, we identified therapeutic candidates for haploinsufficient neurodevelopmental disorders, including a SOX5 enhancer whose CRISPR activation increased transcript and protein abundance. Together, these findings establish a publicly accessible genomic resource for resolving the developmental and cellular contexts of genetic risk and identifying therapeutic targets in the human brain.

title: Chimeric and Outward Reads in Short-Read RNA Sequencing Data: A Unified Circular RNA Assembly Framework
abstract: Circular RNAs (circRNAs) are RNA molecules that play important roles in regulating gene expression, yet detecting and assembling them from short read RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) data remains challenging. Most methods rely on chimeric reads that cross the back-splicing junction (BSJ), but for lowly expressed circRNAs, these reads are often absent, so many circRNAs go undetected. In this work, we propose TERRACE 2.0, a method that addresses this limitation by leveraging an additional but underutilized signal: outward reads. These are paired-end reads that point away from each other when aligned to the reference genome, which is a direct consequence of sequencing a fragment from a circRNA. Together, this multi-signal framework enables circRNAs to be detected and assembled more accurately from short-read RNA-seq data. TERRACE 2.0 infers candidate BSJs from outward reads by testing which ones give a fragment length consistent with the library, reconstructs each full-length circRNA from a splice graph, and combines outward and chimeric reads in a single representation that selects among the candidates jointly. On eight human tissue samples, TERRACE 2.0 has the best average F-score with and without gene annotations. On an alignment that retains more chimeric reads, it is the most accurate assembler in every sample, while its predecessor TERRACE loses much of its precision. Most notably, outward reads are involved in 36% to 56% of the true circRNAs that TERRACE misses, and on simulated data TERRACE 2.0 also has the highest recall and F-score.

title: GatorAnchor: Cross-Modal Uncertainty-Aware Learning of Reliable Cell Neighborhoods in Single-Cell Multi-Omics
abstract: Cross-modal uncertainty challenges single-cell multi-omics integration because molecular modalities differ in sparsity, technical noise, and context-dependent biological informativeness, producing discordant cell-cell relationships. Treating conflicting evidence as equally reliable can propagate uncertain relationships and obscure biologically meaningful cellular heterogeneity. GatorAnchor is a cross-modal uncertainty-aware framework that learns modality-specific probabilistic representations, quantifies disagreement across modalities and neighborhood evidence sources, and refines cell-cell relationships according to their reliability. Across ten paired transcriptome-protein and transcriptome-chromatin datasets, GatorAnchor achieves the highest mean performance across four evaluation metrics among nine representative integration methods, demonstrating improved resolution of cellular heterogeneity. Candidate relations with greater composite unreliability show lower consistency with reference cell-type structure, whereas filtering highly unreliable relations increases same-type edge purity across all datasets. Modality conflict is associated with transcript-protein measurement discordance, while transcriptome-chromatin analyses reveal lineage-dependent contributions of molecular and decoder-derived evidence. A three-modality transcriptome-chromatin-protein analysis characterizes cluster of differentiation 4 (CD4)-related communities with distinct molecular profiles and consistent within-donor contrasts across 12 donors. Under incomplete and mosaic measurements, GatorAnchor preserves informative cell-population structure, while cross-modal correspondence increasingly depends on paired-cell anchors. These findings support uncertainty-aware neighborhood refinement for reliable and interpretable characterization of cellular heterogeneity.

title: Genome architecture and duplication-associated functional diversification in the carnivorous plant Sarracenia purpurea
abstract: The repeated evolution of complex traits raises the question of how genomes generate ecological novelty while preserving developmental organization. We present a chromosome-scale genome assembly and annotation for the carnivorous purple pitcher plant, Sarracenia purpurea, and investigate how two contrasting modes of gene duplication have shaped its genome and functional repertoire: ancient polyploidy, which leaves duplicated genes in conserved chromosomal regions (syntenic duplicates), and local tandem duplication, which generates neighboring gene copies. We compare these duplication classes across nine angiosperms. The genome shows a mosaic of conserved and fractionated duplicated regions reflecting differential retention and loss of genes following ancient polyploidy and later restructuring. Comparison with noncarnivorous Actinidia (kiwifruit) identifies 18 syntenic and nine tandem Gene Ontology (GO) Biological Process term-duplication-class combinations enriched in Sarracenia but not significantly enriched in Actinidia. Syntenic enrichments include meristem maintenance, organ-boundary specification, cuticle development, and hormonal regulation; tandem enrichments include defense responses, oxidative stress, jasmonic-acid biosynthesis, leaf senescence, and oligopeptide transport. Across the carnivorous genera Sarracenia, Nepenthes, Utricularia, and Pinguicula, we identify 19 syntenic and two tandem-associated biological processes showing significant enrichment in all four lineages, revealing striking functional commonalities across multiple evolutionary origins of carnivory despite their divergent trap morphologies and ecological strategies. Among Sarracenia genes differentially expressed in at least one comparison of flower, pitcher-leaf, and root tissues, tandem-class genes exhibit larger maximum absolute expression differences and greater GO richness and effective breadth at matched numbers of annotated homologs. These results highlight the complementary evolutionary contributions of ancient genome duplication and local gene-family expansion to the developmental and ecological diversification of carnivorous plants.

title: Expanding the human T cell receptor germline reference through population-scale pangenome analysis using the gAIRR Suite version 2
abstract: The germline gene set encoding the adaptive immune receptor repertoire (gAIRR) defines the allele space from which the expressed repertoire (exprAIRR) is assembled, so an incomplete gAIRR reference propagates errors into T cell receptor (TR) annotation and genotyping and is also a barrier to studying inherited TR variation in its own right. Human TR gAIRR diversity remains incompletely characterized because the loci resist short-read resolution and because locus-resolved cohorts have been small. We developed gAIRR Suite version 2, in which each gAIRR-annotate query carries 50 bp of germline sequence on either side of the allele core and a call is reported only when the assembly supports the core together with both flanks, and in which gAIRR-call genotypes from Element AVITI libraries whose 500-bp Read 1 spans a complete V core with its flanking anchors. Applying this framework to Human Pangenome Reference Consortium Release 2 (464 haplotype-resolved assemblies from 232 individuals across five superpopulations), we identified 531 novel TR alleles (486 TRV, 45 TRJ), each observed in the targeted-sequencing reads of at least one carrier, of which 298 were absent from our 47-individual Release 1 catalogue. In 216 individuals, targeted genotyping with gAIRR-seq and gAIRR-call recovered 99.985% of the 61,628 evaluated alleles found in the corresponding assemblies, with a precision of 99.995%. Release 2 added few common alleles but many rare ones: 407 of the 531 were restricted to a single superpopulation, and African-ancestry individuals accounted for 51.1% of these (46.0% {+/-} 2.1% after downsampling to equal group size) while comprising 30.2% of the cohort. Population-scale pangenome analysis therefore extends the TR gAIRR reference chiefly by recovering variation that smaller or less diverse cohorts would miss.

title: A Biologically Interpretable Single-Cell Pathology Foundation Model for Molecular Decoding of H&E Images
abstract: The microscopic structure of human tissues encodes molecular information that is not directly accessible by visual inspection. Current pathology foundation models improve histological interpretation but operate at multicellular resolution. It remains unclear whether routine histology contains structured molecular and cellular information recoverable at single-cell resolution, which biological properties are associated with this recoverability, and where its limits lie. Here, we introduce Loki2, a single-cell pathology foundation model trained on UniSeg, a pan-tissue resource integrating 15 million cells with segmentation, lineage annotations and measured or histology-inferred transcriptomic profiles. We examine the above question across cellular representation, molecular recoverability, and patient-level relevance. Loki2 captures cellular identity and continuous morphological variation, with interpretable latent dimensions linked to physical nuclear phenotypes through DAPI validation. Transcriptomic retrieval and in silico protein staining test molecular recoverability, with gene-level analyses revealing the strongest recovery for genes associated with morphologically distinct cellular identities and functions. Then, patient staging and biomarker discovery connect cellular morphology representations to clinical relevance. Together, these findings establish Loki2 as a biologically interpretable single-cell pathology foundation model and provide the opportunities of recovering cellular and molecular information from routine H&E histology at single-cell resolution.

title: Machine Learning Prediction of Antibiotic Resistance Genes: Performance, Interpretability, and Cross-Database Redundancy
abstract: Antibiotic resistance gene (ARG) classifiers are typically developed and evaluated within a single curated database, leaving open how much two independently curated databases agree and what that implies for apparent cross-database generalization. We trained an XGBoost classifier on amino acid trigram frequencies and physicochemical descriptors using the Comprehensive Antibiotic Resistance Database (CARD), the field's largest curated ARG resource. The model separated resistance genes from non-resistance proteins with near-ceiling accuracy (AUROC = 0.982, MCC = 0.886); a label-shuffling null baseline collapsed to chance (AUROC = 0.508) and bootstrap confidence intervals were narrow, confirming genuine signal rather than data leakage or overfitting. SHAP analysis attributed this performance to biologically interpretable features, notably the trigram KTG, isoelectric point, and aromaticity, each consistent with known catalytic motifs in resistance enzymes. Before testing the classifier against ResFinder, one of CARD's most widely used counterparts, we assessed database independence by clustering sequences with CD-HIT, finding that 96.8-98.7% of ResFinder sequences shared substantial protein identity with CARD even at a permissive 50% identity threshold, indicating the two databases largely represent the same sequence population, with direct implications for how cross-database generalization should be measured. On the small subset of ResFinder sequences genuinely non-redundant with CARD (40-100 sequences, depending on threshold), the classifier failed completely, never classifying any as resistance genes; SHAP traced this failure to sequence length, as non-redundant sequences are nearly three times longer than training proteins, and length is among the model's most influential features. The same pattern emerged by resistance mechanism: the model achieved perfect accuracy on beta-lactamases, compact single-domain enzymes well represented in training (100%, n = 351), but correctly identified only 38.5% of efflux pump components (n = 13), a mechanism built from large, multi-domain transporters rather than compact catalytic enzymes. Together, these results describe a capable, interpretable ARG classifier alongside a quantified methodological caution: cross-database redundancy must be measured rather than assumed, and when a sequence-composition classifier fails, the failure is often explained by protein architecture rather than database origin.

title: A full-length isoform atlas of the non-failing and failing human heart
abstract: Dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) and ischemic heart disease (IHD) are leading causes of heart failure, yet isoform-level changes in the failing heart remain poorly defined because reference annotations are derived largely from healthy tissues and short-read sequencing cannot reliably reconstruct full-length transcripts. We sequenced six human left ventricles (non-failing, DCM, and IHD; n = 2 each) with PacBio HiFi long reads and curated 48,232 isoforms across 11,760 genes, including 15,535 novel NIC and NNC isoforms. Independent evidence supported most novel structures: 81.7% of isoforms with novel splice junctions had short-read support for all novel junctions, and a cardiac CAGE atlas supported the 5' ends of 93% of NIC and 86% of NNC isoforms. Novel isoform diversification was concentrated in sarcomere genes and persisted after accounting for gene complexity, expression, sequencing depth, and transcript length. We then augmented GENCODE v43 with 18,637 non-FSM long-read isoforms and re-quantified two independent short-read cohorts (MAGNet and GSE116250). For most genes carrying a transcript that changed more than 2-fold in DCM, the gene itself changed less than 2-fold, so these changes are not apparent at the gene level. Of 626 transcripts differentially expressed in both cohorts, 98% changed in the same direction, including all 100 long-read isoforms among them. The resource is available through CardioIsoMap, an interactive isoform-centric portal (https://cardioisomap.streamlit.app/). This study provides a comprehensive isoform-resolved reference of the human heart in health and disease.

title: Harmonized sample metadata and processed cortical and hippocampal transcriptomes from wild-type and Alzheimer's disease model mice
abstract: Public mouse brain single-cell and single-nucleus RNA sequencing (sc/snRNA-seq) datasets are difficult to reuse across studies because sample annotations are heterogeneous and incomplete. We harmonized sample-level metadata for 2,005 cortex and hippocampus samples from 389 studies, covering wild-type (WT) controls and Alzheimer's disease (AD)-related mouse models. Usable count data from 1,863 samples in 360 studies were uniformly processed into 12,628,942 cell and nuclear profiles with cell-type annotations. Expression-based indicators were consistent with the annotated sequencing protocol and sex, and integrated microglial profiles recovered established AD-associated signatures. To illustrate cross-study use, we asked whether microglial AD--WT expression differences varied with age and between cortex and hippocampus, using covariate-adjusted expression reconstructed with Kanade. Genes separated into groups with predominantly negative or positive AD--WT contrasts, including a group whose age-associated contrasts differed between cortex and hippocampus. These findings demonstrate the utility of harmonized metadata for investigating age- and region-dependent AD-associated transcriptional differences across studies. The resource supports explicit, reproducible cohort definitions across public mouse brain datasets.

title: Diffusion geometry and topology reveal Alzheimer's proteomic states
abstract: ABSTRACT INTRODUCTION: Alzheimer's disease (AD) exhibits substantial molecular heterogeneity. Identifying biologically distinct proteomic states may improve understanding of disease heterogeneity and support precision diagnostics. METHODS: Cerebrospinal fluid proteomic data from ADNI were analyzed. Among 6,361proteins tested between cognitively normal and AD groups, 407 remained significant after Benjamini-Hochberg correction (FDR < 0.05), with 404 retained after missingness filtering. Following preprocessing and outlier removal, 130 individuals were included. Diffusion geometry and persistent homology were applied to characterize intrinsic proteomic structure without predefined clusters. The framework was further evaluated in an independent mass spectrometry cohort. RESULTS: Persistent homology revealed multiscale organization of the AD proteomic landscape. At the selected H0 filtration scale, two dominant proteomic states (n = 71 and n = 42) contained most individuals, alongside smaller components. H1 persistence identified nontrivial cyclic structure, indicating continuous higher-order organization beyond discrete state partitions. The dominant states exhibited distinct proteomic profiles and differed substantially in tau-related biomarkers. Elevated tau pathology in one state was reproduced in the independent cohort, whereas A{beta}42 differences were less consistent across cohorts. DISCUSSION: AD proteomic heterogeneity is characterized by multiscale organization combining dominant group structure with continuous higher-order relationships.

title: Optimal Predictivity of Random Signatures: Causes and Good Modeling Practices
abstract: In high-throughput omics data, randomly-selected sets of markers ("signatures") have large and often optimal phenotypic predictivity. This creates problems of over-interpretation of biological and predictive importance of signatures, of bioinformatics algorithms and expert knowledge-driven selection. We conduct first an empirical study establishing that the phenomenon occurs across a variety of types of datasets/omics types and algorithms (224 combinations, >120 million models fitted). Random signatures are systematically reproducible across datasets. We develop a comprehensive theoretical framework, encompassing definitions, feasibility and impossibility theorems, and analytical formulas. The theory reveals as necessary and sufficient causes of these anomalous behaviors, the existence of large equivalence classes of optimally predictive feature sets, and their structure of information equivalences. We validate the theory with additional experiments and propose good practices intended to strengthen scientific rigor. Our findings apply to both algorithmic discovery and expert knowledge-driven signature selection, and to both existing and future algorithms and expert criteria. They also extend to all types of data with similar equivalence classes of optimal predictors.

title: Infectious Disease Knowledge Graph (IDKG) for Antiviral and Antibacterial Drug Discovery.
abstract: Infectious diseases remain a leading cause of global morbidity and mortality, while therapeutic discovery is hindered by fragmented biomedical data and antimicrobial resistance. To address this challenge, we developed the Infectious Disease Knowledge Graph (IDKG), a queryable platform that integrates curated chemical, biological, pharmacological, and clinical information relevant to infectious-disease drug discovery. Using a customized ORION pipeline, we integrated 20 data sources, including DrugCentral, SMACC, Heli-SMACC, NPASS, ClinicalTrials.gov, and host-virus interaction databases, into a Neo4j graph containing more than 4.6 million nodes and 26 million edges. IDKG supports graph-based reasoning through Clinical Outcome Pathways (COPs) and incorporates curation workflows for small molecules, biologics, and complex mixtures. Illustrative applications include reconstruction of a literature-supported remdesivir pathway for COVID-19 and graph-based mechanistic interpretation of experimentally observed quorum-sensing inhibitor-antibiotic synergies in multidrug-resistant bacteria. The platform provides an interoperable framework for drug repurposing, target prioritization, and mechanism-based hypothesis generation. IDKG is freely available at https://idkg.mml.unc.edu.

title: Mathematical genomics of hidden signatures in NCF1: implications for chronic granulomatous disease
abstract: Inborn errors of immunity (IEIs), such as Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD), impose a disproportionately severe clinical burden in populations with high rates of consanguinity. CGD is caused by defects in the phagocyte NADPH oxidase complex, frequently due to mutations in the NCF1 gene encoding the p47phox protein. While the functional domains of NCF1 are well characterized, the quantitative architectural constraints governing its structural stability remain elusive. This study aimed to decipher the multidimensional quantitative signatures of NCF1, across diverse organisms in order to understand its conserved spatial sequence architecture and the structural basis of variant severity. We analyzed 41 NCF1 sequences using ten distinct quantitative features, integrating primary sequence metrics, biophysical chemistry, and abstract topological geometry. The synthesis of these features revealed a lack of a unified proximity matrix, demonstrating that NCF1 is defined by feature-dependent, multidimensional individual signatures. Primary sequence metrics exhibited rigid phylogenetic conservation, revealing invariant zero-entropy blocks that correlated strictly with severe CGD-causing mutations, while topological metrics exposed a deep spatial architectural convergence. These multidimensional baselines confirmed that the protein requires a highly specific spatial packing to assemble the NADPH oxidase complex; pathogenic mutations therefore disrupt precise structural signatures rather than globally destroying the protein. Consistent with this, the AlphaFold model places the folded PX and tandem SH3 domains in a high-confidence core and the regulatory C-terminal tail in an exposed, low-confidence region, supporting a tail-mediated autoinhibitory mechanism. Ultimately, this quantitative framework offers a useful perspective on NCF1 architecture and may serve as a supportive tool for evaluating the severity of clinical variants, contributing to precision medicine efforts for NCF1-associated diseases.

title: Segment Anything for Microscopy 2
abstract: Foundation models have advanced microscopy image segmentation, but existing models are trained on two-dimensional data, struggle with complex structures in volumetric data, and address only a narrow range of analysis tasks. Here we present Segment Anything for Microscopy 2 (SAM2), a foundation model that adapts SAM2 to joint 2D and 3D segmentation in light and electron microscopy. Trained on annotations of more than 23 million cells and nuclei and 1.6 million cellular structures, SAM2 achieves state-of-the-art automatic and interactive segmentation and outperforms generalist and specialist methods on volumetric data. Dedicated models further enable accurate mitochondrion and nucleus segmentation in electron microscopy. Beyond segmentation, SAM2 supports pixel and object classification from few annotations as well as cell tracking in 2D and 3D time-lapse data. All functionality is available in the user-friendly SAM napari plugin. We demonstrated the capabilities of SAM2 on challenging use cases spanning developmental biology, organoid research, cardiac physiology, and histopathology.

title: WormIE: an Integrated Explorer for multi-source Caenorhabditis elegans annotations and transcriptomic data interpretation
abstract: Interpreting gene lists and expression data from Caenorhabditis elegans experiments usually means writing scripts, searching scattered databases or uploading unpublished data to a remote server. WormIE (Worm Integrated Explorer, https://wormie.bio) is a free, open-source tool for analyzing user-provided data and exploring C. elegans annotations in one browser tab. Starting with gene lists from -omics experiments, genetic screens or other approaches, users can explore what genes have in common and how they interact, test over-representation or ranked-list enrichment in built-in or user-provided gene sets and compare lists by their genes or enriched categories. Of WormIE's nine collections, which include Gene Ontology and CeNGEN neuron types, two are curated sets found in no other worm resource: neuronal genes and synaptic genes. WormIE counts aligned reads from RNA sequencing and tests for differential expression with the same R package as conventional pipelines, then checks the genes for enrichment in those collections. Clicking any gene in a result page opens the gene page gathering seventeen domains from WormBase, the Alliance of Genome Resources and other sources, such as phenotypes, interactions and expression. Everything runs on the user's computer without uploading data and works offline. On simulated data, every analysis agreed with its R counterpart (correlation 0.9999), and in a reanalysis of a germline study of the co-regulator SIN-3, WormIE recovered 99% of the reported differentially expressed genes and all nine WormCat categories. Together, these results show that WormIE reliably links gene lists and expression data to community-curated knowledge without programming or a server.

title: Vecmatch: Balancing Covariates in Multiple Groups Using Vector Matching Algorithm and Generalized Propensity Scores
abstract: Covariate imbalance is a major source of bias in observational studies. This issue arises when confounding variables (e.g., age, sex) are distributed unevenly across compared groups, potentially influencing estimates of between-group differences in other dependent variables. Matching techniques based on propensity scores are widely used to address covariate imbalance and improve the accuracy of causal inferences. These methods work by calculating propensity scores based on imbalanced covariates and then matching observations with the closest propensity scores across compared groups. However, existing matching methods primarily focus on comparisons between at most two groups, and there is currently no widely implemented approach for matching across more than two treatment groups in popular programming languages. In this paper, we present an R implementation of the vector matching algorithm for matching across multiple treatment groups. The implementation includes the core algorithm itself along with several extensions aimed at improving usability and flexibility in applied research. These features include tools for visualizing covariate distributions, functions for estimating generalized propensity scores, and methods for defining rectangular regions of common support. Users can choose among different matching methods and adjust various parameters to improve covariate balance. To support this process, we provide an optimization workflow based on the random search algorithm that identifies parameter combinations yielding the best matching quality and highest percentage of matched samples. In addition, the package includes functions for assessing post-matching quality, offering a comprehensive and flexible framework for robust causal inference in complex observational settings. Keywords: covariate imbalance, bias reduction, vector matching, generalized propensity scores

title: TopoPPI: A geometry-aware platform for visualization and low-distortion mapping of protein-protein interaction interfaces
abstract:
by Shuyu Zhong 

Protein–protein interfaces encode molecular recognition through spatially organized contacts, yet their buried, curved surfaces are difficult to inspect as a whole. Flattening these surfaces can expose interface organization but introduces geometric distortion and may divide individual residues into disconnected regions. We present TopoPPI, a geometry-aware platform that converts interaction surfaces into low-distortion two-dimensional atlases while retaining links to source atoms, residues and contacts. TopoPPI extends OptCuts with a contact-weighted penalty for seam-induced fragmentation of residue footprints—the surface regions assigned to individual residues—jointly balancing continuity, seam length and distortion. In a leakage-controlled benchmark of 2,236 experimental complexes, the geometry-only OptCuts foundation achieved 88.39% lower family-weighted scale-fair distortion than the next-best tested parameterization across 2,209 complete comparable outputs. Across 2,204 exact-domain comparisons, TopoPPI reduced family-weighted residue-footprint fragmentation by 12.81% (95% confidence interval, 11.50–14.05%), with a 2.60% increase in normalized seam length and a 0.061% increase in scale-fair distortion. Continuity gains extended to 1,180 fixed-pose pairs of AlphaFold monomer models and 145 predicted complexes, with fragmentation reductions of 18.60% and 11.65%, respectively. Functionally annotated antibody and colicin–immunity interfaces demonstrated reconnection of the footprints of experimentally characterized binding and specificity residues. Further applications mapped published binding and folding free-energy estimates onto the KRAS–RAF1 interface and compared shared receptor residues across two growth-hormone recognition sites. Available through graphical and command-line interfaces, TopoPPI provides a residue-aware visualization framework for integrating structural contacts and functional annotations within geometrically controlled interface maps.

title: GapCNV: A comprehensive framework for CNV detection in low-input DNA sequencing data
abstract:
by Xuanxuan Yu, Fei Qin, Shiwei Liu, Noah J. Brown, Xiao Fan, Qing Lu, Guoshuai Cai, Jennifer L. Guler, Feifei Xiao 

Copy number variants (CNVs) are prevalent in both diploid and haploid genomes and contribute to genome evolution and phenotypic diversity. However, CNV detection in low-input data, including low-cell and single-cell sequencing data, remains challenging due to the shallow and highly uneven read counts and amplification bias. Another challenge lies in selecting reference samples, which are used to provide a baseline for defining copy-number losses or gains. Normalization using references containing common CNVs can lead to cancellation of true CNV signals or false CNV calls. Here, we develop GapCNV, a statistical framework for CNV detection in low-input DNA sequencing data from both haploid and diploid genomes. GapCNV uses preliminary cell clustering and shared CNV profiles to construct bin-specific pseudo-references from cells inferred to have the copy-neutral state. This strategy reduces the incorporation of common CNVs into the normalization baseline and thereby preserves common CNV signals. We evaluated GapCNV using simulations with and without amplification biases and datasets from  Plasmodium falciparum , human breast cancer and melanoma. In simulations, GapCNV achieved high precision rate while maintaining competitive sensitivity, with advantages for detecting short and common CNVs. In  P. falciparum , GapCNV detected the known CNVs and recovered the short CNV more frequently than the benchmarking methods. In the melanoma cell line and human breast tumors, GapCNV recovered bulk or single-cell derived copy number profile across individual cells. These results show that adaptive, bin-specific pseudo-reference construction can improve CNV detection when reliable normal controls are unavailable.

title: Hierarchical data-driven dynamical surrogate models of social decision-making
abstract:
by Manuel Brenner, Ismail Guennouni, Daniel Durstewitz, Stephanie N. L. Schmidt, Stefanie Lis, Peter Kirsch, Georgia Koppe 

Social decision making is inherently complex, shaped by dynamic trust building, biases, and adaptive strategies. Yet in laboratory settings, its study is often constrained by small datasets that nonetheless encode rich and sophisticated cognitive processes. This scarcity has historically limited modeling approaches to hand-tailored frameworks that embed strong priors about the underlying mechanisms. Recent advances in data-driven modeling of latent dynamical processes provide an alternative, extracting generative models directly from behavioral data without restrictive assumptions. Building on these methods, we derive hierarchical digital surrogates from sparse, non-Gaussian investment sequences in repeated trust games. Our approach proceeds in three stages. First, we demonstrate that, despite the limited data, the inferred models can accurately predict future investments and outperform theory-driven reinforcement-learning and Bayesian cognitive models, establishing predictive validity and providing a solid baseline for subsequent mechanistic analyses. Second, we analyze the latent dynamics of these models and show that they capture mechanistic structure in how investments and choice uncertainty are organized in state space and how social versus non-social cues are represented, in a way that parallels patterns observed directly in the empirical behavior. Third, we exploit the generative nature of the hierarchical digital surrogates to run in-silico experiments beyond the original data, such as probing how specific cues steer participants into trusting or mistrusting states and simulating responses to novel, unobserved cue-outcome combinations and trustee strategies. Together, this work demonstrates how generative digital surrogates open a new path toward mechanistic, data-driven accounts of social interaction dynamics that both reproduce observed behavior and support hypothesis generation in virtual environments.

title: A beam–membrane biomechanical vocal fold model incorporating posturing and glottal conformation
abstract:
by Mohamed A. Serry, Matías Zañartu, Sean D. Peterson 

The posture of the vocal folds produced by laryngeal muscle activation plays a central role in determining the dynamics of voice production. Abnormal vocal fold configurations are frequently associated with inefficient phonation and a variety of voice disorders. Although diverse glottal closure patterns have been observed clinically, the biomechanical mechanisms governing their dynamic behavior and resulting phonatory characteristics remain incompletely understood. Moreover, existing numerical models that incorporate the effects of the intrinsic musculature on posturing and glottal conformation are computationally expensive, which limits their suitability for large-scale parametric investigations. In this work, we introduce a computationally inexpensive vocal fold (VF) model wherein the body and cover VF layers are treated as a composite beam and a coupled membrane, respectively. Intrinsic laryngeal muscle activation, in addition to positioning the arytenoid cartilages and cricothyroid joint, introduces moments at the boundaries of the structure that influence glottal conformation. The model produces phonatory characteristics that are qualitatively consistent with those reported in high-fidelity finite-element models and clinical studies, thereby supporting its predictive capability while offering substantial computational advantage. The proposed framework provides biomechanical insights into the influence of incomplete glottal closure on phonation dynamics and may serve as a computationally tractable tool for investigating mechanisms underlying certain voice disorders.

title: Exploring the potential of bile fluid dynamics analysis to inform clinical strategies for choledochal cysts: Experimental and numerical studies
abstract:
by Yidan Shang, Jiaying Liu, Wentao Sun, Renquan Tu, Xueren Li, Xiaojian Ni, Houbao Liu, Jiyuan Tu 

Surgical intervention is essential for choledochal cysts (CCs) due to their high lifetime risk of progressing to cholangiocarcinoma, yet management strategies vary worldwide. Given bile fluid’s vital role in digestion, investigating bile flow dynamics may provide surgeons with additional insights for treatment planning. In this study, one MRI-based healthy adult scan was used to reconstruct biliary system, which was then modified according to Todani classifications to generate eight CC types. Particle Image Velocimetry was used to first visualize local velocity field, followed by computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations of bile emptying to analyze pathological non-Newtonian bile flow. Wall shear stress (WSS), a key biomechanical parameter, was visualized through 2D surface mapping for comparative evaluation. Results showed consistently low velocity in dilated regions, suggesting bile accumulation in CCs, particularly in Types 1a, 2, 4a, and 4b. While WSS changes were minimal in the healthy biliary system, extreme gradients, up to 10,000-fold emerged in CCs, especially Types 1a, 2, and 4a. These findings highlight that bile flow characteristics are primarily dictated by localized anatomical abnormalities, aligning with surgical interventions that target dilated regions. These findings demonstrate the potential of CFD to provide additional biomechanical insights into bile flow abnormalities associated with different CC types, which may serve as a reference for future clinical investigations.

title: Ontology pre-training improves machine learning-based predictions for metabolites
abstract:
by Charlotte Tumescheit, Martin Glauer, Simon Flügel, Martin Larralde, Fabian Neuhaus, Till Mossakowski, Janna Hastings 

Deep learning has recently led to multiple breakthroughs in longstanding biological problems. Recent advances have shown that integration of expert knowledge can improve deep learning model predictive performance in complex domains such as biology. Bio-ontologies offer a rich source of curated biological knowledge that can be harnessed to this end. Here, we describe an intuitive and generalisable approach to embed the knowledge contained in a classification hierarchy derived from a bio-ontology into a deep learning model as an intermediate training step between general-purpose pre-training and task-specific fine-tuning: a process that we call’ontology pre-training’. We show that this approach leads to an improvement in predictive performance and a reduction in training time for a broad range of prediction tasks related to metabolite functions, activities and properties in living systems, using a range of datasets derived from MoleculeNet. We see the biggest improvement for regression tasks, e.g., prediction of lipophilicity and aqueous solubility of molecules, and a robust improvement for most classification tasks. Our approach can be adapted for a wide range of knowledge sources, models and prediction tasks.

title: Exploring the mechanism of oxfendazole in inhibiting osteosarcoma-induced osteolysis based on single-cell RNA seqsuencing
abstract:
by Jifeng Miao, Pintian Wang, Wenyu Feng, Haiyi Quan, Yunhua Lin, Gejin Wei, Fake Meng, Shanhang Li, Mingxiu Yang, Binyuan Ning, Jingxin Deng, Liang Xiong, Jianming Hu, Yun Liu, Qingjun Wei 

Osteosarcoma-associated osteolysis represents a major obstacle in the management of osteosarcoma. Within the osteolytic microenvironment, interactions between osteoclasts and tumor cells facilitate tumor proliferation and metastatic dissemination, and contribute to the development of pathological fractures. However, conventional osteoclast-targeting agents are insufficient to effectively suppress osteosarcoma-driven bone resorption. In this study, single-cell RNA sequencing was performed to identify critical regulators involved in osteoclast differentiation in the context of osteosarcoma. Using the Beyondcell platform, drugs targeting osteoclast-related signaling pathways were screened, and oxfendazole (OFN) was identified as a potential therapeutic candidate, with ANXA2 recognized as a key associated target. In vitro osteoclastogenesis assays and an in vivo tibial orthotopic osteosarcoma model demonstrated that oral administration of OFN via gavage effectively suppressed osteoclast formation and osteolytic activity, as confirmed by micro-CT and histopathological analyses. But OFN alone did not significantly inhibit osteosarcoma growth but effectively reduced osteoclast-mediated osteolysis. In addition, qRT-PCR and immunohistochemistry confirmed that OFN downregulates ANXA2 expression in vitro and in vivo, thereby impairing osteoclast differentiation. Molecular dynamics simulations combined with in-vitro validation further suggested that OFN may interact with the transcription factor ZNF530, leading to reduced ANXA2 transcription. In conclusion, the integration of single-cell RNA sequencing with the Beyondcell algorithm enabled the identification of OFN as a potent candidate agent for osteosarcoma-induced osteolysis. OFN attenuates osteoclastogenesis and bone resorption by suppressing ANXA2 expression. These findings provide preclinical evidence supporting the therapeutic potential of OFN in the treatment of osteosarcoma-associated osteolysis.

title: Integrating hyperspectral phenomics and genome-wide association analysis reveals a ribosome assembly factor regulating wheat grain protein content under drought stress
abstract:
Background
                      Drought stress threatens wheat grain quality by altering the accumulation of protein and carbon reserves. Deciphering the genetic mechanisms underlying these traits is important for developing climate-resilient wheat varieties. 
                  
                     Results
                      Here we integrate high-throughput hyperspectral imaging (HSI) with genome-wide association studies (GWAS) to investigate the genetic basis of grain quality in a diversity panel of 498 wheat accessions grown under drought and well-watered conditions. To dissect the genetic architecture of these spectral phenotypes, we perform whole-genome re-sequencing of the association panel and conduct GWAS on hyperspectral traits. We identify 828 quantitative trait loci associated with grain spectral traits, including several loci colocalizing with known grain quality genes. Among them, we identify  TaUTP18 , encoding U3 small nucleolar RNA-associated protein involved in ribosome assembly, as a candidate regulator of drought-responsive grain quality. Functional analyses demonstrate that disruption of  TaUTP18  alters grain hyperspectral profiles and significantly reduces grain protein content and grain size under drought stress. Polysome profiling and transcriptome analyses reveal that  TaUTP18  is required for efficient U3 snoRNP-mediated 18 S rRNA maturation, ribosome biogenesis, and translational capacity during grain development under drought. In parallel, machine-learning models trained on hyperspectral data accurately predict grain protein and carbon contents, enabling rapid, non-destructive assessment of grain quality. 
                  
                     Conclusions
                      Our study demonstrates the power of integrating hyperspectral phenomics with GWAS to uncover genes underlying complex quality traits. The identification of  TaUTP18  establishes a mechanistic link between ribosome biogenesis and wheat grain protein accumulation under drought stress, while providing a valuable target for breeding climate-resilient, high-quality wheat varieties.

title: MitoScope: a comprehensive mitochondrial genome analysis workflow for long-read sequencing data
abstract: The mitochondrial genome (mtDNA), rich in repeats and prone to nuclear mitochondrial DNA segments (NUMTs), is implicated in cancer, metabolic syndromes, and neurodegeneration, yet short-read sequencing yields incomplete catalogs, mapping artifacts, and false heteroplasmies. We introduce MitoScope, a scalable end-to-end long-read mitochondrial analysis workflow that integrates mtDNA-read selection, heteroplasmic variant detection, assembly, copy number estimation, read-level haplotyping, and NUMT profiling. Applied to benchmarking data from the Somatic Mosaicism across Human Tissues (SMaHT) Network ,  we reveal high sensitivity and precision compared to existing methods and successfully uncover known mitochondrial biology relevant for variant interpretation, aging, and human disease.

title: STRUCT: a statistical approach to detect conserved RNA secondary structures from raw sequencing data without multiple sequence alignment
abstract: Covariation among orthologous sequences is an established evolutionary signal of conserved RNA secondary structures. We present STRUCT (Statistical Testing of RNA Units with Covariation Traits), a covariation-based statistical test that applies to raw sequencing data, bypassing assembly and multiple sequence alignment required by existing covariation methods. Simulations demonstrate false discovery rate control and high power under matched model assumptions. STRUCT rediscovers known HIV structural elements in provirus sequences, identifies conserved rRNA structures, and prioritizes putative viral RNA structures in metatranscriptomics samples. STRUCT offers a novel approach for high-throughput detection of conserved RNA structures and hypothesis generation for viral discovery.

title: Determining gene specificity from multivariate single-cell RNA sequencing data
abstract:
Background
                      An important application of single-cell genomics experiments is to identify genes specific to biological categories or experimental conditions. We develop ember (Entropy Metrics for Biological ExploRation), an entropy-based framework that uses Shannon’s chain rule across nested biological partitions. Four axioms characterize its  Ψ  score within a class of normalized entropy-decomposition scores. 
                  
                     Results
                      Applying ember to eight tissues from eight founder mouse strains, we find that gene specificity is often unintuitive: canonical markers can be supplanted, housekeeping genes are context-dependent, and mouse strain can drive unexpected cell type switching. Unsupervised learning on entropy metrics uncovers shared genes specialized to male gonads and kidney, as well as genes specific to non-consecutive developmental stages in the kidney. To facilitate further exploration of gene specificity in mice, we have also developed a comprehensive specificity database, along with a web interface, API and MCP server. Extending ember to a human PBMC dataset collected from 255 diverse individuals, we find that variation in PBMCs is largely localized to classical monocytes. We also find genes with unique specificity by sex, age and ancestral background. 
                  
                     Conclusions
                      Together, these applications establish ember as a powerful tool and provide a roadmap for elucidating the impact of human genetic variation using the murine model.

title: A pathogen‐free citrus model recapitulates Huanglongbing‐associated molecular and physiological reprogramming
abstract:
SUMMARY 
 Huanglongbing (HLB) is a devastating citrus disease associated with “ Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus ”, but the contribution of host-driven processes to disease development remains poorly understood. Here, we developed a pathogen-free system to determine whether chloroplast dysfunction can reproduce key molecular and physiological features of HLB. Using  Citrus tristeza virus -mediated silencing of  phytoene desaturase  ( PDS ) and δ-aminolevulinic acid dehydratase ( ALAD ), we simultaneously disrupted carotenoid and chlorophyll biosynthesis in  Citrus macrophylla . Chloroplast dysfunction induced foliar chlorosis resembling that observed in HLB-affected citrus and recapitulated major alterations in pigments, stomatal behavior, primary metabolism, hormone signaling, defense responses, and starch accumulation. Transcriptomic and metabolomic analyses revealed substantial overlap between chloroplast-disrupted and “ Ca. L. asiaticus ”-infected plants. The two conditions shared 1067 differentially expressed genes, with extensive overlap in carbohydrate, amino acid, phenylpropanoid, flavonoid, hormone signaling, and defense pathways. Metabolomic profiles similarly converged, including sucrose depletion, hexose and amino acid accumulation, and extensive remodeling of central carbon metabolism. These findings demonstrate that chloroplast dysfunction can recapitulate a substantial component of the systemic molecular and metabolic phenotype associated with HLB. We hypothesize that chloroplast impairment during HLB contributes to metabolic, hormonal, redox, and defense reprogramming throughout the plant through chloroplast-derived signals, with potential consequences for disease progression. This pathogen-free framework identifies chloroplast stability and chloroplast-to-nucleus signaling as potential targets for further investigation in HLB pathogenesis.

title: Chemical strategies of rhizobacteria to promote plant growth
abstract:
SUMMARY 
 Plants establish intimate relationships with rhizobacteria through the recognition and integration of a wide variety of molecules of different chemical nature, including some of the main phytohormones such as auxins, cytokinins, ethylene and gibberellins, as well as quorum-sensing signals and volatile organic compounds. The emission of bioactive molecules, which serve as communication signals, is species-specific and may change depending upon the composition of the bacterial community. Processes influenced by the bacteriome through their diffusible and/or volatile profiles range from nodulation, lateral root and root hair formation to strengthened immunity and greater resilience and adaptability under stressful environmental conditions. Plant proteins and cellular messengers for recognition of  N -acyl- L -homoserine lactones, cyclodipeptides, and volatile organic compounds of bacterial origin have begun to be identified and include WRKY transcription factors, glycolytic glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase, and signaling through MAP kinases. Understanding the diversity of bacterial signaling molecules and their networks continues to grow, positioning chemical synthesis as a promising approach to spread their application in sustainable agriculture. The strategies and mechanisms of plant growth promotion by rhizobacteria extend and reinforce symbiotic events enabling plants to perceive and integrate microbial information into responses that improve fitness under particular growth conditions and long-term productivity.

title: Splicing factor SMU1 confers cold tolerance by preventing excessive ROS accumulation via chromatin regulation in Arabidopsis
abstract:
SUMMARY 
 Plants activate salicylic acid (SA) signaling cascades and reactive oxygen species (ROS) production upon prolonged cold stress.
