Excessive activation of these pathways severely impairs plant growth, yet mechanisms preventing their overactivation during prolonged cold remain poorly understood. Here, we characterized the splicing factor SMU1 as a key regulator of long-term cold tolerance in Arabidopsis. The  smu1  mutant exhibits severe growth inhibition, excessive ROS accumulation, and hyperactivation of SA biosynthesis regulators ( SARD1 ,  CBP60g ) and the ROS-generating gene  PRX34 , a function likely largely uncoupled from its canonical splicing function. SMU1 binds the chromatin of these three genes, and 3 weeks of cold reduces this association. Loss of  SMU1  decreases histone H3 density and increases H3K9 acetylation (H3K9ac) at these loci after 3 weeks of cold. SMU1 interacts with histone deacetylase HDA9. Although  hda9  mutant exhibits no obvious cold-sensitive phenotype,  hda9 smu1  displays aggravated cold susceptibility and elevates H3K9ac at  PRX34  and  SARD1  after 3 weeks of cold. HDA9 associates with the chromatin of  SARD1 ,  CBP60g , and  PRX34  before cold. Mutation of  SMU1  enhances HDA9 chromatin binding to  PRX34  and  CBP60g  after 3 weeks of cold. Thus, SMU1 and HDA9 cooperatively restrain hyperactivation of SA- and ROS-related genes under prolonged cold. Our findings uncover SMU1 as a chromatin-associated regulator that balances SA and ROS signaling to maintain ROS homeostasis and confers prolonged cold tolerance.

title: Incorporation of the coleoptile purple line trait into the superior haploid inducer HI285 for efficient haploid identification in rice
abstract:
SUMMARY 
 Production of homozygous inbred lines is of great importance for rice breeding. Doubled haploid (DH) technology provides an efficient route to obtain pure lines, drastically reducing the breeding cycle relative to conventional pedigree selection methods. Recently,  in vivo  DH approaches based on intraspecific hybridization using haploid inducers (HIs) have gained momentum in rice, largely owing to the discovery of haploid induction genes and the development of high-performance inducers such as HI285. Nevertheless, the widespread application of this technology remains constrained by the difficulty of haploid identification. Here, we show that haploids are indeed smaller than diploid plants at early developmental stages, but using plant size to identify haploids results in a high false-positive rate, and spontaneous DHs are easily discarded. This prompted us to harness  OsC1 , a key gene involved in anthocyanin biosynthesis. By incorporating the coleoptile purple line (CPL) trait into HI285 via either  OsC1  overexpression or a precise 10-bp insertion, we established a system that maintains high induction efficiency while enabling instant visual scoring. Importantly, the developed HI285-Red, generated via the precise 10-bp insertion in  OsC1 , is transgene-free and allows visual haploid identification at early seedling stage. This advance is expected to remove a major barrier to the routine deployment of DH technology in commercial rice breeding.

title: The F‐box protein FBLA regulates leaf development by promoting ubiquitination and degradation of RLI1 and LBD12‐1 in rice
abstract:
SUMMARY 
 Leaf is crucial for rice yield due to its photosynthetic function, while the details of its development require further exploration. In this study, we identified an  fbla  mutant ( f-box protein for leaf architecture ), which shows increased leaf inclination and narrowed and curled leaves.  FBLA  encodes an F-box protein, which localizes to the nucleus and may function as a component of the Skp1-Cullin1-F-box (SCF) E3 ubiquitin–ligase complex. FBLA interacts with leaf inclination regulator RLI1 and mediates its ubiquitination modification, which is then degraded through the 26S proteasome pathway. Mutation of  RLI1  causes decreased leaf inclination. Further, FBLA interacts with narrow and curl leaf regulator LBD12-1 and mediates its ubiquitination modification, which is then degraded through the 26S proteasome pathway. Overexpression of  LBD12-1  causes narrowed and curled leaves. These findings identified a novel F-box protein and elucidated the molecular mechanism by which it regulates the development of leaf through targeting different substrate proteins, providing a novel theoretical basis and platform resources for molecular breeding of ideal leaf morphology.

title: The genome of tetraploid Hordeum brevisubulatum underpins its evolution and saline–alkali adaptation
abstract:
SUMMARY 
 Saline–alkali stress is a major challenge to crop production. Tetraploid  Hordeum brevisubulatum  is a wild relative of  Hordeum  crops with strong saline–alkali tolerance, but the lack of a reference genome has limited genomic studies and the utilization of its stress-adaptive genetic resources. Here, we generated a chromosome-scale genome assembly of tetraploid  H. brevisubulatum  and resolved its A and B subgenomes. Phylogenomic analyses indicated distinct evolutionary relationships between the two subgenomes, with the A subgenome potentially originating from the  H. brevisubulatum  lineage or a closely related, unsampled or divergent  Hordeum  lineage. Comparative analyses of gene families and transcriptomes revealed functional differentiation and dynamic homeolog-specific expression regulation between the A and B subgenomes under saline–alkali stress. Structural variation analysis further showed that some SVs overlapped gene bodies and regulatory regions, potentially affecting gene function or expression regulation. Transcriptome analysis identified stress-responsive transcription factors, among which  HbNAC29  showed strong induction in both leaf and root tissues and was selected for further investigation. Notably, the  HbNAC29  homoeologs exhibited structural divergence in their regulatory regions, including a subgenome-specific insertion, which may contribute to the divergent expression responses under saline–alkali stress. Heterologous overexpression of  HbNAC29  in rice provided supportive evidence for its potential involvement in saline–alkali stress tolerance. Together, our study provides genomic insights into subgenome divergence, structural variation, and stress-responsive regulatory divergence in tetraploid  H. brevisubulatum , and expands genomic resources for understanding and utilizing this stress-adapted wild relative in crop improvement.

title: Transcription Factor StTCP6 Promotes Potato Tuberization and Axillary Bud Dormancy Through FLOWERING LOCUS T and Symplastic Transport
abstract:
ABSTRACT 
 In plants that form underground storage organs, assimilate partitioning is central to coordinating above-ground vegetative growth and underground storage organs development. However, how plants balance this specialized source-sink relationship, and synchronize it with storage organ formation, remains largely unknown. Here, using potato shoot branching and tuberization as a model, we show that TCP transcription factor StTCP6 orchestrates branching-tuberization trade-offs by coordinating tuber-forming signals and potentially modulating assimilate distribution to axillary buds. StTCP6 activates the expression of tuberigenic  StSP3D  and  StSP6A , and is genetically dependent on  StSP6A  to promote tuberization. Notably,  StTCP6  also suppresses shoot branching through maintaining axillary bud dormancy. Suppression of  StTCP6  in ssp.  tuberosum  promotes increased branching, later maturity and higher yield, while its overexpression leads to opposite effects. Further investigations demonstrate that under long days,  StTCP6  overexpression remarkably induces tuber formation in short-day potato. These findings reveal StTCP6 as a central integrator that coordinates shoot branching and tuberization to optimize plant maturity and tuber yield, providing new insights into how above- and below-ground source-sink relationships are modulated in root and tuber crops.

title: Multiplex Genome Editing Overcomes Photoperiod Sensitivity in Tropical Maize
abstract: Plant Biotechnology Journal, EarlyView.

title: Higher Frequency and Precision of Target Site Integration Using TAHITI
abstract:
ABSTRACT 
 Efficient genomic target site integration, whereby the user selects the locus of transgene insertion, is a long-desired technology in plant biology. Sequence-based selection of the target site allows for the user to designate ideal genomic regions for transgene expression, durability, and downstream breeding, including the stacking of multiple traits. However, the efficiency of target site integration has traditionally been very low, requiring deep pipelines and screening. DNA transposable elements (TEs) naturally cut and paste themselves across genomes, and we previously coupled the activity of the rice TE  mPing / Pong  with CRISPR-Cas programmability and double-strand break formation, resulting in the targeted integration of the  mPing  TE and any associated internal cargo (traits). However, the natural activity of the TE generated a high rate of off-target  mPing  insertion. Here, we improve TE-mediated target site integration through engineering CRISPR-Cas to replace the role of the DNA cleavage activity of the  Pong  TE protein, providing improved on-target integration rates and reduced off-target rates. The combination of a deficient and immobilized TE system with CRISPR-Cas enables highly efficient DNA integration at a user-designated site, and we demonstrate higher accuracy and smaller junction scars compared to the previous version of the technology. We demonstrate additional methods to improve the rate of targeted integration, such as removing one of the two  Pong  proteins, intronizing coding regions, and heat-shocking plants. We demonstrate the next generation of TE-mediated target site integration, called Transposon-Assisted Homology-Independent Targeted Integration (TAHITI).

title: Root gene regulatory network analysis reveals roles for defense hormones and secondary metabolites in establishment of disease‐suppressive soil
abstract:
Hypothetical model of how  Arabidopsis thaliana  establishes soil-borne legacy upon  Hyaloperonospora arabidopsidis  infection.
 
 
 Summary 
 
Plants recruit beneficial microbiota in their rhizosphere to alleviate stresses. In  Arabidopsis thaliana , foliar infection by  Hyaloperonospora arabidopsidis  ( Hpa ) has been shown to establish a disease-suppressive microbiome that promotes protection against  Hpa  infection of the subsequent plant generation grown in conditioned soil – a phenomenon known as soil-borne legacy (SBL). The root responses involved in SBL establishment have remained largely unclear.
In this study, time-series RNA-seq of roots from  Hpa -infected plants grown in natural soil was conducted over 7 d post inoculation. A gene regulatory network of the responding roots was constructed. The role of predicted key components was verified in follow-up assays.
Root transcriptional reprogramming started within 1 d after foliar infection. Genes associated with salicylic acid (SA)-mediated defense were upregulated, while those linked to secondary metabolism and jasmonic acid (JA) responsiveness were downregulated. SA accumulation increased at 1 d post inoculation (dpi), and JA decreased by 3 dpi. Transcriptional regulation occurred in the tips of the roots. Mutant analyses confirmed that SA, JA, indole glucosinolates, camalexin, and flavonoids contribute to SBL establishment.
Our findings reveal systemic transcriptional reprogramming in roots upon foliar pathogen attack, uncovering roles of hormone signaling and secondary metabolism in shaping a disease-suppressive soil beyond their known defense functions.

title: Heterologous small subunits assemble into functional hybrid Rubiscos with altered structure–function in Arabidopsis
abstract:
Overview of heterologous Rubisco small subunits expressed in the Arabidopsis RbcS-deficient mutant  1a2b3b .
 
 
 Summary 
 
Rubisco performs the initial step in CO 2  fixation and is a key target for improving photosynthetic efficiency. In plants, Rubisco is an L 8 S 8  complex composed of four large subunits (RbcL) dimers and eight small subunits (RbcSs). Although the catalytic sites of Rubisco are located within RbcL dimers, RbcS can fine-tune catalytic performance.
Here we used an  Arabidopsis thaliana  mutant severely deficient in native RbcS ( 1a2b3b ) to explore the capacity of nine heterologous RbcSs from a range of species (i.e. plants, algae, diatoms and cyanobacteria) to assemble hybrid Rubisco complexes with Arabidopsis RbcL  in planta .
Five phylogenetically closer RbcSs were able to complement plant growth and photosynthesis, and these complemented plants produced Rubiscos with diverse catalytic properties. We obtained high-resolution cryogenic electron microscopy structures of all five of these hybrid L 8 S 8  complexes.
RbcS variants remodelled the RbcL-RbcS interface and were associated with consistent, long-range conformational differences within RbcL dimers. We identify RbcS-dependent structural pathways that may couple peripheral RbcS variation to the RbcL catalytic core. Our structure–function analyses support that there is significant scope to engineer the RbcS sequence space to modify Rubisco activity.

title: GmSUT4‐GmCyt b5‐2 complex regulates sucrose transport and root pH homeostasis, conferring saline–alkaline tolerance in soybean
abstract:
The GmSUT4–GmCyt b5-2 complex confers saline–alkaline tolerance in soybean by regulating sucrose transport and root pH homeostasis.
 
 
 Summary 
 
Soybean, a major protein and oil source, is severely constrained by saline–alkaline stress. Despite the role of sucrose in energy and signaling, its molecular mechanisms in stress tolerance remain unknown. Here, we characterize the function of  soybean sucrose transporter 4  ( GmSUT4 ) and molecular mechanisms controlling saline–alkaline stress in soybean.
Function analysis showed that  GmSUT4  overexpression (OE) enhances stress tolerance by improving sucrose allocation in roots, reducing electrolyte leakage, and reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation. X-ray computed tomography analysis further revealed that  GmSUT4-OE  lines exhibited increased root volume, root surface area, and reduced root–soil distance.
Interestingly, accumulated sucrose was associated with increased transcription and protein levels of H + -ATPase, thereby enhancing root H + -ATPase activity under saline–alkaline stress. Noninvasive microtest analysis revealed that H +  efflux was significantly increased in  GmSUT4-OE  roots. Root acidification assays further demonstrated that  GmSUT4-OE  lines exhibited stronger acidification capacity. Moreover, we demonstrate that interaction with GmCyt b5-2 enhanced GmSUT4-mediated sucrose transport efficiency, H +  efflux, and improved saline–alkaline tolerance, whereas this synergistic effect was abolished in  GmSUT4-KO  lines.
Together, this study demonstrates that the GmSUT4-GmCyt b5-2 module improves the H + -ATPase abundance and H +  efflux, thereby protecting roots from saline–alkaline injury, advancing our understanding of sugar signal-proton pump, and providing needed genetic resources for breeding saline–alkaline-tolerant soybean.

title: Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungus Rhizophagus irregularis expresses an outward potassium Shaker‐like channel in the interaction with rice (Oryza sativa)
abstract:
Summary diagram of the putative role of RiSKC3 in mycorrhizal K +  transport pathway.
 
 
 Summary 
 
Potassium (K + ) plays crucial roles in many physiological, molecular and cellular processes in plants. Uptake of this nutrient by root cells has been extensively investigated; however, uptake of K +  mediated by the interactions of the roots with fungi in the frame of a mutualistic symbiosis, also called mycorrhizal nutrient uptake pathway, remains poorly understood.
We identified an ion channel in the arbuscular mycorrhizal (AM) fungus  Rhizophagus irregularis . This channel exhibits the canonical features of the Shaker-like channel shared in other living kingdoms and is named RiSKC3. Transcriptionally expressed in hyphae and in arbuscules of colonized rice roots, RiSKC3 has been shown to be located in the plasma membrane.
Functional characterization by voltage-clamp in  Xenopus  oocytes revealed that RiSKC3 is endowed with voltage-gated outwardly rectifying activity with high selectivity for K +  over sodium ions, supporting the hypothesis that RiSKC3 plays an exclusive role in K +  secretion from the fungal cell.
Based on its localization and functional features, the proposed model is that this channel contributes to the secretion of K +  ions taken up by peripheral hyphae of  R. irregularis  into the peri-arbuscular space towards the host root.

title: CvARF3 and CvARF5 antagonistically regulate ray floret morphogenesis in Chrysanthemum vestitum
abstract:
In chrysanthemum, the auxin response factor (ARF) protein CvARF5 activates petal-identity genes to produce tubular petals, and CvARF3 represses the same genes to produce flat petals. This antagonistic regulation explains floral diversity and provides targets for breeding novel flower shapes.
  
 ABSTRACT 
 Flower shape is the most important characteristic of higher plants. The morphology of ray florets in chrysanthemum ( Chrysanthemum  ×  morifolium ) critically determines the diversity of capitulum shapes. However, its regulatory mechanisms remain largely elusive due to the complex genetic background.  C. vestitum , a hexaploid species closely related to chrysanthemum within the genus, exhibits two distinct lines characterized by fully flat and tubular phenotypes of ray florets, which serve as an ideal model material for investigating ray floret morphogenesis. Here, we report that N-1-naphthylphthalamic acid (NPA) treatment converted tubular ray florets to the flat type, accompanied by altered expression of  AUXIN RESPONSE FACTOR 3  ( CvARF3 ) and  CvARF5 . Functional validation showed that CvARF5 promoted the formation of tubular ray florets, while CvARF3 contributed to the development of flat ray florets. We further demonstrated divergent expression of petal identity regulators  PISTILLATA  ( CvPI ) and  SEPALLATA 3  ( CvSEP3 ) between the flat and tubular types. CvARF3 directly repressed the transcription of  CvPI  and  CvSEP3 , whereas CvARF5 activated these two genes, with co-factor CvARF6 enhancing this activation. Notably, CvARF3 and CvARF5 antagonistically regulate their transcription through shared AuxRE elements, suggesting potential competition for promoter occupancy. This transcriptional cascade revealed auxin-mediated regulation of morphological differences in ray florets, providing new insights into the regulatory networks that modulate ray floret development and inflorescence architecture.

title: Microtubule plus‐end tracking proteins EB1c and MOR1/XMAP215 interact to regulate mitosis and cytokinesis in Arabidopsis
abstract:
Arabidopsis  End-binding protein 1C (EB1c) and MICROTUBULE ORGANIZATION 1 (MOR1) interact directly and genetically in regulating plant cell division. The EB1c-MOR1 module is required for bipolar spindle establishment, correct chromosome alignment and segregation during mitosis, and proper phragmoplast expansion during cytokinesis.

  
 ABSTRACT 
 End-binding protein 1 (EB1) and microtubule (MT) polymerase XMAP215 are core components of the MT plus-end protein network. However, whether plant EB1 and XMAP215 homologs interact directly to regulate MT organization remains unclear. Here, we demonstrate a direct interaction between EB1c, an EB1 homolog that specifically associates with MT arrays during cell division, and MICROTUBULE ORGANIZATION 1 (MOR1)/XMAP215 on the spindle and phragmoplast in Arabidopsis, supported by a synergistic genetic interaction between EB1c and MOR1 in regulating plant cell division. Mechanistically, the EB1c−MOR1 module is required for bipolar spindle establishment, correct chromosome alignment and segregation during mitosis, and proper phragmoplast expansion during cytokinesis. Moreover, we discover that EB1c and MOR1 reciprocally yet differentially regulate each other's accumulation on the spindle and phragmoplast. Together, these findings provide direct physical, genetic, and functional evidence supporting the coordinated role of EB1c and MOR1 in spindle and phragmoplast organization and cell division in plants.

title: MaRAV6 controls plant architecture by repressing brassinosteroid biosynthesis in banana
abstract: Abstract The substantial height and dense foliar overlap in banana plants critically constrain light interception and utilization. Optimizing petiole inclination to achieve a compact plant architecture is therefore crucial for enabling high-density cultivation and facilitating mechanized harvesting. However, the underlying genetic and molecular regulatory mechanisms remain largely unknown, owing to banana genome complexity and clonal propagation. In this study, we utilized a panel of 143 accessions exhibiting significant variation in petiole inclination to dissect the genetic architecture through genome-wide association studies (GWAS). This analysis identified 42 significant single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) and 389 candidate genes. By integrating transcriptomic data from the conventional cultivar “Baxi” and its dwarf and erect petiole mutant “R3,” we prioritized MaRAV6, an ABI3/VP1-related transcription factor-encoding gene located on chromosome 4, as a key candidate. Functional validation demonstrated that overexpression of  MaRAV6  confers a dwarf and erect growth phenotype in banana. Combining DNA affinity purification sequencing (DAP-seq) and RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) further revealed that MaRAV6 represses the expression of brassinosteroid (BR) biosynthetic genes, steroid 22α-hydroxylase ( MaDWF4-1 ) and brassinosteroid-6-oxidase ( MaBR6ox1-1 ). This study elucidates first a molecular framework governing petiole angle regulation in banana. It also provides essential genetic resources and molecular targets for breeding compact banana varieties to enhance planting density and harvesting efficiency.

title: Tandem duplication of oxidosqualene cyclases and enzyme promiscuity of cytochromes P450 contribute to the diversity of triterpenoids in Eleutherococcus senticosus
abstract: Abstract Triterpenoid saponins in  Araliaceae  plants exhibit remarkable structural diversity, with species-specific compounds like ginsenosides and ciwujianosides, yet the genetic basis remains elusive. Here, we report a chromosome-scale genome assembly of  Eleutherococcus senticosus  (Rupr. & Maxim.) Maxim. (1.39 Gb, 51,243 genes) and demonstrate that it shares a lineage-specific whole-genome duplication (WGD-α,  K  s  = 0.112) with  Hedera helix . Phylogenomic analyses reveal a 4:4 syntenic relationship between these species, confirming their close evolutionary relationship. Notably, both  E. senticosus  and  H. helix  lack the dammarenediol-II synthase ( DDS ) gene, explaining the absence of ginsenoside-type saponins. Through genome mining and functional validation, we identify eight OSC genes, including a tandemly duplicated cluster on chromosome 18 unique to  E. senticosus . Biochemical assays show that EsOSC4 and EsOSC12 synthesize tirucalla-7,24-dien-3 β -ol, representing the first enzymatic characterization of a tirucallane synthase in Araliaceae, while EsOSC13 produces lupeol. Site-directed mutagenesis establishes residue 372 (valine in EsOSC13, methionine in EsOSC4/12) as critical for this functional divergence. Moreover, we discover three promiscuous CYP716 enzymes (EsCYP716A244/A450/A452) capable of oxidizing  β -amyrin, lupeol, and tirucalla-7,24-dien-3 β -ol at multiple positions, generating diverse oxidized derivatives. These findings reveal tandem duplication and enzyme promiscuity as primary mechanisms driving triterpenoid diversity in  E. senticosus , with implications for synthetic biology applications in saponin production.

title: Spontaneous N-formylation of amines with carbon monoxide in irradiated water
abstract: Abstract  N -formyl amines are crucial synthetic intermediates, yet their production often relies on methods requiring precious metal catalysts, suffering from activation barrier or generating stoichiometric waste. Concurrently, the astrochemical origin of formamide, a prebiotic precursor, remains debated. Herein, we report a catalyst-free, radical-driven  N -formylation strategy that addresses both challenges. Using only water as the solvent and X-ray or electron beam as the energy source, we achieve efficient coupling between carbon monoxide (CO) and amines under ambient conditions. Scaling up with a high-flux electron beam delivers a formamide production rate of 0.35 ± 0.01 mmol L −1  min −1 , with favorable techno-economic analysis indicating industrial potential. The reaction proceeds via the  in-situ  generation of key radicals ( • CHO from CO and  • NR 1 R 2  from amines) generated by species (e aq  − ,  • H,  • OH) produced during water radiolysis, followed by spontaneous C–N coupling. This method exhibits superior C–N coupling reactivity for most derivatives including electron-donating and electron-withdrawing group and achieves a notable radiation-chemical yield up to 4.6 × 10 −7  mol J −1 . Beyond synthesis, this work may offer mechanistic insights into the related radiation-driven prebiotic pathway, demonstrating that radiolysis of simple mixtures (H 2 O, CO, NH 3 ) can efficiently yield formamide, thereby bridging green chemistry and astrochemistry.

title: Van der Waals-modulated integration strategy unlocks scalable fabrication of high-density organic electronic and optoelectronic devices
abstract: Abstract The advancement of organic electronics and optoelectronics fundamentally depends on the development of high-precision integration technologies. However, existing manufacturing approaches for organic semiconductors, particularly conventional photolithography and stencil lithography, are plagued by an intractable trade-off between integration density and device performance. Here we report a van der Waals (vdW)-modulated integration strategy that circumvents this long-standing bottleneck, enabling concurrent high-density and high-performance organic devices. By tailoring the surface chemistry of an ultrathin Parylene shadow mask, we precisely tune interfacial vdW interactions to orchestrate deterministic mask manipulation and high-fidelity patterning. Consequently, organic field-effect transistor (OFET) arrays achieve a device density of 2,500 transistors cm −2  with an average on-state current density of 1.20 μA μm −1 , among the highest reported for integrated organic electronics. Furthermore, this strategy is extended to monolithic OFET-organic light-emitting diode (OLED) integration, yielding efficient light-emitting transistor arrays. This work establishes an integration route that preserves the organic semiconductor interface while avoiding direct photolithographic contact with the active layer, opening a route toward large-scale, multifunctional organic integrated systems.

title: Intelligent hydrovoltaic actuation with proactive ion regulation during solar desalination
abstract: ABSTRACT Solar desalination offers a sustainable approach to freshwater generation, yet it is fundamentally limited by salt accumulation at evaporation interfaces. While common salt-rejecting strategies can mitigate macroscopic fouling, they fail to achieve real-time monitoring and active management of salts at the metastable stage. Local ion enrichment and associated pre-crystallization processes will degrade efficiency through increased mass-transfer resistance and vaporization enthalpy. Herein, we propose active salt management as a proactive system function and fabricate an intelligent dynamic evaporator (IDE) that integrates  in-situ  sensing, adaptive decision-making, and active regulation. The asymmetrically oxidized PPy/cotton is applied for real-time monitoring of ion concentration evolution within nanochannels via hydrovoltaic actuation. Coupled with deep learning algorithms, IDE dynamically correlates electrical outputs with salt enrichment states, enabling advanced intervention before critical accumulation. Dynamic solar tracking enables uniform interfacial evaporation and ion enrichment, elevating the stability of hydrovoltaic potential signals and the recognition precision (93.8%) of salt enrichment states. Overall, radiation-adaptive and self-cleaning IDE delivers an average daily freshwater production of 12.3 kg m −2  over 100 days. This work shifts salt management from static material design to intelligent adaptive control, providing a scalable framework for robust and sustainable water purification.

title: Symmetry-breaking induced highly active Ni sites simultaneously trigger interfacial hydrogen-bond network reconstruction for efficient CO2 electroreduction in strong acidic media
abstract: Abstract Electrocatalytic CO 2  reduction reaction (CO 2 RR) in strong acidic media (pH ≤ 2) offers many unique advantages compared to alkaline electrolytes, but it still remains some significant challenges including the competing hydrogen evolution reaction (HER), low selectivity and poor stability. Herein, we report that symmetry-breaking induced highly active Ni sites incorporated within ultrathin covalent organic polymer nanosheets (p-Ni 1/2 Pc), can simultaneously trigger interfacial hydrogen-bond network reconstruction for efficient acidic CO 2 RR. Direct visualization via scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) reveals the presence of Ni vacancies and uncoordinated pyrrolic N, which collectively break the local symmetry around Ni sites. This asymmetry not only optimizes the electronic structure of Ni sites to kinetically favor CO 2 RR over HER, but more importantly, it reconfigures the interfacial hydrogen-bond network via uncoordinated pyrrolic N. The reconstructed hydrogen-bond network effectively restricts proton transfer, while symmetry breaking creates a CO 2 -enriched local microenvironment. Consequently, p-Ni 1/2 Pc catalyst exhibits a remarkable 97.5% CO Faraday efficiency (FE) and a maximum 402.9 mA cm −2  partial current density ( j  CO ) in strong acidic electrolytes (pH = 1), while maintaining stable operation for 85 h without salt precipitation. This work highlights the critical role of symmetry-breaking in simultaneously engineering active sites and interfacial microenvironments for robust CO 2 RR in acidic media.

title: TyCHE enables time-resolved lineage tracing of B cells and other heterogeneously-evolving populations
abstract: Abstract Phylogenetic methods for cell lineage tracing have driven significant insights into organismal development, immune responses, and tumor evolution. While many methods estimate trees with branch lengths representing mutations, time-resolved lineage trees with branch lengths representing calendar time are more interpretable and could relate events like cellular migration and differentiation to perturbations like vaccines and drug treatments. However, in many evolving systems such as B cells, tumor lineages, and hypermutating bacterial populations, evolutionary rates often vary dramatically by genomic background or cell state, significantly biasing existing methods that build time trees using either a fixed molecular clock rate or uncorrelated relaxed clock models without a mechanistic model of molecular clock rate variation. We introduce TyCHE (Type-linked Clocks for Heterogeneous Evolution), a Bayesian phylogenetics package that infers time-resolved phylogenies of populations in which the molecular clock rate is linked to discrete states like genomic background or cell type. We demonstrate that TyCHE improves the accuracy of estimated time trees using a new simulation package SimBLE (Simulator of B cell Lineage Evolution). We use TyCHE to infer patterns of memory B cell differentiation during HIV infection, dynamics of recall germinal centers following influenza vaccination, evolution of a glioma tumor lineage, and progression of a bacterial lung infection, showing the applicability of our model to a wide range of systems and across different scales. TyCHE and SimBLE are available as open-source software packages compatible with the BEAST2 and Immcantation ecosystems.

title: Box H/ACA snoRNP regulates development and lipid metabolism in Drosophila melanogaster
abstract: Abstract Lipid homeostasis is essential for organismal function, as its disruption drives various metabolic disorders. Using an unbiased genetic modifier screen in  Drosophila , we identified GAR1, a core component of the box H/ACA small nucleolar ribonucleoprotein complex, as a key regulator of systemic lipid storage. H/ACA small nucleolar ribonucleoprotein dysfunction reduces lipid droplet size in the fat body cells and promotes ectopic fat accumulation in the salivary gland cells. Null mutants of  Gar1 ,  Nop60B , and  Nop10  display severe developmental defects, including reduced body size and larval lethality, whereas  NHP2  null mutants die at the embryonic stage, indicating that this complex is critical for normal development. RNA-seq analysis, followed by RT-PCR validation, revealed that  Gar1  dysfunction perturbs the splicing of  sgg , which encodes a key regulator of insulin signaling. Consistently, knockdown of  Gar1  or  Nop60B  impaired PI3K/AKT signaling, as evidenced by reduced membrane localization of the tGPH, a GFP reporter for PIP 3  in the salivary gland cells. Notably, overexpression of  Akt  suppressed the reduction in lipid storage in  Gar1 -silenced flies. These findings reveal a previously unrecognized link between the H/ACA small nucleolar ribonucleoprotein complex and metabolic processes, such as lipid storage and development, and support the role of this complex as a regulator that may be functionally linked to insulin signaling.

title: Mobile group II intron reverse transcriptases: evolution, biochemical activities, and applications
abstract: Abstract Bacterial mobile group II intron-encoded reverse transcriptases are structurally similar to an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase and may have evolved at the time of transition from an RNA to DNA world. Mobile group II intron reverse transcriptases remain prevalent in bacteria, where they diversified into different subtypes, as well as into chromosomally encoded reverse transcriptases that acquired a variety of cellular functions, including phage defense, RNA spacer acquisition in CRISPR systems, and host cell DNA double-strand break and oxidative DNA damage repair. Mobile group II intron and related reverse transcriptases have remarkably beneficial biochemical properties for biotechnological applications, including high-throughput RNA sequencing. Thermostable Group II Intron-encoded Reverse Transcriptases from bacterial thermophiles, the first of these enzymes shown to have such properties, were used to develop a comprehensive RNA sequencing method that enables simultaneous profiling of virtually all RNA biotypes in human cells, extracellular vesicles, and plasma. In recent studies, Thermostable Group II Intron Reverse Transcriptase sequencing identified a novel large class of short (<300 nt) largely structured Full-Length EXcised linear Intron RNAs in human cells and plasma; enabled parallel analysis of transcriptional and post-transcriptional gene regulation by mapping Thermostable Group II Intron Reverse Transcriptase sequencing reads to genome and transcriptome reference sequences and calculating intron/exon depth ratios; and detected numerous differentially expressed RNAs in inflammatory breast cancer patient tumors and peripheral blood mononuclear cells. Differentially expressed RNAs with high intron/exon depth ratios in inflammatory breast cancer patient tumors and peripheral blood mononuclear cells were correlated with pre-mRNA and intron RNA fragments detected in plasma and included the first potential inflammatory breast cancer biomarkers.

title: Chromatin Assembly Factor 1 is required for normal structure and function of facultative heterochromatin in Neurospora crassa
abstract: Abstract Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 (PRC2) is a conserved epigenetic regulator that represses gene expression through methylation of histone H3 lysine 27 (H3K27me3). In animals, plants, and some fungi, PRC2-directed facultative heterochromatin plays essential roles in development and cellular differentiation. Here, we show that the replication-dependent histone chaperone Chromatin Assembly Factor 1 (CAF-1) is required for proper structure and function of facultative heterochromatin in the model fungus  Neurospora crassa . Loss of CAF-1 causes widespread transcriptional misregulation, particularly within PRC2-repressed regions, and leads to redistribution of H3K27me3, reduced ASH1-dependent H3K36 methylation, and accumulation of chromatin marks associated with active transcription. CAF-1 was not required for repressive histone methylation within constitutive heterochromatin. A double mutant lacking both CAF-1 and PRC2 components displayed a synergistic silencing defect, suggesting these complexes make distinct contributions to facultative heterochromatin. Together, our findings indicate that CAF-1 works in concert with PRC2 to silence transcription within  N. crassa  facultative heterochromatin domains.

title: TMCells: A topic-based probabilistic framework for interpretable metacell construction in single-cell data
abstract: Abstract  Motivation Metacells have emerged as an important analytical strategy for addressing the computational barriers posed by the scale and complexity of large-scale single-cell omics data, while preserving biologically relevant information and improving analytical interpretability. However, existing metacell inference methods usually have limited biological interpretability, rely on deterministic assignments that insufficiently capture continuous state transitions, and may lose potential biological signals due to prior feature selection or dimensionality reduction. Results We propose TMCells, an interpretable metacell identification algorithm based on a probabilistic generative framework. TMCells introduces the concept of topic modeling and uses a Gaussian mixture model as the prior for topic distribution, defining metacells as statistical distribution centers in the latent topic space. By modeling the cell generation process, TMCells enables the simultaneous learning of topic representations and metacell partitions in an end-to-end manner, capturing the continuity and uncertainty in cell state transitions. TMCells effectively identifies high-quality metacells, eliminating technical noise while preserving the original biological heterogeneity, thereby enhancing downstream analyses such as differential expression, rare cell type identification, and trajectory inference. Furthermore, TMCells provides an intuitive interpretation of cellular heterogeneity through latent topics associated with biologically meaningful regulatory programs, offering a generative perspective for dissecting regulatory dynamics during cell-state transitions. Availability and implementation The TMCells along with detailed documentation is freely available at  https://github.com/Jinsl-lab/TMCells  with DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24198840. Supplementary Information Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

title: CiliaHub: an updated gold-standard catalogue of ciliary genes with integrated ciliopathy data
abstract: Abstract  Motivation Cilia are specialised cell-surface extensions central to signalling and sensation, and their dysfunction causes ciliopathies, a clinically heterogeneous group of disorders. Progress in the field has been held back by the lack of an updated and expanded gold-standard gene set. Results We present CiliaHub, an open-access platform centered on an expert-curated catalog of over 2,500 ciliary and cilia-associated genes that significantly expands upon the scope of the SYSCILIA Gold Standard v2. For each gene, CiliaHub brings together subcellular localization, protein-complex information, domain architecture, cross-species orthology, functional-screen results, expression profiles, and ClinVar variants, as well as a dedicated ciliopathy module covering over 70 ciliopathies and over 400 disease genes. The data are queried through a rule-based question-answering assistant (CiliAI), gene-list analysis tools, a phenotype-driven search, and open static-JSON endpoints, supporting screen interpretation, variant prioritization, and ciliopathy research from a single point of access. Availability CiliaHub is freely available at  https://ciliahub.org  without registration. Source code is available on  https://github.com/theCiliaHub/theCiliaHub.github.io  and archived at Zenodo version 3 (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23257334). All figures and counts in this manuscript refer to CiliaHub release v9.2 (frozen October 2026). The versions of every external data source used in that release are listed in Supplementary Table S6Supplementary Table S6, and the release version, freeze date and data file are stated at  https://ciliahub.org/about.html . Supplementary information Supplementary data are available at Zenodo online and static-JSON API endpoints ( https://ciliahub.org/api.html ).

title: TAFFISH: shell-native command-level reproducibility for bioinformatics
abstract: Abstract  Summary Bioinformatics analyses often rely on shell commands and small shell scripts whose executable context is difficult to preserve, inspect and reuse. TAFFISH addresses this gap by packaging command-line tool calls and lightweight shell flows as installable, versioned and inspectable executable units. Through a curated public Hub, TAFFISH indexes command interfaces, execution backends, platform constraints, release metadata and smoke-test/validation records. Together, these components provide a command-level reproducibility layer that works directly in ordinary shells and can also be invoked from existing workflow systems. Availability and Implementation TAFFISH is implemented in Common Lisp and released under Apache-2.0. TAFFISH version 0.10.1, together with the source code, documentation and public Hub resources, is available at  https://github.com/taffish/taffish ,  https://taffish.com ,  https://taffish.github.io  and  https://github.com/taffish/ . The submitted software release, frozen Hub snapshot, test data, command logs, checksums and reproducibility package are archived at  https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21054185 . The authors will maintain the software and public resources for at least two years after publication. Supplementary information Supplementary data are available at  Bioinformatics  online.

abstract: Short Summary: LHP1/PCR1 provides a mechanistic lens for examining how Polycomb memory coexists with transcriptional plasticity, a central tension in chromatin biology. We synthesize evidence linking LHP1 to replication-coupled chromatin restoration, 3D genome organization, and lncRNA-mediated chromatin switching, and propose forward-looking models to address this central challenge. Across crops and woody perennials, recurrent LHP1-associated regulatory themes appear redeployed in lineage-specific contexts.

title: Paleogenomics illuminates mobility and changing lifeways in Chalcolithic Anatolia
abstract: Contrary to the stark decline in the archaeological records in Chalcolithic Anatolia (c. 6000–3000 BCE), paleogenomics reveals that populations grew and/or became more mobile, suggesting changing lifeways. Genetic admixture with populations from eastern regions continued throughout this period, and early evidence of movement between Anatolia and the Eurasian Steppe appeared.

abstract: In African lungfish, an evolutionarily repurposed pore-forming toxin, Protop-CrTX-A, switches its source of secretion from goblet cells to infiltrating granulocytes during estivation, driving epithelial remodeling associated with adaptation to terrestrial life.

title: Learning gene co-regulation across cells with Multicellular Transformer
abstract: Understanding how genes coordinate across cells is central to explaining tissue function and disease, yet most existing models still take a single cell as input and therefore emphasize cell-intrinsic regulation. We present the Multicellular Transformer (MCT), a foundation model built around a different assumption: cells function together within tissues, so the appropriate unit of input is not one cell in isolation but a set of cells from the same sample. By jointly modeling multiple cells, MCT learns context-aware gene embeddings that capture gene-gene interactions across the tissue environment. Trained on a large set of tissue samples (>4200) across more than 30 tissue types, MCT recovers ligand-receptor interactions, infers cross-cell signaling programs, and reveals spatial co-localization patterns directly from scRNA-seq data. Its contextual embeddings identify disease-specific rewiring of gene neighborhoods in systemic lupus erythematosus and COVID-19 and predict population-level perturbation effects in cancer without additional training. By linking gene-level regulation to tissue-scale organization, MCT provides a scalable framework for modeling multicellular biology and enables in silico discovery of therapeutic targets and tissue-specific dependencies.

title: Marker direction and donor structure alter genetic cell-stateprioritization in endometriosis: convergent evidence from single-cell chromatin
abstract: Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) identify regions of the genome linked to disease, but they do not tell us which cells are involved. Researchers often address that question by testing marker genes from single-cell atlases. We asked how much the answer changes when those markers are defined differently. Reconstructing a published endometriosis analysis, we found that selecting genes with large fold changes in either direction prioritized venous endothelium, whereas selecting up-regulated genes prioritized decidual stroma (the latter was not significant after within-family false-discovery correction). A calibrated benchmark, six-trait control panel, and donor-level checks showed why neither rule can be trusted on its own. In an independent RNA atlas, stromal programs were repeatedly prioritized, although closely related perivascular states remained plausible. We then examined an independent molecular layer: chromatin accessibility in 36,073 nuclei from 12 endometrial biopsies. The initially specified analysis found enrichment of endometriosis heritability in stromal accessible chromatin (z = 4.11, one-sided p = 2 x 10^-5). In a later, more stringent joint model with baselineLD v2.2, the stromal coefficient remained positive (z = 3.83, p = 6.47 x 10^-5) and exceeded the epithelial coefficient (z = 3.68, p = 1.18 x 10^-4). Both effects remained nominally significant when each biopsy was excluded in turn (12/12 analyses). The association was also seen for leiomyoma, and the endometriosis GWAS share participants. Together, these findings support a broad stromal regulatory context for part of inherited endometriosis risk, but do not establish a unique causal cell state or a lesion cell of origin.

title: Genomic tessellations
abstract: Periodicity is ubiquitous in genomic data. Assembled sequences are dense with homopolymers, microsatellites, and large satellite arrays, which contribute to phenotype, variation, and disease. Third-generation sequencing technologies, such as Oxford Nanopore (ONT) and PacBio HiFi, has enabled longer and increasingly accurate reads, but have brought with them systematic error biases in repetitive regions, where insertions and deletions can distort array lengths and mimic or obscure biological variation. This periodicity is not benign: local repetitiveness makes sequence alignment ambiguous and genome assembly error-prone. In sequence analysis, these two manifestations of periodicity are simultaneously at play, each compounding the challenges of the other; a unified representation of repetitive and non-repetitive sequence is necessary to account for their combined effects consistently. We propose a paradigm under which (either repetitive and non-repetitive) DNA is split into its identity (its irreducible components) and its geometry (how its components are realized). A genomic tessellation {tau} is a canonical factorization of any sequence S of length n over the DNA alphabet into a sequence of tiles partitioning S, where each t in {tau}S is described as a quasi-periodic run of a canonical unit identity ut with geometry consisting of span st, phase {varphi}t, and a set of exceptions Xt. We show that, for a prescribed error bound k [≥] 1 and fixed maximum unit length P, S can be tessellated in O(n) time such that every tile has a unique identity whose periodic expansion differs from the tiled sequence by at most k edits, and that tiles sharing an identity are related by a bounded number of geometric adjustments. We introduce the tessellated Burrows-Wheeler transform (tBWT), which indexes {tau}S by concatenating, over all tiles in order, the identity ut of each tile. For a tessellated query q of m tiles, the tBWT counts the repeat-agnostic occurrences of q in O(m) time, and for sampling interval r locates its h occurrences in {tau}S in O(m + hr) time. We demonstrate that tessellations avoid the well-known speed-accuracy tradeoff and outperform state-of-the-art long-read mappers in repeat-dense regions in both speed and accuracy. On a 20x simulated set of both ONT and HiFi reads on the HG002 maternal X chromosome with synthetically-expanded repeat arrays, locating and chaining exact tile identity matches obtained from the tBWT is up to 57x and 83x faster, respectively, than the state-of-the-art mappers minimap2 and Winnowmap2, with comparable accuracy. Furthermore, by abstracting away differences in geometry, tessellations of a set of input sequences onto itself (an autotessellation) reveals homology otherwise obscured by array-length variation and local sequence divergence. A geometry-only polishing of an an ONT-only assembly of the HG002 maternal X chromosome with [~]50x PacBio HiFi reads improves assembly QV from 45.4 to 60.6 in under a minute using less than 10GB of memory. Tessellated-read evidence over the autotessellation of this assembly organizes 167 mitochondrial contigs totaling [~]4 Mbp into a single family with a [~]16.5kbp representative, which aligns to the HG002 Q100 mitochondrial genome with 100% identity. Genomic tessellations provide a canonical representation of repetitive and non-repetitive DNA and enable efficient sequence analyses while preserving homology.

title: Spectrast: a multiscale spatial statistics toolkit for single-cell spatial transcriptomics
abstract: Spatial transcriptomics resolves gene expression in physical space, but the spatial statistics typically used to quantify spatial organization scale poorly to imaging-based datasets with hundreds-of-thousands of cells and thousands of genes. We recast the standard spatial-autocorrelation statistics as convolutions on a rasterized representation of the gene expression matrix and evaluate them with the fast Fourier transform. Measuring spatial statistics across multiple length scales becomes tractable for every gene using this approach, which extends naturally to differential reorganization testing between two tissue conditions.

title: GRASER: haplotype assignment of graph-aligned short reads
abstract: Existing read phasing tools operate on reads aligned to a linear reference, where reference bias reduces the information available for haplotype inference and read assignment. Pangenome graphs reduce reference bias, but reads falling within non-reference sequence cannot be surjected to a linear reference, so phasing after surjection reintroduces that bias. Here we present GRASER, which phases graph-aligned short reads against haplotype paths inferred for each individual, using established graph genotyping and statistical phasing to build those paths. GRASER phase uses edges unique to one haplotype path as evidence, so reads are phased directly from graph alignments without conversion to a linear reference. Against true parental haplotype paths, GRASER assigned 22.6 to 24.5% of simulated fragments to a haplotype, and more than 96% of those were placed on the correct haplotype. Inferred haplotype paths reduced the assignment rate by about 4 percentage points. GRASER assigned more fragments than a WhatsHap-based linear-reference workflow in every configuration tested. Applied to whole-genome bisulfite sequencing, GRASER recovered allele-specific methylation at imprinted loci and measured haplotype-resolved methylation within a structural variant.

title: Evaluating Language Models as Orchestrators in a Tool-First Biomedical Discovery Platform
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly orchestrate agentic biomedical discovery systems, but cloud deployment raises concerns about inference cost, data privacy, and governance. Small language models (SLMs) that run on-premises are an alternative, provided they orchestrate scientific tools about as well as larger models. We built a tool-first, multi-agent system for scientific discovery in which an orchestrator coordinates six specialized tool systems: differential expression, literature retrieval, pathway enrichment, network-based gene prioritization and knowledge-graph analysis, perturbation signature matching, and structural/druggability assessment. In a tool-first design, specialized tools supply the domain knowledge and computation, so the model's main task is coordination, e.g. choosing tools, passing the right parameters, calling them in the right order, and carrying results across turns. With the tools, prompts, workflow, and benchmark held constant, we compared three orchestrators, Gemma 4 (26B, open-weight and locally deployable), Gemini 2.5 Flash, and Claude Sonnet 5. Evaluation used a custom benchmark of 104 single-turn and multi-turn tests, an LLM-as-judge protocol (groundedness and evidence validity), tool-use accuracy and efficiency metrics, and blind expert review. On single-turn tasks, the three models performed comparably, and reviewers did not rate the SLM below the larger models. In multi-turn tasks, Claude Sonnet 5 showed marginally higher evidence validity, Gemma 4 was weakest when parameters had to be assembled across turns, and all three models struggled with tool ordering on memory-dependent tasks. These differences were illustrated with case studies. Finally, we propose strategies to help SLMs address the multi-turn limitations and support cost- and privacy-aware deployment.

title: Spatial causal discovery reveals novel mechanisms of cellular senescence in human liver
abstract: The complex network of mechanisms that surround cellular senescence, such as its precise causes and effects, are not entirely understood at present. Senescence occurs when a cell permanently ceases dividing, halts apoptosis, stops performing its normal functions, and begins secreting chemicals that can induce other cells in its environment to also become senescent. Senescent cells are present in both healthy and unhealthy tissue, but their abundance is positively correlated with disease and age. A better understanding of senescence could lead to healthier aging, improved recovery from chemotherapy, or increased lifespan. This study used novel machine learning algorithms - with guaranteed properties of correctness under broad assumptions - to investigate senescence in human liver tissue by analyzing Visium spatial transcriptomics data. This produced data-driven models of the causes and effects of senescence, both locally and from nearby tissue. This report includes an assessment of whether the data meet key requirements for causal analysis, the transcripts identified by causal analyses as causes and effects of senescence marker genes, and pathway analyses of those gene sets.

title: One Stop MS Shop (OSMSS): statistical analysis and interpretation of quantitative proteomics data for non-coders
abstract: Open-source statistical methods for proteomic differential abundance analysis are well established. Normalization, missing-value handling, and the statistical model must suit the experimental design and change how proteins are called. Together with the frequent need for data reformatting, coding and bioinformatics expertise, these elements limit the bench scientist's analysis of datasets. Here, we present One Stop MS Shop (OSMSS), a no-code R Shiny application that parses Proteome Discoverer, MaxQuant, FragPipe, DIA-NN or Spectronaut search results for user-driven interactive exploration through transformation and differential analysis. Upon import, OSMSS records the experimental design through user questions, selects the analysis workflow, identifies normalization requirements, runs established statistical methods, and records every analytical step in a case-specific methods text. OSMSS supports label-free data-dependent and data-independent acquisition (DDA, DIA) and tandem mass tag (TMT) group comparisons, affinity-purification comparisons, and DIA and TMT phosphosite analyses. OSMSS runs on local devices or servers and provides volcano plots, heatmaps, trend analysis, kinase prediction, pathway enrichment and kinase activity inference. In seven benchmarks, OSMSS performed comparably to matched reference workflows. OSMSS lets bench scientists apply established statistical models and associated tools transparently and without coding, enabling a more informed analysis of their data.

title: ProtCOVER: Family-Aware Conformal Prediction for Variant Effect Predictors on Unseen Protein Families
abstract: Protein language models and related variant effect predictors (VEPs) increasingly classify missense variants in proteins evolutionarily distant from those used for calibration. Split conformal prediction over variants is valid for its own target, a random variant dominated by well-studied families, but deployment needs coverage for a variant of a new family. On ProteinGym clinical substitutions with five zero-shot predictors, Mondrian conformal comes within 0.005 of that target for four predictors, yet family-weighted pathogenic coverage is only 0.823-0.873 at a 0.90 target for all five, without any shift. We present ProtCOVER, a conformal procedure that treats homology families, rather than individual variants, as the exchangeable unit. ProtCOVER (i) calibrates at the family level over label-free homology clusters, giving marginal coverage for a new family under family exchangeability; (ii) adapts to descriptor shift by calibrating conditionally on an estimated density ratio of label-free descriptors (sequence similarity, alignment depth and embedding distance; a variant reweights by the ratio instead), with finite-sample family-weighted coverage, valid as computed, whenever the true ratio is a nonnegative affine function of the estimate; and (iii) can abstain at low effective calibration support, which proved no better than random abstention. Under a shift of its descriptors, ProtCOVER's mean worse-class shortfall below the target is 0.000, against 0.010 for group-weighted and 0.029 for hierarchical conformal prediction, with larger sets (about equal at matched coverage); on orphan families and held-out embedding regions it matches group weighting (0.002 against 0.003). In evaluations following pre-registered protocols, every shift-aware method met the target on new ClinVar variants of benchmark proteins, which ESM-1b separated better; on 12,225 proteins outside the benchmark, every method fell short for pathogenic variants with either of two predictors, ProtCOVER and a variant conditioned on the descriptors the least, within the 0.01 margin of group weighting.

title: ProtFlap: Structure-based Deep Learning Prediction of Protein Flexibility from Atomic Energy Networks
abstract: Protein flexibility is a key determinant of molecular recognition, catalysis, and regulation, yet remains difficult to characterise at scale. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations provide detailed descriptions of time-dependent dynamics but are computationally expensive. Although recent AI-based structure prediction methods have substantially improved access to high-quality static protein structures, they inherently lack information regarding the dynamic fluctuations essential for functional understanding. There is therefore a need for scalable, structure-based computational approaches that can infer intrinsic protein flexibility without explicit dynamical sampling. We present ProtFlap, a graph neural network framework for predicting relative residue-level flexibility directly from static protein structures. ProtFlap represents proteins as residue interaction graphs and integrates empirical atomic energy features extracted from a single energy-minimised snapshot with structural and sequence-derived descriptors. Central to our approach is the hypothesis that the local atomic energy network encoded in a frozen protein structure contains sufficient information to estimate structural flexibility. Trained using atomic mobility labels, quantified via normalised root-mean-square fluctuation (RMSF) derived from short MD simulations, ProtFlap achieves robust and accurate flexibility prediction across diverse protein domains. Feature attribution analysis reveals that van der Waals-related energy terms are the dominant contributors to the prediction.

title: Thermodynamically Constrained Encoding Improves Reliability in DNA Data Storage
abstract: Synthetic DNA has emerged as a promising storage medium thanks to its exceptional information density and long-term stability. However, sequence-dependent biochemical properties introduced during the encoding process can significantly affect downstream molecular processing and data recovery. Among these properties, the thermodynamic stability of DNA sequences, commonly quantified by the Folding Gibbs free energy ($Delta$G), can influence amplification efficiency, sequencing coverage, and ultimately decoding performance. In this work, we experimentally investigate the impact of $Delta$G constraints applied during the encoding stage on DNA data recovery. We compare the reference JPEG DNA, the future image coding standard on DNA, with a $Delta$G-constrained variant using the same image encoded into synthetic DNA oligonucleotides. Both configurations were synthesized, amplified, sequenced, and decoded under identical experimental conditions. We analyze the relationship between predicted thermodynamic stability, sequencing coverage, and decoding performance to quantify the influence of sequence thermodynamics on the recovery of encoded information. Our results demonstrate that incorporating $Delta G$ constraints during encoding substantially reduces the proportion of sequences with highly negative predicted $Delta G$ values and improves sequencing coverage homogeneity, decreases the number of underrepresented oligonucleotides and dropouts, and consistently reduces the sequencing coverage required for successful decoding across three different synthesis providers, thereby reducing sequencing time. These findings provide experimental evidence that thermodynamic sequence optimization represents an effective design strategy for improving the robustness and efficiency of DNA data storage systems.

title: Somatic mutation probabilities learned from the DNA sequence
abstract: Somatic mutations distribute heterogeneously over genomes, dependent on immediate sequence context, function, and non-genetic factors. Mutations present the foundation for somatic genome evolution towards age-related diseases. Here, we present EAGLE-MUT, a group of DNA language models trained on sparse single base substitution data from esophageal adenocarcinoma (EAC) and melanoma (MELA) samples. In both cancer types, predicted mutation probabilities vary across several orders of magnitude, depending on sequence context. For example, T>G hotspots in EAC localize to A/T-rich ~200 base pair DNA motifs, associated with nucleosome positioning. Coldspots localize to G/C-rich DNA, nucleosome linker DNA, CTCF binding sites, potential origins of replication, and intron-exon boundaries with a transcription strand bias. Fine-tuning EAGLE-MUT for individual patient samples leads to varying mutation distributions relative to genome elements and potential cancer driver mutations. EAGLE-MUT provides new links between DNA sequence, genome function, and stability in individual samples, a foundation for understanding somatic genome evolution, and more personalized strategies for risk-assessment, prevention, and treatment.

title: A conserved matrix-centred core links fibrosis across human organs and mouse models
abstract: Fibrosis develops in many organs through different initiating injuries, yet repeatedly engages inflammation, stromal activation and extracellular-matrix remodelling. Whether these recurring features represent a conserved disease programme, and whether commonly used mouse models reproduce it, remain unresolved. We developed ScarX, an R/Shiny workflow that analyses organ-resolved bulk RNA sequencing, identifies directional overlap across tissues, and ranks human-mouse conserved signals while retaining organ-restricted results. Public RNA-sequencing datasets representing fibrotic or fibrosis-associated disease in human heart, kidney, liver and lung were compared with matched mouse injury models. Differential expression was estimated independently within each organ using DESeq2, followed by cross-organ intersection, functional enrichment, matched-organ effect-profile comparison and a human-first conserved modulation (HCM) score that gives greatest weight to the breadth and magnitude of human disease change, adds support for same-direction mouse effects and penalises discordance. In human disease, 202 genes increased and 35 decreased in the same direction across all four organs. Mouse models contained 409 pan-organ increases and 46 decreases. After gene-symbol harmonisation, 25 gene-direction signatures were conserved across all four organs in both species. These included AEBP1, CDH11, COL1A1, COL1A2, COL3A1, COL5A2, COL6A2, EFEMP2, EMILIN1, LOXL1, LOXL2, TGFB2 and VIM. Matched human-mouse effect profiles varied considerably: Spearman rho was 0.42 for kidney, 0.31 for heart, 0.16 for liver and -0.06 for lung. Despite this uneven gene-level fidelity, 62 same-direction pathways were shared across species, led by extracellular-matrix organisation, collagen fibril organisation, cell-substrate adhesion, wound healing and ECM-receptor interaction. The HCM ranking concentrated structural matrix genes near the top but also identified cell-surface, secreted and regulatory candidates. Among the top 500 candidates, 376 carried at least one local tractability annotation. ScarX therefore separates a compact conserved matrix-remodelling core from a much larger organ- and species-dependent response. The results provide a transparent starting point for target and biomarker selection, while also showing why expression conservation alone cannot establish therapeutic dependence.

title: Know Thy Neighbour: Benchmarking Protein Language Model Embedding-Based Annotation Reveals Anisotropy Substantially Impacts Retrieval
abstract: Functional annotation using protein language models (`pLMs') usually proceeds by transferring the function of a query's nearest neighbour in a reference database. A major drawback is that embedding-based annotation transfer has no null model, i.e. no accepted way to set a cosine-similarity threshold to control false positives. This contrasts with traditional bioinformatics methods, including sequence- and structure-based alignment tools, which rank hits with E-values derived from explicit null models. Here, we benchmark final-layer, mean-pooled embeddings from twelve models against MMseqs2 and Foldseek for remote-homology retrieval on curated datasets based on Swiss-Prot and SCOPe, fixing per-model thresholds at a 1% false-positive rate and probing the score with a ladder of synthetic decoys. On Swiss-Prot, pLMs without retrieval training recover at most 15% of remote homologs at this operating point, against 85% for MMseqs2, and for the ESM-2 and ESM-C families shuffled decoys have higher cosine similarities to their nearest database hits than real remote homologs do. These two pLM families exhibit extreme anisotropy, using fewer than 15 effective dimensions out of 640-2560, and low effective dimensionality is strongly associated with poor performance across models. Applying ZCA whitening, fit on the reference database, to the embeddings sharply raises threshold-free Top-1 superfamily retrieval, e.g. for ESM-2 650M from 59% to 88% on SCOPe, and generally improves remote homology sensitivity at a fixed false-positive rate. As correcting embedding anisotropy requires only the reference database and is compute cheap, it should be considered and tested for any pLM embedding-based annotation task.

title: Bounded by compartment, composition and time: efferocytic transcriptional readouts after ischaemic stroke
abstract: Background. Efferocytosis after ischaemic stroke is usually inferred from bulk tissue transcripts and condensed into one score, which cannot separate a tissue containing more phagocytes from one whose phagocytes are more active; the gene sets behind such scores also mix clearance machinery with the inflammatory output that follows. Methods. We built a decoupled framework scoring apoptotic demand (DEMAND), clearance machinery (CAPACITY), immunogenic output (OUTCOME) and a brake. We assembled 38 datasets across brain, blood, PBMC and sorted parenchyma, admitted a score only where at least 75% of a program's genes were detected, and tested every claim against expression-matched nulls, lineage proxies and cell-level constraints. Because clearance consumes ATP, supply and demand were scored on one scale under one decision rule. Results. After adjustment for five leukocyte lineages the CAPACITY difference survived in one of three cohorts (+0.473, 95% CI +0.350 to +0.588), fell to +0.014 in the second and was unidentifiable in the third; the unadjusted differences (+0.613 and +0.374) exceeded expression- and detection-matched nulls, so the signal is real, but its compositional share differs by cohort. In matched PBMCs the point estimate was negative and not distinguishable from zero. In the only sorted human parenchyma series, non-microglial myeloid cells made up 0.371 of CD45-positive cells against 0.199 in controls, while every microglial layer fell below its expression-matched floor: it moves the composition boundary without testing capacity. In rodent brain it rose with injury: day 3 in microglia, day 7 in macrophages. Energy supply cleared both gates in eleven of eighteen contrasts and demand in eight, concentrated in entering cells (oxidative phosphorylation +1.512 in infiltrating macrophages at day 3). The two scores ranked samples almost identically ({rho} 0.59 to 0.95), and the one significant gap vanished under the same adjustment. Conclusions. Efferocytic transcripts are a measurement bounded by compartment, composition and time, not a flux assay or a biomarker. Energy supply rises with the work of clearance in the cells that carry it, and can rise in cells that do not engulf, but the two scores move closely enough that no transcript design can show one
