title: DeepRNAi: Predicting on- and off-target siRNA activity and establishing a benchmark
abstract: Small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) silence target genes through RISC-mediated hybridization and cleavage, but can silence unintended transcripts and cause toxicity or complicate regulatory approval. In drug development, empirical assessment by qPCR and RNA-seq is slow, forces early candidate prioritization, and is limited by available species- and genome-appropriate cell models. While extensive empirical screening remains standard practice, there is a significant opportunity for modern AI methods to change this paradigm. We introduce DeepRNAi, a deep learning model that accurately predicts on- and off-target knockdown from siRNA and mRNA sequence. Trained on 16 million siRNA-transcript pairs from 2,031 siRNAs designed to interrogate known siRNA failure modes, and incorporating transcript context from biological foundation models, DeepRNAi is the first in silico method that approaches experimental accuracy. It generalizes across cell models, transcripts, genomes and species, and in a small study distinguishes approved therapeutics from hepatotoxic candidates. The value of DeepRNAi for prioritizing better candidates up front is supported by a genome-wide survey of 24.4 million siRNAs targeting 7,946 genes, which indicates that 90.1% of the 100 most potent siRNAs have at least some off-target concerns. To support the community, we are publishing a training and benchmark dataset containing 1.84 million siRNA-transcript pairs from 240 siRNAs.

title: Systematic benchmarks reveal DNA polymerase combinations for high-quality genome assembly
abstract: Background: A fundamental challenge in biodiversity genomics is generating long-read sequencing data and high-quality genome assemblies from samples lacking gold-standard flash-frozen tissue, including ethanol-preserved specimens, minimally invasive biopsies, and small-bodied organisms. Amplification-based library preparation enables long-read sequencing of such samples, but assembly quality critically depends on the polymerase used for amplification. Results: We present a systematic benchmark of eleven long-range DNA polymerases for PacBio HiFi sequencing and genome assembly across three taxonomically diverse species: a springtail, a sea slug, and a bat. We show that polymerase choice substantially affects assembly contiguity and gene completeness, primarily caused by polymerase-intrinsic GC-dependent amplification bias and read coverage heterogeneity. Five polymerases consistently produced assemblies with comparatively high contiguity and completeness, with some enzymes outperforming the polymerase currently used in the PacBio Ampli-Fi protocol. Importantly, combining reads amplified with different polymerases frequently resulted in superior assemblies, because polymerases complement each other by covering regions where others drop out. Combining reads amplified with different polymerases, we generated haplotype-resolved assemblies of the ~1 Gb giant springtail and ~2 Gb bat genome and improved the sea slug reference genome. Using the human GIAB benchmark, we further show that optimized amplification strategies improve variant-calling accuracy, highlighting their utility in medical and clinical research. To facilitate polymerase benchmarking across additional taxa, we provide the polymeval pipeline (https://github.com/casparbein/polymeval), which automates the computational workflow. Conclusion: Our study demonstrates that optimized amplification-based HiFi sequencing generates assemblies with >1 Mb contig N50 and >90% gene completeness, providing a toolkit to produce long-read genome assemblies from challenging samples.

title: Chromatin accessibility predictions reveal lineage-structured effects of noncoding variants across hematopoiesis
abstract: Background. Noncoding variants account for over 90% of genome-wide association study (GWAS) findings, but their mechanisms are often unclear. Sequence-to-function models provide one approach to variant interpretation by predicting the effects of genetic variation on molecular phenotypes. ChromBPNet predicts variant effects on chromatin accessibility, but how these predictions are organized across differentiation hierarchies and relate to orthogonal predictions remains unclear. Results. We trained ChromBPNet models for 17 hematopoietic cell types and scored 302,830 variants. Of 242,307 variants accessible in at least one cell type, 5.6% were predicted to alter chromatin accessibility. Variants active in more cell types had larger predicted effects. Predicted effects also reflected hematopoietic lineage structure, with sharing declining with lineage distance while effect direction was preserved in 99.6% of parent-child comparisons. ChromBPNet predictions agreed with GWAS fine-mapping but largely identified distinct variants. Fine-mapping-only variants were enriched for coding and transcript-associated variation, whereas ChromBPNet-only variants were enriched for regulatory elements, accessible chromatin, and trait-relevant activity. In K562 CRISPRi datasets, predicted accessibility gain showed limited association with target-gene validation. Regulatory elements containing CTCF motifs were less likely to have validated target genes, consistent with a role in chromatin organization rather than gene activation. Conclusions. ChromBPNet and fine-mapping provide complementary information about variant function. Predicted accessibility effects identify the cell types in which noncoding variants are likely to act and capture relationships across the hematopoietic hierarchy, but provide limited information about the genes they regulate. All predictions are available at: https://bloodnnet.ccbr.utoronto.ca/.

title: An oxidative mutational signature in normal tissues of a monoallelic  MUTYH  carrier
abstract: Biallelic loss of MUTYH causes MUTYH-associated polyposis (OMIM: 608456), characterized by the oxidative base-excision-repair mutational signature SBS18, but whether the roughly 1 in 100 individuals who carry a single pathogenic MUTYH allele acquire a mutational phenotype in normal tissue is unknown. Analysis of multi-tissue sequencing of 25 donors from the Somatic Mosaicism across Human Tissues (SMaHT) Network identified three heterozygous carriers of MUTYH p.Gly396Asp. One carrier showed SBS18 across multiple normal tissues, ranking first of 25 donors with three independent methods and remaining significant after adjustment for tissue, without a somatic, epigenetic or transcriptional second hit at the MUTYH locus. A single hypomorphic MUTYH allele can therefore leave a measurable oxidative mutational mark in healthy tissues, supporting tissue-level mutational readouts as an approach to cancer risk stratification within this common carrier state.

title: Empirical optimization of dCas12a-based CRISPRi/a for pooled screening in Yarrowia lipolytica
abstract: Yarrowia lipolytica is an important host for biotechnology and metabolic engineering, valued for its ability to accumulate lipids and produce a wide range of industrially relevant compounds. This creates a growing need for genome-scale tools that can accelerate the identification of genes underlying complex phenotypes. Although Cas9-based CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) and activation (CRISPRa) tools are well established in Y. lipolytica, Cas12a offers a complementary platform with a T-rich PAM that can expand access to promoter regions and facilitate multiplexed regulation. Despite these advantages, Cas12a-based CRISPRi/a remains comparatively underdeveloped in Y. lipolytica, particularly for large-scale functional screening. Here, we establish and systematically benchmark dCas12a-based CRISPRi/a platforms for pooled screening in Y. lipolytica. We first compared two widely used effectors, dLbCas12a and denAsCas12a, across single-gene assays and a pooled CRISPRi library targeting nine essential or conditionally essential genes with 752 crRNAs. Both orthologs supported robust transcriptional repression, but their relative performance was crRNA- and condition-dependent, with dLbCas12a showing more consistent and stronger late-stage depletion across targets. dLbCas12a also enabled enrichment-based CRISPRi and CRISPRa screens, recovering expected drug-resistance and lipid-associated phenotypes. The broad design of the pooled library further enabled identification of crRNA features associated with CRISPRi efficacy. Highly active crRNAs were enriched near transcription start sites, with an effective targeting interval extending from approximately -260 to +50 bp. Intermediate GC content was associated with higher efficacy, while PAM identity showed a weaker but consistent effect, with TTTA and TTTT PAMs linked to stronger depletion than TTTC and TTTG PAMs. Spacer length showed the strongest association with CRISPRi efficacy, with 18-nt crRNAs consistently outperforming matched longer 20-, 23-, and 25-nt variants. Finally, we tested dHyperLbCas12a, an engineered LbCas12a variant with enhanced activity, and found that it produced substantially stronger CRISPRi and CRISPRa phenotypes than dLbCas12a. Together, these results establish Cas12a as a versatile platform for pooled CRISPRi/a screens in Y. lipolytica, identify practical crRNA prioritization rules for improved library performance, and highlight dHyperLbCas12a as a promising effector for future large-scale gain- and loss-of-function screens.

title: Single-cell transfer RNA sequencing reveals principles of translational regulation
abstract: Transfer RNAs (tRNAs) decode genetic instructions from messenger RNA (mRNA) into protein, yet their abundance and regulation across cell states remain largely undefined, as multimodal measures of cellular tRNAs have remained elusive. Here, we develop a massively parallel assay for single-cell translatome and RNA sequencing (sctRNA-seq), which profiles transcriptome-wide mRNA and tRNA abundance simultaneously and chart the tRNA composition of 364,841 cells. Through multimodal perturbation screening of protein-coding genes and tRNA loci, we reveal dynamics across the mRNA and tRNA transcriptomes, delineating distinct tRNA-linked modules regulated by metabolic and Pol III-mediated transcription. Further, we uncover a close correspondence between codon demand and tRNA-mediated anticodon composition during hematopoietic multilineage commitment and differentiation. Tri-modal profiling of mRNA, tRNA, and proteins from primary human T cells reveals tRNA-mediated regulation that partially explains the discordance between mRNA and protein levels, particularly for selenoproteins and transcription factors. Finally, we uncover a stress-responsive tRNA module defined by gene-internal promoter sequences. Together, our analyses resolve tRNAs as a previously undefined layer of translational control underlying cellular identity and cell-state transitions.

title: Elucidating Bat SuperImmunity: Insights from the Bent-Wing Bat Genome Assembly and Multi-Omics Analysis
abstract: Bats have evolved a range of unique adaptations, including powered flight, echolocation, and exceptional longevity. They have also attracted considerable scientific attention, particularly since the COVID-19 pandemic, due to their association with a broad diversity of viruses and their potential role in zoonotic transmission and emerging infectious diseases. Despite hosting numerous viruses, bats often exhibit limited clinical manifestations of infection, suggesting the evolution of distinctive mechanisms of immune regulation and tolerance. Understanding the molecular basis of these mechanisms has become a major focus of current research, with genome-wide analyses providing important insights into the genetic adaptations underlying bat immunity. Nevertheless, the regulatory complexity of bat genomes, particularly the contribution of non-coding RNAs and post-transcriptional RNA editing, remains comparatively underexplored. Here, we present an integrated multi-omic framework for the common bent-wing bat (Miniopterus schreibersii), combining a contiguous chromosome-scale genome assembly with multi-tissue transcriptomic profiling, long non-coding RNA (lncRNA) identification and synteny analysis, endogenous viral elements (EVE) mapping, and same-individual RNA editomic analyses. This study provides a comprehensive resource for investigating genome organization, transcriptional regulation, evolutionary relationships, and post-transcriptional modifications in this species. In particular, it offers an opportunity to explore the potential contribution of non-coding regulatory elements and RNA editing to the molecular mechanisms underlying viral interactions and immune regulation in bats. Collectively, these resources provide a valuable foundation for advancing our understanding of bat genome evolution and the regulatory mechanisms potentially associated with their distinctive responses to viral infections.

title: A chromosome-level genome assembly of northern dragonhead, Dracocephalum ruyschiana L., 1753
abstract: We present a chromosome-level genome assembly for the vascular plant northern dragonhead, Dracocephalum ruyschiana. The assembly comprises two pseudo-haplotypes, hap1 and hap2, of 661 Mb and 681 Mb, with 93.6% and 92.5%, respectively, scaffolded into seven chromosomes each - in line with the known karyotype. Assembly quality was high, with conserved single-copy ortholog completeness scores of 97.9% and 97.8%, combined k-mer completeness of 98.1%, and 38,141 and 38,617 annotated protein-coding genes for hap1 and hap2, respectively. This assembly provides a high-quality genomic resource for future research and conservation of northern dragonhead, as well as the endangered northern dragonhead sap beetle, which depends on the plant for reproduction and whose genome assembly is described in a complementary genome note.

title: MicroDUET: a dual-headed genomic foundation model for pathogen surveillance
abstract: Pathogen genomic surveillance works from raw reads, assembled genomes and alignments, representations that are slow and costly to compare at scale. Compact embeddings from genomic language models offer an alternative, but surveillance requires resolving both evolutionary ancestry (phylogeny) and phenotypic capability (function) - which need not co-vary. Here we present MicroDUET, which adapts a 26.6-million-parameter ProkBERT backbone with two 3.5-million-parameter adapter heads: a phylogeny head trained contrastively on genome windows from the same microbes, and a function head trained to identify genes across taxa. On held-out retrieval benchmarks, the phylogeny head returned the correct species for 80.3% and 66.6% of cellular and viral queries, and the function head the correct gene family for 97.3% and 97.2%, reaching 74.4% accuracy on an independent antimicrobial resistance-class benchmark. Across all three benchmarks MicroDUET outranked 17 other genomic encoders. Without training on lineage, clade or drug-susceptibility tasks, MicroDUET identified Mycobacterium tuberculosis and mpox virus lineages and clades (0.965, 0.975 accuracy), discriminated rifampicin resistance without lineage adjustment (AUROC 0.985), and retrospectively identified an emerging mpox lineage as anomalous (AUROC 0.974). MicroDUET operates 10^3 - 10^4 times faster than single-threaded sequence-based alignments. MicroDUET therefore provides a compact, reusable representation for scalable pathogen surveillance and sequence triage.

title: Longitudinal miRNA-mRNA Profiling Reveals Network Reorganization in Preeclampsia
abstract: Background: Preeclampsia (PE) is a leading cause of maternal and perinatal morbidity. Temporal dynamics of molecular dysregulation across pregnancy remain poorly understood. We performed longitudinal RNA sequencing of maternal whole blood to characterize miRNA-mRNA regulatory network evolution in PE. Methods: Whole-blood samples from early (M1: 10-18 weeks) and late pregnancy (M2: 32-38 weeks) were analyzed from 43 PE cases and 106 normotensive controls, including 109 paired samples (36 PE cases, 73 controls). Differential expression, temporal classification, pathway enrichment, and miRNA-mRNA network integration were performed. Placental expression support was assessed using internal RNA-seq and public databases. Key miRNA-mRNA interactions were experimentally validated in HTR-8/SVneo trophoblast cells. Results: PE exhibited marked temporal reorganization of miRNA-mRNA networks, with strongly opposing temporal effect sizes across overlapping miRNA and mRNA features (Spearman {rho} = -0.82, P < 0.0001). PI3K/AKT/mTORC1 signaling showed biphasic reversal (NES = +1.46, FDR = 0.028 at M1; NES = -1.64, FDR = 0.025 at M2), and heme-metabolism programs showed progressive suppression (2.1-fold NES intensification; FDR < 0.05 at both timepoints). Network analysis identified 29 high-confidence biphasic miRNA-mRNA pairs, including convergent targeting of ADGRA2 by three miRNAs and HSD17B1 by three miRNAs. miR-101-3p overexpression reduced DEPP1 mRNA (~40%) and protein (~26%) in trophoblast cells (P < 0.01), supporting a FOXO-DEPP1 axis. Blood-derived pairs showed pathway convergence with placental VGLL3-centered programs (PI3K/AKT, FOXO, TGF-{beta}, trophoblast differentiation). Conclusions: PE is associated with predominantly stage-specific or biphasic miRNA-mRNA network reorganization, with PI3K/AKT/mTORC1 dynamic remodeling and progressive heme-metabolism suppression. These findings support gestational-age-specific biomarker development and identify regulatory axes, including miR-101-3p [->] DEPP1, for mechanistic investigation.

title: Algorithms for Designing Therapeutic Oligonucleotides on Pangenome Graphs
abstract: Designing therapeutic oligonucleotides that act reliably across human genetic diversity requires more than alignment to a single reference genome. Binding affinity of an siRNA or ASO to a usually complementary site in an mRNA target molecule is one main determinant of drug efficacy. Thus, variation in sub-populations can lead to failures in drug development if this variation reduces binding affinity. We provide a first methodological step towards principled, variant-aware design of therapeutic oligonucleotides. The genetic diversity in target genes, or specific regions thereof, is represented as a pangenome graph. We define individual or small sets of suitable therapeutic oligonucleotides by their ability to cover all paths in a directed acyclic graph within a bounded edit distance <= k. Edit distance is used as an accepted proxy to the commonly used binding affinity. We formalize the resulting computational problem and provide complexity results: NP-hardness of identifying such minimal sets even for k =0, and coNP-completeness of verifying the validity of a given set of oligonucleotides. Further, we propose algorithmic approaches operating on a product graph of an automaton (an Aho-Corasick DFA or an Ukkonen DFA) and the pangenome graph, as well as a dynamic programming-based lossless filter. We evaluate the approaches on gene-specific subgraphs of human pangenome graphs and demonstrate favorable performance compared to naive brute-force computation. Our results show that candidate target sites with a threshold of k <= 3 can be identified even for large, complex graphs where the brute-force computation did not complete within 24h. We observe that the dynamic programming-based lossless filter outperforms both product-graph approaches as well as brute-force baselines while maintaining an average approximation ratio < 1.5 across more than a hundred evaluated subgraphs. We also present examples where a small set of oligonucleotides constitutes a feasible solution where no single oligonucleotide with a threshold of k <= 2 covers all paths.

title: Entangled stoichiometric objectives shape microbial catabolism
abstract:
by Maaike Remeijer, Frank J. Bruggeman 

The understanding of fundamental relationships between energetic and biosynthetic parameters of catabolism and anabolism is a central challenge in microbiology. The large diversity of microbial metabolisms can be compared on the basis of our current definitions of catabolism and anabolism. Catabolism has two functions: synthesising charged energy carriers and carbon precursors. Energy carriers, however, are also involved in precursor synthesis, complicating the analysis. We introduce an unbiased method to quantify stoichiometric relationships between catabolism and anabolism in genome-scale metabolic models. We compare catabolic strategies across diverse (heterotrophic) microbial species and growth conditions, focusing on states of maximal biomass yield per unit of energy source. Catabolic networks turn out to vary greatly, due to variation in the energy and carbon source for growth and the requirement to make suitable precursors for anabolism. We find that the ATP requirement for 1 gram biomass ranges between 72.8 and 148.0 mmol, precursor sets range between 4 and 14 in size, and acetyl-CoA is the only universal precursor across species. An important varying factor is the amount of ATP that is produced or consumed during precursor synthesis. This causes the remaining ATP demand, which is produced in catabolism, to vary. We conclude that the diversity of heterotrophic catabolism results from entanglement between charging of energy carriers and precursor synthesis. The state of maximal energetic efficiency is reached by maximizing the yield of charged energy carriers during precursor synthesis and simultaneously minimizing the demand for charged energy carriers in the conversion of precursors into macromolecules. Our formal analysis of catabolic diversity using a rigorous definition of catabolism’s two functions shows that microbial metabolism cannot be simplified in this manner; it rather shows that these two functions are intertwined due to the precise biochemistry.

title: Handshake: Partner-specific protein-protein binding site prediction at scale using ProstT5 and cross-chain attention
abstract:
by Nurit Haspel 

Partner-specific protein-protein binding site prediction, identifying which residues of a protein form the interface when bound to a specific partner, remains a challenging task with significant implications for drug discovery and understanding of protein structure and function. Existing computational methods are limited by small training datasets, inconsistent redundancy filtering, and reliance on three-dimensional structural information at test time. Here we present a sequence-only, partner-specific protein-protein interface predictor called HandShake. It combines ProstT5, a protein language model pre-trained on structural data, with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), a cross-chain attention mechanism and a contact supervision head. Our method can detect both binding interfaces and pairwise contact matrices. We trained our model on very large datasets of non-redundant protein-protein pairs derived from the PPInterface dataset, the most comprehensive structural protein-protein database to date, and evaluated it on systematically filtered benchmarks at four redundancy thresholds (30%–90% sequence identity). We demonstrate that sequence redundancy inflates reported AUROC by up to 0.079 and MCC by up to 0.145 on identical models, representing a substantial methodological confound in the field. Even at 30% redundancy threshold, our results (AUROC = 0.811, MCC = 0.367, F1 = 0.45) exceed the best published sequence-only result on this convention. Our method also achieves comparable performance to existing partner-specific methods that use explicit structural information. The comprehensive training and evaluation dataset, in addition to the systematic redundancy inflation, can help gain insight into protein-protein interactions and the abilities and limitations of current detection methods.

title: G-quadruplex profiling using single-cell CUT&Tag offers insight into the epigenetic landscape of the developing mouse brain
abstract:
Background
                 G-quadruplexes (G4s) are non-canonical DNA structures that have gained increasing attention for their potential roles in gene regulation and role in neurodegenerative diseases and cancer. Despite their biological significance, G4 structures have not been studied systematically across tissues and cell types. 
              
                Results
                 In this study, we employ G4 single-cell CUT&Tag (G4 scCUT&Tag) to characterize G4 landscapes in postnatal mouse brain cells, leveraging single-cell analytical approaches commonly used in scRNA-Seq and scATAC-Seq datasets. Using conventional single-cell omics workflows to process and explore our data, we distinguish distinct cell lineages based on G4 heterogeneity and establish that a subset of lineage-specific genes show unique promoter G4s. Multi-omics integration with scRNA-Seq gene expression profiles, using both a covariance-based technique (canonical correlation analysis) and a transfer learning-based approach, enables more accurate cell-type annotation. These integrations not only reveal correlations between G4 signal and gene expression, but demonstrate that G4 scCUT&Tag enables detailed examination of G4 heterogeneity in complex tissues and supports integrative analysis of G4 profiles with other omics layers, offering new insights into the epigenomic landscapes of the developing brain. 
              
                Conclusions
                 Our findings establish G4 scCUT&Tag as a framework for investigating the cellular heterogeneity of G4 landscapes in complex tissues and provide a basis for exploring their relationships with gene regulation and other layers of chromatin organization.

title: Structure-guided engineering of eukaryotic Fanzor-ωRNA system enhances in vivo gene editing for dystrophin restoration in a Duchenne mouse model
abstract:
Background
                      Eukaryotic Fanzor (Fz) proteins are compact RNA-guided endonucleases homologous to prokaryotic TnpB/Cas12, offering theoretical advantages for single AAV delivery. However, their low editing efficiency and poorly defined specificity in mammals have hindered therapeutic development. 
                  
                     Results
                      Here, we perform structure-guided engineering of  Spizellomyces punctatus  Fanzor1 nuclease (SpuFz1) to enhance its utility for in vivo genome editing and identify several Fanzor variants whose efficiencies are comparable or only slightly lower than widely-used miniature enAsCas12f1 and large-sized SpCas9. We demonstrate that catalytically dead dSpuFz1-v4.2 can be repurposed for CRISPRa-mediated transcriptional activation in a proof-of-concept manner. Genome-wide PEM-seq in mice reveal low translocation frequencies (below 0.05%, much lower than the background threshold set by the PEM-seq protocol), with no detected events attributable to off-target editing. GUIDE-seq analysis also confirms genome-wide low off-target profile for SpuFz1-v4.2 in human cells, with small amounts of off-target editing due to 3’ terminal sequence tolerability. Embryonic mRNA injection efficiently generates mutant mice. Crucially, single AAV9 delivery of SpuFz1-v4.2 in a humanized Duchenne muscular dystrophy model induces targeted exon skipping, restores dystrophin expression to ~ 10% of wild-type levels, and improves muscle contractile force. 
                  
                     Conclusions
                      Structure-guided optimization overcomes the activity barrier of eukaryotic Fanzors while maintaining low off-target effect. The engineered SpuFz1-v4.2 retains the hypercompact size necessary for single AAV packaging, establishing a robust platform for in vivo gene editing. This work positions Fanzor by a preliminary proof-of-concept therapeutic study as a viable, miniature alternative to CRISPR-Cas systems for genetic disease intervention and functional genomics.

title: Gene-Miner: an evidence-integrating Nextflow pipeline for reference re-annotation and protein-coding gene discovery
abstract:
Background
                      The principal bottleneck in genomics has shifted from assembly to annotation. Reference catalogues reach near-complete gene sets only through billions of reads and years of curation, which most genomes lack. No reference annotation is final, so a reproducible pipeline that re-derives a protein-coding catalogue from modest public data serves both unannotated genomes and audits of existing ones. 
                  
                     Results
                      Gene-Miner, a portable Nextflow workflow, takes the union of RNA-seq transcript reconstruction, two ab initio finders (AUGUSTUS and the evidence-trained GeneMark-ETP) and protein homology, then removes contaminant- and transposable-element-derived models. On identical inputs it matched or exceeded BRAKER3 in conserved-ortholog completeness on all four genomes, while BRAKER3 reproduced reference exon structures more closely — a measure that ranks agreement with the reference rather than correctness. Gene-Miner instead recovered more of every reference annotation and proposed more loci the references lack: on rice, 95.1% BUSCO completeness (poales_odb10), 69% of RAP-DB genes recovered and 16,542 loci RAP-DB does not contain, from four public libraries (118 million read pairs, 2.7% of the reads behind the RefSeq annotation) and Swiss-Prot. Completeness was 92.0% on soybean, 98.8% on  Drosophila melanogaster  and 97.6% on  Caenorhabditis elegans , with 66–88% of each reference annotation recovered. Each locus is released in the GFF3 with its evidence flags and one of three confidence tiers, set by how many of RNA-seq, homology and orthology support it. 
                  
                     Conclusions
                      Gene-Miner extends and audits an existing annotation rather than reproducing it. Curated reference databases remain the authority, and a consensus pipeline such as BRAKER3 stays closer to a reference annotation than a detection-first union does. In 3 h per animal genome, 6 h for rice and 22 h for soybean on one 24-core workstation, it produces an isoform-aware catalogue near-complete in conserved orthologs and candidate model updates for expert review: structural revisions, novel loci and RNA-seq-supported isoforms, each with the evidence behind it.

title: AnnST: robust cross-section tissue domain label transfer in spatial transcriptomics via contrastive learning and optimal transport
abstract:
Background
                      Transferring tissue domain labels across spatial transcriptomics sections remains a challenge. A key problem is how to jointly address technical dropout and inter-section batch effects while preserving spatial tissue organization. Existing methods usually address only part of these challenges and often fail to maintain robust annotation across sections. 
                  
                     Results
                      In this study, we introduce AnnST, a robust framework for cross-section label transfer in spatial transcriptomics. AnnST constructs clean, dropout-perturbed, and batch effect-perturbed expression views. Contrastive learning improves robustness to dropout noise, while optimal transport reduces variation caused by batch effects. Label-aware spatial regularization is further used during supervised fine-tuning to preserve local tissue organization. We evaluate AnnST on the DLPFC Visium, SEA-AD MERFISH, and human breast cancer Visium datasets. AnnST achieves competitive annotation performance across these datasets, while showing stable results across random seeds. It also remains robust under multiple technical perturbations. Downstream analyses further show that the predicted annotations preserve cortical laminar organization and support biologically meaningful functional analysis. 
                  
                     Conclusions
                      AnnST provides a robust and biologically interpretable framework for cross-section annotation in spatial transcriptomics and offers a practical solution for downstream spatial analysis in datasets generated using different ST platforms.

title: EMS‐induced amino acid substitutions in Arabidopsis proteins: what we get and what we miss
abstract: The alkylating agent ethyl methanesulfonate (EMS) is commonly used in Arabidopsis genetics to induce point mutations. It has been known for decades that the mutational spectrum of EMS is highly biased (> 98% G/C→A/T base pair transitions). However, the consequences of this bias on protein sequences have been almost entirely overlooked until now. The graph illustrates this bias, showing that only 29 amino acid substitutions are possible.

title: ROOMIE1 controls rhizobiome assembly in Lotus japonicus and shows a genomic signature distinct from climate‐associated loci
abstract:
Natural variation in  Lotus japonicus  is associated with reproducible differences in rhizosphere microbiome composition, revealing multiple host genomic loci underlying microbiome variation.
 
 
 Summary 
 
How plant genomes accommodate selective pressures across spatial and temporal scales remains poorly understood. Here, we address this by comparing the population-genomic signatures of root microbiome- and climate-associated loci in a natural  Lotus japonicus  population.
We inoculated 155  L. japonicus  accessions with a synthetic community of 107 bacterial isolates and performed genome-wide association analyses of rhizosphere microbiome traits. We then carried out functional validation, testing effects of mutations and natural allelic variation, and compared population-genomic characteristics of microbiome-associated and climate-associated loci.
We identified 355 significant quantitative trait loci associated with rhizosphere microbiome variation. Microbiome-associated loci showed heterogeneous genomic signatures. One subset displayed strong regional differentiation and near fixation of specific haplotypes, whereas another showed low differentiation, and maintenance of multiple haplotypes within populations. The latter pattern was exemplified by  ROOT MICROBIOME ESTABLISHMENT 1  ( ROOMIE1 ). Disruption of  ROOMIE1  reproducibly altered rhizosphere microbiome composition in both synthetic communities and native soil, whereas natural  ROOMIE1  haplotypes were associated with microbiome differences among closely related accessions.
Our findings reveal that microbiome-associated loci can display population-genomic signatures that sharply contrast with those at climate-associated loci, with  ROOMIE1  representing a host gene that controls rhizosphere microbiome composition and shows standing haplotype variation at a local scale.

title: Somatic cell reprogramming to totipotency: molecular logic, emerging models, and future perspectives
abstract:
A mechanistic framework for somatic cell reprogramming toward totipotency during plant regeneration.







Summary
Plant regeneration depends on the capacity of differentiated somatic cells to regain plasticity and acquire totipotency. Although somatic embryogenesis has long been explored, the molecular logic by which a somatic cell converts into an embryo‐forming founder cell remains incompletely understood. Classical studies established the developmental and hormonal basis of regeneration, whereas recent multi‐omics studies have revealed that regeneration is not a simple process of dedifferentiation. Instead, totipotency emerges through ordered reprogramming events involving cell‐type‐specific competence, suppression or redirection of pre‐existing trajectory, activation of embryogenic transcriptional networks, hormonal rewiring, and epigenetic remodeling. We summarize major findings in plant somatic cell reprogramming, discuss the conceptual transition from dedifferentiation to developmental trajectory rewiring, and highlight future directions for engineering totipotency in recalcitrant crops.

title: CaLWD1 forms an MBW complex with CaAMS and CaMS188 to regulate pollen exine formation in pepper
abstract:
Working model for CaLWD1-mediated regulation of pollen exine formation in pepper.
 
 
 Summary 
 
Pollen wall formation is essential for male reproduction in flowering plants. Although several core regulators of pollen wall development have been identified, whether WD40 proteins, which often act as protein interaction scaffolds, contribute to this process remains unclear.
Here, we identified  CaLWD1  (LIGHT-REGULATED WD 1), a WD40 gene highly expressed during early anther development in pepper ( Capsicum annuum ).  CaLWD1  transcripts accumulated mainly in the tapetum and microspores. Silencing  CaLWD1  disrupted the outer exine structure and resulted in male sterility.
Transcriptomic and metabolomic analyses showed that  CaLWD1  silencing significantly reduced the expression of genes involved in fatty acid metabolism and sporopollenin biosynthesis and decreased the accumulation of fatty acid metabolites. CaLWD1 interacted with CaAMS and CaMS188 to form a MYB–bHLH–WD40 (MBW) complex and enhanced CaAMS- and CaMS188-mediated transcriptional activation of  CaFAR2  and  CaCYP703A2 . CaLWD1 was also directly regulated by CaMS188, and this regulation was further strengthened by the CaAMS–CaMS188 interaction, forming a feed-forward module.
These findings reveal a CaLWD1-mediated regulatory module controlling pepper exine formation and define a role for WD40 proteins and MBW complexes in pollen wall development.

title: BpAHL23 promotes shoot branching in white birch by regulating cell cycle
abstract: Abstract Lateral branch development is critical for woody plants, as it determines crown architecture, photosynthetic efficiency, and wood quality. Although auxin and cytokinin are known to regulate lateral branch development in herbaceous plants, underlying transcription factor networks, and the downstream genes that mediate responses to these phytohormones in forest trees remain largely unclear. In this study, we characterized  BpAHL23  (AT-HOOK MOTIF CONTAINING NUCLEAR LOCALIZED 23), a transcription factor that regulates lateral branch development in white birch ( Betula platyphylla ). Loss-of-function  bpahl23  mutants exhibited delayed axillary bud elongation, whereas  BpAHL23 -overexpressing transgenic plants displayed enhanced lateral branching. Transcriptomic and molecular analyses suggest that  BpAHL23  responds to cytokinin and auxin and regulates the expression of the cell cycle - related gene  BpCYCD3;1 . The CYCD3;1 protein can interact with CDKA;1 to control cell cycle progression, thereby promoting cell proliferation in axillary bud and contributing to axillary bud elongation. Overall, these results indicate that  BpAHL23  is induced by cytokinin and auxin, activates  BpCYCD3;1 , and regulates the cell cycle through its interaction with CDKA;1. These findings provide insights into the molecular mechanisms underlying the regulation of tree architecture and suggest potential strategies for the molecular breeding of forest trees.

title: Recognizing and Mitigating Reference Bias in Population Genomics
abstract: Abstract Most population genomic analyses require mapping sequence reads to a reference genome. Mapping to a single reference introduces reference bias, defined as either low-quality read mapping or downstream analytical distortions arising from biased mapping. Although reference bias has been repeatedly documented, its consequences remain insufficiently understood. Its impacts are particularly relevant in biodiversity genomics, where heterospecific references are commonly used to analyse entire clades. Here, we survey the literature to document where reference bias occurs, its sources, and its impacts, focusing on population and biodiversity genomics. We identify five major classes of reference-inference bias impacts: distortions in population genetic inference; alterations to phylogenetic inference; structural variant detection; RNA expression analyses; and gene presence-absence variation. Critically, the direction and magnitude of these impacts are inconsistent across studies, suggesting that generalisations are premature. Reference bias is primarily driven by evolutionary divergence between the reference genome and the mapped samples, and is further aggravated by analytical and biological factors. We suggest several mitigation strategies, including divergence-aware filtering, tool benchmarking, and standardised reporting of reference bias. In the longer term, we advocate expanding reference genome diversity and adopting pangenome-based alignment across taxa.

title: A conserved tetrapolar mating system permits sexual hybridization and recombinant host phenotypes in wheat- and barley-adapted Puccinia striiformis
abstract: Abstract Host specialization can restrict gene flow in fungal pathogens, yet sexual compatibility may persist when mating occurs on a shared alternate host. We tested this possibility by crossing wheat-adapted  Puccinia striiformis  f. sp.  tritici  and barley-adapted  P. striiformis  f. sp.  hordei  on  Berberis vulgaris . Despite contrasting host specialization and genome-wide sequence differentiation, reciprocal crosses produced 18 viable aeciospore-derived progeny. Chromosome-scale parental assemblies revealed physically unlinked homeodomain (HD) and pheromone receptor (PR) mating-type loci, consistent with a conserved tetrapolar mating system. All progeny inherited one HD haplotype from each parent, representing all four parental HD haplotype combinations. Phenotyped progeny displayed host-interaction profiles distinct from either parent, including compatibility with selected genotypes of both wheat and barley. These findings demonstrate that host-associated differentiation in  P. striiformis  can coexist with incomplete intrinsic reproductive isolation between the tested parental isolates, allowing sexual hybridization to generate novel host phenotypes.

abstract: Orlov et al. show that prolonged visual deprivation due to late treatment of congenital cataract does not affect global motion perception. title: A neural circuit mediating altitude control in Drosophila
abstract: Altitude control is a crucial feature of active flight. Erickson et al. use a combination of approaches to characterize a circuit for altitude regulation composed of a single pair of descending neurons that receive input from visual cells sensitive to vertical motion and provide output to motor neurons regulating lift.

title: Sedimentary ancient DNA expands bioarchaeological evidence and interpretation at Roman Harelbeke
abstract: Sedimentary ancient DNA (sedaDNA) can expand archaeological research by recovering broad biological signals from small amounts of sediment. Here, we apply shotgun sedaDNA metagenomics and target capture (also known as hybridization capture) to disused Roman wells from the vicus of Harelbeke, Belgium, dated to ca. 160-300 CE, and integrate the results with existing bioarchaeological datasets. Moving beyond individual introduced taxa as proxies for Roman influence, we reconstruct community-level profiles spanning consumption-related, synanthropic, and environmental organisms. SedaDNA reproduced most established bioarchaeological signals, including cultivated plants and domestic animals, while also recovering additional environmental taxa that established methods underrepresented. Mitochondrial target capture strengthened selected faunal detections and enabled phylogenetic placement of a pig (Sus scrofa) within the European mitochondrial lineage. The predominance of previously established consumption-related taxa is consistent with subsistence continuity and selective adoption of Roman-introduced resources, although taxon counts alone cannot establish their relative importance. Analytical-effort modeling further indicates that batch-based sedaDNA workflows can provide broad biological profiles at lower cost and time investment than established archaeological methods. Overall, sedaDNA complements conventional bioarchaeology by broadening taxonomic recovery, supporting scalable sampling, and providing a broad-spectrum approach to reconstructing settlement ecology, subsistence, and human-environment interaction.

title: Decomposition of the  S. aureus  pangenome reveals evolving genetic repertoire associated with adaptation and virulence
abstract:
by Siddharth M. Chauhan, Bernhard O. Palsson, Jonathan M. Monk 

Bacterial pangenomes are mosaics of vertically inherited chromosomal backgrounds and horizontally acquired mobile elements, yet existing analysis methods either assign each genome to a single phylogenetic group or treat genes independently, failing to resolve this composite architecture. Here, we show that non-negative matrix factorization decomposes the accessory pangenome of 1,398 curated Staphylococcus aureus genomes into 24 additive gene modules (“phylons”) that cleanly separate lineage-defining components from mobile genetic element repertoires, achieving 90% reconstruction accuracy with 96% precision. The additive representation, where each genome equals a primary lineage phylon plus one or more mobilome phylons, recovers known biology (clonal complex structure, immune evasion cluster types) and reveals previously uncharacterized structure, including multiple horizontal transfer events linking the CC30 and hybrid ST239 pandemic lineages. Annotation-independent validation with geNomad confirmed that 75–96% of mobilome phylon gene instances physically reside within prophage regions across all 1,398 genomes, while coordinate-level analysis of the remainder revealed prophage boundary effects, chromosomally integrated elements, and composite mobilome architecture rather than false assignments. External validation on 966 independent draft genome assemblies yielded zero false-positive lineage assignments (mean AUC = 0.996) with no dependence on assembly quality, and mobilome phylons discriminated human from livestock hosts and methicillin-resistant from methicillin-susceptible isolates without retraining. A lightweight projection tool, phylon_assign, enables rapid classification of new genomes. The generalization of this framework from  Escherichia coli  and  Enterobacter  to  Staphylococcus aureus  – species with fundamentally different pangenome structures – establishes non-negative matrix factorization as a scalable, organism-agnostic approach for resolving the modular architecture of bacterial pangenomes.

title: Robust model calibration in large-scale systems biology via an adaptive hybrid algorithm
abstract:
Background
                      Parameter estimation is a central challenge in systems biology, particularly for large dynamic models described by nonlinear ordinary differential equations (ODEs). These global optimization problems exhibit landscapes which are topologically heterogeneous, often exhibiting a pathological mixture of stiff, smooth valleys and rugged, noisy plateaus, making single-strategy hybrids ineffective. While methods like enhanced Scatter Search (eSS) represent the current state-of-the-art, their rigid intensification strategies can limit performance in large-scale or ill-conditioned scenarios. 
                  
                     Results
                      We introduce eLSHADE+, a novel metaheuristic architecture designed to adapt to these topological challenges. The proposed algorithm builds on the well-established Differential Evolution variant LSHADE by incorporating an adaptive multi-strategy hybridization. Unlike standard memetic algorithms, eLSHADE+ uses three distinct operational modes: (i) gradient-based intensification, (ii) derivative-free search, and (iii) pure global exploration. Adaptively switching the intensification strategy allows the algorithm to capture the complementary strengths of different local optimization paradigms while mitigating their individual limitations, achieving precision in differentiable regions, robustness against numerical noise, and saving computational resources in complicated basins. Additionally, a logarithmic parameter space transformation is incorporated to facilitate search across multi-scale biological constants. 
                  
                     Conclusions
                      We evaluated eLSHADE+ using the BioPreDyn benchmark suite, comprising realistic, biologically motivated problems. Within this benchmark suite and under the reported experimental conditions, the proposed multi-strategy approach achieved statistically competitive or superior convergence speed and solution accuracy compared with the methods evaluated. Code and data are available in a publicly accessible repository. These results support eLSHADE+ as a competitive and robust alternative for the model-calibration problems considered.

title: SWANS: a highly configurable analysis pipeline for single-cell and single-nucleus RNA-sequencing data
abstract:
Background
                      Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) is a powerful technique that enables the analysis of gene expression at the individual cell level. Bioinformatic tools for scRNA-seq data analysis have many different options throughout the typical scRNA-seq workflow (normalization, integration, annotation, clustering, and visualization), and the choice of method(s) and parameter(s) at each stage can impact results. 
                  
                     Results
                      Here, we introduce SWANS, a configurable analysis pipeline that, in a single run, can employ multiple analysis methods, resolutions, and modifiable parameters. The resulting clustering arrangements, differential gene expression results, and other quantitative measurements can be dynamically visualized and compared in a Shiny interactive report to assist in choosing a single analysis schema for annotation and downstream analysis. Once a final approach is chosen, SWANS will perform differential gene expression (DGE) analysis based on experimental conditions and gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA). SWANS uses Snakemake as a workflow manager, Cell Ranger for alignment and gene expression quantification, Seurat for single-cell data analysis, and additional R packages for quality control and downstream analysis. 
                  
                     Conclusion
                      SWANS is a tailorable pipeline that integrates quality control, dimensionality reduction, multi-schema clustering comparison, differential gene expression, gene set enrichment, and preliminary trajectory analysis into a single configurable workflow. Additionally, SWANS generates a series of interactive and static HTML reports that facilitate sharing large volumes of complex data in a clear and concise manner to investigators and collaborators.

title: Karst habitat islands drove a largely nonadaptive and allopatric radiation in Petrocodon (Gesneriaceae)
abstract:
Time-calibrated species tree of  Petrocodon .
 
 
 Summary 
 
Whether evolutionary radiations are primarily driven by ecological or neutral processes remains an unresolved question. The karst-endemic genus  Petrocodon , distributed across southern China and northern Indochina, provides a powerful system for testing these alternatives.
We generated whole-genome sequencing data for 54 of the 60 described species and integrated these with morphological, geographic, and paleoclimatic data to evaluate the relative roles of ecological and neutral processes in diversification.
Our analyses revealed a robust nuclear phylogeny but extensive cytonuclear discordance, likely due to pervasive ancient hybridization and introgression. Macroevolutionary and biogeographic analyses indicate that diversification began during a favorable climatic period enabling range expansion, but subsequent species accumulation was primarily driven by geographic isolation and allopatric divergence rather than ecological niche differentiation. Morphological evolution decoupled from lineage diversification, with most morphological diversity accumulating relatively late. Further analyses support genetic drift in small, isolated populations driving morphological evolution, although stabilizing selection cannot be excluded, and reticulate evolution may have additionally contributed to phenotypic innovation.
Together, these results support a largely nonadaptive radiation in  Petrocodon , in which spatial opportunity played a central role in species accumulation, while demographic and reticulate processes may have contributed to its striking phenotypic diversity.

title: Targeted rewiring of the rhizosphere metabolite–microbe axis restores phosphorus acquisition in inefficient citrus rootstock
abstract:
Conceptual diagram of rhizosphere metabolite-mediated recruitment of P-solubilizing bacteria for enhanced P acquisition.
 
 
 Summary 
 
Low phosphorus (P) availability limits citrus production, while genotypic determinants governing rhizosphere P mobilization remain elusive. Here, we investigated P-acquisition strategies in citrus rootstocks.
We performed a systematic screening of citrus rootstocks under P-deficient conditions and identified two contrasting genotypes: P-efficient  Citrus tangerina  and P-inefficient  Citrus junos . Comparative metabolomics, microbiome profiling, targeted strain isolation, and inoculation assays were combined to unravel metabolic and microbial drivers governing P mobilization.
The superior P acquisition of  C. tangerina  stemmed from a unique root-exudate profile enriched in 2-hydroxyflavanone, scopoletin, raffinose, and gallic acid. These metabolites selectively enriched  Methylobacterium  sp. strain HA110, a robust P-solubilizing bacterium. Exogenous exudate application enhanced  C. junos  P acquisition, yet this beneficial effect was abolished under soil sterilization, demonstrating an essential role of microbiota. Combined supplementation of the metabolites and strain HA110 enhanced rhizosphere P activation, which in turn strengthened the P-acquisition capacity of  C. junos  and consequently stimulated its growth.
Collectively, these findings uncover a novel metabolite–microbe axis: P-efficient rootstocks reshape their rhizosphere microbiome through specific exudates. This axis is amenable to rational reconfiguration to restore P acquisition in P-inefficient genotypes, laying a theoretical basis for exudate-derived biofertilizers to boost P-use efficiency in sustainable citriculture.

title: The ZmNAC41‐ZmABC‐ZmCP regulatory module mediates jasmonate‐dependent resistance to southern corn rust in maize
abstract:
A working model of the  ZmNAC41 - ZmABC - ZmCP  module in regulating SCR resistance.
 
 
 Summary 
 
Plant disease resistance is often governed by complex multigene modules, yet their composition and regulation remain poorly defined.
Here, we identify a maize defense module comprising the NAC (NAM, ATAF1/2, and CUC2) transcription factor ZmNAC41, the PADRE domain-containing protein ZmABC, and the cysteine protease ZmCP. This module contributes to resistance to southern corn rust (SCR) caused by  Puccinia polysora  and is linked to jasmonic acid (JA)-associated defense responses.
Upon pathogen infection, ZmNAC41 was rapidly induced and directly activated  ZmABC  transcription. ZmABC physically interacted with ZmCP. Increased JA accumulation and induction of JA biosynthetic and JA-responsive genes were also observed. Silencing any one of the three genes markedly attenuated JA-associated defense responses and compromised resistance, supporting a functional contribution of all three components to maize defense. Importantly, natural variation analysis identified elite haplotypes carrying favorable alleles of  ZmNAC41 ,  ZmABC , and  ZmCP , and these allele combinations were significantly associated with enhanced field resistance.
Together, our findings reveal a maize defense module that integrates transcriptional regulation and protein interaction and contributes to SCR resistance in association with JA-associated defense responses. These findings provide genetic targets for breeding maize with improved resistance to SCR.

title: Novel CRISPR therapy is poised to gain first FDA approval to alter genes inside the body
abstract: Nature, Published online: 12 November 2026;  doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03705-9  Current gene-editing treatments require removal of a participant’s cells — a complex and costly approach.

title: Daily briefing: Are one-person firms the future of biotech?
abstract: Nature, Published online: 12 November 2026;  doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03684-x  Researchers are debating whether small, AI-enabled biotech companies are the future of drug discovery. Plus, even microplastics still reach the wildlife furthest from humanity and an upgrade to AlphaGenome.

title: Record-breaking Ebola outbreak: phone data reconstruct first weeks of spread
abstract: Nature, Published online: 12 November 2026;  doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03666-z  The Bundibugyo virus strain was circulating for weeks before its detection in May, but was missed owing to surveillance failures, testing gaps and funding cuts, researchers say.

title: Who needs sex? Kelp reproduce asexually when no mate is nearby
abstract: Nature, Published online: 12 November 2026;  doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03665-0  Insights into the reproductive modes of brown algae could help in the fight to protect them in warming climate.

title: This little brown mushroom is laced with a hallucinogen — and lethal toxins
abstract: Nature, Published online: 12 November 2026;  doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03639-2  A Florida fungus might combine the psychedelic compound psilocybin with deadly chemicals to defend itself against hungry animals.

title: Found: a protein that drives ageing without unleashing inflammation
abstract: Nature, Published online: 12 November 2026;  doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03638-3  Aged mice engineered to lack granzyme K have improved heart and liver function and less kidney damage.

title: RSV vaccines slash infections: data show jabs’ staggering success against dangerous virus
abstract: Nature, Published online: 12 November 2026;  doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03573-3  Vaccines and monoclonal-antibody injections are cutting hospitalizations linked to the respiratory virus.

title: Massive atlas of brain region linked to a host of diseases is the most detailed yet
abstract: Nature, Published online: 12 November 2026;  doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03565-3  A global team profiled nearly 26 million brain cells from the basal ganglia to build a cross-species reference database that will help to understand conditions from Parkinson’s disease to addiction.

title: Degradation of mucin O-glycans by a human gut symbiont requires a complex enzyme repertoire and promotes colonization
abstract: Schaus et al. reveal how the gut symbiont Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron uses a coordinated repertoire of enzymes to degrade colonic mucin O-glycans. Enzymes that act on terminal O-glycan decorations are important for colonization, identifying key steps that may shape host-microbiota interactions at the intestinal mucus barrier.

title: Sub-second dopamine reinforcement shapes juvenile social play
abstract: Dopamine acts moment by moment to reinforce the specific actions that make up juvenile social play. Disrupted reinforcement underlies social deficits in a Shank3-deficient autism model, and correcting it in real time restores normal play.

title: From the human genome to the human brain cell atlas
abstract: The BRAIN Initiative Cell Atlas Network (BICAN) is establishing an evolving reference for neuroscience by integrating cell identities, anatomy, and multimodal evidence across species. In analogy with the Human Genome Project, the BICAN basal ganglia atlas is a model for a federated reference to advance understanding of brain organization, function, variation, and disease.

title: Harmonized brain ontology and 3D atlases for human, macaque, and marmoset basal ganglia
abstract: A Harmonized Ontology of Mammalian Brain Anatomy (HOMBA) enables consistent creation of structural and cellular brain atlases and ontologies as well as the integration of multimodal data and samples across species.

title: Collaboration across scales: More than the sum of its parts
abstract: Science is collaborative by nature, but some questions require coordination on an exceptional scale. Among them is the challenge of creating a comprehensive reference framework for the human brain. In this issue of Cell, together with papers published in Cell Genomics, Cell Reports, Cell Reports Methods, Cell Systems, and Neuron, we present the first publication package from the NIH BRAIN Initiative Cell Atlas Network (BICAN).

title: Toward an integrated framework for a human and mammalian brain cell atlas
authors: The BRAIN Initiative Cell Atlas Network (BICAN)
abstract: The BRAIN Initiative Cell Atlas Network integrates molecular profiles, spatial maps, and anatomical frameworks into a curated cell-type taxonomy of the human, macaque, and marmoset basal ganglia. This multimodal atlas offers a blueprint for comparing brain cell types across species and for scaling to the whole brain.

title: Mesoscale molecular architecture of the striatum across cell types and adult aging
abstract: Using Slide-tags spatial transcriptomics across 19 human donors, this study shows that the striatum is organized into six molecularly distinct zones that are conserved in macaque and mouse, align with brain-wide projection inputs, and lose their transcriptional distinctiveness with age.

title: Morphoelectric diversity and specialization of primate striatal neuron types
abstract: Patch-seq in the macaque striatum links transcriptomic cell-type identity to neuronal form and function, revealing non-canonical spiny projection neurons, specialized interneurons, spatially organized morphoelectric gradients, and features that distinguish macaque from mouse neuron types.

title: Disruption of cell-type-specific molecular programs of striatal spiny projection neurons in autism
abstract: Cross-species single-cell profiling identifies molecular disruptions among striatal spiny projection neurons in genetically defined autism. D1 striosome spiny projection neurons are identified as the most affected, with altered synaptic and energy metabolism programs linked to reduced EGR1/EGR3 activity, partly reproduced by EGR1/EGR3 loss in organoids.

title: Common variation of cell abundances and gene expression in the human striatum
abstract: Single-cell analyses of the adult human striatum and prefrontal cortex reveal substantial inter-individual variation in cell-type abundance and gene expression. Most aspects of donor-associated cellular and molecular features recur across brain regions, while age and common genetic variation have distinct effects across cell types.

title: Conserved striatal mechanisms underlying ASD
abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) involves changes in social and stereotypic behaviors regulated by striatal circuitry. Using an innovative cross-species approach, in this issue of Cell, Yuan et al. identify alterations in specific striatal neurons and astrocytes, opening new avenues for investigating cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying striatal dysfunction in ASD.

title: Deploying liquid intelligence in cancer: Finding answers in our blood
abstract: Liquid biopsies provide a noninvasive way to screen for disease. This review explains how AI-powered multimodal foundation models will help to identify robust tumor signals from liquid biopsies at scale, but clinical and infrastructural hurdles will need to be addressed to deliver their promise to the clinic.

title: Spatial transcriptomics reveals molecular organization of human and nonhuman primate basal ganglia
abstract: A cellular-resolution spatial transcriptomics atlas of the basal ganglia in human, rhesus macaque, and common marmoset highlights a conserved molecular organization and introduces an accessible resource for the research community. This atlas reveals complex gene expression gradients that coexist with discrete cell-type specializations.

title: An integrative single-cell epigenomic atlas annotates the regulatory genome of the adult mouse brain
abstract: A comprehensive single-cell epigenomic atlas integrates four histone modifications, chromatin accessibility, DNA methylation, the 3D genome, and the transcriptome, and resolves functional chromatin states of the adult mouse brain. This integrative framework, together with sequence-based deep learning, identifies active and repressive regulatory mechanisms and their dynamic deployment underlying cell-type-specific gene regulation.

title: Mapping primate brain aging across cell types, regions, and sexes
abstract: Aging is the major risk factor for neurodegenerative disease, yet how it affects different cells in the primate brain remains unclear. In this issue of Cell, Yang et al. present a single-nucleus atlas of the aging macaque brain that, together with recent work by Zhang et al., reveals context-dependent aging programs, sex-biased transcriptional aging, and molecular links to Alzheimer’s disease.

title: Stepping (hi)stones: Charting a single-cell multiomic path toward understanding the human brain
abstract: In this issue of Cell, two single-cell multiomic atlases jointly profile transcription and histone modifications across different regions of the adult human brain, revealing cell-type-specific regulatory landscapes, developmental epigenetic memory, and improved interpretation of neurological variants. These studies establish a framework for understanding human brain cell identity, evolution, and pathology.

title: Multimodal single-cell epigenomic and 3D genome atlas of the human basal ganglia
abstract: A single-cell atlas of DNA methylation and 3D genome architecture across the human basal ganglia defines the regulatory signatures of its cell types, including a distinct striatal projection neuron subtype, and predicts cell-type-specific gene regulatory networks. Spatial transcriptomics further reveals interneuron types that differ between the striatal matrix and striosomes.

title: Cross-species multiomic atlas of the primate basal ganglia
abstract: A cross-species multiomic atlas of the primate basal ganglia aligns 1.8 million nuclei from human, macaque, and marmoset into 61 cell types conserved over 76 million years. The atlas reveals that dorsal-ventral spatial identity is more evolutionarily constrained than direct and indirect pathway or striosome and matrix identity, identifies a distinct SMYD2-HTR7 spiny projection neuron type, and links regulatory sequence grammars and psychiatric risk variants to specific cell populations.

title: A single-cell and spatial 3D multi-omic atlas of developing human basal ganglia
abstract: Single-cell and spatial profiling of the developing human basal ganglia show that their principal neurons, spiny projection neurons, mature through unusually synchronized epigenomic remodeling; that oligodendrocytes pass through a transient chromatin state during differentiation; and that spiny projection neurons carry an elevated genetic risk for schizophrenia and bipolar disorder.

title: Spatial and regulatory organization of cell identity across the primate subcortex
abstract: Dense multimodal profiling of the marmoset subcortex reveals how spatial context and gene regulatory programs jointly shape cell identity across the primate brain. By linking transcriptional states, chromatin accessibility, and anatomy, this atlas uncovers regulatory principles underlying spatial gradients, neuronal convergence, and evolutionary specialization.

title: Circuit-aligned specialization of human basal ganglia astrocytes
abstract: Astrocyte diversity in the human basal ganglia reflects both large-scale brain identity programs and local microcircuit specialization. Integrated transcriptomic, epigenomic, and spatial analyses link these astrocyte populations to subgroup-specific regulatory features and enhancer logic, providing a framework for understanding and targeting astrocyte heterogeneity.

title: Multiscale spatial atlas of human basal ganglia cell types and communities
abstract: This study combines MERFISH+ and Stereo-seq to generate a multiscale spatial transcriptomic atlas of the human basal ganglia. It reveals cellular community organization, conserved and species-specialized features of striosome-matrix architecture, and projection-associated molecular signatures inferred from subcellular RNA localization.

title: Single-cell, multi-region profiling of the macaque brain across the lifespan
abstract: Yang, Watkins et al. generate a 5.3 million cell transcriptomic atlas of the aging primate brain, which reveals that glia drive most age-related compositional shifts. These data uncover region-, cell-type-, and sex-specific molecular trajectories linked to neurodegenerative disease, providing key insights into the cellular mechanisms underlying brain aging and vulnerability.

title: Single-cell analysis of chromatin state and transcriptome in the human basal ganglia
abstract: A single-cell multi-omic atlas spanning eight regions of the human basal ganglia maps cell-type-specific chromatin landscapes and gene regulation, revealing the regulatory programs that shape cell identity. The atlas provides a framework for interpreting noncoding variants linked to basal ganglia traits and diseases, and it enables the construction of a deep-learning model for predicting how variants affect gene regulation and function.

title: Single-cell multimodal atlas reveals regulatory programs in the human brain
abstract: A multimodal, integrative framework for understanding gene regulatory mechanisms across diverse cell types in the adult human brain. This framework helps elucidate how regulatory programs govern neuronal and glial functions, encode developmental trajectories, underlie neurological phenotypes, and change during evolution.

title: Early Retinal UCHL1 Dysregulation Coupled With Synaptic Loss Reflects Alzheimer's Disease Severity (Adv. Sci. 63/2026)
abstract:
Retina as an Early Site of AD Synaptopathy  
 This frontispiece illustrates the newly identified early and progressive excitatory synaptic loss and UCHL1 dysregulation in the retinas of patients with Alzheimer's disease, highlighting the close connection between retinal synaptic pathology and the severity of brain disease. More details can be found in the Research Article by Maya Koronyo-Hamaoui and co-workers (DOI:  10.1002/advs.202600020 ).

title: The Natural Product Corramycin Acts as a DNA Gyrase Poison and Overcomes Fluoroquinolone Resistance in Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Adv. Sci. 63/2026)
abstract:
Corramycin Overcomes Fluoroquinolone Resistance  
 The natural product corramycin, whose mechanism of action remained elusive for 15 years, is identified as a DNA gyrase poison. Corramycin stabilizes a previously uncharacterized post-cleavage conformation of gyrase, preventing DNA religation and causing lethal double-strand breaks. By acting through a mechanism distinct from fluoroquinolones, corramycin retains activity against resistant bacteria, expanding the chemical and mechanistic space of gyrase poisons. More details can be found in the Research Article by Jennifer Herrmann, Rolf Müller, Jan Rybniker, Stéphanie Petrella, and co-workers (DOI:  10.1002/advs.76832 ).

title: Issue Information: (Adv. Sci. 63/2026)
abstract: Advanced Science, Volume 13, Issue 63, 12 November 2026.

title: Symbiont‐Induced HSP83 Establishes Two‐Tiered Control of Antifungal Immunity in an Invasive Beetle–Fungus Complex (Adv. Sci. 63/2026)
abstract:
Host-Microbe Interactions  
 Embedded within a pine-bark gallery, a protected sanctuary symbolizes the  Dendroctonus valens-Leptographium procerum  mutualism amid antagonistic fungal threats. The mutualist induces host HSP83, which mediates two-tiered control by associating with selected fungal recognition receptors and restraining Dorsal-driven antimicrobial peptide transcription, thereby limiting excessive responses while maintaining immune homeostasis and supporting host survival. More details can be found in the Research Article by Zhen Zou, Le Kang, Jianghua Sun, and co-workers (DOI:  10.1002/advs.77421 ).

title: Diverging Liquid–Liquid Phase Separation Behavior of Different Recombinant Major Ampullate Spidroins (Adv. Sci. 63/2026)
abstract:
Liquid-Liquid Phase Separation Behavior  
 The cover shows an  Araneus diadematus  at the center of its web. Dimerized spidroins (right circle), produced in the silk gland tail, undergo liquid-liquid phase separation (upper left circle) in the reservoir and duct facilitating their transition to a solid fiber (lower left circle). More details can be found in the Research Article by Tim Schiller, Cheryl Hayashi, and Thomas R. Scheibel (DOI:  10.1002/advs.77295 ).

title: Multiplexed Profiling of Individual Extracellular Vesicles Reveals Lung Cancer‐Associated Protein Signatures (Adv. Sci. 63/2026)
abstract:
Multiplexed Profiling of Individual Extracellular Vesicles  
 Imaging multicolor-stained extracellular vesicles (EVs) is akin to gazing at countless stars in the night sky. Named after the constellation, the Cygnus platform enables immersive exploration of the molecular complexity of single EVs. More details can be found in the Research Article by Yoonjeong Choi, Miles A. Miller, Hakho Lee, and co-workers (DOI:  10.1002/advs.77301 ).

title: Tailored Stereo‐Configuration of Crosslinkable Polyester‐Based Solid Polymer Electrolytes for All‐Solid‐State and Binder‐Free Li Metal Batteries (Adv. Sci. 63/2026)
abstract:
Crosslinkable Polyester-Based Solid Polymer Electrolytes  
 The cover illustrates a multiscale view of an all-solid-state lithium metal battery enabled by a crosslinkable polyester-based solid polymer electrolyte. Molecular-level control of the polyester stereo-configuration creates a favorable ion-transport environment, while the interconnected polymer network intimately integrates the electrode components. This tailored architecture promotes efficient lithium-ion transport and enables robust, binder-free solid-state battery operation. More details can be found in the Research Article by Sang Uck Lee, Pil J. Yoo, Patrice Rannou, and co-workers (DOI:  10.1002/advs.202600063 ).

title: Saturation barcoding of ribosomal DNA resolves the nucleolar organizer regions of the human genome
abstract: The nucleolus is the hub for ribosome biogenesis in eukaryotic cells. It is assembled on nucleolar organizer regions (NORs), tandem arrays of ribosomal DNA (rDNA) units. In humans, each rDNA unit is ~45 kb and encodes the 47S ribosomal RNA (rRNA) precursor. Hundreds of rDNA units are present per germline genome, spread across 10 NORs positioned on the short arms of the five acrocentric chromosomes. However, their precise count and structure are unknown. In fact, twenty-five years after the first draft of the human genome, NORs are the only regions of the human genome that remain incompletely resolved, represented in telomere-to-telomere (T2T) reference genomes as gaps or modeled sequences rather than bona fide assemblies. Here we use prime editing to insert degenerate 6-bp DNA barcodes to 99% of taggable rDNA units in a clonal derivative of the leukemia-derived K562 cell line. Following ultra-long-read sequencing, these barcodes serve as molecular identifiers that guide the end-to-end assembly of all 18 NORs of K562s pseudotriploid genome. The assembly yields: (i) a precise rDNA copy number for each NOR (range 5-43; total 290); (ii) the cis- and trans- architecture of intragenomic variation in rDNA sequence, both structural and fine-scale; and (iii) patterns of divergence and homogenization within and across NORs that may have arisen during cancer evolution and the subsequent passaging of this line. Finally, by reading the same tags from RNA, we define the relationship between DNA methylation and Pol I transcription at the resolution of individual rDNA units. Together, our study demonstrates how the final tangles of the human genome can at last be resolved, and opens the door to more extensive investigations of how genetic, epigenetic and functional rDNA variation contributes to health and disease.

title: Single-nucleus long-read RNA sequencing reveals isoform usage shifts in mouse acute kidney injury
abstract: Introduction Single-cell and single-nucleus short-read RNA sequencing has elucidated transcriptomic changes across kidney cell types at the gene expression level. However, its limited read length precludes reliable isoform identification, hindering the characterization of individual protein-coding isoforms and non-protein-coding isoforms. We combined long-read sequencing with single-cell and single-nucleus RNA sequencing technologies to investigate isoform regulation in healthy and acutely injured mouse kidneys. Methods Single-cell and single-nucleus long-read RNA sequencing datasets were generated from kidneys of three healthy adult male C57BL/6J mice. An additional three adult male C57BL/6J mice underwent bilateral renal ischemia-reperfusion injury, and kidneys were subjected to single-nucleus long-read RNA sequencing. Results A total of 1.3 billion reads were generated, with a median read length of 757-884 bases across samples. Single-nucleus libraries yielded a smaller proportion of reads assigned to isoforms than single-cell libraries, reflecting their larger proportion of intronic reads. Nevertheless, single-nucleus libraries detected more distinct isoforms and greater isoform expression diversity, partly owing to the near absence of mitochondrial gene-derived transcripts. Single-nucleus analysis of healthy and injured kidneys revealed that ischemia-reperfusion injury downregulated oxidative phosphorylation-associated genes in proximal tubule cells both at the gene expression level and through shifts in isoform composition. Beyond oxidative phosphorylation-associated genes, Fut9 and Prrc2b were identified as genes exhibiting prominent shifts in isoform usage after ischemia-reperfusion injury. Conclusion Single-nucleus long-read RNA sequencing detected injury-induced shifts in isoform usage in mouse kidney, adding a layer of transcriptomic information that is largely inaccessible to conventional gene-level short-read analysis.

title: The chromosome-scale genome of the drought-adapted Caatinga tree Spondias tuberosa reveals a conserved, unduplicated architecture within Anacardiaceae
abstract: Spondias tuberosa (umbu) is a tree endemic to the semi-arid Caatinga of north-eastern Brazil, adapted to recurrent drought and high temperatures. Although genomes of mango (Mangifera indica), pistachio (Pistacia vera) and cashew (Anacardium occidentale) are available, comparative analyses of genome evolution across Anacardiaceae remain scarce. We aimed to generate a chromosome-scale reference genome for S. tuberosa and use it to examine genome architecture, meiotic recombination and gene family evolution within the family. We assembled the genome of a single individual using PacBio HiFi and Omni-C (Hi-C) data, mapped meiotic crossovers by single-nucleus RNA sequencing of pollen, and compared the genome with those of six other Sapindales species through orthology, synteny, synonymous substitution (Ks) and gene family expansion/contraction analyses within a dated phylogenomic framework. The assembly anchors 288 Mb onto 16 chromosomes (98.8% BUSCO completeness) and contains 24,232 protein-coding genes, 52.01% repetitive DNA and 1.78 million heterozygous SNPs (0.62%). We identified 1,740 crossovers in 153 pollen nuclei (4.01 cM.Mb1), which were depleted in repeat-rich pericentromeric regions.
