Ks analyses revealed a whole-genome duplication shared by Mangifera and Anacardium that is absent from S. tuberosa, which retains only the ancient {gamma} triplication. The 97 gene families expanded in S. tuberosa, mostly through tandem duplication, include receptor-like kinases, glutathione S-transferases and disease-resistance proteins, consistent with roles in environmental sensing and stress tolerance. Genome structure has remained highly conserved across Sapindales, except in the mango cashew lineage, which underwent extensive rearrangements following a whole-genome duplication. As sister to the remaining Anacardiaceae sampled and with an unduplicated, largely collinear architecture, S. tuberosa provides a reference for comparative mapping and for transferring genomic information to economically important woody relatives.

title: A chromosome-level genome assembly of the endangered northern dragonhead sap beetle, Thymogethes norvegicus (Easton, 1959)
abstract: The northern dragonhead sap beetle (Thymogethes norvegicus) is believed to be endemic to Norway and is classified as endangered. Its life cycle is closely tied to the host plant northern dragonhead (Dracocephalum ruyschiana), itself classified as vulnerable in Norway. Here, we present a chromosome-level genome assembly of a male T. norvegicus. The assembly comprises two pseudo-haplotypes, hap1 and hap2, of 1,142 and 1,109 Mb, with 96.3% and 96.8% scaffolded into chromosomes, respectively. Hap1 contains 8 autosomes and the X chromosome, while hap2 contains 8 autosomes. Assembly quality was high, with conserved single-copy ortholog completeness scores of 96.6% and 90.7% and combined k-mer completeness of 98.1%. A total of 13,484 and 12,550 protein-coding genes were annotated in hap1 and hap2, respectively. This assembly provides a valuable genomic resource for the conservation of this endangered endemic species totally dependent on the vulnerable plant, the northern dragonhead.

title: RNA Small-Molecule Binding-Site Prediction by Integrating RNA Language Models and Structural Geometry
abstract: RNAs are emerging as promising therapeutic targets, and small-molecule binding can modulate their structure and function, creating opportunities for therapeutic development. Accurate identification of RNA small-molecule binding sites is therefore important for understanding RNA-ligand interactions and facilitating RNA-targeted drug discovery. However, the structural complexity of RNA and the limited availability of experimentally characterized RNA-ligand complexes pose challenges for computational binding-site prediction. In this study, we propose RSMBind, a graph attention-based deep learning framework for nucleotide-level prediction of RNA-small molecule binding sites. The model integrates geometric descriptors of the local three-dimensional environment with pretrained RNA language model embeddings to capture complementary structural and sequence information. We investigate three pretrained RNA language models RNA-BERT, ERNIE-RNA and RNA-FM and assess the contributions of sequence representations and geometric features through feature-level ablation experiments. The model is developed using the TR60 and HARIBOSS datasets and evaluated on four independent benchmark datasets: RB9, TE18, TL12 and JL10. RSMBind achieves the highest MCC among the compared methods on three of the four benchmarks, with relative improvements of 17.1% on RB9, 7.2% on TL12 and 16.0% on JL10 over the best previously reported results, while achieving competitive performance on TE18. Furthermore, RSMBind retains predictive capability when using only pretrained RNA language model embeddings, highlighting their potential utility when explicit tertiary structural features are unavailable. Structural analysis indicates differences in prediction performance across RNA structural regions, with loop-associated binding sites generally being captured more effectively than those embedded within stem regions. Additionally, 100 ns molecular dynamics simulations of selected RNA-ligand complexes provide insights into the relationship between predicted binding probabilities and dynamic ligand proximity, further highlighting the role of conformational dynamics in evaluating structure-based predictions. The source code is available at [ https://github.com/sharma-nandita/RSMBind].

title: Leveraging state-of-the-art AI structure predictors to generate atomic resolution ensembles of intrinsically disordered proteins
abstract: Intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) are central to many biological processes, but their function depends on dynamic conformational ensembles rather than a single structure. Despite the impact of artificial intelligence on protein structure prediction, determining these ensembles at atomistic resolution remains challenging. Recently, we introduced bAIes, a framework that leverages the structural information encoded in AlphaFold2 distograms to generate conformational ensembles of IDPs at atomistic resolution. Here, we extend this framework to six state-of-the-art structure prediction tools (AlphaFold2, AlphaFold3, Boltz-1, Boltz-2, ESMFold, and ESMFold2) and systematically compare the structural information encoded in their predicted inter-residue distance distributions. Despite differences between predictors, we show that bAIes generates ensembles with comparable accuracy against experimental NMR and SAXS data, and competitive performance relative to state-of-the-art all-atom simulations and alternative IDP ensemble generation methods. These results demonstrate that bAIes is robust to the choice of structure predictor and that the distance distributions generated by different deep learning architectures contain valuable information about the conformational preferences of disordered proteins. More broadly, our work highlights the potential of combining AI-derived structural information with physics-based modeling to generate atomistic ensembles of intrinsically disordered proteins and regions.

title: Rise and Fall of a Superbug: Analyzing the epidemic success of a distinct clone of vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium ST117/CT71 in Germany, 2017 - 2024.
abstract: Vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium (VREfm) is a major cause of healthcare-associated infections, yet outbreak analysis remains challenging, particularly for prevalent lineages. One of the most striking examples is the Sequence Type (ST) 117/Complex Type (CT) 71/vanB lineage, whose rapid expansion across Germany coincided with a sharp rise in VRE prevalence observed around 2019. Defining reliable genomic thresholds remains particularly difficult, as current core-genome Multi-Locus Sequence Typing (cgMLST) cutoffs are based largely on expert consensus or limited case series. Here, we evaluate the discriminatory performance of cgMLST and split k-mer analysis (SKA) for resolving relatedness within ST117/CT71 and investigate whether low core-genome diversity represents a lineage-specific trait or a population-wide property of E. faecium. While cgMLST captures the overall population structure of ST117/CT71, SKA provided higher resolution, distinguishing isolates identical by cgMLST. Analysis of 2,505 genomes showed that ST117/CT71 does not exhibit reduced allelic variability compared with other hospital-adapted lineages, suggesting that limited core-genome diversity is a broader population characteristic. Complementary transposon analyses further identified two temporally distinct ST117/CT71 sublineages carrying different Tn1549-like structures. To assess allelic variation within confirmed transmission events, we analyzed 138 outbreak clusters from 96 hospitals. Outbreak-associated isolates showed sharply compressed allelic differences (median = 1), with 90% of pairwise comparisons falling within [≤]9 alleles. Thus, the commonly applied [≤]20-allele threshold risks overestimating genomic relatedness and grouping unrelated isolates. Based on these data, we propose lowering the cgMLST alert threshold to [≤]9 alleles for initial cluster detection of local outbreaks, followed by confirmatory high-resolution analyses such as SKA.

title: Non-coding RNA controls long-range enhancer-promoter interactions
abstract: Transcription regulation depends on interactions between enhancers and gene promoters, which often occur over large genomic distances. The molecular drivers of long-range enhancer-promoter interactions remain poorly understood. Enhancers themselves are known to be transcribed into non-coding RNAs, but the function of these transcripts is unclear. Here, we use acute genetic and chemical perturbations of transcription elongation and termination to study the role of non-coding RNA in enhancer-promoter interactions. By integrating high-resolution 3D genome mapping, transcriptomics, proteomics, biochemistry and live-cell super-resolution imaging in these perturbation contexts, we demonstrate that a strong increase in RNA molecules at enhancers disrupts their long-range interactions with gene promoters, whereas decreased RNA levels lead to stabilization of these interactions. Using separation-of-function perturbations, we show that this regulatory function of RNA is independent from the process of transcription and the proteins recruited to initiate transcription. Functionally, we show that RNA-mediated disruption of enhancer-promoter interactions is associated with reduced transcription of target genes, indicating a regulatory feedback mechanism. Together, our results uncover an additional regulatory principle of enhancer-promoter interactions mediated by non-coding RNA.

title: Pocket similarity guided selection of protein targets for systematic protein ligand dataset generation
abstract: The scarcity of large, diverse, and unbiased protein ligand binding datasets limits the performance of machine learning approaches in drug discovery, particularly for understudied proteins. The Target 2035 initiative aims to address this gap by generating open-access binding data for more than 2,000 human proteins, a goal whose value depends on maximizing the diversity of the selected targets. Because proteins with different folds can share chemically analogous binding sites, we reasoned that pocket similarity, rather than sequence or fold similarity, is the appropriate criterion for selecting representative targets that maximize coverage of the human pocketome. Here, we use PocketVec, an alignment-free descriptor of binding sites, to map the human globular pocketome, identifying 51,535 predicted druggable pockets across 15,559 proteins. A two level hierarchical clustering, first within protein families and then across the whole proteome, grouped these pockets into 1,865 clusters of chemically similar binding sites. After discarding 533 clusters containing pockets with known ligands, we selected the 100 most populated of the remaining 1,332 ligand free clusters and chose two high quality representative pockets per cluster, ranked by their resemblance to known ligand-binding sites. Finally, we implemented two complementary prioritization strategies, one favoring structurally unexplored proteins and the other proteins amenable to experimental follow up, and selected 200 pockets from 100 different clusters from each strategy, with 89 clusters in common. Both selections cover over 10,000 pockets in ~5,600 proteins, approximately 36% of the human proteins with annotated druggable pockets, which represents a 2.8- to 4.4-fold increase in the number of covered pockets, domains, and proteins than random selection baselines. This pocket based framework offers a principled strategy to select diverse targets for Target 2035 and other large scale protein ligand data generation efforts in chemical biology.

title: CellVocal Attributes Transcriptional Dynamics to Spatial Signalling
abstract: Understanding how local signalling shapes cell-state transitions requires linking spatial context to transcriptional dynamics. Here we present CellVocal, a framework that integrates spatial RNA velocity with cell-cell communication to decompose cell-state transitions into intrinsic and communication-associated components and further attribute their contributions to signalling modules and neighbouring sender cells. CellVocal recovered complex trajectories and communication perturbations in simulations and reconstructed coherent dynamics and spatially restricted ligand-receptor programmes across the mouse brain, gut and lung. Further analyses linked inferred NCAM1-NCAM1 signalling to lower cell-cycle-associated RNA velocity during embryonic neurogenesis. In melanoma, inferred local MIF-CD74+CD44 signalling corresponded to a predicted decline in the melanocytic programme. Analysis of acute liver failure identified hepatocyte-derived ANGPTL4-SDC1 signalling in association with acetaminophen-related communication enrichment and predicted matrix-remodelling RNA dynamics. By converting static ligand-receptor maps into velocity-constrained networks of signalling influence, CellVocal provides a general strategy for generating spatially resolved hypotheses about how intercellular communication contributes to predicted transcriptional changes.

title: Detection of Maximal Exact Matches in Terabases of Genome Assemblies in Compressed Space and Sublinear Time
abstract: Detection of long exact matches between a pair of genomes has historically been a fundamental operation in genomics. Similarly, detection of long exact matches between all pairs of haplotypes in a large panel of genotyping array data or whole-genome sequencing variant calls is a fundamental operation in population genetics. Thanks to various recent pangenome efforts, for the first time, large panels of high-quality genome assemblies are being constructed. Therefore, we propose the intersection of these two approaches: detection of long exact matches between all pairs of assemblies in panels of hundreds to thousands of high-quality assemblies. Since these datasets would contain trillions of basepairs, practically detecting all exact matches requires algorithms operating in at most linear time and compressed space. Previous methods such as Mumemto achieve this, but running them on terabase-sized pangenomes still took very large space and long time. Here, we describe more efficient algorithms for outputting all long exact matches between all pairs of assemblies in compressed space and sublinear time given a compressed index of the panel. Given the construction of an O(r) space compressed index--a one-time cost that can be done in compressed space and close to linear time with previous work--we describe three algorithms taking O(r) words of memory: (1) computing all supermaximal exact matches (SMEMs) in O(r) time, (2) computing all supermaximal exact matches and their occurrences in O(r + occ) time, and (3) computing all maximal exact matches (MEMs) in O(r + occ) time, where r is the number of runs in the Burrows-Wheeler transform of the panel of assemblies and occ is the number of occurrences or matches outputted. Our algorithms use 7.5 times less memory than state-of-the-art competitors on a dataset of human centromere assemblies from 625 haplotypes. They are also 20 times faster if index construction time is counted, and 2,500 times faster if index construction is excluded. Finally, we perform an analysis of all-vs-all MEMs in all well-assembled centromeres of the Human Pangenome Reference Consortium Release 2 dataset that reveals multiple novel insights into structural variation in centromeres. For example, we find that the active -satellite higher-order repeat (HOR) array of Chromosome 2 is flanked by a ~200 kbp inversion on one side and a ~200-300 kbp pseudopalindromic sequence on the other. We also detect large segmental duplications in the centromere of every chromosome except Chromosome Y. These segmental duplications range in size from hundreds of kbp to multiple Mbp and occur both in and out of the active -satellite HOR arrays. Our computational results make pairwise MEM analyses possible in pangenomes, while our biological results show they are likely to be useful. Our algorithms are implemented as TeraMEM in the TeraTools suite available at https://github.com/ucfcbb/TeraTools.

title: Basic-peptide depletion and precursor masking in bottom-up proteomics
abstract: Biomarker proteomics studies report protein identities at the canonical precursor level, yet the underlying mass-spectrometry evidence consists of peptides whose physicochemical properties may diverge from the annotated protein. We reanalyzed peptide-level evidence from public datasets with a proteoform-aware pipeline that maps detected peptides to canonical sequences under a five-level confidence taxonomy, computes sequence-derived physicochemical features for precursors, peptides, and detected regions, and tests class-composition bias against digestion-matched backgrounds. Across ten public studies spanning five result-file formats and 70,020 peptide-evidence rows, detected peptides are depleted in the basic isoelectric-point class relative to their own proteins' theoretical tryptic peptides (fixed-effect odds ratio 0.45, 95% CI 0.44-0.46; leave-one-study-out envelope 0.44-0.49). The depletion is absent among fully tryptic peptides (OR 1.06) and concentrates in missed-cleavage peptides (OR 0.62-0.57), is invariant to detected-abundance stratification, and retains its direction under three independent pI-calculator models. Case studies reveal both directions of precursor-centric masking. Two orthogonal validations ground the framework: a digestion-free synthetic-peptide analysis (basic-class odds ratio 0.73, 95% CI 0.71-0.76 under standard DDA) and a paired top-down benchmark, in which detected regions recover top-down sequence space (90% of spans overlapped) but do not delimit proteoform boundaries (8% containment). Pipeline, data, and code are public.

title: Investigating the causal and consequential role of the nuclear encoded mitochondrial genome in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis
abstract: Mitochondrial dysfunction is implicated in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), but which mitochondrial pathways are involved, and whether their involvement is a cause or a consequence of disease remains unclear. We investigated whether nuclear-encoded mitochondrial gene (NEMG) pathways are enriched for ALS genetic risk, which are dysregulated in ALS tissue, whether pathway activity defines patient subgroups that differ in survival, and whether co-expression between the nuclear and mitochondrial genomes is altered. We tested MitoCarta3.0 pathways for enrichment of ALS genetic risk using MAGMA and the largest European ALS GWAS to date (27,205 cases and 110,881 controls), using hierarchical testing across pathway tiers, and annotated the direction of gene-level effects using published TWAS and SMR results. In >1,500 bulk RNA-seq samples from post-mortem motor cortex and spinal cord (KCL Brain Bank, NYGC ALS Consortium) and iPSC-derived motor neurones (Answer ALS), we performed cell type adjusted gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA), gene set variation analysis (GSVA)-based clustering with exploratory survival analysis, and nuclear-mitochondrial co-expression analysis. Of seven broad mitochondrial categories, only the mitochondrial central dogma was enriched for ALS risk after correction (Padj = 0.044). Hierarchical testing within this pathway localised the signal to translation (Padj = 0.008) and the mitoribosome (Padj = 0.014). Genetically predicted expression pointed in opposite directions for different mitoribosomal genes (lower MRPS33 and higher MRPL28 expression with increased risk), and did not agree in direction with differential expression in ALS tissue more often than expected by chance. A nominal enrichment in ROS and glutathione metabolism was largely attributable to SOD1. In tissue, mitochondrial genes were broadly more highly expressed in ALS motor cortex in both cohorts, largely as a global shift across mitochondrial genes. OXPHOS subunits and the mitoribosome were enriched beyond this shift in ALS Consortium motor cortex (both PFDR = 0.027), as were OXPHOS subunits in iPSC-derived motor neurones (PFDR = 2.4 x 10-), whereas spinal cord showed no genome-wide enrichment. GSVA based clusters were associated with diagnosis in motor cortex, and nominally with survival in lumbar spinal cord (adjusted HR 0.69, Punadj = 0.013), where cluster structure was weakest. No individual pathway was associated with survival after correction in adjusted models. In all four post-mortem tissues, nuclear-encoded mitochondrial genes were more negatively co-expressed with mtDNA-encoded genes in ALS than in controls, most strongly in lumbar spinal cord, whereas iPSC-derived motor neurones showed the opposite pattern. In conclusion, inherited ALS risk shows a modest enrichment centred on mitochondrial translation, with gene specific rather than uniform directions of effect. The same pathway, alongside OXPHOS, is more highly expressed in end-stage ALS motor cortex, which may reflect a response to disease, residual differences in cell composition, or both. At the gene level, genetically predicted and observed expression changes did not agree in direction, so whether inherited risk and these tissue changes are linked remains unresolved.

title: scDeepSim: Deep Generative Simulation for Controlled Benchmarking of Single-Cell Methods
abstract: Benchmarking single-cell computational methods requires both realistic data and reliable ground truth. However, annotating real datasets is costly and, even when available, may not fully represent the diverse settings where methods are used. Simulators address this gap by generating synthetic data that has fully specified ground truth and whose structure can be tailored to challenge competing methods. Existing single-cell simulators can broadly be divided into statistical and deep generative classes. Statistical simulators offer interpretable parameters for controlling simulated data, but their modeling assumptions may not accurately represent real data. Deep generative models can learn complex expression patterns, but it remains unclear how to transparently control individual biological or technical factors without introducing unintended effects. We introduce scDeepSim, a simulator that combines a structured variational autoencoder with latent diffusion to generate synthetic single-cell expression profiles. It allows users to intervene on selected biological or technical factors at user-specified strengths, producing realistic datasets with benchmark ground truth. We demonstrate this capability by benchmarking batch correction and trajectory inference methods, showing how batch-effect strength affects batch mixing and cell-type preservation, and how trajectory geometry and noise affect pseudotime recovery. scDeepSim therefore enables researchers to vary selected biological and technical factors in realistic simulated data and assess how these changes affect the performance of single-cell analysis methods, helping understand when such methods may be appropriately applied. Code for the scDeepSim simulator and experiments is available at https://github.com/LangtianM/scDeepSim.

title: Assessing the Capacity of Genomic Language Models to Generate Informative Embeddings of Viral Genome Fragments
abstract: Genomic language models (gLMs) trained on large volumes of nucleotide sequences are becoming an alternative to classical methods in metagenomic analysis, particularly for studying genomic "dark matter". In this work, we investigate the ability of four gLMs (DNABERT-2, DNABERT-S, ViraLM, and Evo2-7B) to generate taxonomically informative vector representations of short viral genome fragments. We constructed a balanced reference dataset of viruses based on the ICTV Virus Metadata Resource and compared the representations generated by gLMs with conventional k-mer profiles and MinHash sketches using clustering and neighborhood-based metrics (adjusted Rand index (ARI), precision@k, and CROSS precision@k). On the reference dataset, three of the four gLMs outperformed the 4-mer profile in terms of ARI and precision@5 under the same evaluation protocol. The best performance was generally achieved by intermediate model layers. Conventional k-mer profiles consistently outperformed MinHash sketches. We further evaluated the methods on two viral orders (egoviruses and mriyaviruses) absent from the reference dataset, with model layers and k-mer lengths selected exclusively on the reference dataset. DNABERT-S showed the most consistently strong performance across these two orders, ranking first on mriyaviruses and second on egoviruses, while k-mer profiles with Jensen-Shannon distance remained competitive. We also observed the consistency of representations between forward fragments and their reverse complements. Overall, the best-performing gLMs surpassed conventional baselines, although their advantage depended on the dataset and evaluation metric. The consistently strong performance of DNABERT-S suggests a potential benefit of contrastive fine-tuning and indicates that larger models are not necessarily more effective for generating taxonomically informative representations.

title: SIFT: Syncmer-Informed Selection of Haplotypes for T2T Imputation
abstract: Genome patching improves the completeness of fragmented assemblies by filling unresolved gaps with sequences from reference genomes. Pangenome panels provide diverse candidate haplotypes for this task, but identifying suitable references efficiently becomes increasingly challenging as these panels grow. We present SIFT, a compressed indexing method for selecting reference haplotypes for genome patching with ImpuT2T. SIFT combines closed-syncmer parsing, phrase-level indexing, and pseudo-maximal exact match (pseudo-MEM) queries. Closed syncmers provide a context-independent parsing rule with bounded distances between consecutive selected positions, enabling consistent parsing of reference and query sequences. We demonstrate that two closed syncmers determine the distance at which they can occur consecutively in any string, so that equal substrings of two parses represent identical sequences and no gap sequence need be stored. SIFT indexes the reference parse and its reverse using run-length compressed suffix arrays and adapts the Boyer-Moore-Li search procedure to identify pseudo-MEMs between the reference parse and query parse. It then aggregates matching evidence to identify candidate reference haplotypes for downstream patching. This framework connects compressed sequence indexing with haplotype selection and provides a basis for querying large reference panels at the phrase level. SIFT is publicly available under the GNU license at https://github.com/EddieFerro/SIFT.

title: CellChat Hotspot: A Targeted Approach to Cell Cell Communication Analysis With Spatial transcriptomics Validation.
abstract: Abstract. In recent years, single cell RNA sequencing (scRNA seq) has enabled the investigation of intercellular communication through Cell Cell Communication (CCC) tools such as CellChat. Despite their potential, these approaches remain challenging to interpret, particularly when global analyses generate complex interaction networks that may include biologically irrelevant signals. To address this limitation, we developed a framework termed CellChat Hotspot, designed to improve the biological interpretability of inferred communication networks. This approach integrates gene set enrichment analysis with a context driven filtering strategy, selecting both genes and cells based on their functional relevance prior to communication inference. Applied to stage II colon cancer data, CellChat Hotspot enabled the identification of condition-specific interaction patterns associated with recurrence. Non recurrent patients showed enrichment of immune related processes, whereas recurrent cases were characterized by pathways associated with invasion and metastasis. Notably, a loss of interaction in the HSPG pathway between CALB1+ and stromal cells was observed in recurrent patients, suggesting a potential disruption of cell matrix adhesion mechanisms. To verify the reliability of this finding, we applied the framework to spatial transcriptomics data, which confirmed the presence of the HSPG2 DAG1 interaction in non-recurrent tumors and its near absence in recurrent ones. Overall, this framework provides a biologically guided strategy for studying intercellular communication in complex systems such as the tumor microenvironment.

title: Using Oyster Genomics to Understand Human Health
abstract: As sessile filter feeders that experience continuous environmental exposure, oysters, particularly Crassostrea virginica, offer a unique opportunity to understand how environmental exposure alters the genome and influence health. Furthermore, oysters must be sorted by size for market value for premium size and taste. However, it requires intensive labor, specialized equipment (tumblers), and is susceptible to environmental risks like pollution. Therefore, it is desirable to produce uniform oysters without machines. However, limitations in the previous reference genome [2] have constrained our understanding of how genes are organized and maintained in oyster populations. To this end, we harvested 240 adult oysters in same location, 120 extremely large size and 120 extremely small, controlled with all confounding factors such as age and water temperature. We perform a genome wide associate study (GWAS) using next generation whole genome sequencing, aiming to discover genomic regions associated with oyster size. Using PacBio HiFi, Illumina, and Hi-C technologies, we generated a 99.7% complete chromosome-level genome assembly for C. virginica (NCBI RefSeq GCF_053477285.1) [75]. We identified a ~13 Mb region on chromosome 1 uniquely expanded in C. virginica and enriched for innate immune and stress-response genes. To evaluate whether these structural features are reflected at the population level, we then conducted a k-mer analysis. This revealed differential sequence patterns by size, including enrichment of bacterial DNA in smaller individuals and host variation at the RNF213 locus within this region. By highlighting genome structure as a mediator of immune resilience, this work supports the use of oysters as sentinels to advance out understanding of how the dynamic reassembly of the genome due to environmental exposures influence health in human populations.

title: Long-read analysis of complete human 5S rDNA arrays reveals a zoned organization with two-state unit methylation linked to chromatin architecture
abstract: Despite the fundamental importance of the 5S ribosomal DNA (rDNA) to all cellular life, the landscape of its units by position along its array has remained poorly understood. Here, recent telomere-to-telomere long-read sequencing is used to resolve 5S rDNA arrays from flank to flank and to follow the state of each unit along single molecules. The array is zoned at both the sequence and the epigenetic level. Notably, methylation is bimodal at the level of the unit, and the combination of low-methylation and high-methylation units gives rise to the overall methylation pattern of the array. Moreover, the average number of low-methylation units remains relatively constant regardless of array length. Chromatin fiber sequencing (Fiber-seq) data further show that low-methylation units are more accessible, have lower nucleosome occupancy and are more frequently footprinted at the TFIIIB-binding site, consistent with analyses of ATAC-seq and ChIP-seq data from cell lines. Across species, this pattern is shared among apes, whereas other species show diverse patterns. These results provide a unit-resolved view of the human 5S rDNA array and reveal a zone-specific organization of unit methylation that is associated with chromatin architecture.

title: Genome-wide diversity across 130 years reveals drastic post-bottleneck genetic erosion in a recovering population of golden eagles (Aquila chrysaetos)
abstract: Many wild populations have experienced severe human-induced declines, but the genetic consequences of such bottlenecks are often poorly understood. In Finland, as well as in many other countries, golden eagles were heavily persecuted during the 19th-20th centuries, disappearing from southern regions and reaching their lowest population size in the 1950-1960s. Although conservation efforts facilitated demographic recovery, the long-term genomic consequences of the bottleneck remained unknown. Here, we used whole-genome sequencing data spanning 136 years to evaluate patterns of genetic diversity in 26 Finnish golden eagles before, during, and after the mid-20th century bottleneck. We found substantial loss of genetic variation, including an 82% reduction in genome-wide heterozygosity, a 42% decline in nucleotide diversity, a 67% reduction in Watterson's theta, and a substantial loss of variable sites. Analyses of the site frequency spectrum and Tajima's D confirmed historical population contraction, and runs of homozygosity analysis indicated elevated post-bottleneck inbreeding. These results indicate strong genetic erosion in Finnish golden eagles despite the census size recovery. Therefore, incorporating genomic indicators in conservation monitoring and performing regional assessments are necessary to guide management and preserve biodiversity in line with the Global Biodiversity Framework's goal of maintaining genetic variation.

title: Pepti-DrugPhAI: Multimodal AI-evaluator for functional pharmacokinetics and toxicity of peptides
abstract:
by Elizaveta A. Bogdanova, Timofei F. Lukianov, Artem V. Chernukhin, Alexey K. Shaytan 

Peptide drugs exhibit exceptional selectivity for biological targets and high functional activity making them among the most promising therapeutic agents. However, unsatisfactory pharmacokinetic characteristics remain a critical barrier to their implementation. They often become the primary reason for the failure of promising candidates in preclinical and clinical trials. To address this issue, we present Pepti-DrugPhAI – a comprehensive algorithm for the precise prediction of the pharmacokinetics and toxicity of a wide range of peptide compounds. Unlike many existing solutions, the proposed algorithm is multimodal and can simultaneously process both SMILES representations of chemical structures and amino acid sequences. This ensures efficient processing not only of canonical peptides but also of non-canonical modifications, cyclic structures, and peptide-like small molecules. We also created an original dataset for model training integrating data from public databases and relevant scientific publications. The algorithm simultaneously predicts key parameters including membrane permeability (Caco-2 and PAMPA penetration), distribution and excretion (half-life, clearance, volume of distribution), as well as general and specific toxicity profiles (neurotoxicity, hemolytic activity). A key innovation of the study is the integration of functional pharmacokinetic scoring. The model not only predicts ADMET values but also calculates an adaptive suitability rating for a compound in the context of its specific biological activity. We have conducted a comparative analysis of various data encoding strategies implementing a stack of models ranging from classical machine learning methods to modern transformers and language models in classification modes. Results from testing on independent test sets demonstrate high prediction accuracy and interpretability of features making Pepti-DrugPhAI a powerful tool for more robust selection of promising peptide drug candidates. All data and the code are available in the GitHub repository at https://github.com/EABogdanova/Pepti-DrugPhAI.

title: Sphinx: An R package for adaptive spatial neighborhood modeling and functional analysis in spatial omics
abstract:
by Mengyi Yan, Xiaoxiu Tan, Zhenhao Liu, Siwen Zhang, Yiwen Du, Hong Li, Lanming Chen, Lu Xie 

Spatial omics enables analysis of tissue microenvironmental heterogeneity, but most spatial tools are optimized for transcriptomics and poorly suited to proteomics data. We developed Sphinx, an R package providing a comprehensive workflow for spatial proteomics, including preprocessing, cell annotation, adaptive spatial neighborhood modeling, and functional characterization. Importantly, it introduces an adaptive parameter selection framework guided by spatial statistical metrics and incorporates computational optimizations for large-scale datasets, enabling robust neighborhood modeling. Notably, Sphinx offers improved computational efficiency and scalability. Across lung adenocarcinoma, colorectal cancer, and mouse spleen datasets, Sphinx robustly identifies cell types and spatial functional units, including tertiary lymphoid structures. We also explored the application of Sphinx to paired high-resolution spatial transcriptomics datasets, illustrating its potential applicability. Sphinx provides a flexible and efficient framework for spatial proteomics, enabling robust characterization of spatial organization and tissue microenvironments.

title: Burst-to-burst information resetting in sequential rhythmic neural activity
abstract:
by Pablo Sanchez-Martin, Irene Elices, Alicia Garrido-Peña, Carlos Garcia-Saura, Rafael Levi, Francisco B. Rodriguez, Pablo Varona 

In multiple neural systems, networks of bursting neurons generate and coordinate robust sequential rhythms, such as those observed in central pattern generators (CPGs) that control motor activity. In this paper, we combine electrophysiological experiments and biophysical models of the pyloric CPG to investigate cycle-by-cycle coordination resetting in sequential rhythms. In particular, we focus our analysis on the variability constraints of sequence intervals defined by the burst onset and offset time references, which structure the timing of the rhythmic CPG sequence cycle-by-cycle. We identified the conditions under which sequential dynamical invariants emerge as robust relationships between specific intervals within the same cycle, and when such relations reset at each cycle or extend between intervals of consecutive cycles. Our results help understand the mechanisms underlying the autonomous cycle-by-cycle sequential coordination and the relationships between intervals from consecutive cycles when a slow modulatory action establishes a common trend across the rhythm.

title: An antigen-specific protein language model guides CDR optimization for antibody design
abstract:
by Faisal Bin Ashraf, Karen Paco, Sanaz Zebardast, Zihao Zhang, Ryan Mooney, Christian J. Dávila Ojeda, Mariana Paco Mendivil, Rashid M. Alam, Eva Chen, Iraneus Ogu, Jordan A. Lay, Tristan Y. Yang, Fernando L. Barroso da Silva, Malkiat Johal, Ilya Tolstorukov, Matthew H. Sazinsky, Animesh Ray, Stefano Lonardi 

The capacity of an antibody to recognize and bind an antigen with high specificity and strength (i.e., its  binding affinity ) is a key determinant in the design and optimization of neutralizing antibodies against pathogenic targets. Here we introduce Ab-Affinity, a fine-tuned protein language model (PLM) that predicts the binding affinity of an antibody against a target peptide within the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein. Cross-validation results shows that that Ab-Affinity outperforms other PLM-based affinity predictors when evaluated on a held-out validation and independent test sets. When integrated with a genetic algorithm and simulated annealing for sequence diversification and fitness optimization, Ab-Affinity enables the generation of candidate antibodies exhibiting over 100-fold improvement in predicted binding affinity relative to its parental (natural) antibody. More broadly, antibodies designed with Ab-Affinity attain higher predicted binding affinities than those produced by alternative mutational strategies, yielding synthetic antibodies with favorable predicted biophysical characteristics. Molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations for the strongest synthetic candidates indicate enhanced interactions and increased stability with the target peptide epitope within the spike protein. Experimental validation  in vitro  for a top-ranked candidate reveals an apparent increase in binding relative to its parental antibody. All model weights, source code, and analysis pipelines are publicly released to allow full reproducibility.

title: PhysInfer: A physics-constrained neural network for adaptive inference of transcriptional bursting from single-cell RNA-seq
abstract:
by Xiaodong Zeng, Jingwen Zhang, Shan Li, Haohua Wang 

Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) has established that gene expression is driven by stochastic transcriptional bursting. However, inferring burst dynamics from static scRNA-seq snapshots is fundamentally constrained by parameter unidentifiability and model topology mismatch. Here, we propose PhysInfer, an unsupervised framework that integrates a physics-constrained neural network with adaptive model selection and parameter decoupling. A physics-informed loss function, combining stationary-distribution likelihood with zero-count anchoring, reparameterizes the optimization from unidentifiable microscopic rates to an interpretable macroscopic burst-quantity representation of burst size and burst frequency, thereby providing an interpretable parameterization for assessing practical recoverability in static data. Validation on synthetic data with known ground-truth parameters confirms high inference accuracy in low-to-medium activation regimes and shows that recovery of BS and productive BF becomes increasingly condition-dependent as the ON-state probability approaches saturation; under different recovery criteria, the condition-specific upper Pon limit for simultaneously recovering BS and productive BF varies with cell number and capture efficiency. Applied to a mouse embryonic fibroblast (MEF) dataset, PhysInfer reconstructs a transcriptional dynamic manifold across the 2,137-gene secondary BIC analysis set, showing cross-gene variation in fitted burst frequency and burst size. A model-specific stationary likelihood combined with zero-count anchoring improves robustness to zero-heavy observations. The adaptive topology module further identifies a distinct subset of genes with stable support for an effective sequential 3-state representation, revealing distributional structure beyond that captured by standard 2-state fitting. PhysInfer thus provides a robust, topology-adaptive, and interpretable solution for characterizing transcriptional kinetic patterns from static single-cell transcriptomic snapshots.

title: FDTest: Fluctuation-dissipation theorem as a test for memory effects in brain dynamics
abstract:
by Sebastian Manuel Geli, Juan Manuel Monti, Adrián Ponce-Alvarez, Gustavo Deco, Yonatan Sanz Perl 

A central challenge in neuroscience is to understand how the brain flexibly balances local and distributed information processing to support diverse cognitive and conscious states. We hypothesize that a key signature of this balance is the presence of memory effects, which arise when a brain region’s future activity depends not only on its current state, but also on past information fed back from the wider network. Here we introduce the FDTest, a method for assessing local memory effects in multidimensional systems by measuring violations of a generalized Fluctuation–dissipation theorem (FDT). We first apply this framework to whole-brain models fitted to human neuroimaging data, demonstrating that the brain’s memory structure reflects its underlying connectivity. We then extend the analysis to individualized models of subjects during wakefulness and deep sleep. Memory effects are consistently stronger in wakefulness, indicating richer inter-regional dependencies and more integrated dynamics. These findings establish local memory as a dynamical marker of brain state and position the FDTest as a principled tool for probing the hidden structure of neural dynamics.

title: Spatial transcriptomics defines segmental and temporal dynamics of pig intestinal epithelium
abstract:
Background
                      The pig ( Sus scrofa ) is widely studied as a large-animal model for human gastrointestinal biology, including gut physiology, pathology and disease. However, the spatial and developmental organisation of the pig intestine is not yet fully understood. 
                  
                     Results
                      Here, we generate a comprehensive spatiotemporal atlas of pig intestinal development by applying spatial transcriptomics to three intestinal segments across five developmental stages and an additional four intestinal segments at the adult stage. We identify spatial separation among enterocytes, plasma cells and stem cells, observing more pronounced separation in the small intestine compared to the large intestine. Pseudotime analysis of enterocyte-enriched regions reveals a gradient along the crypt-villus/crypt axis as early as post-conception day 70 in the jejunum, becoming fully evident across all intestinal segments by birth in the large intestine, with all three intestinal segments reaching a mature state by postnatal day 33. Our analysis indicates that the maturation of enterocytes during migration along the crypt-villus axis involves transcriptional programs similar to those governing enterocyte maturation across developmental stages, suggesting conserved molecular mechanisms governing both spatial and temporal differentiation. In the large intestine, nutrient transport-related gene expression declines progressively during development, transitioning from jejunum-like levels at early stages to markedly reduced levels in adulthood, consistent with functional specialization of distinct intestinal segments. 
                  
                     Conclusions
                      Our study provides a high-resolution spatiotemporal framework of pig intestinal development and establishes a valuable resource for comparative biology and translational research.

title: Track display jockey (trackDJ): a user-friendly R package for visualization of epigenomic data
abstract:
Background
                      Visualization of epigenomic data such as coverage tracks, peak calls, and chromatin interactions is a critical task in genomic data analysis. Although genome browsers such as the Integrative Genomics Viewer (IGV) and the UCSC Genome Browser permit user-friendly exploration of genomic tracks, they are not optimized for fully programmatic and reproducible generation of publication-quality figures. In contrast, existing programmatic tools lack a user-friendly interface and require extensive configuration. 
                  
                     Results
                      We present trackDJ (Track Display Jockey), an R package for visualization of epigenomic data.  trackDJ  prioritizes usability by favoring convention over configuration; it provides high-level plotting functions with sensible defaults, aiming to allow users with minimal programming experience to generate clear, publication-quality figures with relatively little coding. Within a unified plotting framework, users can stack and align multiple data types, including coverage tracks, peak annotations, chromatin loops, and gene annotations.  trackDJ  allows users to select plotted genomic regions by coordinates or by gene name, enabling rapid visualization without knowledge of precise locus boundaries. 
                  
                     Conclusions
                       trackDJ  complements existing epigenomics toolkits by providing a user-friendly, reproducible alternative to interactive genome browsers for epigenomic visualization. By enabling scripted generation of clean, customizable genomic illustrations,  trackDJ  readily integrates into R-based analysis workflows to streamline the creation of publication-quality figures.

title: BactFlow: a graphical workflow for bacterial genome assembly and annotation
abstract:
Background
                      Bacterial genome reconstruction increasingly uses short-read, long-read, and hybrid sequencing strategies. However, coordinating read processing, genome assembly, quality assessment, and downstream characterization across these data types can require substantial bioinformatics expertise. 
                  
                     Results
                      We developed BactFlow ( https://github.com/farhadm1990/bactflow ), an open-source interactive app for bacterial single isolate genome assembly and downstream analysis. It supports Nanopore and PacBio long reads, Illumina short reads, and Nanopore-Illumina data for hybrid assembly. A single local browser interface integrates read processing and quality assessment, genome assembly, and post-assembly analysis, with run-status monitoring. BactFlow combines genome-quality assessment, taxonomic classification, gene annotation, plasmid prediction, and interactive genome visualization. We demonstrated four assembly routes using publicly available Nanopore, Illumina, and PacBio datasets, as well as Nanopore-Illumina hybrid assembly. 
                  
                     Conclusions
                      After initial setup on Linux, BactFlow can be launched with a single command line using Docker, Apptainer/Singularity, or Conda. Users can then configure and run analyses through the user interface (UI) without manually invoking each bioinformatics tool. The integrated interface supports bacterial isolate genome analysis across multiple sequencing strategies.

title: TADDM-WMHHGCN: a weighted multi-head hypergraph convolutional network for predicting triple associations among drugs, diseases, and miRNAs
abstract:
Background
                      Associations among drugs, diseases, and microRNAs (miRNAs) are important for elucidating disease mechanisms and supporting drug repositioning. Several computational models predict pairwise drug-disease, drug-miRNA, or miRNA-disease associations. However, few models have addressed associations involving all three entity types, and no model has specifically focused on triple associations among drugs, diseases, and miRNAs (TADDMs). 
                  
                     Results
                      We developed TADDM-WMHHGCN, a weighted multi-head hypergraph convolutional network for predicting TADDMs. Candidate TADDMs were constructed by integrating validated drug-disease, drug-miRNA, and miRNA-disease pairwise associations and were represented using a three-dimensional (3D) adjacency matrix. Raw drug, disease, and miRNA features were derived from this matrix as 3D Gaussian interaction profile (GIP) kernel matrices. We then constructed a weighted heterogeneous hypergraph from the adjacency and GIP kernel matrices. After linear transformation, the raw features were passed through a multi-head hypergraph convolutional network to obtain high-level representations, and a multilayer perceptron decoder generated the predictions. In internal cross-validation on four datasets containing different categories of unlabeled triples of drugs, diseases, and miRNAs, the model achieved AUROC and AUPR values above 0.94 for every dataset. 
                  
                     Conclusions
                      TADDM-WMHHGCN outperformed several existing triple-association prediction models across most evaluation metrics, demonstrating its potential as a tool in the research on the associations among drugs, diseases, and miRNAs.

title: Benchmarking precision matrix estimation methods for differential co-expression network analysis
abstract:
Background
                      Gene expression profiling is widely used to investigate disease mechanisms, but classical approaches such as differential expression or pairwise correlation analyses provide limited interpretability. Network-based differential co-expression methods that model conditional dependencies through partial correlations offer richer insights, yet their application in high-dimensional settings requires estimation of precision matrices. Numerous precision matrix estimation methods (PMEMs) have been proposed, but these are typically validated in a narrow range of simulation settings and benchmarked against only a small number of competing methods, so their relative performance under diverse conditions remains unclear. 
                  
                     Results
                      Simulated gene expression datasets with known ground truth correlation structures were used to benchmark a broad set of PMEMs for their suitability in differential co-expression network analysis of transcriptomic data. Performance was strongly affected by data characteristics, including covariance structure, matrix density, covariance values, sample size-to-dimension ratio, and sampling distribution. Among the evaluated methods,  GLassoElnetFast  generally achieved high accuracy in recovering differential edges across the simulated scenarios, although high signal-to-noise ratios and sufficient sample sizes remain essential for reliable inference. Applying a subset of these methods to a real transcriptomic dataset reproduced this estimator-dependent variability, with limited overlap between the differential edges recovered by different methods. 
                  
                     Conclusions
                      Evaluation across diverse simulation conditions demonstrated that no single metric or condition was sufficient to assess PMEM performance. Therefore, less extensive evaluations may only capture part of this variability and limit the generalizability of their conclusions. Our simulation and benchmarking framework supports future method development and ensures reproducible evaluation of newly developed approaches.

title: LoRA-BERT: a natural language processing model for robust and accurate prediction of long non-coding RNAs
abstract: Long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) are key regulators in many biological processes. While they share some sequence features with messenger RNAs (mRNAs), lncRNAs have distinct functions, opening new research opportunities. Recent advances in next-generation sequencing have made it easier to detect lncRNAs, and deep learning methods are increasingly used to classify these transcripts. Although these methods have significantly improved the efficiency of identifying lncRNAs, they often lack robustness, and the prediction accuracy tends to vary significantly depending on the quality of the transcript. To tackle this issue, we introduce LoRA-BERT, a novel lncRNA prediction algorithm built on the bidirectional encoder representation from transformers (BERT). LoRA-BERT is designed to effectively capture information at the nucleotide level that is important for lncRNA classification, leading to more robust and accurate prediction outcomes that are not significantly affected by the quality of the input transcript. Through performance evaluations on comprehensive benchmarks, we demonstrate that LoRA-BERT outperforms existing schemes in terms of accuracy, efficiency, and robustness. Especially, unlike other methods, LoRA-BERT retains good predictive capability for partial transcripts, a critical feature that makes it applicable for reliable lncRNA prediction even when the sequencing depth is relatively low. Availability and implementation: The code repository is available at  https://github.com/Nick-Jeon/LoRA_BERT .

title: PHI: a Galaxy-based workflow for reproducible prophage-host interaction analysis and standardized viral-genomics reporting
abstract:
Background
                      Viruses that infect bacteria, known as bacteriophages or phages, are widespread in nature and play important roles in shaping microbial communities and ecosystem functions. Some phages can integrate into bacterial genomes as “prophages”, where they may influence the biology of their host by carrying genes that affect metabolism, virulence, or environmental adaptation. Despite their importance, studying prophages and their interactions with bacterial hosts remains challenging because it typically requires combining many complex computational tools and can be resource-intensive. 
                  
                     Results
                      In this study, we introduce the Prophage-Host Interaction Toolkit (PHI), a user-friendly and automated workflow available through the Galaxy platform. PHI brings together multiple established tools into a single, reproducible pipeline that identifies candidate prophages, evaluates their quality, predicts host relationships, and characterizes key functional genes. Importantly, all results are summarized in an interactive report that simplifies interpretation. Applied to the MBARC22 mock community of 22 bacterial reference genomes as a workflow demonstration, PHI identified 41 candidate prophages across 14 hosts, including high- and medium-quality viral genomes. Most host genomes exhibited > 99% completeness and < 1% contamination, while DefenseFinder identified between 3 and 24 antiviral defense systems per genome. To further evaluate applicability to metagenome-derived assemblies, PHI was also applied to three MAGs and their matched reference genomes. Differences in candidate prophage counts and sequence-level correspondence between MAGs and references demonstrated that prophage recovery can be strongly influenced by genome fragmentation and assembly continuity, even in otherwise high-quality MAGs. 
                  
                     Conclusions
                      By removing installation barriers and consolidating the outputs of multiple established tools, PHI lowers the barrier to advanced phage analysis, enabling both specialists and non-experts to explore phage-host interactions and their implications in areas such as microbiome research, biotechnology, and environmental science.

title: Check my sample sheet: a web application for validating illumina sample sheets before demultiplexing
abstract:
Background
                      Proper configuration of an Illumina sequencing run is crucial for ensuring successful outcomes, with the sample sheet serving as a vital component by summarizing sample metadata. Accurate demultiplexing and downstream analysis depend heavily on the correctness of this sample sheet. To address this need, validation of the sample sheet becomes essential to prevent errors during sequencing processes. 
                  
                     Results
                      We present a browser-based web application built using Streamlit, which incorporates the IEM Python module from the Sequana Python library to perform comprehensive sanity checks on Illumina sample sheets. This application allows users to upload or paste sample sheet files through a simple interface that requires no installation, where automated validation checks are performed. These checks assess key parameters such as sample duplication, consistency, and adherence to Illumina formatting standards. 
                  
                     Conclusions
                      HierHGT-DTI provides an effective multiscale relation-aware framework for cold-start DTI predictiConclusions. The “Check My Sample Sheet" web application enables users to preemptively detect and resolve potential issues in their sample sheets, reducing errors and improving sequencing outcomes. The application supports both the legacy bcl2fastq (v1) and the newer bclconvert (v2, BCL Convert) sample sheet formats, detecting the version automatically. Additionally, the application’s open-source nature supports extensibility, making it adaptable to specific workflow requirements.

title: Beyond leaf mass per area: anatomical and economic drivers of toughness in evergreen and deciduous oaks
abstract:
SUMMARY 
 We examined how leaf habit (deciduous versus evergreen) shapes the structural, mechanical, and chemical traits of oaks (genus  Quercus ), aiming to determine whether evergreen leaf toughness arises from intrinsic chemical investment or greater tissue allocation per unit area. Leaves from 33 oak species were sampled, focusing on interveinal lamina. Morphological traits (LMA, thickness, density), mechanical properties, and cell wall composition (cellulose, hemicellulose, lignin, cutin, nitrogen) were measured. The fiber fraction composition was used to estimate the construction costs and heat of combustion. Comparisons between deciduous and evergreen species were made on area- and mass-bases. Evergreen leaves had higher leaf mass per area, thickness, and toughness than deciduous leaves, with partial overlap in LMA. Area-based investments in cell wall polymers and construction costs were consistently higher in evergreens. Mass-based fiber construction costs were lower in evergreens, reflecting the dominance of metabolically inexpensive polysaccharides, whereas deciduous fibers contained more energetically costly compounds such as lignin and cutin. Evergreen leaf toughness is primarily driven by tissue quantity (LMA) and specific anatomical reinforcement rather than intrinsic fiber cost. Deciduous leaves are mechanically weaker, despite higher mass-based fiber cost. These results highlight a decoupling between chemical investment and mechanical properties and show how leaf structural design underpins functional divergence between leaf habits.

title: Speciation and biogeographical history in the European Alpine System: the radiation of Ranunculus sect. Euromontani (Ranunculaceae)
abstract:
Biogeographical analysis of species of  Ranunculus  sect.  Euromontani  and related taxa.
 
 
 Summary 
 
High mountain systems provide manifold preconditions for allopatric and sympatric speciation. We hypothesize that allopatric speciation due to geographical isolation of mountain chains, and sympatric speciation via allopolyploidy played major roles for a radiation within  Ranunculus  sect.  Euromontani  within the European Alpine System (EAS).
We used target enrichment of 1249 nuclear gene loci on 81 samples for phylogenomics, biogeographical analysis, species delimitation, SNPs for genetic structure and NeighborNet analysis, flow cytometry for ploidy determination, and morphometrics for selected species pairs. We also included type material.
The core  R . sect.  Euromontani  comprises 12 monophyletic species, most of them (sub)endemic to one mountain system. The section originated probably from a widespread lineage and diversified 1.39 million years ago. Founder-event speciation was the most common mechanism; only one species ( Ranunculus montanus ) originated likely  in situ  via allopolyploidy. In the West Carpathians, the new species  Ranunculus tatrimontanus  was recognized as different from  Ranunculus gruinalis  (=  Ranunculus pseudomontanus ) in the South Carpathians. In the Pyrenees, clinal variation suggested inclusion of  Ranunculus ruscinonensis  into  Ranunculus gouanii .
Peripatric speciation during the Pleistocene was the predominant mechanism for this geographical/climatic radiation in the EAS, whereas sympatric speciation via allopolyploidy happened only in the Alps.

title: A human-specific TAF8 isoform diversifies the composition of the TFIID general transcription factor
abstract: Abstract Despite its central role in RNA polymerase II transcription, the composition and function of the TFIID general transcription factor can vary across tissues and developmental stages. Such variability may provide a substrate for evolutionary innovation and contribute to human-specific regulatory functions. Here, we identify a human-specific short isoform of TAF8 (TAF8s), a scaffold subunit of TFIID, generated through the use of an intronic polyadenylation site (iPAS). Comparative genomic analyses reveal that the genomic substrate for this isoform originated with the insertion of a FLAM-C  Alu  element into intron 5 in the common ancestor of anthropoid primates (Simiiformes), whereas subsequent small sequence changes at the  Alu -associated iPAS coincide with the emergence of  TAF8s  expression in the human lineage.  TAF8s  lacks nearly half of the canonical  TAF8  coding sequence, is widely expressed across human tissues, and accounts for a substantial fraction of  TAF8  transcripts. It encodes a truncated protein lacking the canonical nuclear-localization signal and localizes predominantly to the cytoplasm. Despite retaining interactions with its histone-fold partner TAF10 and other core TFIID subunits, TAF8s loses interaction with TAF2, providing a molecular basis for alternative TFIID sub-complex formation. Together, our findings identify a recently evolved human-specific regulatory innovation at the  TAF8  locus that diversifies the composition of a conserved general transcription factor. This example illustrates how evolution of transcript isoforms can generate new protein interactions and molecular complexity in essential cellular machineries, with potential implications for the functional diversification of TAF-containing complexes and the genetic basis of TAF-related developmental disorders.

abstract: Kunik et al. discover that a little brown mushroom found in Florida’s swamps co-produces the psychedelic compounds of “magic mushrooms” and amatoxins like those found in the world’s deadliest mushrooms. Evolutionary analyses suggest that the psychedelic genes were acquired via horizontal gene transfer from unrelated fungi rather than passed down.

title: Lateral orbitofrontal cortex enables new learning to overwrite previously acquired information
abstract: Mahmoudi et al. show here that contingency degradation is resistant to spontaneous recovery and reinstatement and that its learning, but not retrieval, depends on the lateral orbitofrontal cortex. Together, these findings suggest that unlike extinction, degradation overwrites initial learning and offers a potential approach to the development of relapse-resistant treatments.

title: A microbial sugar tips the metabolic scales
authors: Annika M. Weber, Sean P. Spencer
abstract: Obesity and metabolic disorders are linked to the microbiome, but the underlying pathways remain poorly defined. In this issue of Cell Host & Microbe, Tan et al. identify a Clostridium immunis-derived exopolysaccharide that reduces interleukin-22 signaling to reshape visceral adipose immunometabolism, and their findings link microbial chemistry to host energy balance.

title: Baby’s first toxin
authors: Kelsey M. Kershner, Skye R.S. Fishbein
abstract: The consequences of early-life enteric pathogen colonization are not well understood. In a recent Science paper, Semon et al. reveal how Clostridioides difficile toxin restructures the early-life development of intestinal tissue that persists into adulthood.

title: Beyond who is there: Industrialization shifts gut microbial ecology and evolution
abstract: The relationship between industrialization and the gut microbiome remains incompletely understood due to limitations in cohort design involving host physiology and bacterial isolates. Two recent studies from the Global Microbiome Conservancy link industrialization to lower microbiome diversity and stability, altered host immune markers, and gene gain in gut bacteria.

title: Locking away a fungal poison to protect cereal crops
abstract: In this issue of Cell Host & Microbe, Xia et al. show that the Fusarium toxin deoxynivalenol (DON) hijacks NAD⁺-dependent metabolic enzymes to disrupt plant central metabolism. They further reveal that myo-inositol metabolism promotes PI(4,5)P2 production, which drives DON trafficking into vacuoles for sequestration and confers Fusarium resistance in crops.

title: A gut mucin muncher signals protection in the uterus
abstract: Microbial communities occupy distinct anatomical niches, yet their byproducts can influence distant tissues. In this issue of Cell Host & Microbe, Qu et al. link the gut bacterium Akkermansia muciniphila to tyrosol production. In a mouse model, tyrosol reaches the uterus and protects against endometritis, inflammation of the uterine lining.

title: Molecular mimicry arrests the phage packaging AppA-ratus
abstract: Among characterized phage defenses, those that interfere with phage genome packaging and virion assembly remain comparatively underexplored. Wang et al. show that a small Salmonella Gifsy-1 prophage protein, AppA, disrupts late-stage virion assembly by mimicking the terminase assembly interface and arresting phage DNA packaging, supporting bacterial fitness during intestinal infection.

title: Timing the feast: Circadian control of rhizosphere nitrogen supply
abstract: The challenge of nitrogen use efficiency stems from a “handshake” problem between soil supply and plant demand. In this issue, Du and colleagues reveal how the rice circadian regulator Nhd1 uses rhythmic chemical signals to synchronize microbial nitrogen cycling with plant uptake and assimilation, providing an example of “chronoculture.”

title: The blood-brain barrier imports diverse neuroprotective proteins through pathways impaired early in Alzheimer’s disease models
abstract: Bioorthogonal proteomics reveals that the blood-brain barrier (BBB) imports diverse plasma proteins to specific brain cell types through receptor-mediated transport, a process dysregulated early in an Alzheimer’s model. Restoring one diminished protein, liver-derived apolipoprotein A1, rescues Alzheimer’s glial and neuronal dysfunction, recasting the BBB as an interface recruiting peripheral signals for brain health.

title: Gradient‐Integrated High‐Strength and High‐Toughness Cellulose Triboelectric Materials for Enhanced Charge Storage and Transport
abstract:
Inspired by the gradient structure of sea urchin spines, a gradient-integrated cellulose/multi-walled carbon nanotube (MWCNT) triboelectric material is constructed. A compatible interface and built-in electric field synergistically suppress charge dissipation, achieving 20.5 nC cm −2  surface charge density, 8044-cycle stability, 126.33 MPa tensile strength, and 9.11 MJ m −3  toughness, providing a foundation for interfacial design in green self-powered wearable electronics.

 
 
 ABSTRACT 
 The rapid advancement of wearable electronics places ever-increasing demands on the electrical and mechanical properties of materials. Cellulose offers renewability, low cost, and high durability for green wearables, but its weak electron-donating ability and poor charge-transport efficiency limit triboelectric performance. Interfacial mismatch between the electrode and triboelectric layers also induces charge dissipation, further aggravating this problem. Inspired by the Janus structure found in sea urchin spines, a gradient-integrated triboelectric material (MWCNT/T-CNFs) was fabricated via vacuum-assisted layer-by-layer filtration. The resulting gradient electric field forms a highly compatible interface between the triboelectric layer and the electrode layer, providing a low-impedance path that effectively suppresses charge dissipation. Consequently, the material achieves a surface charge density of 20.5 nC cm −2  (931.8% that of pure T-CNFs) and excellent cycling stability (8044 cycles). The integrated interface offers strong adhesion, far outperforming conventional electrode tapes, while the gradient design alleviates stress concentration, yielding a tensile strength of 126.33 MPa and toughness of 9.11 MJ m −3 (535.9% that of pure T-CNFs). The material also exhibits good water stability and high-temperature resistance. This study addresses the key limitations of low surface charge density and interfacial mismatch in cellulose materials, providing a solid foundation for interface design in wearable electronics.

title: Reframing Porous Carbon as a Transport Framework for High‐Rate CO2 Electroreduction
abstract:
Hierarchical integration of Cu nanodomains with porous carbon frameworks promotes reactant transport during high-rate CO 2  electroreduction. Compared with a physically mixed benchmark, the integrated architecture shortens effective transport paths, mitigates local CO 2  depletion, and lowers cathodic overpotential, enabling higher ethylene Faradaic efficiency and partial current density. Multiphysics simulations provide a consistent mechanistic interpretation of these transport benefits.

 
 
 ABSTRACT 
 Porous carbons are widely used as supports for Cu-based CO 2  reduction electrodes, yet how their pore structures regulate reactant transport within the catalyst layer remains insufficiently understood. Here, carbon blacks with distinct hierarchical textural characteristics are systematically investigated, revealing a consistent association between more developed pore architecture and higher C 2 H 4  productivity. Guided by this trend, a hierarchically integrated Cu/C catalyst is designed by forming Cu nanodomains throughout the carbon framework and compared with a benchmark prepared by physically mixing commercial Cu nanoparticles with the same carbon support. The integrated Cu/K6 catalyst achieves a C 2 H 4  partial current density of 355 mA cm – 
 2  with a C 2 H 4  Faradaic efficiency of 50.7% at a total current density of 700 mA cm −2 . Under these conditions, Cu/K6 exhibits a cathode potential approximately 0.3 V less negative and a 20% higher C 2 H 4  partial current density than the physically mixed benchmark. Mixed kinetic-transport analysis indicates that the integrated architecture shifts the apparent transport-limitation threshold to higher current densities. Multiphysics computational fluid dynamics simulations further reveal shorter effective CO 2  diffusion paths and mitigated local CO 2  depletion. These findings establish hierarchical Cu–carbon integration as an effective strategy for alleviating CO 2  transport limitations and enhancing C 2 H 4  production.

title: LFA‐1‐Engineered Extracellular Vesicles Deliver CD59 to Protect Endothelial Integrity in Acute Lung Injury
abstract:
LFA-1-engineered extracellular vesicles preferentially target pulmonary endothelium and deliver CD59, thereby inhibiting membrane attack complex formation, preserving vascular integrity, and attenuating acute lung injury. This strategy reveals a targeted approach for protecting the pulmonary vasculature from complement-mediated damage.

 
 
 ABSTRACT 
 Acute lung injury (ALI) is a life-threatening disorder characterized by pulmonary endothelial injury, vascular leakage, and hypoxemia, yet no targeted therapies are available to protect the lung vasculature. Dysregulated complement activation contributes to endothelial dysfunction through excessive deposition of the membrane attack complex (MAC), which disrupts endothelial barrier integrity. CD59 is a membrane-bound complement inhibitor that protects endothelial cells (ECs) from MAC-mediated injury, but its role and therapeutic potential in ALI remain unclear. In this study, we found that endothelial CD59 was significantly reduced during bacteria-induced ALI and that  Cd59  deficiency exacerbated pulmonary vascular leakage in mice. To supplement endothelial CD59, we engineered extracellular vesicles (EVs) expressing lymphocyte function-associated antigen-1 (LFA-1) (EV LFA−1 ) to enhance delivery to activated endothelium. CD59-loaded EVs (EV LFA−1 -CD59) preferentially targeted ECs, reduced endothelial MAC deposition and apoptosis, and preserved endothelial barrier integrity in experimental ALI. EV LFA−1 -CD59 also improved survival following bacterial infection. Collectively, these data establish diminished endothelial CD59 levels as a critical driver of complement-driven vascular injury and highlight EV LFA−1 -mediated CD59 delivery as a promising therapeutic strategy for ALI.

title: Hierarchical Organization of Biomaterials in the Formation of Photonic Nanostructures
abstract:
Natural organisms create vibrant structural colors through precisely organized nanostructures formed under mild biological conditions. This review explores how cellulose, chitin, corneous beta‐protein, and melanin form complex nanostructures across molecular, mesoscale, and tissue levels. By integrating biological, physical, and computational perspectives, it establishes a framework for understanding and engineering hierarchical photonic nanostructures.








ABSTRACT
Biological organisms produce diverse nanostructures, some of which generate structural color through their interaction with light. The distinctive properties of structural color have inspired efforts across multiple fields to reproduce these effects through bottom‐up approaches using natural and synthetic materials. Despite substantial research on the optical mechanisms of structural coloration, how natural photonic nanostructures develop, particularly how molecular interactions and biological regulation enable higher‐order organization, remains incompletely understood, despite their potential to inspire new low‐cost methods of manufacturing nanostructures. This review provides a comprehensive overview of organization into photonic nanostructures, focusing on four of the most prevalent biomaterials (cellulose, chitin, corneous beta‐proteins (CBPs), and melanin). We first examine their formation using a common hierarchical framework encompassing: 1) biological regulation and synthesis, 2) molecular building blocks, 3) intermediate structural units, 4) mesoscale organization, and 5) photonic architecture and optical function. We then discuss the molecular interactions and mesoscale assembly mechanisms that connect these hierarchical levels, together with computational approaches ranging from atomistic and molecular simulations to continuum modeling and artificial intelligence. By integrating biological, physical, and computational perspectives, this review clarifies how natural photonic nanostructures develop and provides a foundation for biomimetic approaches to nanostructural fabrication.

title: Activation of DNMT1 by Chemically Synthesized Dual‐Monoubiquitinated PAF15 Protein
abstract:
DNA methyltransferase 1 (DNMT1) propagates DNA methylation patterns during replication and is stimulated by dual‐monoubiquitinated PCNA‐associated factor 15 (PAF15Ub2). We chemically synthesized PAF15Ub2 with native isopeptide linkages. Cryo‐EM analysis of DNMT1 bound to the synthetic PAF15Ub2 and hemimethylated DNA revealed an active conformation with the autoinhibitory replication foci targeting sequence (RFTS) domain released from the catalytic domain.








ABSTRACT
Replication‐coupled DNA methylation maintenance by DNA methyltransferase 1 (DNMT1) is mediated by dual‐monoubiquitinated PCNA‐associated factor 15 (PAF15Ub2). However, the molecular mechanism of DNMT1 activation by PAF15Ub2 remains unclear. Here, taking advantage of chemical protein synthesis, we prepare PAF15 protein bearing dual‐monoubiquitination through native amide linkages and determine the active conformation of DNMT1 complexed with the synthetic PAF15Ub2 and hemimethylated DNA by cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo‐EM). With an optimized convergent synthetic route, the 262 amino‐acid protein PAF15Ub2 was assembled from six synthetic peptide segments, including two branched peptides. By employing a one‐pot ligation technique and deselenization chemistry, we obtained the native sequence of PAF15Ub2 in high purity and good yield. The chemically synthesized PAF15Ub2 was shown to bind to DNMT1 and stimulate its methyltransferase activity in biochemical assays. Cryo‐EM analysis of DNMT1 in complex with PAF15Ub2 and hemimethylated DNA revealed that DNMT1 adopts an active conformation in which the RFTS domain is released from the catalytic domain, thereby relieving the autoinhibition.
