title: An Iontronic Bimodal Afferent Nerve for Cross‐Modal Neuromorphic Fusion and Robotic Sorting
abstract:
A flexible iontronic pressure–temperature sensor is integrated with pulse encoding and a multi-gate SnO 2  nanowire synaptic transistor to create a near-sensor neuromorphic platform. Pressure and temperature cues are encoded, temporally integrated, and fused for accurate multimodal object recognition and robotic sorting, establishing a compact pathway from tactile sensing to neuromorphic perception and embodied intelligent action.

 
 
 ABSTRACT 
 Inspired by the multisensory perception and fusion strategy of the biological tactile system, we present a bimodal iontronic afferent nerve that integrates a flexible pressure–temperature sensor patch, pulse-encoding electronics, an electrolyte-gated synaptic transistor and a dual-branch neuromorphic classification framework. The flexible sensor patch enables pressure and temperature perception over broad ranges, covering mechanical stimuli from 0 to 300 kPa and thermal stimuli from 0°C to 80°C. Rather than functioning as an isolated sensor, the system converts mechanical and thermal tactile cues into unified iontronic/spiking representations, enabling neuromorphic encoding, synaptic modulation and cross-modal feature fusion. By integrating pressure and temperature features through a dual-branch neuromorphic network, the system achieves 92.00% accuracy under within-recording contiguous-block validation with dual-feature fusion and outperforming single-modal classification. Finally, the integrated afferent nerve is applied to feed-forward robotic tactile sorting, where objects with different color-derived thermal states and mechanical stiffness are identified and classified. This work demonstrates a flexible bimodal neuromorphic tactile system capable of sensing, encoding, fusing and acting on multimodal tactile information, providing a promising route toward artificial skin for intelligent robotic perception.

title: CD34+ Progenitors Promote Ageing‐Associated Valve Sclerosis through the PDGFR–JNK–JUNB Pathway
abstract:
In age-related aortic valve sclerosis, non-bone marrow CD34 +  progenitor valvular interstitial cells (VICs) undergo transdifferentiation into periostin +  myofibroblast-like VICs via the PDGFR-JNK-JUNB axis, driving leaflet thickening and fibrosis. Ablating non-bone marrow CD34 +  cells attenuates this remodeling. Targeting this axis or preserving progenitor holds promise to halt early calcific aortic valve disease progression.

 
 
 ABSTRACT 
 Aortic valve sclerosis (AVS), characterised by fibrocalcific remodelling without significant hemodynamic obstruction, represents a critical window for early clinical intervention; however, its underlying cellular drivers during ageing remain poorly understood. Here, genetic lineage tracing and single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) techniques were used to examine the temporal and spatial functions of CD34 +  valvular interstitial cells (VICs) in ageing-associated AVS. Human scRNA-seq datasets were used in combination with natural ageing and D-galactose (D-gal)-induced mouse models, and a significant age-dependent downregulation of CD34 in VICs was identified. Lineage tracing and bone marrow (BM) chimeras confirmed that non-BM CD34 +  progenitor VICs (prog-VICs), rather than bone marrow-derived cells, serve as the origin of periostin +  myofibroblast-like VICs (myo-VICs) during ageing. Functionally, the systemic or non-BM-specific ablation of CD34 +  cells or the CD34 + Periostin +  transitional subpopulation markedly attenuated age-related leaflet thickening and fibrotic remodelling. Mechanistically, the JNK–JUNB signalling pathway, mediated by PDGFR, was found to be crucial for the pathological transdifferentiation of CD34 +  prog-VICs into periostin +  myo-VICs. Non-BM CD34 +  prog-VICs were found to aggravate senescence-associated AVS; thus, targeting the PDGFR–JNK–JUNB axis or preserving the prog-VIC identity may offer therapeutic avenues to arrest early calcific aortic valve disease (CAVD) progression.

title: Chip‐Level Voltage Controlled Magnetic p‐Bits Array with Variation Compensation for Stochastic Neural Network Computation
abstract:
A chip‐level VCMA‐MTJ array is demonstrated for stochastic neural‐network computing. Combined with a tail‐truncation strategy to compensate for device‐to‐device variations, it establishes a hardware–software co‐design approach for scalable probabilistic computing.








ABSTRACT
The increasing computational and energy‐efficiency demands of artificial intelligence are driving the development of new computing paradigms based on emerging memory devices. Probabilistic bits (p‐bits) based on magnetic tunnel junctions (MTJs), benefiting from energy efficiency, CMOS compatibility, and fast sampling, show broad potential in stochastic neural networks. However, unavoidable device‐to‐device variations in MTJ switching probabilities hinder the realization of scalable p‐bit chips. Here, we integrate a high‐density array of voltage‐controlled magnetic anisotropy MTJs (VCMA‐MTJs) and employ a tail truncation strategy to compensate for their variations in probabilistic switching ranges, enabling chip‐level p‐bit functionality. Our VCMA‐MTJ chip (VM‐chip) successfully implements restricted Boltzmann machines (RBM) and deep belief networks (DBN) for image recognition, anomaly detection, image completion, and image generation, demonstrating the practical utility of this chip in stochastic neural networks. Furthermore, we propose a dual‐control strategy that tunes both the amplitude and duration of the voltage pulse, significantly enhancing network performance and performing comparably to conventional software‐generated pseudo‐random numbers. Our work enhances the tolerance of probabilistic computing to variations in MTJ switching probabilities, offering flexibility in device selection and array integration. This approach may provide a promising pathway toward scalable p‐bit hardware and cost‐effective manufacturing in future probabilistic computing systems.

title: Experience Filter: Translating Heterogeneous Signals into Motion
abstract:
The  Experience Filter  is a signal-agnostic framework with modality-specific feature extraction and a modality-agnostic shared encoding that maps heterogeneous media—music and images—into structured 3-DoF motion. Each signal is reduced to three descriptors (intensity, dominant spectral feature, distance from neutral) and encoded into a hardware-independent trajectory through a fixed, training-free pipeline, enabling synchronized, user-adjustable image-audio-motion experiences renderable on robotic platforms of arbitrary morphology.

 
 
 ABSTRACT 
 Human experience is inherently rich and multisensory, composed of intertwined visual, auditory, and kinesthetic feedback. Digital media capture only its audiovisual dimensions, omitting its mechanosensory dimensions. While full-body (kinesthetic) haptic feedback can enrich media, no general method exists for deriving structured motion from heterogeneous signals and combining it with the audiovisual content for rendering. The Experience Filter maps multimedia signals into structured motion trajectories through a common pipeline of modality-specific feature extraction followed by a modality-agnostic shared encoding, recombining them into a synchronized multisensory experience: each signal is reduced to a shared descriptor space – signal intensity, dominant spectral feature, and distance from neutral axis – then mapped to a trajectory via a fixed, deterministic, training-free encoding. Because this encoding space is hardware-independent, the motion can be retargeted to robotic platforms of arbitrary degrees of freedom and morphology. A feature-sensitivity analysis shows that the descriptor axes are independent and the encoding-space topology follows from the chosen descriptors rather than being fixed. The framework is demonstrated on real-world music and images, producing continuous, synchronized image-audio-motion experiences without manual authoring. The Experience Filter thus provides an analytical mapping from multimedia signals to combined image-audio-motion rendering, enabling expressive, user-adjustable experience across robotic platforms.

title: ADISSP Drives Metabolic Reprogramming and Immune Suppression to Regulate Hepatocellular Carcinoma Progression and Immunotherapy Sensitivity
abstract:
In HCC, ADISSP sustains IKKβ/NF‐κB signaling by inhibiting PPP1CA‐mediated IKKβ dephosphorylation, thereby inducing the expressions of SLC16A3 and CCL20. SLC16A3‐driven lactate remodeling promotes glycolysis, ferroptosis resistance, and M2 macrophage polarization, whereas CCL20 facilitates macrophage recruitment. More important, targeting ADISSP markedly enhanced the therapeutic efficacy of anti‐PD‐1 plus lenvatinib for HCC.








ABSTRACT
Metabolic reprogramming and immune evasion are critical drivers of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) progression and therapeutic resistance, yet the upstream regulators linking these processes remain poorly understood. Here, we identify adipogenesis‐associated secreted signaling protein (ADISSP) as a previously unrecognized oncogenic regulator in HBV‐related HCC. ADISSP was markedly upregulated in HCC tissues and associated with poor prognosis, while its inhibition suppressed tumor progression in vitro and in vivo. Mechanistically, ADISSP interacted with PPP1CA to sustain NF‐κB activation, resulting in transcriptional induction of SLC16A3 and CCL20. The ADISSP/SLC16A3 axis promoted glycolytic adaptation and lactate‐mediated STAT3 activation, thereby driving macrophage M2 polarization, whereas CCL20 facilitated macrophage recruitment. Together, these pathways established an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment characterized by enhanced M2 macrophage infiltration and impaired antitumor immunity. More important, targeting ADISSP markedly enhanced the therapeutic efficacy of anti‐PD‐1 plus lenvatinib in HCC. Collectively, our findings identify ADISSP as a central regulator integrating metabolic reprogramming and immune suppression through the PPP1CA/NF‐κB axis and highlight ADISSP as a potential therapeutic target for increasing immunotherapy sensitivity in HCC.

title: Negative Gauge Factor Piezoresistance in Soft Strain and Pressure Sensors: Mechanisms, Materials, and Emerging Applications
abstract:
Negative-gauge-factor materials reverse the usual rule of piezoresistive sensing: their resistance falls, rather than rises, under deformation. This review organizes such behavior into four mechanistic classes spanning intrinsic semiconductors, composites, conducting polymers, and engineered architectures. The unifying theme is that strain activates conduction, opening a path toward switch-type, event-triggered sensors that consume almost no standby power.

 
 
 ABSTRACT 
 Soft strain and pressure sensors underpin wearable electronics, soft robotics, and human-centered healthcare, yet most piezoresistive devices rely on a positive gauge factor (pGF), in which resistance increases as deformation disrupts conductive pathways and continuous power is needed to register an event. Negative-gauge-factor (nGF) materials, whose resistance decreases under deformation, offer a fundamentally different route. Importantly, a negative gauge factor does not by itself imply low power: continuously conducting nGF devices still require an applied bias and constant monitoring, whereas near-zero-standby-power, event-triggered operation is enabled specifically by switch-type nGF devices that are insulating at rest and turn on only under strain. This review classifies reported nGF systems into four mechanistic categories: intrinsic nGF from strain-induced band-structure modulation (Si, MoS 2 , PtSe 2 /PdSe 2 , SiC); composite nGF that transfers this response into polymer matrices and textiles; polymer-reorganization nGF in conducting polymers; and architecture-induced nGF engineered through tunneling barriers, contact closure, and compliant geometries. We discuss how these mechanisms enable low-power switch-type sensors, wearable health and motion monitoring, electronic skins, and smart textiles, and outline the challenges to establishing nGF piezoresistance as a design principle for energy-efficient soft electronics.

title: Next Generation Antimicrobial Coatings for High Touch Surfaces: Application, Benefits, Risks, Environmental Impacts and Sustainability Aspects
abstract:
Antimicrobial coatings for high touch surfaces promise infection control but are too often validated only in the lab. This review shows that active‐agent release governs both human toxicity and environmental impact and argues that durability and real‐world performance must be primary design criteria, placing a safe‐and‐sustainable‐by‐design framework (SSbD) at the heart of responsible coating development.








ABSTRACT
Antimicrobial coatings for high‐touch surfaces are a promising strategy to reduce the burden of infectious pathogens, limit human exposure, and mitigate transmission in public, healthcare, and other shared environments. This review outlines current antimicrobial coating strategies and their modes of action with attention to their rational applications on high touch surfaces. Because standard laboratory efficacy tests often fail to capture end‐use conditions, the review points to the need for application relevant testing approaches that account for factors such as humidity, temperature, contamination level, inoculum volume, and repeated touching. Beyond efficacy, safe use also depends on how active components are released and on the resulting exposure to humans and the environment, both during their use and at end‐of‐life. Human safety endpoints, such as cytotoxicity, immunotoxicological effects, skin sensitization, and skin irritation, are examined under short‐ and long‐term exposure, in relation to current testing standards and regulatory expectations. In parallel, the review addresses environmental concerns, including potential persistence, bioaccumulation and the transport of released substances into soil, sediments, air and water. Building on these considerations, the review concludes by outlining key principles for applying a safe‐and‐sustainable‐by‐design (SSbD) approach to antimicrobial coatings.

title: A Novel Immunosuppressive Effector Functions as a Bio‐Adjuvant to Enhance the Activity of Bacillus Thuringiensis and Chemical Insecticides
abstract:
A previously unrecognized link between quorum sensing and host immune suppression is revealed in  Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt). The PlcR-PapR system induces the novel immunosuppressive effector PisP, which inhibits DAF-16 nuclear translocation and downstream immune defenses, thereby promoting Bt pathogenicity. PisP also enhances the activity of Cry5Ba toxin and chemical insecticides.

 
 
 ABSTRACT 
 Host innate immunity is a major barrier to microbial infection and often limits the efficacy of biological and chemical pest-control agents. While microbial immunosuppressive effectors have been described, whether quorum-sensing systems coordinate virulence and immune suppression during host infection remains largely unknown. We demonstrated that the PlcR-PapR quorum-sensing system acts as a master regulator that promotes both processes (virulence and immune suppression) to enhance  Bacillus thuringiensis  (Bt) pathogenicity. During infection, PlcR-PapR signaling induces production of the heptapeptide PapR 7 , which activates expression of patatin-like protein PisP, a previously uncharacterized and widely conserved protein. PisP suppresses host immunity by inhibiting nuclear translocation of the transcription factor DAF-16, thereby attenuating the expression of antimicrobial defense genes. Consistent with this mechanism, Bt strains overexpressing  pisP  display enhanced virulence against both nematodes and insect hosts. Importantly, exogenous PisP markedly potentiates the activity of Bt Cry5Ba toxin and several commercial chemical insecticides, enabling effective pest control at reduced doses. Together, these findings reveal a quorum-sensing-controlled mechanism that links virulence regulation to immune suppression during Bt infection and identify PisP as a conserved Bt-encoded immunosuppressive effector with strong potential as a bio-adjuvant for improving the efficacy and sustainability of biological and chemical pest-management strategies.

title: Natural Variation in ZmASB1 Links Tryptophan Metabolism to Root Growth and Drought Tolerance in Maize
abstract:
Natural variation in the maize  ZmASB1  promoter regulates tryptophan accumulation, root development, and drought tolerance through a tryptophan–auxin pathway. A 5-bp InDel alters ZmDOF17 binding and promoter activity, and the favorable allele is enriched during breeding. These findings reveal a cis-regulatory mechanism linking amino acid metabolism with hormone signaling and provide a target for drought-resilient root improvement.

 
 
 ABSTRACT 
 Root amino acid metabolism is important for maize adaptation to water deficit, but the genetic mechanisms underlying this relationship remain poorly understood. We profiled 18 free amino acids in the roots of 192 diverse maize inbred lines and integrated genome-wide association analyses with root transcriptome data. This approach identified 118 metabolite QTLs and prioritized  ZmASB1 , which encodes the β-subunit of anthranilate synthase, as a candidate regulator of tryptophan (Trp) accumulation. A cis-regulatory locus in the  ZmASB1  promoter was associated with variation in  ZmASB1  expression and root Trp abundance. Functional analyses indicated that  ZmASB1  promotes Trp accumulation and root growth through Trp-dependent auxin biosynthesis.  ZmASB1 -overexpressing lines showed enhanced root development and drought tolerance, whereas the mutant exhibited the opposite phenotypes. Exogenous Trp or auxin partially rescued the root-growth and drought-sensitive phenotypes of the mutant. We identified a 5-bp insertion/deletion (InDel-178) in the  ZmASB1  promoter that affects promoter activity by altering the binding of the transcription factor ZmDOF17. The favorable  ZmASB1 
 InDel+  allele was enriched in modern maize inbred lines relative to teosinte and landraces. Together, these findings identify a natural cis-regulatory mechanism controlling  ZmASB1  expression and support a  ZmASB1 -tryptophan-auxin module that contributes to root development and drought responses in maize seedlings.

title: Integrating evolutionary and protein language model representations for thermodynamically consistent stability prediction
abstract: At fixed thermodynamic conditions, protein stability changes obey reversal antisymmetry and path independence, but learned predictors need not satisfy these properties. Explicit alignment-derived evolutionary information may also complement single-sequence protein language model representations, motivating their integration under clearly defined physical constraints. Here, we develop a training-free strategy that combines thermodynamic constraints with complementary sequence representations. We first introduce EvoPhi-DDG, a potential-based adaptation of the alignment-conditioned evolutionary predictor MSAesm_ddG. By antisymmetrizing its predictions and setting the hidden biases to zero, we express stability changes as differences of a learned, evolution-informed effective potential conditioned on the mutation site and alignment context. This guarantees exact reversal consistency and exact same-site transitivity under fixed alignment contexts while preserving predictive accuracy. We further extend the adapted predictor to multiple substitutions through a background-aware construction that preserves whole-variant antisymmetry. We then combine EvoPhi-DDG with the previously published JanusDDG using fixed, equal weight averaging to test predictive complementarity without additional training. The ensemble preserves exact antisymmetry and reduces multisite pathway-closure RMSE relative to JanusDDG across all evaluated path lengths. Furthermore, the ensemble outperforms both components on S669 and S96, achieving Pearson correlations of 0.59 and 0.55, respectively, compared with 0.55 and 0.52 for JanusDDG and 0.53 and 0.48 for EvoPhi-DDG. On the multiple-substitution benchmark PTmul-NR, the ensemble achieves a Pearson correlation of 0.66, improving on JanusDDG's 0.61 and matching the EvoPhi-DDG extension at the reported precision. Together, these findings distinguish two benefits: averaging complementary predictions improves accuracy, whereas the potential-based reformulation strengthens physical consistency. They support the integration of alignment-conditioned and single-sequence representations without additional training, while separating predictive improvements from mathematical guarantees.

title: Parallel transcriptome profiling of soybean cyst nematodes (SCN) during a three-way interaction among SCN, soybean aphids, and soybean
abstract: The soybean cyst nematode (SCN), Heterodera glycines (Ichinoe) (Rhabditida: Heteroderidae) is arguably the greatest yield-limiting factor for soybean (Glycine max [L.] Merr.) production in the United States. Previous research found that the impact of SCN infestation on yield is exacerbated during concurrent infestations with soybean aphids (SBA), Aphis glycines (Matsurmura) (Hemiptera: Aphididae). Although recent research has characterized the host root transcriptomic response during these infestations little is known about the corresponding in planta gene expression dynamics of either pest. This study examines the transcriptomic expression of SCN in soybean cultivars' roots under single or combined SBA infestations at two different time points: 5 and 30 days post-infestation (DPI). The SCN transcriptomics for SCN-susceptible (S) PI 518671 (Williams 82) cultivar reacted equivalently to both SCN and SCN + SBA treatments. However, transcriptomics in SCN-resistant (R) MN1806CN (H. glycines HG type 0/race 3 resistant) demonstrated an elevated significant expression pattern under the SCN + SBA combined treatment. During the early infestation period (i.e., sampled at 5 DPI), both S and R cultivars reacted similarly, irrespective of treatment conditions. The functional enrichment analysis of 1829 differentially expressed genes/transcripts showed that during the early co-infestation period (5 DPI), SCN genes were significant and mapped towards resistance breakage, whereas in the late stage (30 DPI), the gene flux oriented towards nematode dormancy. Together, these results suggest that SCN activity is amplified when combined with SBA, offering foundational data for molecular breeding to produce SCN resistant soybean cultivars.

title: DaliScope: Distilling Biological Insights from Deep Structural Alignments
abstract: Structural similarity searches reveal protein relationships that sequence alignments miss, but treating DALI results as isolated match lists misses deeper connections. We present DaliScope, an interactive Python framework that treats complete DALI target sets as structured populations for systematic analysis of protein structural neighbourhoods. DaliScope combines structural community detection with sequence profiling, Pfam annotation, residue mapping, and 3D visualization, enabling target sets to be subdivided and examined at the residue level. We demonstrate two applications. In a multidomain protein with sparse domain annotation, structural analysis uncovered previously unannotated domains. A structurally anchored HxD...H signature occurred in 697 of 1,093 Pfam-annotated CUPIN domains and in 15 domains lacking Pfam annotation; relaxing the central residue constraint recovered 96% of Pfam-annotated CUPIN domains among the DALI targets. In a second application, a DALI search with transitive closure returned >12,000 hits. Applying an 80% coverage criterion to a conserved structural core reduced this set to 6,708 domain instances, resolved into 23 structural communities. (80% was chosen instead of the default 50% because the GOLD domain has a compact core with short loops.) Many communities were strongly enriched for individual Pfam families while providing structural context for 1,097 targets lacking Pfam assignments. Three-dimensional superimposition revealed structural continuity among related {beta}-sandwich architectures through progressive changes in sheet geometry and auxiliary elements. Together, these examples show how a single DALI query provides a structural anchor for organizing large neighbourhoods, extending interpretation beyond sequence-based annotations, and deriving structurally anchored sequence signatures from defined populations.

title: Automated Continuous LLM-driven Biomedical Literature Mining for a Large-Scale Hepatotoxicity Knowledge Base
abstract: Predicting whether a chemical disturbs liver and mitochondrial function matters for drug safety and environmental risk assessment, but the data available for training such models are small and mostly curated by hand. We describe an automated pipeline that uses a large language model (LLM) to collect hepatotoxicity findings from the biomedical literature. The pipeline runs a PubMed/PMC query, downloads the matching full texts or abstracts, asks the LLM to record each reported effect in a fixed schema (tested chemical, biomarker, direction of change, and related fields) with controlled vocabularies, and writes de-duplicated records to a database that is updated as new papers appear. The current snapshot holds 189,212 findings on 17,002 chemicals from 53,575 articles (1995-2026), covering 235 biomarkers reported for at least 20 chemicals. In a manual check of 217 findings from 35 articles, 208 findings (from 33 articles) were fully correct; the other 9, all from 2 articles, were incorrect. As a use case, we train structure-based QSAR models, both graph neural networks and classic baselines, for each biomarker; at this data scale the classic models remain competitive. The pipeline and the knowledge base will be made publicly available.

title: Batch, Prefetch, Skip, Orient, Squeeze: Faster, Smaller k-mer dictionaries via the Spectral Burrows-Wheeler transform
abstract: Looking up k-mers in an index is a core operation in genomics, underlying read mapping, metagenomic classification, and many other tasks. Queries are often streaming: the k-mers come from a longer sequence such as a sequencing read, and consecutive k-mers overlap. The fastest index for such queries is currently the hashing-based SSHash; indexes based on the spectral Burrows-Wheeler transform (SBWT) are competitive in space but slower. We show how to make SBWT indexes both faster and smaller. First, we process queries in small batches and prefetch the memory each will need next, hiding the latency of the dependent random accesses that dominate a lookup; together with a new rank structure that reads one cache line per query, this makes k-mer lookups about seven times faster than unbatched SBWT search. Second, we extend batching to streaming search and show that one failed lookup can rule out many k-mers of a read at once, which removes the need for the longest common suffix array. Third, we build an SBWT that stores only one orientation of each k-mer, thereby halving its size, with a modified search that exploits how rarely the orientation changes along a read. Finally, we adapt a compact subset rank structure to batched search. On the collections of the SSHash benchmark, and on two collections up to 15 times larger, our fastest index answers streaming queries for 31-mers faster than SSHash on every read set, by up to 4.9 times, using 12 bits per canonical k-mer against SSHash's 7.4-11.1. We also show that a 6.1-bit index is still faster than SSHash on most read sets, and that our smallest index needs about 4 bits per canonical k-mer. Unlike that of SSHash, the space of our indexes barely varies across collections. Our code is available at https://github.com/anadis504/sbwt-squeeze-rs.

title: EMtrace: offline nanopore metagenomics on a laptop for rapid viral diagnostics, genome recovery and 16S profiling
abstract: Nanopore sequencers produce reads within minutes, but metagenomic analysis remains challenging where internet access is limited, data are sensitive or computing resources are modest. EMtrace is an offline pipeline that runs on a laptop during sequencing: it classifies MinKNOW reads, estimates taxon abundance by expectation-maximization (EM) and assembles reference-based consensus genomes. We benchmarked it against five virome and four 16S rRNA tools on simulated, mock-community and clinical data. On field isolates and 16 SARS-CoV-2 clinical samples, EMtrace had the highest species-level F1 score (1.00 and 0.97) and one false-positive species, against 3-7 for the comparators. It recovered divergent viruses as completely as ViMOP, and low-titre field libraries more completely, at [≥]99.7% identity. In replayed runs, it identified the target virus in the first 4,000-read batch (5-13 min). With a shared 16S reference, EMtrace reported two to three times fewer false-positive species than Emu.

title: LIGR-Nue for the global mapping of the bacterial sRNA targetome in vivo
abstract: Interactions between regulatory small RNAs (sRNAs) and their target transcripts are central for post-transcriptional regulation in bacteria. Based on RNA-seq analysis, we determined the relative abundance of several sRNAs in the photosynthetic cyanobacterium Synechocystis sp. PCC 6803 under photoautotrophic growth conditions and after transfer to darkness. We observed an increase in the abundance of the sRNAs DsiR1 to 58.6% and of CsiR1 to 19% of the sRNA transcriptome after transfer to darkness. We then developed a duplex-directed, transcriptome-wide mapping strategy of RNA-RNA interactions in vivo, called LIGR-Nue, which involves aminomethyltrioxsalen-mediated UV cross-linking, proximity ligation, crosslink reversal, reverse transcription and sequencing. The data were analysed using the RNANUE pipeline for the detection of chimeric reads and mapping, and benchmarked against known targetome data for the sRNAs PsrR1 and NsiR4. Using this methodology, we identified RNA-RNA interactions, such as PsrR1 as a regulator of carbon assimilation, and DsiR1 as a global silencing factor of photosynthesis-associated mRNAs in the dark. This data enables the comprehensive analysis of sRNA functions in post-transcriptional gene regulation. LIGR-Nue is broadly applicable to map RNA-RNA interactions in bacteria.

title: Membrane Geometry Reveals Strengths and Limitations of AlphaFold-Predicted Transmembrane Protein Complexes
abstract: High-confidence protein complex predictions do not necessarily represent physically or biologically plausible assemblies. This limitation is particularly relevant for transmembrane (TM) proteins, whose interactions are constrained by the lipid bilayer. Here, we systematically evaluated membrane compatibility in the recently expanded AlphaFold Protein Structure Database, analysing 189,469 high-confidence AlphaFold-Multimer TM-TM complexes and additional TM-soluble assemblies. Most predictions exhibited plausible membrane geometry: among 125,657 evaluable complexes with TM proteins possessing more than two TM helices, 95.4% had joint hydrophobic thicknesses within the expected range of 15-35 angstroms. Nevertheless, some complexes displayed substantial inconsistencies in membrane positioning or protomer orientation despite favourable prediction confidence. Interactions between TM proteins, particularly those containing only one or two TM helices, were frequently dominated by extramembrane contacts. Among TM-soluble complexes, 77.4% showed no penetration of the soluble partner into the hydrophobic membrane core. We further investigated whether AlphaFold3 (AF3) could overcome limitations of AlphaFold-Multimer. Although AF3 recovered an experimentally supported SERCA-phospholamban interaction, it failed to reproduce the cholesterol-mediated norepinephrine transporter homodimer. A benchmark of 173 cholesterol-containing membrane protein targets further revealed limited accuracy in predicting cholesterol-binding poses, particularly for structures released after the AF3 training cutoff. Together, these findings demonstrate that membrane-specific geometric constraints provide a valuable complement to conventional confidence metrics and highlight the persistent challenges of predicting assemblies involving lipids.

title: spSheaf: sheaf-theoretic spatial domain inference from raw molecules without cell segmentation
abstract: Spatial-transcriptomics pipelines usually require cell segmentation and discard 20-60% of transcripts. We introduce spSheaf, a segmentation-free spatial domain inference method built on cellular sheaf theory. Within a domain, neighbouring regions have compatible local expression structure; across a transition between programs they remain discordant after alignment of their local subspaces. spSheaf quantifies this alignment-adjusted disagreement and attenuates transitions during clustering. On the MERFISH hypothalamus benchmark it attains mean ARI 0.571 and NMI 0.655, ranks first of twelve on NMI, and leads SSAM, Points2Regions and FICTURE by 0.16 ARI on held-out slices. On three further annotated sections, every method tuned, it leads on one, ties on one and trails SSAM by 0.06 ARI. The sheaf weighting adds +0.102 ARI where domains are distinct programs and is neutral on laminar cortex. One domain above the annotated count, it divides the BST into the territories of two atlas neuronal populations on both adjacent sections.

title: Cross-state representation learning enables prospective discovery of dynamic protein allosteric sites
abstract: Allosteric regulation offers multifunctional induction in therapeutic interventions, yet conformational plasticity hinders computational identification of allosteric sites. Machine learning models rely on static holo (ligand-bound) structures, generalizing poorly to apo or substrate-bound states where binding pockets are transient or cryptic. We present AsBench2, a cross-state site-recognition benchmark, and AllositeUltra, a deep learning framework integrating multimodal protein representations (combining structure-aware language models with physical dynamics) and residue-guided candidate supplementation, effectively decoupling site detection from static pocket geometry. AllositeUltra demonstrates superior generalization, achieving Top-3 site recovery rates of 65.2% and 70.6% on apo and substrate-bound structures, respectively, representing relative improvements of 36.4% and approximately 50% over the best-performing baselines. Prospective application to MAGI2 identifies a previously unrecognized interdomain allosteric pocket, validated at atomic resolution through small-molecule screening and X-ray crystallography. Proteome-wide application yields a high-confidence atlas of targetable allosteric sites, bridging the gap between structural representation learning and prospective AI-driven drug discovery.

title: Long-range regulatory sequence models reveal a phylogenetic boundary in vertebrate genome evolution
abstract: Regulatory activity at a locus depends on local sequence and on long-range interactions with sequence further away, but how long each kind of information stays shared between genomes over evolution is unknown. Here we use sequence-to-function models as a comparative assay, training FunFormer, a long-context binary classifier that reads 20 kb, together with an architecture- and parameter-matched control that reads only the central 1 kb, in six vertebrates spanning 435 million years, and measuring what each retains when applied to another genome. Within species, the long-context model outperformed three published 1 kb classifiers by 1.0 to 3.8 percentage points in every genome, a gain that came from context rather than architecture. Across species, its contribution decayed with divergence, was near zero at the amniote split and reversed between 320 and 435 Mya, while local sequence still transferred into fish. Zebrafish and Atlantic salmon, which share their divergence from tetrapods but differ by the salmonid genome duplication, behaved alike, so the reversal is not explained by the salmonid duplication. An in silico flank intervention showed that replacing the flank with GC-matched sequence from the target genome cost 8 percentage points among mammals. When a mammalian model was applied to fish, a flank drawn from the source genome on average performed as well as the target's own flank, so the model drew nothing from the fish flank that an arbitrary source-genome flank did not provide. The long-range information that these models learn therefore stops being shared between vertebrate genomes well before the local information does. The same boundary sets a practical rule for reusing models in species without their own data, where long context helps among close relatives but is a liability across deep splits, and in variant scoring most foreign models matched a native model in data-limited pig but none did in human.

title: HV-MultiScaleGNN: A Multi-Scale Graph Neural Network Framework for Host-Virus Protein-Protein Interactions Prediction
abstract: Accurate identification of HV-PPIs is essential for understanding viral infection mechanisms and for developing antiviral therapeutic discovery. However, the experimental identification process is often time-consuming and expensive, while many computational approaches depend on incomplete protein sequences, structural and interaction information. Here, we present HV-MultiScaleGNN, a topology-driven multi-scale GNN framework for HV-PPIs prediction that operates exclusively on the topology of a heterogeneous interaction network. The framework formulates HV-PPIs prediction as a heterogeneous link prediction problem by integrating the human interactome with experimentally validated HV-PPIs. HV-MultiScaleGNN systematically investigates three complementary graph representation strategies, viz. Local view, Global view and an integrated Local+Global view. The Local view employs one-hop relation-aware graph attention to model fine-grained neighbourhood interactions. The Global view captures higher-order structural dependencies through propagation-based neighbourhood aggregation. The integrated representation combines both views to jointly encode local connectivity and global topological context within a unified embedding space, enabling relation-specific link prediction without relying on sequence- or structure-derived features. Experiments on large-scale HV-PPIs datasets evaluate all three strategies using discrimination, calibration, and ranking metrics. The Local view achieved the best discriminative performance (AUROC = 0.9444, AUPRC = 0.9422), whereas the Global view exhibited the lowest ECE (0.0379). The integrated Local+Global view provided consistently strong predictive performance (AUROC = 0.9378, AUPRC = 0.9356). Comparative evaluation against representative graph representation learning methods showed competitive predictive performance. Furthermore, interfacial interactions were identified using protein-protein docking and atomistic-level understanding was explored. Moreover, GO and KEGG enrichment provided additional functional insights into the selected host proteins. The proposed framework enables systematic evaluation of complementary graph representation strategies for heterogeneous biological link prediction and helps experimental researchers to delineate novel HV-PPIs.

title: Reticulation-Aware Dissimilarities for Phylogenetic Networks
abstract: Dissimilarity measures play a critical role in phylogenetics. They help quantify the accuracy of inferences when the ground truth is known, allow comparisons of inferences obtained using different methods, and provide a tool for summarizing sets of phylogenies. A wide array of dissimilarity measures has been introduced for phylogenetic trees over the past half-century, and they vary in their mathematical properties, empirical behavior, and computational complexity. When the evolutionary history involves reticulate processes, such as hybridization and horizontal gene transfer, it is represented by phylogenetic networks. Although the study of phylogenetic network dissimilarity is less established than its tree counterpart, the past two decades have seen an increasing number of measures developed for phylogenetic networks. However, while some have established mathematical properties---for example, metricity on certain classes of phylogenetic networks---none properly separates reticulation disagreement from tree-like disagreement. This is the rationale behind the introduction of the hybrid ancestry error (HAE) measure by Dai and Molloy. The HAE measure, however, is too simplistic to distinguish different reticulation scenarios. In this work, we propose a novel family of network dissimilarity measures that explicitly account for reticulation differences while being more informative than HAE. We prove that our measures are pseudometrics on rooted binary phylogenetic networks on a fixed taxon set, with two instantiations yielding metrics on binary level-1 networks. Empirically, the measures remain sensitive to reticulation errors as network size grows and respond to changes in hybrid identity and parental placement. Calibration experiments further characterize the measures' behavior under network edits of various magnitudes. Data Availability: The dissimilarities are implemented in the PhyNetPy library, available at https://github.com/NakhlehLab/PhyNetPy. All the data simulated for the study is available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23933421. Funding: This work was supported in part by the NSF grants DMS/NIGMS-2153704 and DBI-2420499. Declaration of AI-assisted technologies: During the preparation of this work, the authors used OpenAI's Codex (GPT-6 Astra) and Anthropic's Claude (Fable 5) to assist with editing manuscript text, developing proofs and analysis code, and preparing figures. The authors reviewed and edited the resulting material, verified the analyses, and take full responsibility for the content of this article.

title: Genomes2Genes: A Progressive Cactus Gene Analysis Pipeline
abstract: Whole-genome alignments are fundamental resources in comparative genomics, because they place genes and their surrounding sequences in a shared evolutionary context. Progressive Cactus aligns large numbers of genomes without a reference genome and reconstructs ancestral sequences along the input phylogeny. However, its Hierarchical Alignment Format output has mainly been used for visualization, phylogenomics, and pangenome studies, and gene-level analyses of these alignments remain difficult. Here, we present Genomes2Genes, a pipeline that converts Progressive Cactus graph-based alignments into validated coding sequence alignments of extant species and their reconstructed ancestors. The pipeline extracts exon alignment blocks, handles atypical genomic jumps, stitches exons into transcripts, and reports start codons, stop codons, and frameshifting indels across species, with validation steps throughout and a base-by-base audit of the final alignments. It catches both biological and technical artifacts and can be run on any part of the genome. We anticipate that this pipeline will be useful in identifying and removing problematic regions used in the potential reconstruction of species or gene phylogenies. We developed and tested the pipeline on a whole-genome alignment of 21 Brassicaceae species and 2 outgroups and found that, among 45,491 lineage-specific genes, the pipeline supported 22,376 candidate de novo genes, of which 1,811 had complete evidence of enabler mutations. Genomes2Genes is publicly available and extends whole-genome alignments to gene-level questions in comparative genomics and evolutionary biology.

title: In situ single-cell CRISPR screens uncover context-dependent rewiring of glioma states and immune recruitment
abstract: In vivo single-cell CRISPR screens can resolve perturbation effects in native tissues, but few combine cell-type-restricted delivery, somatic tumor initiation, and combinatorial perturbation. Here we developed an RCAS-TVA-based single-cell CRISPR screening approach coupling oncogenic transformation with single- or dual-guide perturbation in defined neural progenitors. In glioma, tumor suppressor loss produced distinct genotype-dependent transcriptional states, including an NF1-loss-associated increase in mesenchymal programs. Introducing a fixed Cdkn2a(ARF) perturbation altered malignant-cell state composition, immune-cell abundance, and the effects of additional tumor-suppressor perturbations, including increased representation of Pten- and Rb1-deficient cells, suggestive of the relief of an ARF-dependent genetic barrier. These perturbations converged on transcriptional states resembling pharmacologic p53 activation in human glioblastoma. Across mouse tumors and human glioblastoma models, this response was associated with increased astrocyte-like state representation. These findings establish a framework for single-cell analysis of context-dependent somatic perturbations during tumor initiation in vivo.

title: OmniT2I: a unified table-to-image framework for survival prediction and cross-modal inference with incomplete multimodal cancer data
abstract: Molecular profiles and histopathology provide complementary information about cancer prognosis, but these data are often incomplete for individual patients. Here we present OmniT2I, a table-to-image framework for survival prediction and cross-modal inference from incomplete multimodal cancer data. Each molecular profile was converted into a three-channel image representation with correlation-based feature placement. OmniT2I combines available molecular and histopathology embeddings through availability-aware fusion and predicts missing modalities from those observed. Across 10,373 patients with 32 cancer types, the C-index was 0.631 within cancer types and 0.783 with all cancers pooled (0.660 and 0.787 in 5,605 patients with all five modalities). A single model handled all 31 modality combinations and, compared with nine survival methods trained separately for each, achieved higher C-indices in 240 of 279 pooled and 226 of 279 within-cancer comparisons. Adding predictions of withheld modalities to observed inputs improved pooled C-indices in all 180 pairings of observed and withheld modality sets and within-cancer C-indices in 164. Adding measured histopathology to RNA produced the largest within-cancer C-index gain among the four additional modalities evaluated, whereas adding copy number variation reduced it. In seven external cohorts, frozen RNA-only C-indices differed from test performance in the corresponding cancer type in TCGA by a median of -0.003 (range, -0.092 to +0.079). OmniT2I enables prognostic modeling with incomplete multimodal data.

title: LingoCell interprets gene perturbations through natural language and tissue niches
abstract: Single-cell foundation models are general tools for resolving cell identities and disease states, but struggle to interpret changes in expression magnitude in biological language, to transfer to sparse spatial measurements, and to explain cellular niches. We introduce LingoCell, a foundation model connecting single-cell and spatial transcriptomics. It aligns cell representations with language while keeping gene expression editable, supporting cell annotation, cross-batch integration, description generation, and disease-language readouts of single-gene and combinatorial in silico perturbations. Extended to tissues, it annotates cells without single-cell references, learns identity-conditioned niche embeddings, and performs spatial in silico perturbation by replacing and editing neighbor expression. In lung adenocarcinoma, LingoCell revealed synergistic disease responses to jointly weakening alveolar differentiation programs and strengthening malignant programs. In colorectal cancer, it revealed different programs conveyed by the same fibroblast state to T cells, macrophages, and tumor cells. LingoCell provides a unified framework for prioritizing target combinations and stromal intervention programs.

title: Gene-level structure of prior knowledge and perturbation responses informs target-level predictability in prior-informed models
abstract: Background: Predictive models of transcriptional responses to unseen genetic perturbations increasingly incorporate biological prior knowledge. However, it remains unclear how well prior knowledge reflects each target's perturbation-response relationships and how closely prior-derived measures track target-level predictive performance. Here, we develop a gene-similarity framework to quantify agreement among eight sources of biological prior knowledge and between prior knowledge and co-function or co-regulation relationships derived from six Perturb-seq datasets. Results: In genome-wide and essential-gene screens, prior agreement accounted for 30-47% of the variance in co-function agreement and 35-43% in co-regulation agreement. Agreement with Perturb-seq responses was higher for essential genes, lower for transcription factor and signaling genes, and varied with gene expression characteristics and cellular context. We compared prior agreement and prior-derived train-test similarity with measures based on the observed test response in tracking target-level predictive performance. Across three prior-informed models, predictions were more accurate for targets whose observed perturbation-response relationships better matched prior knowledge and that were more similar to training perturbations. Notably, prior agreement and prior-derived train-test similarity, calculated without the test response, tracked relative differences in target-level predictive performance. The strength of these associations varied across models and datasets and, for train-test similarity, across prior sources. Conclusion: Our framework reveals gene- and context-level heterogeneity in how biological knowledge aligns with perturbation responses, and provides an a priori basis for assessing relative perturbation predictability before perturbation responses are measured.

title: ProClust provides reliable statistical significance of clusters for single-cell transcriptomic data
abstract: Clustering of single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data is widely used to identify cell populations. However, overclustering can partition a single cell population into multiple clusters, potentially leading to spurious identification of cell subpopulations. Assessing the statistical significance of clusters is therefore needed to support their biological interpretation. We propose ProClust, a statistical test for clustering significance in scRNA-seq data. ProClust defines a single cluster as a log-concave distribution and adopts a projection-based approach to quantify clustering uncertainty through p-values. These projections can also provide interpretable visual evidence for individual clusterings. ProClust merges clusters when there is insufficient evidence to reject the single-cluster null hypothesis, refining an initial overclustering without prespecifying the final number of clusters. Across parametric and PBMC-based semi-synthetic simulations, ProClust avoided false subdivisions under single-population null settings while consistently recovering the underlying population structure across different numbers of true populations. In real scRNA-seq datasets from the Human Lung Cell Atlas, Tabula Muris, and Hydra, ProClust produced clustering solutions that showed overall agreement with reference annotations while retaining supported substructure and merging groups with insufficient evidence for separation. Together, these results demonstrate that ProClust provides a statistically principled and interpretable framework for refining an initial overclustering and distinguishing supported cellular heterogeneity. The ProClust R package is available at https://github.com/Anonym027/ProClust.

title: DecoyOpt: A two-stage pipeline for decoy-aware enzyme discrimination and EC number prediction
abstract: Accurate and efficient EC number prediction is essential for elucidating the catalytic roles of enzymes. Although similarity-based and deep learning-based approaches have advanced this task, they often fail to distinguish active enzymes from closely related decoys inactivated by local functional-site mutations, leading to high false-positive rates (FPRs). We propose DecoyOpt, a two-stage pipeline for decoy-aware enzyme discrimination and EC number prediction. Specifically, we generated putatively inactive functional-site decoys using ESM3 and evaluated 16 protein language models across three splits. An MLP trained with classification and ranking losses distinguishes enzymes from unannotated proteins and decoys before a contrastive learning model assigns EC numbers to predicted enzymes. On the most stringent GraphPart 40% split, DecoyOpt achieves an MCC of 0.899 and a D0 decoy FPR of 6.17%, outperforming retrained baselines. Across all splits, it outperforms these baselines in EC number prediction on the full test set while maintaining performance close to CLEAN on the enzyme subset. It also correctly annotates all four wild-type enzymes and rejects all eight inactive or nearly inactive variants. We believe that DecoyOpt has potential for annotating uncharacterized proteins and their variants, with applications in genomics, synthetic biology, and biocatalysis.

title: CPDD: Adapting an autoregressive DNA language model for bidirectional phage genome modeling
abstract: Autoregressive DNA language models generate sequences ef[fi]ciently from left to right, but many genome-analysis and sequence-editing problems are naturally conditioned on both [fl]anks. We introduce CreatiPhage, a 144.5M-parameter autoregressive DNA language model for bacteriophages, and its diffusion extension, CreatiPhage Diffusion DNA-LM (CPDD). CPDD is a 147.5M-parameter bidirectional discrete diffusion model initialized from the six-epoch CreatiPhage checkpoint. CPDD retains the pretrained Transformer, block attention residuals, and Engram conditional memory, while introducing non-causal attention, a MASK-aware base-5 Engram, centered depthwise convolution, and position-aligned nucleotide readout. Training combines masked and GIDD-style uniformly substituted bases with nucleotide- and amino-acid-level losses over a 10 kb, 32 kb, and whole-source context curriculum. On a screened panel of 522 phage CDSs, CPDD achieves higher random-mask restoration accuracy than a comparable diffusion model and performs well above codon-level references. In a mixed-corruption test, it restores 42.4% of visible incorrect bases. Frozen CPDD representations also support infA [fi]tness prediction and seven-class phage virion protein subtype classi[fi]cation. Controlled evaluations further characterize how restoration depends on visible context and identify opportunities to improve longer-range sequence recovery. Together, these results support scaffold-conditioned sequence modeling as a step towards modular design of phage genomes.

title: KLONE: An Imbalance-Robust k-NN Ensemble for Cross-Modal Single-Cell Clone Assignment
abstract: Single-cell DNA sequencing (scDNA-seq) and single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) enable the inference of copy number clones and transcriptional states in tumor studies. However, these two assays usually profile different cells of the same tumor, requiring computational assignment of unpaired scRNA-seq cells to clones identified by scDNA-seq to link clonal genotypes with transcriptional profiles. This task is challenging because the only connection between the two modalities is a weak, gene-dependent dosage effect, and the absence of clone labels for RNA cells precludes supervised learning of this relationship. Moreover, clonal distributions may differ between the two modalities because the cells are profiled independently, while the inherent clonal imbalance of real tumors can leave minority subclones underrepresented, further compromising assignment accuracy. To address these challenges, we present KLONE, a per-clone $k$-nearest-neighbor ($k$-NN) ensemble that assigns RNA cells directly to copy-number clones based on cross-modal Pearson similarity, without the need for a parametric model or clone labels for RNA cells. To ensure a fair assessment of each clone's compatibility with a given RNA cell, KLONE allocates an identical neighborhood budget to every clone, preventing majority clones from dominating the affinity assessment solely through their greater abundance. We compare KLONE with six existing methods on three colorectal cancer patients, using cells profiled in both modalities as ground truth. KLONE is the most accurate method and recalls minority clones at 100%. Despite discrepancies in clonal distribution between the two modalities, KLONE recovers the clonal distribution of RNA cells almost perfectly ($rho = 0.99$).

title: Telotrons: spliceosomal introns composed of telomeric repeats
abstract: Spliceosomal intron numbers vary widely across eukaryotes, but the only established mechanism for large bursts of intron gain is the spread of transposable introner elements. We describe telotrons, spliceosomal introns composed predominantly of telomeric repeats. In a survey of 10,310 eukaryotic genome assemblies, we identified 7,008 introns with >85% telomeric repeat coverage and an additional 44,423 with >50% to [≤]85% coverage, in 25 genomes spanning haptophytes, dinoflagellates, a cryptophyte, stramenopiles, the apicomplexan Eimeria, and the nematode Mesorhabditis. Most telotrons carry GT-AG or GC-AG splice boundaries, and RNA-seq supports their splicing. Their repeat orientations are consistent with telomerase extension of broken DNA ends, and intron absence at corresponding positions in orthologs supports widespread de novo gain. In Eimeria and Mesorhabditis, telotrons instead occupy positions where orthologs carry ordinary introns, suggesting modification of existing introns. Telotrons thus point to telomerase as an endogenous driver of structural innovation through intron creation and remodeling.

title: Disentangled generative modeling of single-cell perturbation responses across dynamic cellular states
abstract: Single-cell perturbation studies are increasingly conducted across complex, multi-condition biolog-ical systems, offering a powerful lens into how interventions reshape cell states and molecular pro-grams. However, standard computational models compress single-cell profiles into unified repre-sentations where treatment effects are obscured by cell division, lineage progression, donor varia-tion, and cellular stress. Here, we present Disentangled Variational Inference for Perturbation Re-sponse (PertVI), a deep generative model that separates baseline mitotic phase, cellular state, and batch effects from treatment-induced shifts while isolating aberrant off-manifold responses in or-thogonal anomaly space. This structured design tackles two intertwined tasks: (1) quantifying treatment-induced changes in cell-state composition, and (2) inferring state-gated transcriptional changes in response to treatment. Across simulated benchmarks, PertVI accurately disentangles coupled biological axes and recovers weak treatment signatures. In conditional chemical and genet-ic screens of primary human CD8+ and CD4+ T cells, PertVI separates memory-precursor adju-vants from toxic phenocopies, resolves co-clustered regulators into directional kinetic trajectories and biphasic rebounders obscured by standard workflows, and reveals that treatment-induced phe-notypic shifting is decoupled from broad transcriptional perturbation responses and instead gov-erned by state-specific impulses. Altogether, PertVI brings unique mechanistic granularity to sin-gle-cell perturbation response modeling, serving as a proof of principle for biology-informed, struc-ture-guided variance disentanglement in dynamic cellular systems.

title: ASD Neuro Agentic (ANA): An Agentic Framework for Feature Discovery and Cross Site Generalization in Autism fMRI Classification
abstract: Classifiers of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) from resting state functional MRI rarely generalize across sites, and many reported accuracies are inflated by data leakage.We show that an agentic artificial intelligence framework, ASD Neuro Agentic (ANA), whose language model agents propose features from the literature and researcher input while fixed tools perform every calculation, can search auditably for site independent classifiers while controlling the leakage. In 1,028 participants from 17 ABIDE I centers, ANA tested 71 pipelines and selected a ComBat harmonized ensemble of tangent space connectivity models from six parcellations and 98 public connectivity derivatives. In leave one center out testing, the ensemble reached an area under the curve of 0.814 (95% CI, 0.773 to 0.841), outperforming ASD DiagNet and ASD SAENet. Predictive connectivity was mainly reduced in ASD. Agentic AI offers a systematic and efficient approach to exploring, evaluating, and identifying pipelines as model selection grows complex.

title: Statistical significance testing for spatial domain detection in spatial transcriptomics
abstract: In spatial transcriptomics, domain-detection methods group platform-specific spatial measurement units--cells, bins or multicellular spots--into spatial domains for comparing molecular programs, cellular composition and interactions among tissue regions. However, the number of candidate domains detected in the same tissue can vary with user-specified parameters or model-selection criteria. Whether candidate domains should be merged can be framed as a test of a single-domain null hypothesis, under which each gene has constant mean expression across all spatial units in the combined region. However, testing candidate domains on the same gene-expression data used to detect them may induce post-selection bias and yield anti-conservative p-values, increasing the risk of oversegmentation. To address these challenges, we introduce SigDoTS (statistical Significance testing for Domain deTection in Spatial transcriptomics), a hypothesis-testing framework for spatial domain detection. SigDoTS uses hierarchical testing to determine which candidate domains to retain or merge, with adjustment for family-wise error control. It accounts for gene-gene covariance and spatial dependence and computes p-values by rerunning the upstream domain-detection pipeline on datasets simulated under the fitted single-domain null. In simulations, SigDoTS controlled the type I error rate at the root node under the single-domain null and improved recovery of the true spatial domains when multiple domains were present. In human dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, SigDoTS retained superficial and deep Layer 6 domains but merged Layer 3 candidate domains across different initial numbers of candidate domains. In ovarian and colorectal cancers, SigDoTS retained epithelial domains with different gene-expression programs and local immune environments, together with immune, stromal and vascular domains.

title: Uncovering Viral Signals Across Cell Populations in Colorectal Cancer
abstract: Viral sequences have been detected in colorectal cancer, but their cellular and anatomical distribution remains poorly resolved. We aimed to establish a cell-type-resolved map of viral reference-associated RNA signals across colorectal cancer, tumour-adjacent normal tissue, and healthy colon. We repurposed human-unmapped reads from single-cell RNA sequencing libraries generated in ten publicly available studies. We retained cell-barcode and unique molecular identifier information, removed duplicate molecules, and aligned reads to a curated human-associated viral reference using three aligners. Viral signals were analysed across cell types, tissue conditions, and colorectal segments. We used participant-grouped repeated cross-validation to evaluate tissue-condition classification and screened an independent paired colorectal cancer proteomics cohort for compatible peptide matches. The study included 547 libraries from 112 participants, including 49 with matched colorectal cancer and tumour-adjacent normal samples, and approximately 415,000 cells spanning ten major cell populations. Viral reference-associated RNA signals differed across epithelial, immune, stromal, and vascular compartments, tissue conditions, and anatomical regions of the colon. Of 318 independent healthy-reference viral-load comparisons, seven involving six virus-cell-type groups remained significant after Benjamini-Hochberg correction, including plasma-cell HHV-7 and HHV-6B and mast-cell HCV-2. Cell-type-resolved viral features distinguished colorectal cancer, tumour-adjacent normal tissue, and healthy colon in participant-grouped validation; random forest achieved a macro-AUC of 0.957 (SD 0.028), with HERV-K113 as the leading quantitative feature. An independent proteomic screen identified peptide matches compatible with 20 candidate viral groups. We established a cell-type-resolved map of viral reference-associated RNA signals across colorectal tissue conditions and anatomical regions. By identifying candidate viral signals in epithelial and immune compartments, this map provides a basis for investigating virus-host pathways involved in tumour biology, immune regulation, and antigen-presentation states, and could help prioritise future combination strategies pairing virus-directed or virus-mimetic approaches with standard treatment or immune checkpoint blockade.

title: Lifestyle-mediated shifts in the gut microbiome and host genetics modulate gene expression in intestinal organoids
abstract: Industrialization-associated shifts in the gut microbiome have been linked to disease, but the mechanisms by which microbial communities influence host gene regulation remain poorly understood. We developed a live microbiome-colonic organoid (colonoid) co-culture system to investigate genotype-dependent host responses to gut microbial community variation. Colonoid 2D monolayers from healthy donors were co-cultured with live gut microbial communities from individuals living urban or rural lifestyles, followed by RNA-sequencing. Urban and rural microbiomes elicited largely shared transcriptional responses, however they induced distinct host genetic effects on gene expression. We identified 511 host genes with microbiome-dependent allele-specific expression (ASE) which were involved in epithelial architecture, cell-matrix interactions and structural integrity. Notably, 149 host genes had distinct allelic effects between Urban and Rural microbiomes (urban-rural condition specific ASE or cASE), revealing genotype-dependent host responses to lifestyle-associated microbiomes. Urban-rural cASE was associated with microbial community composition, predominantly involving Prevotella and Bacteroides species. Targeted Prevotella copri spike-in recapitulated Prevotella-associated allelic effects at specific loci, including one in the IBD-associated autophagy gene, ATG4B. Together, these findings establish an experimental framework to investigate genotype-by-microbiome interactions, and demonstrate that lifestyle-mediated shifts in the microbiome modify host cis-regulatory genetic effects on gene expression.

title: A population-scale isoform atlas enables isoform-based trait association and regulatory analysis in lettuce
abstract: Genomic variation shapes phenotypic diversity, yet how genetic variation contributes to transcript isoform diversity remains poorly understood at the population scale. Here, we integrated transcriptomic data from 240 lettuce accessions with a lettuce pangenome to construct a comprehensive pan isoform atlas comprising 531,657 isoforms from 49,729 transcribed loci. Isoform presence absence variation (iPAV) captured extensive transcript diversification during domestication and horticultural differentiation, providing additional resolution beyond locus-level analyses, particularly within loci shared across the population. To facilitate the systematic analysis of isoform trait associations, we developed ISONET-GWAS, a computational framework that integrates isoform-based association mapping, functional annotation, and network-based candidate prioritization. ISONET-GWAS recovered the known chlorophyll regulator LsGLK, identified 455 metabolite isoform associations across 77 metabolites, and prioritized candidate regulators of chlorophyll metabolism supported by functional validation. Genome-wide splicing quantitative trait locus (sQTL) mapping identified 10,498 sQTL associations, revealing widespread distal genetic associations with alternative splicing and candidate trans-sQTL hotspots. Notably, we identified a trans-sQTL hotspot overlapping LsPPR, which encodes a pentatricopeptide repeat RNA-binding protein. Perturbation of LsPPR resulted in widespread changes in alternative splicing of floweing-related genes, accompanied by delayed bolting and flowering and altered splicing of flowering-related genes. Together, our study establishes a population-scale pan-isoform resource and a broadly applicable analytical strategy for isoform-level trait association, candidate prioritization, and complementary analysis of the genetic regulation of alternative splicing in crops.

title: A Y-specific translocated gsdf copy is a candidate master sex-determining gene in common dab (Limanda limanda)
abstract: Sex-determining systems in flatfishes are highly diverse, and even closely related species can differ in both sex-determining loci and heterogametic systems. In common dab (Limanda limanda), the genetic basis of sex determination has not yet been established. Here, we investigated sex determination using pooled whole-genome sequencing combined with long-read genome sequencing of females and males from Iceland and Norway. Genome-wide allele-frequency analyses identified sex-associated regions consistent with male heterogamety (XX/XY), with the strongest signal on chromosome 16. Comparison of the existing reference assembly, which represents an X haplotype at this locus, with a haplotype-resolved male PacBio HiFi assembly revealed a [~]21.5 kb Y-specific insertion on chromosome 16. The insertion showed complete coverage in male pools but little or no coverage in female pools from either population. It contained a translocated genomic segment including a copy of gonadal soma-derived factor (gsdf) and a predicted gene of unknown function. Comparative genomic analyses were consistent with this segment originating from an autosomal gsdf-containing region on chromosome 1. Given the recurrent recruitment of gsdf as a sex-determining factor in teleosts, we designate the Y-linked copy gsdfY and identify it as the strongest candidate for the master sex-determining gene in common dab. Additional broad sex-associated differentiation on chromosome 19 was restricted to the Icelandic samples and may reflect population-specific expansion of the sex-linked region, although its structural basis remains unresolved. Together, these findings provide the first genomic characterization of sex determination in common dab and demonstrate how gene duplication and translocation can contribute to the evolution of novel sex-determining systems in flatfishes.

title: Time-resolved single-cell screening reveals the dynamic regulatory architecture of human cardiogenesis
abstract: Congenital heart disease (CHD) originates during early embryogenesis, yet when disease genes act cannot be determined from existing data. Human fetal heart atlases lack critical time points, and perturbation screens that systematically assess gene function currently profile at most a few time points. Here we combined single-cell CRISPR screening of 400 disease-relevant genes in cardioids, sampled daily over seven developmental days (~975,000 cells), with a matched multiome atlas. Perturbation phenotypes were strongly dependent on developmental stage. Perturbations that reshaped cell-fate allocation or gene expression were enriched for CHD-linked genes, and most acted already during progenitor stages. Timing was largely independent of the target gene's own expression, marking instead when a cell state became functionally dependent on it, and some effects persisted after expression declined. Consensus gene regulatory networks integrating perturbation and multiome data recovered stage-specific regulators and nominated HOXB2 and HOXB3 as candidate cardiac regulators. Many perturbations converged on shared downstream programmes, which were reorganised through differentiation. Effects correlated in progenitors were maintained in differentiated cells, split into distinct programmes, converged with other perturbations or disappeared entirely, indicating that gene function is highly context dependent. Beyond advancing our understanding of the developmental regulatory logic underlying CHD, our work provides a resource for developing context-dependent models for in silico prediction of perturbation effects.

title: Contig-Resolved Genetic Context of Antimicrobial Resistome in Sediments of Two Contrasting Wastewater-Impacted Rivers
abstract: River sediments harbor diverse antimicrobial resistance (AMR) determinants; however, gene abundance alone provides limited insight into their genomic context, mobility potential, and associated bacterial hosts. This study employed an assembly- and read-mapping metagenomic framework to surface-sediment metagenomes (40.78 Gb clean data) from two contrasting wastewater-impacted Indian rivers, Adyar (Chennai) and Musi (Hyderabad), retaining sample-, contig- and open reading frame level provenance. ARG-carrying contigs (ACCs; n = 2,402) were annotated for mobile genetic elements (MGEs), biocide/metal resistance genes (BMRGs), virulence factor genes (VFGs), nitrogen-cycling genes (NCycGs), and putative host taxonomy. The resistomes exhibited substantial diversity (264 ARG subtypes) and spatial heterogeneity, with subtype richness in the Adyar (up to 171 subtypes) than in the Musi, where richness progressively declined downstream. Rank IV determinants dominated ARG abundance (77.82%), whereas Rank I determinants accounted for only 9.89%. MGEs were detected on just 3.12% (75/2,402) of ACCs, predominantly comprising plasmid-like contigs and proximal ARG-MGE associations. Co-occurrence with BMRGs was observed on 386 ACCs, whereas VFGs were uncommon (26 ACCs) and primarily represented dual-annotated efflux and envelope-integrity determinants rather than independent virulence loci. NCyc annotations were sparse (12 ACCs), with no evidence of complete nitrification or denitrification pathways. Taxonomic classification resolved 217 ACCs to the species level, with no matches to curated human pathogenic bacteria. Only two Acinetobacter-assigned ACCs exhibited both genus-level pathogenicity and mobility evidence. These findings highlight the importance of integrating mobility and host-taxonomic information to distinguish baseline environmental resistance from potential priorities for AMR surveillance.

title: Beyond unseen entities: Auditable cold-start evaluation for drug interaction prediction
abstract:
by Xiaoqing Ru, Yansu Wang, Quan Zou, Mengting Niu 

Reliable generalization is essential for deploying drug–drug interaction (DDI) and drug–target interaction (DTI) models in drug discovery, pharmacovigilance, and clinical decision support. However, strong performance on random splits or weakly constrained evaluations may not reflect how well a model generalizes to new drugs, targets, or deployment conditions. In pairwise prediction, test instances may still resemble training examples in molecular structure, sequence, or network context. Such overlap can inflate performance estimates and make interpolation appear to be extrapolation. In this Perspective, we argue that cold-start evaluation should be treated as an auditable deployment claim. We organize common evaluation settings by their source and scope of novelty, ranging from random splits and entity-disjoint protocols to structure-level, temporal, domain-disjoint, and many-domain evaluations. The L0–L5 framework clarifies which deployment claim each setting is designed to test. Coverage, overlap, and distance quantify the resulting train–test discrepancy. We further provide a practical checklist for leakage control, validation alignment, candidate-pair construction, and domain-level risk reporting. This Perspective clarifies the boundaries and evidential scope of cold-start evaluation, providing a common basis for interpreting and comparing results across DDI and DTI studies.

title: Estimating rates of SARS-CoV-2 lineage spread using graph spectra from genetic sequence data
abstract:
by Emma E. Goldberg, Michael D. Kupperman, Ruian Ke 

The modern enormous scale of viral genomic data, as exemplified by SARS-CoV-2, presents unique opportunities for epidemic inference and real-time monitoring. A key challenge is to wade through the extremely large stream of sequence data in order to identify small subsets of sequences that may represent rapid population growth of newly emerged lineages. To address this challenge, we developed a new approach that combines techniques in graph theory and machine learning. We represent distances between small subsets of sequences as graph Laplacians and identify from them features of rapid population growth. From early sequence data collected in the US and the UK between 2021 and mid-2022, we identified two features—genetic diversity and graph connectivity—that allow us to reliably estimate growth rates of newly emerged lineages. To test our model, we used data collected from mid-2022 to end-2024 and accurately inferred the growth rates of lineages that appeared during this period. Furthermore, we demonstrate that for data collected in 2023 when the sequencing efforts were relatively high (thousands of sequences per day) in the US and the UK, our model correctly identified the most rapidly expanding lineages when they were still at low frequencies. Overall, our work provides a scalable and adaptable tool to estimate the growth rate of newly emerged SARS-CoV-2 lineages.

title: Short-read sequencing benchmarking with donor-specific assemblies
abstract:
Background
                      High-throughput short-read sequencing has become a core technology for genomics, but the rapid expansion of available platforms has made it increasingly important to benchmark them under standardized conditions. A major challenge is that conventional reference-based comparisons confound true sequencing errors with inherited variation and reference bias, making it difficult to isolate platform-intrinsic performance. 
                  
                     Results
                      We benchmark nine short-read chemistries across seven DNA sequencers using two highly characterized benchmark samples, HG002 and COLO829BL, together with donor-specific assemblies to measure sequencing errors against sample-matched genomic references. This strategy separates authentic platform errors from biological divergence and reveals substantial differences in substitution, indel, read-position, and sequence-context error profiles. Element AVITI UltraQ and Roche SBX-D show the lowest substitution error rates, whereas Ultima and Roche chemistries exhibit the strongest indel-associated biases.
